1: The most famous gaze in Dutch art may belong to a woman who never existed.
She is not a portrait of anyone. Vermeer painted a 'tronie', an imagined face, and the most famous gaze in Dutch art may belong to a woman who never existed.
2: It is not night at all: darkening varnish turned the daylight into darkness.
It is not a night scene. Centuries of darkening varnish turned Rembrandt's daylight into night, and the name stuck before anyone cleaned it.
3: Caravaggio's Judith hesitates. Artemisia's rolls up her sleeves.
Caravaggio painted Judith hesitant. Artemisia, who survived a rape and then a trial where she was tortured to test her testimony, painted her with her sleeves rolled up.
4: The most famous touch in art never happens.
The most famous touch in art never happens. Michelangelo left a gap between the two fingers, and for five centuries every viewer has been standing inside it.
5: That smear on the floor is a skull. Stand at the right edge and look back.
That smear across the floor is a skull. Stand close to the right edge and look back: death snaps into focus, and the two powerful men dissolve.
6: Perhaps the most stolen artwork ever, and one panel is still missing.
It may be the most stolen artwork in history. One panel, the Just Judges, vanished in 1934 and was never found; the one in Ghent today is a copy.
7: Mary faints in the very same curve as her son's body.
Look at Mary: she faints in the very same curve as her son's body. And in the corners hide tiny crossbows, because Leuven's archers' guild ordered it.
8: Rough, unidealized shepherds that stunned Florence.
Shipped from Bruges to Florence in 1483, its rough, unidealized shepherds stunned the city; Ghirlandaio soon borrowed them for his own Nativity.
9: Music written on a sinner's backside, finally played after five centuries.
In the hell panel, a line of music is written on a sinner's backside. In 2014 a student transcribed it, and a tune silent for five centuries was finally played.
10: Only a piece: the rest of the panel hangs an ocean away.
This is only a piece. The panel was cut from a larger wing, and its lower part, a glutton floating in a barrel, now hangs at Yale, an ocean away.
11: She turns the pages of a prayer book, but her eyes have drifted to the coins.
She is turning the pages of a prayer book, but her eyes have drifted to the coins. In the little mirror on the table, a man by a window watches them both.
12: A magic square that adds up to 34 every way, with the year hidden inside.
The magic square on the wall adds up to 34 in every direction, and its bottom row hides the year: 15 14. Even genius, here, cannot think its way out of gloom.
13: Death holds up an hourglass, and the knight does not even turn his head.
Death holds up an hourglass, a devil creeps behind, and the knight does not even turn his head. Dürer cut every hair of it into copper by hand.
14: In its eye, the reflection of a window: the hare sat in his workshop.
Look into its eye: Dürer painted the reflection of a window there. The hare was sitting indoors, in his workshop, more than five centuries ago.
15: Christ covered in sores, so the sick in the hospital would see God suffer like them.
It stood in a hospital for victims of St Anthony's fire, a disease that ravaged the skin. Grünewald covered Christ in sores, so the sick would see God suffer as they did.
16: Over a hundred proverbs, and someone is still banging his head against a wall.
More than a hundred proverbs hide here, and many still speak to us: one man bangs his head against a wall, another fills in the well after the calf has drowned.
17: Skeletons sweep away kings, and two lovers keep making music.
An army of skeletons sweeps away kings, soldiers and peasants. Only two lovers in the corner keep making music, unaware that a skeleton is playing along.
18: Old women step into the pool and come out young. The men never get in.
Old women arrive on carts and wheelbarrows, step into the pool and come out young on the other side. The men never get in; they wait for them by the tents.
19: The Battle of Alexander at Issus
A sky that curves like the Earth itself, and Napoleon carried it off to Paris.
Thousands of soldiers, under a sky that curves like the Earth itself. Napoleon, who idolized Alexander, carried it off from Munich to Paris in 1800.
20: The Body of the Dead Christ in the Tomb
Dostoevsky thought a man could lose his faith looking at it.
Dostoevsky stood frozen before it in Basel. In The Idiot, one of his characters says that looking at this painting, a man could lose his faith.
21: Whose face is it? A legend about a beauty who died at 22 never let go.
Florentines whispered that Venus has the face of Simonetta Vespucci, the city's beloved beauty who died at 22. There is no proof, and the legend has never let go.
22: Some 500 plants in one meadow, most blooming around Florence in spring.
Botanists have counted some 500 plants in its meadow, nearly 200 of them different flowers, most of which bloomed around Florence in spring.
23: In 1652 the friars cut a doorway through the wall and took Jesus's feet.
In 1652 the friars cut a doorway through the wall and took away Jesus's feet. The painting was already crumbling: Leonardo had skipped true fresco, and the wall did not forgive.
24: There are two of them, probably because of a fight over payment.
There are two of them, in Paris and London. A long fight over payment with the brotherhood that ordered it is the likely reason Leonardo painted the scene twice.
25: Plato may wear Leonardo's face, and at the edge Raphael looks right at you.
Plato is widely thought to wear Leonardo's face, and the brooding man on the steps is probably Michelangelo. At the far right, Raphael himself looks straight at you.
26: Two bored little angels at the bottom stole the show from the Madonna.
Raphael tucked two bored little angels at the bottom, and they became some of the most reproduced angels on Earth. In 1945 the Soviets took the painting to Moscow for ten years.
27: Beautiful models were scarce, so he painted 'a certain idea' instead.
In a famous letter attributed to Raphael, he says that beautiful models are scarce, so for Galatea he painted 'a certain idea' that came into his mind.
28: The face on that empty, flayed skin is widely believed to be Michelangelo's.
St Bartholomew holds up his own flayed skin, and the face on that empty skin is widely believed to be Michelangelo's: a self-portrait hidden in the saddest spot on the wall.
29: Mark Twain called it the vilest picture in the world. Manet borrowed the pose.
Mark Twain called it the vilest, most obscene picture the world possessed. Three centuries later Manet borrowed her pose for Olympia and shocked Paris all over again.
31: No one knows what it means, and X-rays found a bathing woman under the young man.
No one knows what it means, and Giorgione left no clue. X-rays only deepened the riddle: where the young man stands, he first painted a naked woman bathing.
32: The feet are deliberately too small, or they would hide the body.
Mantegna deliberately shrank the feet, since true perspective would have hidden the body behind them. The painting was still in his studio when he died.
33: Christ is whipped in the background. Who are the three men chatting in front?
The whipping of Christ happens far in the background, while three men in front talk as if nothing were happening. Who they are is one of art's great unsolved riddles.
34: Called to bed, he answered: "Oh, what a sweet thing perspective is!"
Broken lances lie on the ground in a neat perspective grid. Vasari tells that when Uccello's wife called him to bed, he answered: 'Oh, what a sweet thing perspective is!'
35: At the top of the friars' stairs, it asks each one who passes to stop and pray.
It was painted for friars, at the top of the stairs in their own convent. An inscription below asks every friar who passes to stop and say a Hail Mary.
36: The Medici rode into the Christmas story, and the painter signed his cap.
The Medici painted themselves into the Christmas story, riding with the Magi through Tuscan hills. Gozzoli joined the crowd too, with his name written on his cap.
37: Dead at 26, and for a century artists came here to learn from him.
Masaccio painted it in his early twenties and was dead at 26, yet for a century artists came to this chapel to learn from him, the young Michelangelo among them.
38: A Sicilian painted so Flemish that experts thought it was Van Eyck.
In 1529 a Venetian collector noted that some thought it was by Van Eyck or Memling. Antonello, a Sicilian, had mastered Flemish oil painting so well that he fooled the experts.
39: A golden ray through a slit in the wall, and in front, a giant cucumber.
A golden ray shoots from the sky through a tiny slit in the wall to reach Mary. And right at the front, for no obvious reason, Crivelli set down a giant cucumber.
40: The Louvre's largest painting, and most visitors stand with their backs to it.
The largest painting in the Louvre hangs facing the Mona Lisa, and most visitors stand with their backs to it. Napoleon's troops cut it in two to carry it from Venice.
41: Everything is stretched, and one column holds up nothing at all.
Parmigianino stretched everything: the neck, the fingers, the sleeping child. He died before finishing it, which is why a lone column at right holds up nothing.
43: A face of peaches and cherries, with a pea pod for teeth.
Summer's face is built of peaches, cherries and a pea pod for teeth. Arcimboldo signed it on the collar, weaving his name and the year into the straw.
44: Women were meant to embroider. Her sisters play chess.
Sofonisba painted her sisters playing chess, a game of the mind, at a time when women were expected to embroider. Vasari wrote that they lacked only speech.
45: Barred from drawing nude men, she painted a whole crowd of them.
Women were barred from drawing nude men, yet Michaelina Wautier painted a whole crowd of them. The only woman looking out at us is thought to be the artist herself.
46: Which one is Matthew? Scholars still argue.
Which one is Matthew? For centuries everyone said the bearded man pointing at himself; some scholars now argue it is the young man at the end, still bent over the coins.
47: The fruit basket teeters at the table's edge, about to fall into your lap.
The fruit basket teeters on the very edge of the table, about to fall into your lap. Caravaggio wanted the miracle to happen in your space, not in a faraway picture.
48: A wormhole in the apple, leaves drying out: beauty already starting to decay.
Look closely: the apple has a wormhole and the leaves are drying out. In one of the first pure still lifes in Italian art, Caravaggio painted beauty already starting to decay.
50: Painted at about 17: her Susanna is not coy, just disgusted.
Artemisia signed and dated it 1610, when she was about 17. Painters usually showed Susanna coy; hers twists away in plain disgust from the two men leaning over the wall.
51: Timoclea Kills the Captain of Alexander the Great
Headfirst into the well: all we see of her attacker is his kicking legs.
Timoclea pushes the officer who raped her headfirst into a well; we see only his kicking legs. Sirani ran one of Europe's first painting schools for women, and died at 27.
52: A year before Galileo's telescope news, the Milky Way here is already separate stars.
Painted in 1609, a year before Galileo published what his telescope saw, it shows the Milky Way as countless separate stars and the Moon with its real markings.
53: Japanese visitors still come to Antwerp because of a boy in a cartoon.
In the novel A Dog of Flanders, the poor boy Nello dies before Rubens's paintings in this cathedral. Japanese visitors, raised on the story's anime, still come to Antwerp to see them.
54: Credited to an assistant for centuries, then sold for £49.5 million.
For centuries it was credited to one of Rubens's assistants. Recognized as his own in 2002, it sold that year for £49.5 million, then a record for an Old Master.
55: Still Life with Cheeses, Almonds and Pretzels
Her name is engraved on the knife handle. Elsewhere, her face hides in goblets.
Clara Peeters engraved her name on the knife handle. In other works she hid tiny self-portraits in the reflections on goblets, as if to say: I was here.
56: This bouquet never existed: its flowers bloom in different seasons.
This bouquet never existed. Its flowers bloom in different seasons, so Bosschaert painted each one separately and gathered them together only in paint.
57: The Return of the Prodigal Son
Look at the father's hands: one strong, one gentle.
Look at the father's hands: many see one broad and strong, the other slender and gentle, as if he holds his son as both father and mother.
58: Hebrew on the wall, but written in columns, maybe a rabbi neighbor's idea.
The writing on the wall is Hebrew, but set in vertical columns. Rembrandt probably took the idea from his neighbor, the Amsterdam rabbi Menasseh ben Israel.
59: The Storm on the Sea of Galilee
His only seascape was stolen in 1990. The empty frame still waits on the wall.
Rembrandt's only seascape was stolen from a Boston museum in 1990. It has never been found, and its empty frame still hangs on the wall, waiting.
60: He painted jugs and a basket, then erased them for one nail and its shadow.
Vermeer first painted a rack of jugs on the wall and a big willow basket on the floor, then painted them out. Scans revealed them in 2022: he chose a bare wall, one nail and its shadow.
61: His widow hid it from creditors. Hitler's copy ended up in a salt mine.
Vermeer's widow tried to keep it from his creditors. Three centuries later Hitler bought it for his planned museum, and it was found in 1945 in an Austrian salt mine.
62: Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window
For centuries the wall was bare. Under the paint, a Cupid was watching.
For centuries the wall behind her was bare. In 2021 restorers removed paint added after Vermeer's death and found a large Cupid watching over her letter.
63: The year it was painted, a gunpowder blast killed the painter and wrecked his studio.
Painted the year Fabritius died, at 32, when the Delft gunpowder store exploded and wrecked his studio. Only about a dozen of his paintings survive; the little chained bird is one.
64: He offers coins. She keeps sewing and will not look up.
A man leans in, offering coins; she keeps sewing and will not look up. For two centuries Leyster's paintings were sold as Frans Hals, until her monogram was noticed in 1893.
65: Ten children, painting into her eighties, and outselling Rembrandt.
Rachel Ruysch raised ten children and kept painting into her eighties, proudly adding her age to her signature. In her lifetime her flowers sold for more than Rembrandt ever got.
66: As the Old Sing, So Pipe the Young
The man teaching a little boy to smoke is the painter himself.
The man teaching a little boy to smoke a pipe is Jan Steen himself. In Dutch, 'a Jan Steen household' still means a chaotic, messy home.
67: Only small things, always on the same stone ledge, by a man we barely know.
Coorte painted only small things, a few strawberries, some shells, this bundle of asparagus, always on the same stone ledge. Almost nothing is known about his life.
68: A swan guarding its eggs, until someone labeled one egg 'Holland'.
A swan fights off a dog to guard its eggs. Later someone added labels: the swan became statesman Johan de Witt, an egg became 'Holland'. It was the first painting the Dutch nation bought.
69: Trompe l'oeil: The Reverse of a Framed Painting
Not the back of a painting, but a painting of one, waiting for you to turn it.
This is not the back of a painting. It is a painting of the back of a painting, made to lean against a wall and wait for someone to try to turn it around.
70: In 1914 a suffragette walked in with a meat cleaver.
In 1914 a suffragette walked into London's National Gallery with a meat cleaver and slashed her seven times, protesting the arrest of Emmeline Pankhurst.
71: The egg whites are just turning opaque: a few seconds, frozen for 400 years.
Velázquez was about nineteen. Look at the eggs: the whites are just turning opaque in the hot oil, a few seconds frozen for four hundred years.
72: No altar, no knife, only a bound lamb in the dark.
Zurbarán painted this bound lamb several times. There is no altar and no knife, only a dark void, and yet the whole story of sacrifice is in it.
73: Fruit on strings in a stone window, and a year later he became a monk.
Fruit hangs on strings in a stone window, the old Spanish way of keeping food cool. A year later Sánchez Cotán gave up his career and entered a Carthusian monastery.
74: The Burial of the Count of Orgaz
The boy pointing is the painter's son. His birth year is on the handkerchief.
The boy pointing at the scene is El Greco's son. On the handkerchief in his pocket, his father wrote the year he was born: 1578.
75: Arms flung wide, a wound in his palm. The soldiers have no faces.
The man in white throws his arms wide like a crucifix, and in his palm Goya painted a wound like a stigma. The soldiers have no faces.
76: Painted straight onto a wall of his house, probably the dining room, for no one's eyes.
Goya painted it straight onto a wall of his own house, probably the dining room, never meant for anyone to see. It was moved to canvas decades after his death.
77: The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters
When reason sleeps, monsters take wing.
Goya first planned it as the opening image of his Caprichos, then made it plate 43. The words on the desk sum up the series: when reason sleeps, monsters take wing.
78: Almost all empty space, and one small head looking up.
Goya painted it on a wall of his house near Madrid and never gave it a title. Almost everything is empty space; only a dog's head rises above the slope, looking up.
79: The Cheat with the Ace of Diamonds
An ace slides out of a belt while the women trade glances.
The cheat slides an ace from his belt while the women trade glances behind the rich boy's back. La Tour was so forgotten that he was only rediscovered in 1915.
80: A tomb in paradise: 'Even in Arcadia, I am here.'
Shepherds trace an inscription on a tomb: 'Even in Arcadia, I am here.' The speaker is usually read as Death, reminding them that no paradise is without it.
81: The Academy had no box for it, so it invented a new genre.
The Royal Academy did not know how to classify it, so it invented a new genre: the fête galante. And the couples may be leaving the island of love, not arriving.
82: The first painter refused the commission. Fragonard said yes.
A courtier asked for his mistress on a swing pushed by a bishop, with himself placed to look up her skirt. The first painter he asked refused; Fragonard said yes.
83: A famously slow painter, devoted to a bubble that lasts a second.
A boy blows a bubble that will burst in a second. Chardin, a famously slow painter, spent his time on the most fleeting thing there is, and painted it at least three times.
84: A mother too drunk to notice her baby falling over the rail.
A mother too drunk to notice her baby falling over the rail. Hogarth's print came out in 1751 to back the campaign that soon passed that year's Gin Act.
85: Freud is said to have hung a copy in his Vienna apartment.
Shown in London in 1782, it caused a sensation and was copied in prints across Europe. Freud is said to have hung an engraving of it in his Vienna apartment.
86: The boy lost his leg to the shark, became Lord Mayor and bought this painting.
The boy in the water, Brook Watson, lost his leg to a shark in Havana harbor at 14. He survived, became Lord Mayor of London, and owned this painting.
87: Modern uniforms instead of togas, and most of these men were never there.
Critics told West that heroes must wear togas; he painted modern uniforms, and history painting changed. Yet most of the men around the dying general were not actually there.
88: A guest shows off her jewels. Cornelia points to her sons.
A rich visitor shows off her jewels; Cornelia points to her sons: these are mine. Kauffman was one of only two women among the founders of London's Royal Academy.
89: The painting that opened the Academy's door, with a queen's push.
This painting won Vigée Le Brun a place in the Royal Academy in 1783, backed by Marie Antoinette, on the same day as her rival Labille-Guiard. Only four women were allowed in.
90: The brothers swear to fight. One of the weeping women loves the enemy.
Three brothers swear to fight to the death for Rome. On the right the women already weep: one of them is engaged to a man from the enemy family.
91: Critics joked about extra vertebrae. A 2004 study found her back impossibly long.
Critics joked that she had three extra vertebrae. A medical study in 2004 measured her and agreed that her back is impossibly long; Ingres chose grace over anatomy.
92: About 150 adrift, 15 rescued. He studied corpses in a morgue to paint them.
Of about 150 people set adrift on the raft, 15 were rescued. Géricault interviewed survivors, built a model of the raft and studied corpses in a morgue to paint it.
93: Bonaparte Visiting the Plague Victims of Jaffa
A bare hand on a plague sore, like a king healing by touch.
The scene is Jaffa, 1799: Napoleon touches a plague sore with his bare hand, like a medieval king healing by touch. It was propaganda, commissioned and painted five years later.
94: The god with the compass is no hero here, but a tyrant of cold reason.
Blake hand-colored a copy of this image days before he died. The god measuring the world with a compass is no hero to him: he named him Urizen, tyrant of cold reason.
95: The bride glows under a paper crown. Where is the groom?
The bride is easy to find, glowing under a paper crown before a green cloth. The groom is the mystery: scholars still argue over which guest, if any, he is.
96: A steep diagonal table, and angels made of smoke.
Tintoretto set the table on a steep diagonal and filled the dark with a smoking lamp and angels made of smoke. He painted it in the last years of his life.
97: The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp
The body is a thief hanged that same day.
The body belonged to Aris Kindt, a thief hanged for armed robbery the same day. Rembrandt was 26, and this commission made him Amsterdam's most sought-after painter.
98: The red cross on his chest was added later. Legend says by the king.
The red cross on Velázquez's chest was added after he finished: he was knighted three years later. Legend says King Philip painted it on himself.
99: A scream painted on a real shield, perhaps from the painter's own face.
Painted on a real wooden shield, as a gift for the Grand Duke of Tuscany. Many believe the screaming face is Caravaggio's own, studied in a mirror.
100: Stabbed in the bath where he soaked for hours, then painted as a martyr.
Marat was stabbed in his bath by Charlotte Corday; he soaked there for hours because of a skin disease. David, his friend, painted him as a martyr within months.
101: A critic's insult that became the name of a revolution.
A critic used its title as an insult: mere 'impressionists'. The painters liked the word, and a sneer became the name of a revolution.
102: Painted from memory, by day: a night sky he could only see by remembering it.
Van Gogh painted it from memory, by day, in an asylum near the window he watched at night. The sky he gave us was one he could only see by remembering it.
103: Not a cathedral, but the hours: the stone is just where the light lands.
Monet painted this same façade more than thirty times. He was not painting a cathedral; he was painting the hours, and the stone was just where the light landed.
104: Dozens of versions, and at 67 he wrote he was still making progress.
Cézanne painted this mountain dozens of times and, at 67, wrote that he was still making progress. Weeks later he collapsed in a storm while painting outdoors.
105: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte
No mixed colors at all: your eye does the mixing, a few steps back.
Seurat never mixed his colors. For two years he set countless tiny dots side by side and left the mixing to your eye, a few steps back.
106: When he painted a woman with a parasol again, years later, he left her face blank.
This is Camille, Monet's wife, with their son Jean on a windy hill. She died four years later at 32, and when Monet painted a woman with a parasol again in 1886, he left her face blank.
107: A lawyer could not tell what it showed, and soon quit law to paint.
In 1896 a young Russian lawyer saw one of these in Moscow and could not tell what it showed. The shock helped push Wassily Kandinsky to quit law and paint his way toward abstraction.
108: Bridge over a Pond of Water Lilies
He did not find this pond. He dug it, then painted it for the rest of his life.
Monet did not find this pond; he dug it, diverting a stream despite neighbors who feared his exotic water lilies would poison their water. Then he painted his own creation for the rest of his life.
109: Snow full of blue and lilac, and the only true black is one small bird.
The Salon jury rejected it in 1869. Look at the snow: it is full of blue, lilac and yellow shadows, and the only true black in the whole field is one small magpie perched on the gate.
110: The woman cooing at the little dog would later marry the painter.
The young woman cooing at the little dog is Aline Charigot, a seamstress Renoir later married. The man straddling a chair at right is Caillebotte, the painter who bought his friends' work.
111: The dancer in red watched the painters so closely that she became one.
The dancer in red is Suzanne Valadon, a former circus acrobat turned model. She watched the painters so closely that she became one, the first woman admitted to the Société Nationale des Beaux-Arts.
112: Critics saw grease stains. It is sunlight falling through leaves.
Critics in 1877 sneered that the pale patches on her dress and the ground looked like grease stains. They are sunlight falling through leaves, exactly how it looks when you stand under a tree.
113: They are not sisters, and the little girl has never been identified.
They are not sisters. The young woman was an 18-year-old actress, Jeanne Darlaud, and the little girl beside her has never been identified.
114: After seeing Raphael, he feared he had never learned to draw.
After seeing Raphael in Italy, Renoir feared he had never learned to draw. He spent about three years on this canvas, outlining every body sharply, and many of his Impressionist friends were baffled.
115: Two hungry painters, side by side, and out of that summer came Impressionism.
In summer 1869 Renoir and Monet set up their easels side by side at this riverside bathing spot. Renoir wrote that they did not eat every day; out of that hungry summer came Impressionism.
116: Hardly anyone is dancing: they scratch, yawn and fix their bows.
The old man leaning on a stick is Jules Perrot, once one of Europe's most celebrated dancers. Look at the girls: hardly anyone is dancing; they scratch, yawn, fan themselves and fix their bows.
117: Half hidden in the wings stands a man in black.

Half hidden in the wings stands a man in black. He was probably an abonné, a wealthy subscriber allowed backstage, and for many poor young dancers such men were patrons, protectors and danger at once.
118: Two friends posed as lost drinkers, and their reputations paid for it.
The two lost drinkers are Degas' friends posing: the actress Ellen Andrée and the engraver Marcellin Desboutin. When the painting caused a stir in England in 1893, their reputations suffered for it.
119: A Cotton Office in New Orleans
His own family's business, and the first Degas a museum ever owned.
Degas painted his own family's business in New Orleans: his uncle tests cotton in front, his brother reads the paper. In 1878 the museum in Pau bought it, the first Degas any museum ever owned.
120: One irons with all her weight. The other just yawns.
One woman presses down with all her weight; the other yawns and grips a bottle. Degas painted Paris laundresses again and again: the long shifts, the heat, the boredom few other painters noticed.
121: Women seen as if through a keyhole, unaware of any viewer.
Degas said he wanted to show women as if seen through a keyhole, absorbed in themselves and unaware of any viewer. Shown in 1886, these bathers shocked a public used to nudes who pose.
122: Both sisters trained as painters. One stopped; the other painted her.
The young mother is Edma, Berthe Morisot's sister. They trained as painters together, but Edma gave it up when she married; Berthe kept going and painted her watching her baby sleep.
123: Two students walked out of the Tate with it. Now two cities take turns.
In 1956 two Irish students walked out of London's Tate with this painting to protest a disputed will. Today London and Dublin share it, taking turns showing it.
124: Manet admired this small painting so much that she gave it to him.
The woman under the parasol is Edma, Morisot's sister, on the harbor wall in Brittany. Manet admired this small painting so much that Berthe gave it to him as a gift.
126: The oar, his arm, the boat's lines: everything points to the child.
The rower's dark back fills half the canvas, and the oar, his arm and the boat's lines all point to the child. Cassatt, an American in France, painted it on the Riviera at Antibes.
127: She aims her opera glasses. Behind her, a man aims his right at her.
She aims her opera glasses at the stage, or at someone. In a box behind her, a man is aiming his own glasses right at her: Cassatt turned the theater into a game of who gets to look.
128: A pond full of ducks, at the house where she would live the rest of her life.
Cassatt painted it the year she bought a country château north of Paris, with a pond full of ducks. She lived there for the rest of her life and died there in 1926.
129: A village under the flood, turned into some of his calmest paintings.
In spring 1876 the Seine flooded the village of Port-Marly. Sisley turned the disaster into some of his calmest paintings, returning to the same flooded inn several times.
130: A lifetime in France, and he died without French citizenship.
Sisley was born in Paris to English parents and spent nearly his whole life in France. Near the end he applied for French citizenship and never got it; he died a British subject in 1899.
131: A war ruined his rich father, so sunny bridges like this had to pay the rent.
Sisley grew up rich, until the war of 1870 ruined his father's business. From then on he had to live from paintings like this sunny bridge, and money stayed tight for the rest of his life.
132: A village hidden behind bare branches, with a friend's solid colors in it.
The village hides behind bare branches, like a screen. Pissarro and Cézanne painted side by side around Pontoise in these years, and you can feel Cézanne's solid blocks of color in his friend's work.
133: Soldiers destroyed most of his paintings. He started over with orchards.
When Pissarro returned to Louveciennes after the war of 1870, he found that soldiers had used his house and destroyed most of the paintings he left behind. He started over with orchards like this.
134: Born on a Caribbean island, he became the Impressionists' father figure.
Pissarro was born to a Jewish family on the Caribbean island of St. Thomas. He became the father figure of the Impressionists, and the only one who showed in all eight of their exhibitions.
135: Rejected as vulgar, yet the curls of shaved wood still look freshly fallen.
The 1875 Salon rejected it as vulgar: workers, bare to the waist, scraping a floor. Caillebotte showed it with the Impressionists instead, and the curls of shaved wood still look freshly fallen.
136: Centuries of women bathing, and then a man drying his back.
Painters had shown women bathing for centuries. Caillebotte turned it around: a man drying his back, wet footprints on the floor, painted with the same plain, unembarrassed attention.
137: Nothing but rain: rings spreading on the water, one by one.
Caillebotte spent his youthful summers at the family estate on the Yerres river. Here he paints nothing but rain: rings spreading on the water, one by one, overlapping.
138: He squeezed himself in at the far left edge. Three years later he was gone.
Bazille painted his whole family on their terrace near Montpellier and squeezed himself in at the far left edge. Three years later he was killed in the Franco-Prussian War, at 28.
139: The tall man is Bazille, but another painter painted him in.
The tall man in the middle is Bazille, but he did not paint himself: Manet took the brush and added him. Around him friends talk art in the studio he shared with Renoir, months before the war.
140: He quietly kept his friends afloat, buying Monet's work in monthly installments.
Bazille came from a wealthy family and quietly kept his friends afloat. To help Monet, he bought his big Women in the Garden, paying for it in monthly installments.
141: Crowds came to laugh, and modern art found its first audience.
Rejected by the Salon of 1863, it hung in a special Salon of the Rejected that the emperor allowed. Crowds came to laugh at it, and modern art found its first audience.
142: Mocked as a model, she also painted, and the Salon took her over Manet.
The woman staring back is Victorine Meurent. Mocked as Manet's model, she also painted, and in 1876 the Salon accepted her own work in the same year it rejected Manet's.
143: Look at the mirror: the reflection never quite adds up.
Look at the mirror: the barmaid's reflection drifts far to the right, facing a man who should be standing where you are. Manet's last major painting never quite adds up.
144: The only train is a cloud of steam, and Olympia is now dressed, reading.
The title promises a railway, but the only train is a cloud of steam behind the bars. The woman is Victorine Meurent, Olympia's model, now dressed, reading, and looking right at us.
145: No horizon at all: the water climbs to the top of the canvas.
Manet spent the summer of 1874 at Argenteuil beside Monet and finally tried painting in bright outdoor light. There is no horizon at all: the water climbs to the top of the canvas.
146: Overpaid for asparagus, he sent the missing spear.
A collector paid Manet 1,000 francs for a painted bunch of asparagus priced at 800. Manet sent him this single spear with a note: 'There was one missing from your bunch.'
147: Painted to welcome a guest. The visit ended with part of an ear.
Van Gogh painted these to decorate the room for Gauguin, who was coming to stay in Arles. The visit lasted about two months and ended the night Vincent cut off part of his ear.
148: A room meant to suggest rest, painted again from an asylum.
Van Gogh wrote to his brother that this room should suggest rest and sleep. He loved it enough to paint it three times, the last two from the asylum, when he could no longer go home.
149: For a baby named Vincent: blossoms to hang above his bed.
When his brother Theo had a son and named him Vincent, the painter in the asylum sent this: blossoming branches against a blue sky, to hang above the baby's bed.
150: The same hands dug the earth and now reach into the dish.
Van Gogh wanted you to feel that these peasants dug the earth with the same hands they now reach into the dish with. He thought it his best work; most people at the time found it ugly.
151: Painted in his first week at the asylum: a lightning conductor for his illness.
Van Gogh painted it in his first week at the asylum in Saint-Rémy, calling painting the lightning conductor for his illness. In 1987 it became the most expensive painting ever sold.
152: Farmhands playing cards, and one version reportedly sold for $250 million or more.
Cézanne painted farmhands from around his family's estate playing cards, in five versions. One of them was sold in 2011 to the royal family of Qatar for a reported $250 million or more.
153: Follow the table's edge under the cloth: the two sides do not line up.
Follow the table's edge under the cloth: the left side and the right side do not line up. Cézanne bent perspective on purpose, and the painters after him took it as permission.
154: Seven years of work, unfinished, and modern painting grew from it.
Cézanne worked on this canvas for about seven years and left it unfinished when he died in 1906. Picasso and Matisse studied his bathers closely, and modern painting grew from them.
155: Skulls stacked like fruit on a cloth, painted with the calm he gave apples.
In his sixties, ill with diabetes, Cézanne painted skulls with the same calm he gave to apples, stacked like fruit on a cloth.
156: The Bay of Marseille, Seen from L'Estaque
'Like a playing card': red roofs against the blue sea.
'It is like a playing card,' Cézanne wrote to Pissarro from L'Estaque, 'red roofs against the blue sea.' He returned to this bay again and again, flattening it into blocks of color.
157: Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?
Three questions, painted after his daughter's death, and still open.
Gauguin painted this in Tahiti in 1897, after learning that his daughter Aline had died. He later wrote that he then went into the mountains to die; he survived, and the questions stayed open.
158: Women leaving church still see the sermon, on a field of pure red.
Breton women leave church still seeing the sermon: Jacob wrestling the angel on a field of pure red. Gauguin offered the painting to a local church; the priest turned it down.
159: A wooden crucifix that still hangs in a chapel, moved into a yellow field.
The model was a painted wooden crucifix in the Trémalo chapel near Pont-Aven, which still hangs there. Gauguin moved it outdoors into an autumn field and turned it bright yellow.
160: He went looking for an untouched paradise and found a French colony.
Gauguin went to Tahiti in 1891 looking for an untouched paradise and found a French colony. One woman wears a pareo; the other, a high-necked dress of the kind missionaries introduced.
161: He could barely sell it. In 2015 it reportedly fetched about $210 million.
In 2015 it was reported sold for about $210 million, among the highest prices ever paid for a painting. In his lifetime Gauguin struggled to sell his Tahiti pictures at all.
162: Parisians laughed at the red dog. Its name means 'joyfulness'.
Arearea means 'joyfulness' in Tahitian. When it was shown in Paris in 1893, visitors laughed at the red dog; today it is one of the treasures of the Musée d'Orsay.
164: Everything rises in upward lines, meant to feel joyful. He died before finishing.
Seurat was still working on it when he died suddenly in 1891, aged 31. Everything rises in upward lines, which he believed would make a picture feel joyful.
165: A wild dance frozen into identical diagonals, mustache tips included.
The chahut was a high-kicking dance that shocked Paris. Seurat froze it into rows of identical diagonals: legs, coattails, mustache tips and bows all tilted upward together.
166: He sailed into a small fishing port, and painters came long before the yachts.
Signac sailed into a small fishing port called Saint-Tropez in 1892 and fell in love with it. He settled there, and painters followed long before the yachts did.
167: The Pine Tree at Saint Tropez
Dots grown into mosaic tiles of pure color.
By 1909 Signac's dots had grown into bold mosaic tiles of pure color. Matisse spent a summer painting beside him in Saint-Tropez in 1904 and came away ready to set color free.
168: The small man in the background beside a very tall one is the painter.
The small man walking in the background beside a very tall one is Lautrec himself, with his cousin. At some point the strip with the green-lit face at right was cut off; it was later reattached.
169: His first poster went up across Paris and made him famous almost overnight.
Lautrec's legs stopped growing after he broke both as a teenager. In 1891 this, his first poster, went up on walls across Paris and made him famous almost overnight.
170: Later, in a clinic, he drew the circus from memory to prove he was sane.
This circus scene hung in the entrance of the Moulin Rouge when it opened in 1889. Years later, confined to a clinic, Lautrec drew circus acts from memory to prove he was sane.
171: Two heads on one pillow, from the painter of cancan nights.
Two heads on one pillow, one blanket pulled up to the chin. Lautrec, famous for nightlife and cancan, painted here one of the tenderest pictures of closeness in his work.
172: Salon in the Rue des Moulins
No customer appears. The waiting is the subject.
Lautrec sometimes lived for weeks at a time in Paris brothels, and he painted the women between clients: slumped, bored, waiting. No customer appears; the waiting is the subject.
173: He never left France: his jungle grew in a Paris hothouse.
Rousseau never left France. His first jungle, a tiger crouching in a storm, grew out of visits to the hothouses and zoo of the Jardin des Plantes in Paris.
174: A folding screen between them, and nearly fifty years together.
This is Bonnard and his lover Marthe in their bedroom, divided by a folding screen. They stayed together for nearly fifty years, and he painted her hundreds of times.
175: Room, garden and woman melt into one warm afternoon, painted from memory.
Bonnard rarely painted from life; he worked from memory and small pencil notes. Here the room, the garden and Marthe leaning at the window melt into one warm afternoon.
176: Interior, Mother and Sister of the Artist
His sister sinks into the wallpaper, while their mother sits solid in the middle.
Vuillard lived with his mother almost all his life. Here his sister in a checked dress seems to sink into the patterned wallpaper, while their mother sits solid and dark in the middle.
177: A woman sweeping almost dissolves into the wallpaper.
His mother ran a corset-making workshop from the family apartment, and Vuillard painted its quiet chores. A sweeping woman almost dissolves into the patterns of wallpaper and cloth.
178: A Loge at the Théâtre des Italiens
Manet's only formal pupil died less than a week after him.
Eva Gonzalès was Manet's only formal pupil. She died in 1883 at 34, days after giving birth, and less than a week after her teacher Manet.
179: No crushing rock, only longing: one huge, shy eye.
In the myth, the one-eyed giant Polyphemus loves the nymph Galatea and crushes his rival with a rock. Redon keeps only the longing: one huge, shy eye gazing at a sleeping woman.
180: Decades of black charcoal, then color: a drowned girl floating in a bouquet.
For decades Redon worked almost only in black charcoal, drawing dreams and monsters. Around fifty he discovered color, and here drowned Ophelia floats inside a bouquet.
181: Critics found it bleak and clumsy. Seurat, Gauguin and Picasso learned from it.
Critics in 1881 found it bleak and clumsy. Younger painters saw a way forward in its flat, silent sadness, and Seurat, Gauguin and later Picasso all learned from it.
182: A calm sacred grove, and a young Lautrec crowded it with Parisians in parody.
When the full-size mural was shown in Paris in 1884, the young Toulouse-Lautrec and friends painted a cheeky parody of it, crowding the calm grove with modern Parisians.
183: Is that tree yellow? Then use your finest yellow. On a cigar-box lid.
Gauguin stood beside Sérusier and asked: how do you see that tree? Yellow? Then use your finest yellow. Painted on a cigar-box lid, it became the founding relic of the Nabis.
184: Painted at 20, it started a lifelong quarrel over who influenced whom.
Émile Bernard was 20 when he painted these women in flat color. Gauguin saw it in Pont-Aven and soon painted his Vision After the Sermon; who influenced whom became a lifelong quarrel.
185: A child chases a red ball while the shadow of the trees closes in.
A child runs after a red ball in sunlight while the shadow of the trees closes in. Vallotton probably worked from snapshots taken with a Kodak he bought in 1899, which explains the strange high view.
186: Painters gathered around a still life. Cézanne himself is absent.
The painters gathered around this Cézanne still life are the Nabis, and the still life itself once belonged to Gauguin. Cézanne is absent; the older Redon stands at far left, listening.
187: Painted only in a few minutes of dusk each evening, over two summers.
Sargent painted only in the few minutes of dusk each evening, when the light matched the lanterns. It took two summers, and he kept replacing the dying flowers.
188: His wife and daughter, painted fast while the sea wind tugged at their dresses.
The woman in white is Sorolla's wife Clotilde, and the girl is their daughter María. He painted them fast, outdoors, while the wind off the sea at Valencia tugged at their dresses.
190: Summer Evening on Skagen's Southern Beach
Two painters on the beach, in the blue hour when sea and sky become one.
The two women are painters: Anna Ancher and Marie Krøyer, the artist's wife. Krøyer loved Skagen's 'blue hour', when sea, sand and sky melt into one color.
191: Dancing near midnight, in a half-light where the sun barely sets.
On Midsummer Eve in Sweden the sun barely sets. Zorn painted the people of his home district around Mora dancing in that strange half-light near midnight.
192: His hometown turned it down. Now it hangs at MoMA.
Rousseau, a self-taught toll collector, offered this painting to his hometown of Laval. The town said no; today it is one of the treasures of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
193: A garden dissolving in fog, a woman barely visible among the flowers.
A garden dissolving into morning fog, a woman bent over the flowers barely visible. Sisley, the purest landscape painter of the group, painted almost nothing but places like this.
194: A woman sews, but the true subject is the blue light.
Backer painted this in Paris; the woman sewing is her friend, the painter Asta Nørregaard. The true subject is the blue light; Backer later taught a generation of Norwegian painters to see it.
195: A girl knits in the corner, but the real subject is a square of sunlight.
The girl knitting in the corner is Helga, Anna Ancher's daughter. The real subject is the square of sunlight on the wall, and Anna, born in Skagen, painted that light more patiently than anyone.
196: Three Impressionist shows, and then she stopped, to keep the peace at home.
Marie Bracquemond showed with the Impressionists three times. Her husband, an engraver, resented her work, and she largely stopped painting; their son said it was to keep the peace.
197: A city clerk painting factory smoke, until he won the lottery.
Guillaumin painted factory smoke in a burning sunset while working for the city of Paris to survive. In 1891 he won 100,000 francs in a lottery and could finally paint full time.
198: Born a Delacroix, he translated 'croix' into English to escape the name.
His real name was Henri-Edmond Delacroix. To avoid confusion with the famous Delacroix, he translated 'croix' into English and signed as Cross.
199: Painted from the deck: the sea broken into thousands of dots.
Théo van Rysselberghe, a Belgian who loved to sail, painted this from the deck: the helmsman braced, the sail slicing the sky, and the sea broken into thousands of dots of green and white.
200: Decades later, watching the Nazis march, he wanted to throw up more than he could eat.
Max Liebermann spent his summers in Holland painting work like this. Decades later, watching the Nazis march in 1933, he said: 'I cannot eat as much as I would like to throw up.'
201: 'Can only have been painted by a madman', written faintly by Munch himself.
On this version a faint pencil line reads: 'Can only have been painted by a madman.' In 2021 handwriting experts confirmed that Munch wrote it himself.
202: More than thirty studies, then four days. He wanted you to hear this one.
Kandinsky made more than thirty studies for it, then painted the final canvas in about four days. He believed colors could sound, and he wanted you to hear this one.
203: Real gold leaf, and the couple kneels one step from the cliff's edge.
Klimt used real gold leaf, and the couple kneels at the edge of a flowered cliff. Vienna's most famous embrace is also a moment one step from the fall.
204: Blue was the spirit's color, and animals saw the world more truly than we do.
For Franz Marc, blue was the color of the spirit. He painted animals because he believed they saw the world more truly than we do. He was killed at Verdun at 36.
205: He painted himself as Death, holding the woman he was about to leave.
Schiele painted himself as Death, holding Wally, the woman he was about to leave, in the year he married someone else. Three years later he was dead at 28.
206: Three women, three stages of love: white, red and black.
Three women, three stages of love: innocent white, passionate red, mourning black. Munch set the drama on a summer shore, under a moon that lays a pillar of light on the sea.
207: Over twenty years he came back, trying to hold one bright night still.
The bridge stood in Åsgårdstrand, the seaside village where Munch spent his summers. He came back to this scene again and again for over twenty years, as if trying to hold one bright night still.
208: A crowd of pale, masklike faces, and one dark figure walking the other way.
Oslo's grand promenade, and the crowd comes at you with pale, staring faces like masks. One dark figure walks the other way, alone, and many see Munch himself in him.
209: For decades, the Nobel Peace Prize was handed out beneath this sunrise.
Munch painted this sunrise over the Norwegian coast for the great hall of the University of Oslo. From 1947 to 1989 the Nobel Peace Prize was handed out beneath it.
210: The silent sibling of The Scream: no figure, no cry, only breathing darkness.
Painted in 1893, the year of The Scream, this is its silent sibling: no figure, no cry, only the shore at Åsgårdstrand, a few stars and a darkness that seems to breathe.
211: Years before the group had a name, this little rider was already crossing the meadow.

Years before Kandinsky and Franz Marc named their group The Blue Rider, this small rider was already crossing a meadow. Kandinsky later explained: we both loved blue, Marc loved horses, I loved riders.
212: Look again: lances, Cossacks, a castle on a hill, a rainbow.
It looks abstract, but look again: two black lances, Cossacks on horseback, a castle on a blue hill, a rainbow. Kandinsky was erasing the world one step at a time, until only its music remained.
213: Ten years after the storm, the storm became an orchestra.
Ten years after the storm of Composition VII, Kandinsky, now teaching at the Bauhaus, turned to circles, lines and triangles. He saw it as a high point of his work: the storm had become an orchestra.
214: Circles drift like planets, and wherever they overlap, a new color is born.
Kandinsky called the circle 'the synthesis of the greatest oppositions'. Here circles drift through dark space like planets, and wherever they overlap, a new color is born.
215: Yellow rushes at you, blue pulls away, and red keeps the balance.
On the left, a yellow that for Kandinsky rushed toward the viewer. On the right, a deep blue that pulls away into the distance. Between them, red keeps the balance. He believed colors move.
216: It won first prize, and he kept painting it anyway.
It won first prize at the 1911 international exhibition in Rome, and Klimt kept working on it anyway. He painted over its gold background, and Death, in a robe of crosses, still watches the sleepers.
218: Painted to be destroyed after the show. It survived.
Klimt painted it on the walls of the Vienna Secession for a 1902 Beethoven show, to be destroyed afterward. It survived, ending with Schiller's line from the Ninth: 'this kiss to the whole world'.
219: A golden tree in a private dining room, known to most only through designs like this.

This golden tree spirals across a dining room in a Brussels mansion, laid in marble, gold and enamel mosaic. The house is private, so most of us know it only through Klimt's working designs, like this one.
220: Framed through a telescope, a garden flattens into a wall of flowers.

Klimt spent his summers on Lake Attersee and painted about fifty landscapes, nearly all square. He often framed them through a telescope or opera glass, which flattens a garden into a wall of flowers.
221: After a fire, a friend repainted the burned part. You can still see where.
On the back Marc wrote: 'And all being is flaming suffering.' After his death a fire damaged the painting, and his friend Paul Klee repainted the burned part. You can still see where.
222: A tiger built of crystal planes, perfectly still and ready to spring.
In 1912 Marc took the sharp planes of Cubism and built a tiger out of them, like a crystal. It lies perfectly still among the rocks, yet every angle of its body is ready to spring.
223: On the eve of war, red and black collide. He never came home.
In 1914, on the eve of war, a red force and a black one collide. Marc volunteered that August, and from the front he could manage only a small sketchbook. He never came home.
224: How does a deer see the world? A forest broken into shards of light.
Marc asked: 'How does a horse see the world, or an eagle, a deer, or a dog?' Here he tries to answer, breaking the forest into shards of light around the resting deer.
225: Last seen in Berlin around 1945. Does it still exist?
The Nazis seized it as 'degenerate art', and it was last seen in Berlin around 1945. Nobody knows if it still exists; old color reproductions like this one are all that is left.
226: A man, a woman, and a child who was never born.
Schiele painted himself, a woman, and a child who was never born. In autumn 1918 his wife Edith died of the Spanish flu while six months pregnant, and he died three days later.
227: The painter of anxious bodies, for once holding on without fear.
Schiele, famous for anxious, angular bodies, painted something rare for him here: two lovers simply holding each other on a rumpled white sheet, without fear.
228: The painter of nervous nudes, suddenly very quiet before four trees.
Four trees stand in a row against an autumn sunset, their leaves already thinning. The painter of nervous nudes could be very quiet when he faced a landscape.
229: The town drove him out for living with his lover. He kept painting its roofs.
Schiele loved Krumau, his mother's hometown on the Vltava, but in 1911 its residents drove him out for living there unmarried with his lover. He kept painting its crowded roofs anyway.
230: Four birds on a wire, and a crank that makes them sing.

Four birds on a wire, and a crank that makes them sing. Berlin's National Gallery bought it in 1923; the Nazis removed it as 'degenerate' in 1937, and by 1939 it was in New York's Museum of Modern Art.
231: A line went for a walk and built a castle.

A whole castle built of squares, triangles and one red sun. Klee taught at the Bauhaus, where he famously described drawing as taking a line for a walk; here the line went for a walk and built a city.
232: Look closely: a clock hangs among the fish.
Look closely: a clock hangs among the fish, beside flowers and faces in the deep. Klee glued a square of muslin to the center of the canvas, like a curtain over the sea.
233: Painted on gauze, so the weave shows through like an old memory.
A red balloon floats over a town of colored blocks. Klee painted it on gauze, not canvas, so the weave of the fabric shows through like the grain of an old memory.
234: On this trip he wrote: 'Color and I are one. I am a painter.'
In Tunisia in April 1914 Klee wrote in his diary: 'Color has taken possession of me... Color and I are one. I am a painter.' This watercolor comes from that trip.
235: Before the grids, a blood-red tree.
Before the grids and primary colors, Mondrian painted trees. This blood-red tree against a blue dusk is where his long walk toward pure abstraction begins.
236: Three years after the red tree, the branches have become rhythm.
Three years after the red tree, the branches have turned into a web of gray curves. Mondrian had seen Cubism, and the tree was slowly becoming a drawing of rhythm.
237: No blossoms, no fruit, hardly a tree. Without the title, you would never guess.
No blossoms you can see, no fruit, hardly a tree: just curved strokes and ovals. Without the title you would never guess, and that was exactly where Mondrian was heading.
238: A pier, the North Sea, and the waves, all reduced to pluses and minuses.
Hundreds of small pluses and minuses inside an oval. Mondrian was watching a pier run into the North Sea and the waves move around it, and he reduced it all to crosses.
239: Composition II in Red, Blue, and Yellow
Only verticals and horizontals. A diagonal helped end a friendship.
Only three primary colors, plus black, white and gray, and only horizontal and vertical lines. Mondrian later broke with his friend Theo van Doesburg, partly because van Doesburg let diagonals in.
240: Hung in the corner where Russian homes kept the holy icon.
At its first show in 1915 Malevich hung it high across a corner of the room, the spot where Russian homes kept their holy icon. A black square had taken the place of a saint.
241: A tilted red square, and he insists it is a peasant woman.
Its full title is 'Painterly Realism of a Peasant Woman in Two Dimensions'. A slightly tilted red square, and Malevich insists it is a woman: half joke, half a new way of seeing.
242: Feet, hands and stairs repeated like frames of a film.
Malevich shows a knife grinder at work by repeating his feet, hands and the stairs again and again, like frames of a film. Within three years he would drop the human figure altogether.
243: Morning in the Village after Snowstorm
Snowdrifts are metal cones: a winter morning turned into a gleaming machine.
The snowdrifts are metal cones, the peasants polished tubes. Malevich, who grew up among Ukrainian villages, turned a winter morning into a gleaming machine.
244: A few colored rectangles, and the title says they are flying.
A handful of colored rectangles on white, and the title is 'Airplane Flying'. Malevich wanted painting to float free of the earth, just as people had only recently learned to fly.
245: Ten canvases over three meters tall, kept hidden at her own request.
Hilma af Klint painted this series of ten canvases, each over three meters tall, in about two months of 1907. She asked that her abstract work stay hidden until twenty years after her death.
246: She dreamed of a spiral temple for them. A century later, the Guggenheim.
A golden sun above a rainbow triangle. Af Klint dreamed of a spiral temple for her paintings that was never built; in 2018 New York's spiral Guggenheim finally gave them one.
247: Two swans, black and white, slowly turned into pure geometry.
The Swan series begins with two birds, one black and one white, and slowly breaks them into pure geometry. By number 17 the swans have become circles divided between light and dark.
248: Painted, she said, under guidance from spirits.
Af Klint said she painted these under guidance from spirits she contacted in séances with four women friends, a group called The Five. She was 44, and the world would not see them for decades.
249: Paris and the Eiffel Tower, dissolved into panes of colored light.

The poet Apollinaire coined a name for paintings like this: Orphism, after Orpheus the singer. Delaunay looked at Paris and the Eiffel Tower through a window, then dissolved it all into panes of colored light.
250: A hymn of spinning discs for the man who flew the Channel.
In 1909 Louis Blériot became the first to fly an airplane across the English Channel. Five years later Delaunay painted him a hymn of spinning discs, propellers and suns.
251: A tower too new and too tall to fit a single point of view.
Delaunay painted the Eiffel Tower again and again. Here it bends and breaks as if seen from below, from the side and from the clouds at once, a tower too new and too tall to fit a single view.
252: The Three Graces of ancient Greece, standing naked beside the Eiffel Tower.
Four meters wide, with the Three Graces of ancient Greece standing naked between the Seine and the Eiffel Tower. Delaunay fused old Paris and new Paris into one shattered, glowing view.
253: Planes of color stacked like sheets of glass leaning on one another.
Lyubov Popova stacked planes of color like sheets of glass leaning on one another. She died of scarlet fever in 1924, at 35, days after her young son died of the same disease.
254: Lines like beams of force, and that same year she declared easel painting finished.
Lines cut through space like beams of force. That same year Popova and her circle declared easel painting finished and went to design for the theater and for textile factories.
255: One green stripe on white, decades before such paintings made headlines.
One green stripe glowing on white, decades before such paintings made headlines in America. Olga Rozanova painted it in 1917 and died the next year of diphtheria, at 32.
256: Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge
A red triangle pierces a white circle, and graphic design took notes.
A red triangle pierces a white circle: a poster from the Russian Civil War, Reds against Whites. With almost no words, it became a model for a century of graphic design.
257: Huge red horses strain as a new city rises.
Huge red horses strain, workers haul, a new quarter rises on the edge of Milan. Boccioni wanted the noise and speed of the modern street; six years later he died at 33 after a fall from a horse.
258: Somewhere in this whirl of color is a footballer in full stride.
Somewhere in this whirl of color is a footballer in full stride. Boccioni wanted the body and the air around it to move as one force; two years later he enlisted in a volunteer cyclist battalion.
259: Don't look for the bicycle. This is speed itself.
Don't look for the bicycle: there are only arcs, wedges and color rushing forward. Boccioni wanted to paint not a cyclist but speed itself, the rider dissolving into the wind he makes.
260: The man who painted this crowd later gave up painting for noise machines.
The man who painted this red wedge of crowd smashing into a city later gave up painting for sound. In 1913 Luigi Russolo wrote 'The Art of Noises' and built machines that roared and hissed.
261: Five dancers, three colors, and two hands that fail to meet.
A Moscow collector, Sergei Shchukin, ordered it for the staircase of his mansion. Five dancers, three colors, and a ring that almost breaks where two hands fail to meet.
262: It caused an uproar, and the young Picasso may have painted an answer.
Its wild colors caused an uproar in Paris in 1906. The young Picasso saw it, and many historians think his Demoiselles d'Avignon was partly an answer to this dream of joy.
263: First blue-gray, then flooded with red, leaving the furniture as ghosts.
Matisse first painted his studio as it looked, in blue-gray and ochre. Then he flooded it all with red, leaving the furniture as faint ghost lines and only his own artworks in full color.
264: Luxury, calm and pleasure, borrowed from a poem and painted in dots.
The title comes from Baudelaire: 'There, all is order and beauty, luxury, calm and pleasure.' Matisse painted it after a summer in Saint-Tropez, in dots of pure color.
265: A window over a harbor, and a critic called the painters wild beasts.
Shown in Paris in 1905, works like this made a critic call their painters 'fauves', wild beasts. All Matisse had done was paint a window over a harbor in the colors he felt, not the ones he saw.
266: A fish bowl, meant to give you the calm of a long gaze.
Matisse painted goldfish again and again around 1912. In Morocco he had watched people gaze into fish bowls for long stretches, and he wanted a painting to give you that same calm.
267: Sent to repeat Monet's foggy Thames, he burned the fog away with color.
The dealer Ambroise Vollard sent Derain to London, hoping to repeat the success of Monet's foggy Thames. Derain came back with the fog burned away by pure color.
268: A few summer weeks in a fishing village, and Fauvism was born.
In the summer of 1905 Derain and Matisse painted side by side in Collioure, a fishing village near the Spanish border. Fauvism was born there, in a few weeks by the Mediterranean.
269: Colors as sticks of dynamite, meant to explode into light.
The Thames as a harbor of jade and orange. Derain later said that for the Fauves, colors became 'sticks of dynamite', meant to explode into light.
270: A girl in red ran past, and the red stayed in his eye longer than she did.
Dufy said he once watched a girl in red run along a harbor and noticed that the red stayed in his eye longer than her shape. From then on he let colors spill past the lines.
271: A newspaper, a glass, a bottle, sliding past each other like stained glass.
Juan Gris, who died at 40, made Cubism orderly and full of light. On this table a newspaper, a glass and a bottle slide past one another like pieces of a stained-glass window.
272: A poor 19-year-old moved into Picasso's building and learned to slice guitars into planes.
Gris came to Paris at 19, poor, and moved into the ramshackle studio building where Picasso lived. A few years later he was painting guitars split into planes of wood grain and shadow.
273: Find the newspaper: it is real paper, glued in, and the painting grew around it.
Look for the newspaper: Gris glued real paper into this still life by an open window, then painted the striped sunblind around it. Collage let real life walk into the painting.
274: Gassed at Verdun, he came home dazzled by the beauty of machines.
Léger came back from Verdun, where he was gassed, dazzled by the beauty of guns and machines. Here Paris becomes posters, girders and stenciled letters, a city built like an engine.
275: Over three and a half meters of villagers, mountains and harvest, woven into one.
More than three and a half meters wide, it was Cubism's grand epic: villagers, mountains and the harvest woven into one landscape. That same year Gleizes co-wrote the first book on Cubism.
276: Two men chat outdoors while a balloon carries the dream of flight past them.

Two men talk at a table in the open air as a balloon with a French flag drifts by. Roger de La Fresnaye painted the dream of flight in 1913; he came back from the war with tuberculosis and died at 40.
277: The faces are masks, and the street is a pink river.
The faces are masks and the street a pink river. Kirchner was a founder of Die Brücke, 'The Bridge', a group of young painters who wanted art to cross from the old world to a new one.
278: Feathered hats, circling men: a street that works like a market of glances.
Two women in feathered hats, men circling them: Kirchner's Berlin street is a market of glances. In 2006 the painting was returned to the heirs of its Jewish owner and sold for 38 million dollars.
279: He came up the mountain to recover, and never came down again.
After a breakdown during the war, Kirchner went up to the Swiss mountains near Davos to recover. He painted the town in pink and blue snow and stayed there for the rest of his life.
280: Such joyful colors, from a man who would take his life in these same valleys.
In 1937 the Nazis removed more than 600 of Kirchner's works from German museums. In 1938, in the Swiss valleys he painted in such joyful colors, he took his own life.
281: Not oil but glue paint, dry and chalky like an old fresco, for a world without cities.
Otto Mueller painted with glue-based distemper instead of oil, for a dry, chalky surface like an old fresco. His bathers live in a world with no cities, the dream all of Die Brücke shared.
282: Nobody in this park looks at anyone, and a peaceful world is about to end.
Nobody in this park looks at anyone else, and the lady in green doesn't look at us. August Macke, killed in the first weeks of the war at 27, painted a peaceful world about to end.
283: Tunisian light turned his color into sunshine. Five months later he was dead.
In April 1914 Macke traveled to Tunisia with Paul Klee, and the light there turned his color into pure sunshine. Five months later he was dead on the Western Front.
284: Parrots, deer and people in hats, all sharing one transparent light.
Parrots, deer and people in hats, all sharing the same transparent light. For Macke, a Sunday at the zoo was a small paradise where people and animals live in peace.
285: People stroll, the water glows, and nothing bad can happen yet.
Macke painted it on Lake Thun in Switzerland, where he spent his last peaceful months, from autumn 1913 to spring 1914. People stroll, the water glows, and nothing bad can happen yet.
286: She put down the brush for ten years for his career. Then she came back like this.
Marianne von Werefkin stopped painting for ten years to promote the career of her partner, Alexej von Jawlensky. When she picked up the brush again, she painted like this.
287: She painted mothers like the earth itself, and died 18 days after becoming one.
Paula Modersohn-Becker painted mothers and babies as few had before: naked, heavy, of the earth. In 1907 she gave birth to a daughter and died eighteen days later, at 31.
288: Peat canals taught her big, simple shapes. Buyers were few.
In the artists' colony of Worpswede, among the peat canals of northern Germany, the young Paula learned to see big, simple shapes. She sold only a handful of paintings in her lifetime.
289: Police shut his only solo show on opening day, because of nudes like this.
In December 1917 police closed Modigliani's only solo show in his lifetime on its opening day, because of nudes like this one in the window. He died two years later, poor, at 35.
290: Can you find Christ? He is almost lost in the mob of masks and brass bands.
Christ rides into Brussels almost lost in a mob of masks, slogans and brass bands. Ensor's own avant-garde group refused to show it, and it was not exhibited publicly until 1929.
291: Skeletons Fighting over a Pickled Herring
A pun in French: 'hareng saur' sounds like 'art Ensor'. The skeletons are his critics.
In French 'hareng saur', smoked herring, sounds like 'art Ensor'. The two skeletons tearing at it are his critics, fighting over his art like scavengers.
292: A reflection so exact that the sky seems to go on under the water.
Hodler believed the world is built on repetition and symmetry, and called the idea Parallelism. Here Lake Thun mirrors the mountains so exactly that the sky seems to continue under the water.
293: A staircase that twists out of the world, from a man who could not sleep.
A woman in black on an endless staircase that seems to twist out of the world. Léon Spilliaert, an insomniac from Ostend, painted his nights in ink and watercolor, and they still feel like dreams.
294: Yes, the playwright. With a palette knife, he cut a hole of light into a forest.
Yes, that Strindberg: the playwright of Miss Julie also painted, mostly with a palette knife. Here a dark forest opens onto a glowing hole of light, which he called Wonderland.
295: He painted when the words stopped coming: a dark town on a strip between storm and sea.
Strindberg painted mostly in the years when his writing stalled. Here a dark town clings to a thin strip of land between a stormy sky and black water.
296: Youth, painted not as a face but as spirals and buds unfolding.
Number 3 of ten giant canvases that follow a human life from childhood to old age. Af Klint painted youth not as a face but as spirals, petals and buds unfolding on a field of orange.
297: A stroke left his hand trembling. He painted this lake about sixty times anyway.
A stroke in 1911 left Lovis Corinth's hand trembling, and he painted on, wilder than before. From his house above Lake Walchensee in the Bavarian Alps he painted this lake about sixty times.
298: Battle of Lights, Coney Island, Mardi Gras
Futurism came home from Paris and found itself at night in Coney Island.
Joseph Stella, an Italian immigrant, brought Futurism home from Paris and found it at night in Coney Island. Electric bulbs, rides and crowds explode together into one roaring fireworks.
299: On the bridge at night he felt 'on the threshold of a new religion'.
Stella said that standing on the Brooklyn Bridge at night he felt 'as if on the threshold of a new religion'. He painted its cables and Gothic arches like a cathedral of steel.
300: No face, only flags, medals, initials, and an age: 24.
There is no face here. Marsden Hartley mourned a young German officer he loved, killed in the first months of World War I, through flags, medals, his initials and his age: 24.
301: Made at about seventy, by a man who said nothing before seventy counted.
Hokusai made it at about seventy and later wrote that nothing he drew before seventy was worth noticing. At 110, he hoped, every line would be alive.
302: Not a mountain, but the few minutes a mountain turns red.
Three colors, almost no detail, and a mountain that turns red for a few minutes on late-summer mornings. Hokusai did not paint a mountain; he painted a moment.
303: Van Gogh copied this cheap print in oil, stroke for stroke.
Van Gogh copied this print in oil, stroke for stroke. A Japanese woodblock sold cheaply in Paris helped teach Europe a new way of seeing.
304: The signature hid in the leaves for nearly a thousand years.
Find the travelers: a tiny mule train at the bottom, almost lost. For nearly a thousand years no one knew who painted it, until in 1958 a scholar found Fan Kuan's signature hidden in the leaves.
305: Along the River During the Qingming Festival
More than 800 people on one scroll, and each is doing something different.
The whole scroll is over five meters long and holds more than 800 people, each doing something different. Emperors guarded it like treasure; it is still called China's Mona Lisa.
306: A fisherman, his rock and his lines make a small triangle that echoes Fuji.
The fisherman, his rock and his taut lines form a small triangle that echoes Fuji above. Early impressions were printed almost entirely in Prussian blue, a pigment newly imported into Japan.
307: One gust: a hat flies, papers escape, and Fuji shrinks to an outline.
Hokusai froze a single gust: a hat flies, papers escape a traveler's hands, and Fuji shrinks to an outline. In 1993 Jeff Wall restaged the scene as a huge photograph.
308: Clear sky at the summit, lightning at its feet.
Clear sky at the summit, lightning at its feet. Hokusai shows one mountain in two weathers at once, as if to say the storm is only one layer of what is happening.
309: Water like long fingers clawing down the rock, and tiny pilgrims looking up.
Hokusai drew the falls as long fingers of water clawing down the rock, with tiny pilgrims gazing up from below. He made his waterfall series in his early seventies.
310: A pool drawn as a perfect halo, and people picnicking at the edge of the abyss.
The falls are named after Amida Buddha, and Hokusai drew the pool at the top as a perfect circle, like a halo. Below, tiny figures picnic at the edge of the abyss.
311: Fuji from Kanaya on the Tōkaidō
No bridge, on purpose. Travelers crossed the river on porters' shoulders.
There was no bridge here, on purpose: the shogunate banned one over the Ōi River for defense. So travelers, luggage and all, crossed on the shoulders of porters.
312: A hundred ghost prints were planned. Only five are known.
A laughing demon woman bursts out of a moon-round frame, clutching a child. Hokusai planned a hundred ghost prints for this series in his seventies; only five are known.
313: On his deathbed he reportedly begged for five more years. The tiger dances anyway.
Painted in 1849, the year Hokusai died at 88. On his deathbed he reportedly asked heaven for five more years, so he could become a real painter. The tiger is dancing anyway.
314: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake
Two sets of rain lines at slightly different angles, so the downpour seems to move.
Look at the rain: two sets of fine lines cut at slightly different angles, so the downpour seems to shift as you watch. On the bridge, everyone runs bent under hats and mats.
315: Edo's fireworks began as a memorial for the dead of famine and disease.
Edo's summer fireworks over the Sumida began in 1733 as a memorial for victims of famine and disease. Here a single burst opens over the dark river, and the boats below look up.
316: You fly beside a diving eagle, more than a century before drones.
Hiroshige lifts you into the sky beside a diving eagle, talons spread, over an empty snowy plain. A landscape seen through the eyes of a hunter, more than a century before drones.
317: The giant red lantern hangs right over your head.
The giant red lantern of the Thunder Gate hangs over you, as if you were standing beneath it. Beyond, snow covers Sensō-ji, said to be Tokyo's oldest temple, founded in 628.
318: The whirlpools are real, and can reach about 20 meters across.
The whirlpools are real: tides squeezing through the narrow Naruto Strait spin up vortexes that can reach about 20 meters across. Hiroshige turned them into pure pattern.
319: Only greys, black and white, and still you can hear the silence of snow.
Almost no color, only greys, black and white, and still you can hear the silence that snow brings. Bent travelers trudge uphill as the night swallows the village.
320: Look at the umbrella: a little 1830s advertising, caught in the storm.
Rain, wind, bamboo and running men all lean the same way. Look at the umbrella: it carries the publisher's name and the series title, a little 1830s advertising caught in the storm.
321: Japanese prints almost never showed shadows. Here the full moon casts every one.
Look at the shadows. Japanese prints almost never showed them, but here a full moon throws every figure's shadow onto the street of Edo's kabuki theater district.
322: A pine branch that grew into a full circle, so people could see the moon through it.
The pine branch really grew into a full circle, and people came to see the moon through it. A typhoon destroyed it in the Meiji era; in 2012 a new one was trained into the same loop.
323: Three Beauties of the Present Day
Real celebrities of 1790s Edo, each with her own crest so fans could tell them apart.
They were real celebrities of 1790s Edo: a famous geisha and two teahouse girls crowds came just to look at. Utamaro gave each her own crest so fans could tell who was who.
324: Shaved eyebrows mean she is married. So who is she thinking about?
Her shaved eyebrows mark her as a married woman, and Utamaro's title for this print is 'Deeply Hidden Love'. He leaves us to guess who she is thinking about.
325: Takiyasha the Witch and the Skeleton Spectre
The legend summons an army of skeletons. He drew just one, enormous.
In the legend, the witch princess summons an army of skeletons. Kuniyoshi made it one: a single giant skeleton leaning through the ruined palace, with bones drawn almost like an anatomy book.
326: At First Glance He Looks Very Fierce, but He Is Really a Nice Person
Look closer: the whole face is made of people.
Look closer: the face is made of people. Kuniyoshi built it entirely out of human bodies, and the title says it all: at first glance he looks very fierce, but he is really a nice person.
327: Ōtani Oniji III as Yakko Edobei
About 140 prints in ten months, then he vanished. No one knows who he was.
Sharaku made about 140 prints in roughly ten months, then vanished. No one knows for sure who he was, and the clawed hands of this villain still look ready to strike.
328: Woman Admiring Plum Blossoms at Night
Full color had just arrived, and he spent it on a black night.
