In the 1760s Harunobu helped launch full-color woodblock printing in Edo. Here he spends it on darkness: a young woman with a lantern, searching for plum blossoms in a black night.
329: Fujiwara no Yasumasa Playing the Flute by Moonlight
A bandit creeps up to rob him, and the flute music stops him cold.
A bandit creeps up to rob the nobleman, but the flute music stops him cold. In the old tale he follows Yasumasa all the way home without ever daring to strike.
330: He went out to sketch the fire, and while he drew, his own house burned down.
On 26 January 1881 a fire swept through Tokyo's Ryōgoku district. Kiyochika went out to sketch the flames, and while he drew, his own house burned down.
331: Hokusai reportedly admitted that his daughter painted women better than he did.
Hokusai's daughter Ōi worked beside him for decades, and he reportedly admitted she painted women better than he did. This glowing night is one of the few works signed with her name.
332: A few splashes of ink, and out of them rise a mountain, a flag and a boat.
Sesshū, about 75, painted this as a parting gift for a pupil going home. A few splashes of ink, and out of them rise a mountain, a tavern flag and a small boat.
333: One jagged line slashes down the sky, and scholars still argue what it is.
A single jagged ink line slashes down through the sky and cliff, and scholars still argue what it is. Five centuries later it looks startlingly modern.
334: Copied, and then the copy was copied a century later.
Two gods dance on an empty field of gold: wind with his bag of gales, thunder with his drums. Decades later Kōrin copied it, and a century after that Hōitsu copied Kōrin's copy.
335: He left out the poet, the bridge and the story. Only the flowers remained.
It illustrates a scene from a 10th-century tale: a homesick poet sees irises by a bridge. Kōrin left out the poet, the bridge and the story. Only the flowers remained, on gold.
336: The dark river was once silver, darkened by age.
The dark river between the trees was once silver that has darkened with age. An old white plum on one side, a young red one on the other, painted by Kōrin late in his life.
337: A grocer's son who is said to have kept chickens just to study them.
Jakuchū, son of a Kyoto grocer, is said to have kept chickens in his yard to study them. This rooster belongs to a set of thirty scrolls he painted over about a decade and gave to a temple.
338: Mostly empty paper, and that is the point: pines dissolving in fog.
Most of it is empty paper, and that is the point: pines appear and dissolve in fog. Scholars think it may have started as a draft, and it became a National Treasure of Japan.
339: Warlords wanted trees as mighty as themselves.
Eitoku painted for warlords like Nobunaga and Hideyoshi, who wanted trees as mighty as themselves. He died in 1590 at 47, reportedly worn out by commissions.
340: Night Attack on the Sanjō Palace
A century after the fire, a painter turned that night into flames and stampeding horses.
In 1159 rebels set fire to the Sanjō Palace and seized a retired emperor. A century later a painter turned that night into flames and stampeding horses. The scroll is now in Boston.
341: The roofs are missing on purpose, so we can look inside.
The roofs are missing on purpose: 12th-century painters 'blew them off' so we could look into the rooms of The Tale of Genji, written by a woman and often called the first novel.
342: There were no tigers in Japan. He painted one anyway.
There were no tigers in Japan, so Rosetsu painted one he had never seen: a huge striped cat leaping across the sliding doors of a seaside temple in Kushimoto.
343: A landscape meant to make you want to live in it. One story says his paintings became dust rags.
Guo Xi wrote that a great landscape should make you want to walk in it and live there. Later his style fell from favor, and one story says palace servants used his paintings as dust rags.
344: Cranes over the palace, a good omen. Fifteen years later the capital fell.
In 1112 a flock of cranes circled the palace gate, and Emperor Huizong painted them as a good omen. Fifteen years later his capital fell, and he died a prisoner of the Jurchen.
345: Its owner wanted it burned with him. It was saved, split in two.
A collector loved this scroll so much he ordered it burned with him when he died. A nephew pulled it from the fire, split in two. The halves, in Taipei and Hangzhou, met again in 2011.
346: Still fighting its tether after 1,200 years, ringed by collectors' red seals.
This was the favorite horse of a Tang emperor, and it is still fighting its tether after 1,200 years. Each collector who owned the scroll added a seal, until the horse was ringed in red stamps.
347: Court Ladies Preparing Newly Woven Silk
Look under the stretched silk: a little girl ducks beneath it to peek.
The Tang original by Zhang Xuan is lost; we know it through this copy attributed to Emperor Huizong. Look under the stretched silk: a little girl ducks beneath it to peek.
348: He gave away a fortune to drift on a houseboat. His landscapes hold no one.
Ni Zan gave away his family fortune and spent some twenty years drifting on a houseboat. His landscapes hold an empty hut, a few trees, water, and not a single person.
349: Clouds Rising from the Green Sea
Twelve leaves, and every one is only water.
Twelve album leaves, and every one of them is only water: still, rippling, flooding, boiling. Eight centuries before abstract art, Ma Yuan made motion itself the subject.
350: He reportedly hung the top honor on the wall and walked away.
The story goes that Liang Kai received the golden belt, the court academy's top honor, hung it on the wall and walked away. His drunken immortal is a few wet strokes and a grin.
351: Born a prince, he became a monk. His fish still glare at us sideways.
Bada Shanren was born a Ming prince. When the dynasty fell he became a monk and reportedly stopped speaking. His fish still glare at us sideways, as if they know.
352: The world's oldest dated printed book, paid for 'on behalf of his two parents'.
The world's oldest dated printed book, made in 868. A man named Wang Jie paid for it 'on behalf of his two parents', and it waited sealed in a desert cave for some nine centuries.
353: Five-Colored Parakeet on a Blossoming Apricot Tree
A poor emperor, a brilliant artist, with a script of his own invention.
Huizong was a poor emperor and a brilliant artist. Beside the bird he wrote a poem in 'slender gold', a script he invented himself, with strokes as fine as wire.
354: An alchemist moves to the mountains to brew immortality. The painter died in prison.
The Daoist alchemist Ge Hong moves his family into the mountains to brew the elixir of immortality. The painter Wang Meng had no such luck: he died in a Ming prison in 1385.
355: A Solitary Temple Amid Clearing Peaks
A critic once counted two genuine works by him, and three hundred fakes.
Already in the 11th century, the critic Mi Fu said he had seen two genuine Li Chengs and three hundred fakes. This temple among the peaks, attributed to him, is one of the strongest candidates.
356: Autumn Colors on the Qiao and Hua Mountains
A homeland, painted for a friend who had never seen it.
Zhao Mengfu painted it in 1295 for his friend Zhou Mi, whose family came from these hills near Jinan but who had never seen them. A homeland, given as a gift.
357: A lamp-lit hall at dusk, and guests who have not yet come.
A silk fan glowing at dusk, a lamp-lit hall, someone waiting for guests who have not yet come. Ma Lin, son of Ma Yuan, was the fifth generation of a family of court painters.
358: Not an imagined Chinese mountain, but the real one near his home.
Instead of the Chinese mountains Korean painters usually imagined, Jeong Seon painted the real peak near his Seoul home, at 75, mist still rising after rain. It is a National Treasure of Korea.
359: 12,000 peaks squeezed into one view, like a crown of stone.
Jeong Seon squeezed the traditional '12,000 peaks' of Mount Geumgang into one bristling view, like a crown of stone. He walked these mountains himself, and it shows.
360: Check the man at lower right: his hands appear to be swapped.
A ring of spectators watches two wrestlers, and you can almost tell who is about to fall. Check the man at the lower right: his left and right hands appear to be swapped.
361: Only in winter do you see that the pine stays green.
Exiled to Jeju island, Kim Jeong-hui painted this for a former student who kept sending him books from China. The title echoes Confucius: only in winter do you see the pine stays green.
362: The ears and body faded away. The gaze survived.
No ears, no body, just an intense face and a beard that seems to burn. Scientific study found the ears and body were drawn once and faded away; the gaze survived.
363: Women wash their hair in a stream, and two young monks peek from the rocks.
It is the Dano festival: women wash their hair in a stream and swing high on a rope, while two young monks peek from behind the rocks. Shin Yun-bok loved what polite art left out.
364: The king sat in front of it, and completed the cosmos.
This screen stood behind the throne of Joseon kings: sun, moon, five peaks, waterfalls. The king sat at its center, completing the cosmos. One appears on Korea's 10,000 won note.
365: Just skin over bones, the emperor wrote. He died the next day.
Emperor Jahangir wrote that his courtier, wasted by opium and wine, was just skin over bones, and ordered painters to record him. Inayat Khan died the next day.
366: These are European squirrels, which do not live in India.
Look closely: these are European red squirrels, which do not live in India. Abu'l Hasan probably studied them from imported prints, then added a hunter climbing the trunk.
367: Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings
An emperor turns away from kings, and the painter hides himself in the corner.
Jahangir turns away from kings, including an Ottoman sultan and England's James I, to hand a book to a Sufi sage. The painter Bichitr put himself in the corner, holding a picture.
368: About 1,400 giant paintings for a king who could not read.
Emperor Akbar ordered about 1,400 giant paintings for the adventures of the hero Hamza, a project of some fifteen years. Only around 200 survive. Akbar, who could not read, loved stories read aloud.
369: The bridge of boats sank under them, and both emperor and elephant survived.
At nineteen Akbar rode a raging elephant named Hawa'i in pursuit of another, onto a bridge of boats over the Yamuna. The boats sank under them, and both emperor and elephant survived.
370: That halo came from European Christian pictures, borrowed for a Mughal king.
Shah Jahan, the emperor who built the Taj Mahal, rides with a golden halo around his head. Mughal painters borrowed the halo from European Christian pictures and gave it to their own kings.
371: Studied so closely that naturalists still admire it four centuries later.
Emperor Jahangir called Mansur 'Wonder of the Age' for paintings like this: a chameleon gripping a branch, studied so closely that naturalists still admire it four centuries later.
372: Radha and Krishna in the Boat of Love
Those long lotus eyes may belong to a real singer, loved by a raja.
Kishangarh painters gave Radha long lotus eyes and a sharp profile, a look said to be modeled on Bani Thani, the singer loved by Raja Savant Singh. Here she floats with Krishna on the lake.
373: Maharana Jagat Singh II in Procession
A king who had his painters record his days the way we use phone cameras.
Maharana Jagat Singh II of Mewar had his painters record his days much as we use phone cameras: processions, hunts, festivals and parties. Here he rides out among his court.
374: A morning melody, painted as a woman getting ready for her lover.
Ragamala paintings turn music into pictures: each raga, with its mood and hour, gets its own scene. Vilaval Ragini, a morning melody, appears as a woman adorning herself for her lover.
375: Not a color photograph: a black-and-white negative, colored stone by stone.

This is not a color photograph. It is a photochrom: a black-and-white negative printed in color from a series of lithographic stones, one per tone. The subject: the tomb Shah Jahan built for his wife.
376: The first king, among people in leopard skins. The book was later sold page by page.
Gayumars, the first king in Persian legend, sits on a mountain where people wore leopard skins and lived among the animals. The book it comes from was later broken up and sold page by page.
377: No kings, no heroes, just two lovers close enough to share a breath.
Reza Abbasi turned from kings and heroes to ordinary lovers, close enough to share a breath. He signed and dated this one in 1630, only a few years before his death.
378: Seven rooms, every door locked, and as he flees, each lock springs open.
Zulaikha has led Yusuf through seven rooms and locked every door behind them. Behzad paints the moment he flees and, as the poem tells it, each lock springs open.
379: Stay up with a whole city after dark: some sleep, some work, some keep watch.
Stay up with a whole Persian city after dark: some sleep, some work, some keep watch. Mir Sayyid Ali later moved to India and helped found Mughal painting.
380: The Simurgh Arrives at the Birth of Rustam
A giant bird explains a caesarean, then heals the wound with a feather.
In the Shahnameh, the giant bird Simurgh explains how to deliver baby Rustam by cutting open his mother's side, then heals her wound with a feather. A caesarean, told a thousand years ago.
381: Bahram Gur in the White Pavilion
Seven pavilions, seven colors, seven princesses with seven stories. Friday was white.
King Bahram built seven domed pavilions, each a different color, and spent each day of the week with a different princess, hearing her story. Friday belonged to the white one.
382: Millions of knots, and the maker's name woven into one end.
Millions of hand-tied knots, and a signature woven into one end: Maqsud of Kashan, in the year 946 of the Hijra, about 1540. William Morris urged London's museum to buy it.
383: Ursa Major, Book of Fixed Stars
The first known written mention of the Andromeda galaxy: a 'little cloud'.
Al-Sufi's star catalogue of 964 contains the first known written mention of the Andromeda galaxy, which he called a 'little cloud'. This copy, from about 1009, is one of the oldest of its kind.
384: This is a signature: a sultan's name, grown into a garden.
This is a signature. The monogram spells 'Suleiman Shah, son of Selim Shah Khan, ever victorious', and court artists filled its loops with spiraling flowers until a name became a garden.
385: An old man patiently training tortoises. Often read as a joke about slow reform.
Osman Hamdi painted himself as an old man trying to train tortoises, often read as a joke on slow Ottoman reform. In 2004 it became the most expensive Turkish painting sold to date.
386: Every mosque and tower of Istanbul, and not a single person.
Matrakçı Nasuh was a mathematician, historian and champion swordsman who invented a martial game. He drew Istanbul from above, every mosque and tower, and not a single person.
387: What Ottoman art rarely showed: a woman alone, off duty, simply asleep.
Istanbul's 'Tulip Era', when the elite paid fortunes for rare bulbs, also produced Levni. He painted what Ottoman art rarely showed: a woman alone, off duty, simply asleep.
388: A raised, brilliant red that faded away when the workshops did.
Iznik potters perfected a raised, brilliant red, made from an iron-rich clay slip, in the mid-1500s. As the workshops declined in the next century, that red faded with them.
389: Gold letters on indigo parchment, and no one knows exactly who made it.
Gold letters on parchment dyed deep indigo, made over a thousand years ago, probably in North Africa. Its leaves are scattered across museums, and no one knows exactly who made it.
390: A whole room moved from Damascus to New York. Its poems still welcome guests.
This whole winter reception room, dated 1707, was taken from a house in Damascus and rebuilt in New York. Poems painted on its panels still welcome guests, now museum visitors.
391: Twelve marble lions, 124 columns, built by Spain's last Muslim kingdom.
Twelve marble lions hold up the fountain, and 124 slender columns ring the court. When it was built in the 1300s, Granada was the last Muslim kingdom in Spain.
392: The Rock in the Dome of the Rock
Under the golden dome, bare bedrock, sacred to two faiths.
Under the golden dome lies bare bedrock. Jews revere it as the Foundation Stone of the Temple Mount, Muslims as the place of Muhammad's Night Journey; the shrine was finished around 691.
393: Not one white brushstroke: the snow is made of nothing at all.
Look for the snow and you will not find a single white brushstroke. Ōkyo left the paper bare and painted only around it, so the snow is made of nothing at all.
394: A temple you could roll up and carry.
Thangkas were painted on cloth to be rolled up and carried, a portable temple for monks on the move. Guhyasamaja, 'the secret assembly', has three faces and six arms, each holding a symbol.
395: She wore the torments of hell on her robe, and became a Zen monk's disciple.
Legend says the courtesan called Hell wore a robe painted with the torments of the underworld, and she became a disciple of the Zen monk Ikkyū. Kyōsai painted her again and again.
396: An old plum twists across four doors, in pain and in bloom.
The old plum twists across four sliding doors like a living thing in pain and in bloom. Kanō Sansetsu painted it in 1646 for a temple in Kyoto; today it lives in New York.
397: A demon whose blood can cure a king's blindness, at the end of seven trials.
At the end of seven trials, Rustam enters a cave to fight the White Div, a demon whose blood can cure his king's blindness. He wins, and tears out its liver.
398: Poem Written in a Boat on the Wu River
He called a strange rock 'elder brother'. Here his brush races like a boat in the wind.
Mi Fu was famous for bowing to an oddly shaped rock and calling it 'elder brother'. Here his brush lurches and races like the boat in his poem, caught by wind on the Wu River.
399: Mehmed the Conqueror Smelling a Rose
The conqueror of Constantinople chose to be shown smelling a rose.
The sultan who conquered Constantinople in 1453 chose to be shown smelling a rose. He had invited the Venetian painter Gentile Bellini to his court, and Italian realism crept in.
400: Thousands of hairs, painted one by one. The pine may be his teacher's.
Every hair of this tiger was painted one by one, thousands of fine strokes. Tradition credits the tiger to Kim Hong-do and the pine above it to his teacher Kang Se-hwang.
401: Wanderer Above the Sea of Fog
We never see his face, so you can stand where he stands.
We never see his face. Friedrich turned him away so that you would stand where he stands, and look at the fog as if it were your own future.
402: People paid admission to see one painting, and brought opera glasses for the leaves.
In 1859 people paid admission to see this one painting. They brought opera glasses to study the leaves, and more than 12,000 came in three weeks.
403: The deadliest wave has passed, and the sky takes the color of hope.
Sailors believed the ninth wave is the deadliest. Aivazovsky painted the survivors just after it, clinging to a mast, and gave the sky the color of hope.
404: A ghost of Trafalgar, towed to its death by a small smoking tug.
A ghostly warship that fought at Trafalgar is towed to the breakers by a small, smoking steam tug. Turner called it his 'darling' and refused to sell it.
405: Painted in Rome, of a valley that does not quite exist.
Bierstadt painted it in a studio in Rome, stitching sketches into a valley that does not quite exist. The paradise that drew Europe's eyes west was partly an invention.
406: Ships once sailed this sea. He painted them out.
The writer Heinrich von Kleist said that looking at it felt as if your eyelids had been cut away. Friedrich had first painted ships on that sea, then erased them.
407: Look right of the ice: a crushed ship is sinking beneath the slabs.
Look to the right of the ice tomb: the stern of a crushed ship is sinking beneath the slabs. Friedrich could not sell it, and it stayed in his studio until he died.
408: Painted the year he married, after a honeymoon on these cliffs.
Friedrich painted it the year he married, after a honeymoon on Rügen. The three figures are often read as the painter, his young wife Caroline and his brother.
409: Two men and a long wait. Beckett reportedly called it the source of Godot.
Two men, a bare tree, and a long wait for something. Samuel Beckett, seeing this painting, reportedly said it was the source of Waiting for Godot.
410: Look low in the mist: monks are carrying a coffin.
Look low, in the mist: monks carry a coffin toward an open grave. The 15-year-old crown prince of Prussia urged his father to buy this and The Monk by the Sea.
411: Snow Storm: Hannibal and his Army Crossing the Alps
A Yorkshire storm on the back of a letter. 'In two years, you'll call it Hannibal.'
Turner watched a storm over the Yorkshire hills and sketched it on the back of a letter. 'In two years,' he told a friend, 'you will see this again, and call it Hannibal.'
412: Snow Storm: Steam-Boat off a Harbour's Mouth
He claimed he was tied to a mast for four hours. A critic saw only soapsuds.
Turner claimed he had himself tied to a mast for four hours to watch this storm. A critic called the result 'soapsuds and whitewash'; Turner wished he had been in it.
413: Look at the water: shackled legs, sinking among the fish.
Look at the water: shackled legs sinking among the fish. Turner is thought to have had in mind the Zong, whose crew threw more than 130 enslaved Africans overboard for the insurance.
414: Find the hare running ahead of the train, about to lose.
Find the hare. Just ahead of the train, a tiny hare runs along the tracks, the fastest creature in the fields about to be overtaken by a machine.
415: Never exhibited, left unfinished, and a century later it looked like the future.
Turner never exhibited it. It was found among the unfinished canvases he left to the nation, and a century later it looked like the future: a castle dissolving into light.
416: No buyer in London. A gold medal in Paris.
The cottage on the left still stands in Suffolk. The painting found no buyer in London, but in Paris it won a gold medal, and French painters began to look at the sky differently.
417: Months after his wife died: 'The face of the world is totally changed to me.'
Constable painted it months after his wife Maria died, leaving him with seven children. 'The face of the world is totally changed to me,' he wrote. The ruin stands alone.
418: The commission that finally let him marry, after seven years of waiting.
This commission helped Constable finally afford to marry Maria Bicknell, after a seven-year courtship her family opposed. He even widened the canvas to fit in everything the owner wanted.
419: On the back he noted the hour and the wind, like a weatherman.
On the back of his cloud studies Constable noted the date, the hour and the wind, like a weatherman. He spent two summers on Hampstead Heath doing almost nothing but 'skying'.
420: Before the painting, a full-size sketch, just as huge, to work out every cloud.
The last of Constable's 'six-footers', huge canvases of the river Stour where he grew up. Before painting it he made a full-size sketch, just as big, to work out every cloud.
421: Bent by the wind but still rooted. A whole country saw itself in it.
A lone birch on a Norwegian mountainside, bent by the wind but still rooted. Norwegians came to see in it their own country: battered by weather, refusing to fall.
422: Painted far from home, from sketches and memory, by Norway's father of landscape.
Dahl lived in Dresden, in the same house as Caspar David Friedrich, and painted his native Norway from sketches and memory. Norway calls him the father of its landscape painting.
423: On the far hill, logging scars seem to spell a word in Hebrew: נח.
Look at the far hill: logging scars seem to spell the Hebrew נח, Noah, and upside down שדי, Shaddai. Cole also painted himself in, tiny, at his easel on the rocks.
424: A giant stone goblet with a lake and sailboats on its rim. Nobody knows why.
A giant stone goblet stands in an ordinary valley, and on its rim are a lake with sailboats, trees and tiny buildings. No one has ever settled what Cole meant by it.
425: The empire is gone. Only the boulder on the cliff never changed.
The last of five paintings: the mighty city of the earlier canvases is gone, and nature has taken it back. Only the boulder on the cliff, there in all five, has not changed.
426: No rock, no railing, nothing between you and the edge.
Church left out the foreground: no rock, no railing, nothing between you and the edge. Over two meters wide, it puts you right at the lip of the falls.
427: A blood-red sky as a nation slid toward civil war, and not one person in it.
Painted in 1860, as America slid toward civil war. Many viewers have read that blood-red sky as a premonition, and Church left no people in it at all.
428: About 78 years, almost forgotten, in a boys' home in Manchester.
For about 78 years it hung, almost forgotten, in a house in Manchester that became a boys' home. Rediscovered in 1979, it sold for $2.5 million, a record for an American painting.
429: The sun fights through volcanic ash like a red eye.
Church followed the explorer Alexander von Humboldt to Ecuador. Here the sun fights through volcanic ash like a red eye, painted in 1862 while America tore itself apart.
430: He never saw this place. His friend's frozen ship is right there under the lights.
Church never saw this place. He painted it from the sketches of his friend, the Arctic explorer Isaac Hayes, whose schooner sits frozen in the ice beneath the lights.
431: A peak named for a fallen expedition leader, and a record price.
Bierstadt named the peak after Frederick Lander, the expedition leader killed in the Civil War. In 1865 it sold for $25,000, then the highest price paid for an American painting.
432: A Storm in the Rocky Mountains, Mt. Rosalie
He named the mountain after his friend's wife. Later, she married him.
He named the mountain after Rosalie, wife of his travel companion, the writer Fitz Hugh Ludlow. A few years later she divorced Ludlow and married Bierstadt.
433: Almost two and a half meters of valley, glowing like a cathedral.
Bierstadt's first large Yosemite canvas, almost two and a half meters wide, painted from sketches made two years earlier. El Capitan guards the right, and the valley glows like a cathedral.
434: The Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone
Congress bought it, and the painter started signing as 'Yellowstone'.
Congress bought it for $10,000 in 1872, the year Yellowstone became the world's first national park. Moran began signing himself 'Thomas Yellowstone Moran'.
435: Bought by Congress to hang beside his Yellowstone in the Capitol.
In 1873 Moran joined John Wesley Powell's survey to the Grand Canyon. Congress bought this canvas too, for another $10,000, to hang beside his Yellowstone in the Capitol.
436: Trappers spoke of a giant cross of snow. A photograph proved it real.
For years trappers told of a giant cross of snow somewhere in the Rockies. Once a photograph proved it real, Moran climbed to see it and painted the cross as a pilgrimage.
437: Calm so smooth that hardly a brushstroke shows.
Kensett painted calm so smooth that hardly a brushstroke shows. Three years later he died, his health broken, it is said, after he plunged into cold water to save a drowning woman.
438: A Gorge in the Mountains (Kauterskill Clove)
The year he went to war, he painted a valley holding its breath.
Gifford painted this golden haze in 1862, the same year he went off as a Union soldier with New York's Seventh Regiment. In a year of war, he gave America a valley holding its breath.
439: Found in an antiques shop, and it made a forgotten painter famous again.
Heade was nearly forgotten after his death. In 1943 a New York dealer found this canvas in an antiques shop, and its black water and bright sails made him famous again.
440: He lost the use of his legs as a toddler, and still traveled the coast to paint this.
As a toddler, Lane lost the use of his legs, probably after eating a poisonous plant. He still traveled the Maine coast to paint this stillness, where even the water seems to hold its breath.
441: A memorial: the painter who just died, on the ledge with his poet friend.
A memorial: the painter Thomas Cole, who had just died, stands on the ledge with his friend the poet William Cullen Bryant. In 2005 the New York Public Library sold it for a reported $35 million.
442: The English doubted trees could be this red, so he had real leaves shipped over.
When it was shown in London, the English doubted any trees could be this red. Cropsey had real autumn leaves sent from America and displayed them beside the painting.
443: He did not paint the bears. Someone erased the signature of the man who did.
Shishkin did not paint the bears: his friend Konstantin Savitsky did. The collector Tretyakov erased Savitsky's signature, and today every Russian knows the scene from a candy wrapper.
444: On a sketch for it, Shishkin wrote: 'Expanse, space, land. Rye. God's grace. Russian wealth.' The son of a merchant from Yelabuga, he painted his homeland's fields like a hymn.
445: A lone pine on a northern cliff, dreaming of a palm in a faraway desert.
Shishkin painted it for Lermontov's poem, itself a version of Heine: a lone pine on a northern cliff, dreaming of a palm tree in a faraway desert.
446: Pines straight enough for ship masts. His last great canvas.
These pines, tall and straight enough for ship masts, grew near Yelabuga, Shishkin's hometown. It was his last great canvas: he finished it early in 1898 and died that March.
447: 'I am all in it, with my whole psyche.'
Levitan wrote to Tretyakov that he was 'all in it, with my whole psyche'. A tiny wooden church stands against a vast river and a gathering storm, and the graves are almost lost in the grass.
448: No one here, a door left open, and you can almost hear the first drip of spring.
There is no one in it: just a horse waiting by a sunlit porch, blue shadows on the snow, a door left open. You can almost hear the first drip of spring.
449: His best friend was Chekhov, until Chekhov wrote a story mocking him.
Levitan's closest friend was Anton Chekhov, until Chekhov wrote a story mocking a painter much like him. They stopped speaking for years, then made up.
450: An empty country road, where convicts once walked in chains to Siberia.
This empty country road was the Vladimirka, where convicts walked in chains to Siberia. Levitan, a Jew just expelled from Moscow himself, painted no people, only the road.
451: The moonlight glowed so strongly that people looked behind it for a lamp.
Kuindzhi showed it alone, in a darkened room lit only on the canvas. The moonlight glowed so strongly that people looked behind the painting for a hidden lamp.
452: An orphan who herded geese to survive, painting sunlight you could touch.
Kuindzhi, the son of a poor Greek shoemaker, was orphaned at about six and herded geese to survive. Here sunlight falls on the grass like something you could touch.
453: At the height of his fame he stopped showing, and painted in private for thirty years.
At the height of his fame Kuindzhi stopped showing his work and kept painting in private for nearly thirty years. This sunset belongs to that long silence.
454: He never painted the sea outdoors. All of it came from memory.
Aivazovsky never painted the sea outdoors. He worked from memory in his studio, sometimes finishing a canvas in a day, and left some 6,000 paintings.
455: No ship, no shore, no survivors: only water and light, painted at 81.
No ship, no shore, no survivors: only water and light. Aivazovsky painted it at 81, two years before he died, and it hangs in the gallery he gave his hometown, Feodosia.
456: It made him famous. Reportedly, only two people came to his funeral.
This plain spring scene made Savrasov famous. He later sank into drink and poverty, and reportedly only two people came to his funeral: a school doorman and Pavel Tretyakov.
457: A rain-soaked Russian meadow, painted from memory in sunny Crimea, by a dying man.
Fyodor Vasilyev painted this rain-soaked Russian meadow in sunny Crimea, from memory, while dying of tuberculosis. He was 23 when he died, a year later.
458: A king who had seen it as a young exile asked for this view decades later.
As a young exile, the future French king Louis-Philippe traveled all the way to the North Cape. Decades later he asked Peder Balke to paint the place for him.
459: He saw the Arctic once and painted it for the rest of his life.
Balke was a poor farmhand's son who saw Arctic Norway once and painted it for the rest of his life. Forgotten after his death, his bare, foggy peaks now look startlingly modern.
460: The ice reached right down into the valley. Today you could not paint this view.
When Fearnley painted it in 1838, the glacier's ice reached right down into the valley. It has since retreated so far that you could not paint this view today.
461: Famous for Alpine storms, here he painted the calm instead.
Calame made his name with Alpine storms, one of them hailed in Geneva as a 'national painting'. At Lake Thun he painted the calm instead: still water, and the snowy Bernese peaks beyond.
462: Each level seen from its own height, so your eye climbs the whole mountain.
Koch stacked the Alps vertically, each level seen from its own height: valley, forest, falls, glacier. Your eye climbs the whole mountain in one look.
463: Over thirty years of coming back, summer and winter, to the same islands.
Anna Boberg first came to the Lofoten Islands in 1901 and kept returning, summer and winter, for over thirty years. This study comes from the last year of that long love affair.
464: Others painted pretty pines. He painted rot, and died the same year, at 24.
Where others painted pretty pines, August Cappelen painted rot: fallen trunks, dead branches, black water. He died that same year, aged 24.
465: Dozens of seascapes in one summer, many of them the very same wave.
In one summer at Étretat Courbet painted dozens of seascapes, many of them the same breaking wave. Two years later he was jailed for helping topple the Vendôme Column.
466: The Cliff at Étretat after the Storm
'Show me an angel and I will paint one.'
The storm has passed, the boats are pulled up, and the stone arch stands in washed air. 'Show me an angel and I will paint one,' Courbet said; he painted only what he saw.
467: A river bursts out of a dark cave, as if the earth itself were opening.
A river bursts out of a dark cave near Courbet's hometown of Ornans. He painted this cave mouth again and again, a place where the earth itself seems to open.
468: The painter of exhausted peasants gave the land a rainbow.
Millet, the painter of exhausted peasants, gave the land a moment of grace: a rainbow after the storm over a blossoming orchard. It was among his last works.
469: Painters fought loggers for these oaks, and helped create an early nature reserve.
Rousseau and his Barbizon friends fought to save these oaks from loggers. In 1861 part of the forest was protected by imperial decree, one of the first nature reserves anywhere.
470: She needed a police permit to wear trousers, and gave oxen the dignity of kings.
To study animals in markets and slaughterhouses, Rosa Bonheur needed a police permit to wear trousers. Here she gave the oxen the dignity painters usually saved for kings.
471: Not a place, but the memory of one, painted in a studio.
The title means 'Memory of Mortefontaine'. Corot painted it in his studio from memories of a place, and Emperor Napoleon III bought it at the Salon of 1864.
472: The tombs are real and still in use. The storm and the rainbow are not.
The tombs are real: they stand in Beth Haim, the Portuguese Jewish cemetery at Ouderkerk near Amsterdam, still in use. Ruisdael added the ruin, the storm and the rainbow.
473: The Windmill at Wijk bij Duurstede
In a country without mountains, he made the sky the landscape.
Ruisdael set the horizon so low that a plain Dutch windmill towers like a cathedral against the clouds. In a country without mountains, he made the sky the landscape.
474: View of Haarlem with Bleaching Fields
Those white strips are linen bleaching in the sun, and they made a city rich.
Most of it is sky. Below, the white strips are linen laid out in the sun to bleach, a trade that helped make Haarlem rich.
475: By then he had a day job gauging wine. This became his masterpiece.
By the time he painted it, Hobbema had a steady job as a wine gauger for Amsterdam and painted only now and then. This late canvas became his masterpiece.
476: Painted by a man who could not hear or speak, full of people talking and flirting.
Avercamp was deaf and mute, known in his town as 'the mute of Kampen'. He spent his life painting frozen Holland in the Little Ice Age, packed with people talking, falling and flirting.
477: No saint, no story, no people. Around 1520, that was almost unheard of.
No saint, no story, no people. Around 1520 that was almost unheard of, and Altdorfer's small panel is one of the very first pure landscapes in Western painting.
478: Look at the cliff on the left: some see a face hidden in the rock.
Dürer painted this watercolor on his way home from Italy, simply because the place moved him. Look at the cliff on the left: some see a face hidden in the rock.
479: A whole day's hunt, and they come home with a single fox.
The hunters come home with almost nothing, a single fox. Andrei Tarkovsky loved this painting so much that his camera lingers over it in Solaris.
480: Lunch at noon, and one man sleeps sprawled under a pear tree.
One of six paintings of the seasons made for an Antwerp banker's house; five survive. At noon the harvesters eat, and one man sleeps sprawled under a pear tree.
481: Ships are wrecked in the storm, and in the village someone eats a waffle.
A storm wrecks ships in the estuary, yet in the village it is Carnival: a man eats a waffle and a child wears a paper crown. Life goes on at the edge of disaster.
482: Landscape with the Fall of Icarus
Find Icarus: two legs splashing in the sea. The ploughman never looks up.
Find Icarus: just two legs splashing in the sea, bottom right. The ploughman never looks up. Experts now think this is an early copy of a lost Bruegel.
483: Will he survive the sharks? Homer's sarcastic answer: happily ever after.
When anxious viewers asked whether the sailor would survive the sharks, Homer replied, with sarcasm, that he would be rescued and live happily ever after.
484: The hunt is reversed: starving crows close in on the fox.
The hunt is reversed: starving crows close in on a fox floundering in deep snow. It was the first Homer painting bought by a museum.
485: Two men once stood on these rocks. He painted them out and left only the sea.
Homer first painted two men in oilskins on these rocks. Years later he painted them out, leaving only the sea crashing into the coast of Maine.
486: After the storm, two sailors read the sun to learn where on Earth they are.
Eight bells marks noon at sea. After the storm, two sailors take a reading of the sun to find out where on Earth they are.
487: He saw the volcano stir once, and painted it more than thirty times.
Wright saw Vesuvius stir during one visit to Naples in 1774, and kept painting it for the rest of his life, more than thirty times, mostly back home in Derby.
488: The British Channel Seen from the Dorsetshire Cliffs
An astronomer painted the sea the way he studied the sky: as light, measured.
Brett was an astronomer as well as a painter, a fellow of the Royal Astronomical Society. He painted the sea the way he studied the sky: as light, measured.
489: One painted the fjord, the other the wedding. A country saw its own portrait.
Two painters made it together: Hans Gude painted the fjord and mountains, Adolph Tidemand the wedding party in the boats. Norway took it as a portrait of itself.
490: 'A picture for dreaming.' Rachmaninoff saw only a print and wrote music to it.
Böcklin never explained it; he called it 'a picture for dreaming'. Rachmaninoff saw only a black-and-white print and composed a symphonic poem after it.
491: Rejected for being so bright it might burn a hole in the wall.
Vienna's jury first rejected it as too bright, joking it would burn a hole in the wall. In Paris a year later, Tina Blau won an honourable mention at the Salon.
492: Yosemite Valley from the Best General View
Hauled into the valley by mule, these photographs helped protect it.
Watkins hauled a camera for huge glass plates into Yosemite by mule. His photographs helped persuade Congress, and in 1864 Lincoln signed a law protecting the valley.
493: Mountain of the Holy Cross, Colorado
A rumored cross of snow, until he hauled his camera up the facing peak.
For years the cross of snow was a rumor. In 1873 Jackson hauled his heavy camera up a facing peak and photographed it, the proof that the mountain was real.
494: The tiny man on the terraces is a painter, and together they made a national park.
The man on the terraces is the painter Thomas Moran. His paintings and Jackson's photographs from this 1871 expedition reached Congress, and in 1872 Yellowstone became the first national park.
495: The wagon is his darkroom, the footprints are his. Before this, he photographed Gettysburg.
The wagon is O'Sullivan's own darkroom, and the footprints are his. A few years earlier, the same man had photographed the dead at Gettysburg.
496: Ancient Ruins in the Cañon de Chelly
Houses under the cliff, about 900 years old, developed on glass in the desert.
The houses tucked under the cliff, now called White House, were built by Ancestral Puebloans about 900 years ago. O'Sullivan had to develop each glass plate on the spot, in the desert.
497: The whole north face slid away, and the volcano exploded sideways.
On the morning of 18 May 1980 the whole north face of the mountain slid away and the volcano exploded sideways. It lost about 400 meters of height; 57 people died.
498: A fountain of lava taller than the Empire State Building.
In the 1959 eruption of Kīlauea Iki in Hawaii, the lava fountain at one point reached about 580 meters, taller than the Empire State Building and the highest ever measured there.
499: The rainbow is alive, and a microbe from Yellowstone's springs is in every PCR test.
The rainbow rings are living microbes. A bacterium found in Yellowstone's hot springs made PCR possible, the technique behind DNA tests and the COVID tests in our noses.
500: The first tornado followed by scientists from birth to death.
This 1973 Oklahoma tornado was the first ever documented from birth to death by scientists, with Doppler radar and chase teams on the ground. Modern tornado warnings began here.
501: In Proust, a dying writer comes for one last look at a patch of yellow wall.
In Proust's novel, a dying writer drags himself to see this painting for one last look at a 'little patch of yellow wall', and dies in front of it.
502: A lamppost splits the city in two, and no one looks at anyone.
Look at the lamppost: it splits the painting in two, and no one on either side is looking at anyone. Caillebotte painted the loneliness of the modern city before it had a name.
503: A starry night painted on the spot, without a touch of black.
His first starry sky, painted on the spot, at night, without a touch of black. 'The night is still more richly coloured than the day,' he wrote to his sister.
504: An eye infection kept him indoors, so he painted the night from a hotel window.
Kept indoors by an eye infection, Pissarro painted the boulevard from a hotel window. It is the only night scene in the series, and the street glows like wet paint.
505: The back side of the postcard: dust, laundry, a mother running to a fallen child.
Canaletto usually sold tourists the postcard Venice. Here he painted the back side: dust, laundry, and a mother running to a fallen child. Many call it his finest work.
506: For centuries no one knew which street this was. Tax records on canal dues gave it away.
For centuries no one knew which Delft street this was. In 2015 a historian found it in old tax records of canal dues: Vlamingstraat 40 and 42, where houses still stand.
507: Made perhaps for a peep box. Two years later a gunpowder blast killed him.
The strange stretched perspective suggests it was made for a peep box. Two years later Fabritius, Rembrandt's most gifted pupil, died at 32 when Delft's gunpowder store exploded.
508: The Golden Bend in the Herengracht
Look at the gaps: the city's most expensive street, still waiting for buyers.
Amsterdam's most expensive street, painted while it was still half empty. Look at the gaps between the mansions: those lots were waiting for buyers who had not yet arrived.
509: The Market Place and the Grote Kerk at Haarlem
Go to Haarlem today and you can stand exactly where he stood.
Berckheyde painted this square again and again, the way a photographer returns to one corner. Visit Haarlem today and you can stand exactly where he stood; the church has hardly changed.
510: A perfect city, and not a single person in it.
A perfect Renaissance city, and not a single person in it. No one knows who painted it, and the empty piazza feels less like a dream than like the moment after everyone left.
511: Effects of Good Government in the City
Painted where the rulers met, so they would see good government every day.
It was painted on the wall of the room where Siena's rulers met, so they would see daily what good government looks like: shops open, builders on the roofs, dancers in the street.
512: Crumbling at the bottom while they are still building at the top.
Bruegel had seen the Colosseum in Rome, and his Babel is built like it: arches on arches. The tower is already crumbling at the bottom while workers still build at the top.
513: St Mark's as Venetians saw it in 1496. All but one of those mosaics are gone.
This is a precious record of St Mark's façade as Venetians saw it in 1496. Of the golden mosaics over its doors, all but one were later replaced.
514: Miracle of the Relic of the Cross at the Ponte di Rialto
That wooden drawbridge is the old Rialto, before it collapsed.
That wooden drawbridge is the old Rialto. It collapsed in 1524, and the stone bridge every tourist photographs was not finished until 1591.
515: Dresden from the Right Bank of the Elbe Below the Augustus Bridge
When the city burned, his precise views became its memory.
Bellotto was Canaletto's nephew and signed with his uncle's name. When Dresden burned in 1945, his precise views became precious records of the city that was lost.
516: Krakowskie Przedmiescie with the Church of the Holy Cross, Warsaw
Warsaw was razed, and architects rebuilt it using these paintings.
When the Nazis razed Warsaw in 1944, Bellotto's paintings survived. After the war architects used them to rebuild the old city, sometimes down to the details of a façade.
517: The Ruins of the Old Kreuzkirche, Dresden
He once painted this city at its most beautiful. Now he paints its ruins.
Prussian cannon wrecked this church in 1760. Bellotto painted the shell as workers pulled it down, the same artist who once painted Dresden at its most beautiful.
518: Vienna Viewed from the Belvedere Palace
A whole capital spread like a carpet on a long golden afternoon.
Empress Maria Theresa hired Bellotto to paint Vienna, and he gave her this: a whole capital spread like a carpet, seen from the palace garden on a long golden afternoon.
519: Imaginary View of the Grande Galerie of the Louvre in Ruins
The Louvre's own curator painted it in ruins.
The Louvre's own curator painted it in ruins. Hubert Robert had just survived prison during the Terror, and he showed this next to a picture of the same gallery restored.
520: The Bastille in the First Days of Its Demolition
A fortress that held prisoners for centuries, half shadow and half smoke.
Robert painted the Bastille while it was being torn down in July 1789. The fortress that held prisoners for centuries is shown already half shadow, half smoke.
521: Demolition of the Houses on the Pont Notre-Dame
Bridges once carried whole streets. Here the river reappears.
Paris bridges once carried whole streets of houses. In 1786 the city tore them down for light and air, and Robert was there to paint the moment the river reappeared.
522: A dome already 1,600 years old, and the hole at its top has no glass.
The dome over these tourists was already 1,600 years old when Panini painted them. It is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome on earth, and the hole at its top has no glass.
523: A gallery that never existed, hung with all of ancient Rome.
A gallery that never existed, hung with all of ancient Rome. The patron, a French count who later became a powerful minister, sits in the middle of his imaginary collection.
524: Staircases that lead nowhere, and ten years later he made them darker.
Staircases that lead nowhere, bridges into darkness. Piranesi first printed these prisons in 1750, then reworked the plates a decade later and made them much darker.
525: View of the Colosseum (Vedute di Roma)
Some travelers who reached Rome found the real ruins smaller than these.
These prints were souvenirs for rich travellers on the Grand Tour. Some who reached Rome afterwards found the real ruins smaller than Piranesi's.
526: The Bucintoro at the Molo on Ascension Day
Once a year, this golden barge carried the Doge out to marry Venice to the sea.

Once a year the Doge sailed out in this golden barge and threw a ring into the sea, marrying Venice to the water. After Napoleon ended the Republic in 1797, French troops burned the barge to strip its gold.
527: The Entrance to the Grand Canal, Venice
The great white church is a thank-you note for surviving a plague.
The great white church was a thank-you note. Venice built Santa Maria della Salute after a plague killed about a third of its people in 1630 and 1631.
528: London: The Thames from Somerset House Terrace towards the City
His London looked so unlike his Venice that a rumor said he was an impostor.
When war closed Venice to English tourists, Canaletto came to London instead. His painting was so different from what buyers expected that a rumour spread he was an impostor.
529: Fire at the Oil Depot at San Marcuola
Venice watches a warehouse burn, while Paris is in revolution.
On a November night in 1789 an oil warehouse caught fire in Venice. Guardi, then 77, painted the blaze and the crowd watching, while Paris was in revolution.
530: View of the Giudecca Canal and the Zattere
Venice trembling with flicks of light, sold cheaply in his lifetime.
Canaletto painted Venice sharp as a map; Guardi painted it trembling, with flicks of light. He sold cheaply in his lifetime, and only later generations prized that tremble.
531: The painter of these canals also lit them, with about 1,800 street lamps.
The painter of these quiet canals also lit them. In 1669 Amsterdam adopted his plan for about 1,800 street lamps, and his system lit the city until 1840.
532: Rembrandt lies in this church, and no one knows exactly where.
Van der Heyden also invented a fire engine with flexible hoses. Rembrandt was buried in this church in 1669, in a grave whose exact place has never been found.
533: The Interior of St. Bavo, Haarlem
Measured like a surveyor, then quietly stretched, so the silence feels bigger.
Saenredam measured churches like a surveyor, then quietly stretched them. His pillars rise a little higher than the real ones, so the white silence feels even bigger.
534: The Old Town Hall of Amsterdam
When he painted it, the building had been gone for five years.
When Saenredam painted this town hall, it had already been gone for five years. It burned in 1652, and he worked from a drawing he had made on the spot in 1641.
535: Interior of the Church of St Odulphus, Assendelft
Near the front, in the floor, lies his father's gravestone.
In the floor of this village church, close to the front, lies the gravestone of Saenredam's father. He painted the place where his family began as a vast, calm, light-filled room.
536: Interior of the Oude Kerk, Amsterdam
Children play and dogs wander in during the sermon.
Dutch churches were public living rooms: people strolled, children played and dogs wandered in during the sermon. De Witte painted the light, and let life go on beneath it.
537: A View of Delft after the Explosion of 1654
About 40 tonnes of gunpowder blew a hole in a city. He painted the ruins again and again.
On 12 October 1654, about 40 tonnes of gunpowder blew a hole in Delft. Van der Poel, whose daughter is believed to have died in the blast, painted the ruins again and again.
538: The Courtyard of a House in Delft
The tablet over the arch is real, and asks passers-by for patience.
The stone tablet over the arch was real: it came from a Delft convent and invited passers-by to patience and gentleness. It still survives in the city today.
539: View of Piazza del Popolo, Rome
A Dutchman so at home in Rome that Italians renamed him Vanvitelli.
A Dutchman from Amersfoort became Rome's great view painter, and Italians called him Vanvitelli. His son Luigi became one of the leading architects of 18th-century Italy.
540: Monet put on his best clothes and got the trains held for more smoke.
Renoir later recalled that Monet put on his best clothes, told the station master he was a famous painter, and got trains held with their fires stoked for more smoke.
541: Painted from a hospital terrace, many canvases at once, chasing the fog.
Monet painted it from a hospital terrace across the Thames, working on many canvases at once as the fog changed. He finished most of them years later, back home in Giverny.
542: Painted from the very rooms where Impressionism made its public debut.
Monet looked down on this boulevard from photographer Nadar's studio, the very rooms where the Impressionists held their first exhibition in 1874.
543: The Rue Montorgueil, Paris, Celebration of 30 June 1878
A street turned into flags, and a few kilometres away Manet painted the same day.
Paris was celebrating its recovery after war and the Commune, and the whole street turned into flags. On the same day, a few kilometres away, Manet painted the same holiday.
544: Too beautiful to be painted, he reportedly said. He painted it anyway.
Monet first saw Venice at 68 and is said to have called it too beautiful to be painted. It was his only visit; his wife Alice, who travelled with him, died less than three years later.
545: A new iron bridge, a man, a woman, and a dog with somewhere to be.
A brand-new iron bridge over the railway, a man, a woman, and a dog with somewhere to be. Below these tracks, Monet was painting the Saint-Lazare station at about the same time.
546: His brother looks out over Paris. He died that same year, at 26.
The man looking out over Paris is Caillebotte's younger brother René. He died that same year at 26, and the painting became the last image of him.
547: The Boulevard Montmartre on a Winter Morning
One hotel window, about fourteen paintings, every kind of weather.
Pissarro rented a hotel room above this boulevard and painted it about fourteen times, in rain, sun, night and fog. This is one window, many weathers.
548: Avenue de l'Opéra, Snow Effect, Morning
His eyes kept him indoors, so Paris came to him through a hotel window.
A chronic eye infection kept Pissarro from painting outdoors, so he painted Paris through hotel windows. His late city views exist because his body forced him inside.
549: Paris's oldest bridge, painted by a man over seventy with a year to live.
Pissarro painted Paris's oldest bridge from an apartment window on Place Dauphine. He was over seventy, and within a year he was dead.
550: Three sleepless nights, to paint the terrible passions of humanity in red and green.
Van Gogh stayed up three nights to paint it. He wrote to his brother that he had tried to express the terrible passions of humanity with red and green.
551: A dream of a house full of artists. Gauguin came, and they quarrelled.
Van Gogh rented these rooms in Arles dreaming of a house of artists. Gauguin came, they quarrelled, and in 1944 the house itself was wrecked by bombing.
552: The road splits around the church, and neither path leads in.
Van Gogh painted this village church in June 1890. The road splits around it and neither path leads in; seven weeks later he was dead.
553: View of Paris from Vincent's Room in the Rue Lepic
Theo gave him a home in Paris. Paris gave him color.
This was the view from the flat Van Gogh shared with his brother Theo in Montmartre. Theo gave him a home in Paris; Paris gave him color.
554: Flags everywhere, and in the corner a man on crutches limps past the party.
Manet painted the flag-draped street below his studio window. In the corner a man on crutches limps past the party, possibly a veteran of the war France had just lost.
555: Rue Halévy, Seen from the Sixth Floor
Six floors above a Paris so new the paint had barely dried.
Caillebotte looked down from six floors up on Haussmann's brand-new Paris. The street is named for Fromental Halévy, the Jewish composer whose opera La Juive was one of the century's great hits.
556: His brother stopped strangers to ask the time, so Renoir could sketch them standing still.
Renoir's brother Edmond stopped strangers on the bridge to ask the time or the way, so Renoir, watching from a café upstairs, could sketch them while they stood still.
557: For fifty years the world believed it was lost. It was in the Hermitage.
Soviet troops took this painting from Berlin in 1945, and for fifty years the world believed it was lost. In 1995 it reappeared at the Hermitage.
558: Boulevard des Capucines, Evening, outside the Café Napolitain
The boulevard painter who stood as Proust's second in a pistol duel.
Béraud painted the boulevards with the eye of a society reporter. In 1897 he served as Marcel Proust's second when the young writer fought a pistol duel.
559: The scaffolding is real: Paris, healing its burns.
The scaffolding is real: this wing of the Louvre was being rebuilt after the Commune set it on fire in 1871. De Nittis painted Paris healing its burns.
560: View of Paris from the Trocadéro
A city just out of siege and civil war, shrunk to a pale strip behind two women and a child.
A city that had just survived a siege and a civil war, seen from a quiet hill. Morisot, who lived nearby, shrank Paris to a pale strip and gave the foreground to two women and a child.
561: Moscow grew into a megacity. The white church is still there.
Polenov painted this from the window of his rented flat near the Arbat. Moscow has since grown into a megacity of millions, but the white church in the background still stands.
562: Nocturne in Black and Gold: The Falling Rocket
Called a pot of paint flung in the public's face. Whistler sued, and won one farthing.
Ruskin accused Whistler of flinging a pot of paint in the public's face. Whistler sued for libel and won one farthing in damages, and the legal costs helped bankrupt him.
563: Nocturne: Blue and Gold, Old Battersea Bridge
The real bridge was low and squat. Whistler made it soar.
The real wooden bridge was low and squat. Whistler raised it into a tall T against the night, borrowing a trick from the Japanese woodblock prints he collected.
564: Night paintings named like music, meant to work on you the way a melody does.
Whistler's patron suggested calling these night paintings 'nocturnes', a word from music. Whistler loved it: he wanted a painting to work on you the way a melody does.
565: Whistler thought he invented nocturnes, until he reportedly saw these.
Whistler reportedly said he considered himself the inventor of nocturnes until he saw Grimshaw's moonlit pictures. Grimshaw taught himself to paint while working as a railway clerk.
566: Industrial Leeds after rain, glowing like a dream.
Wet pavements, gaslit shop windows, a city glowing after rain. Grimshaw made industrial Leeds look like a dream, and he barely ever painted it any other way than at dusk.
567: The Burning of the Houses of Lords and Commons
Parliament burned because clerks were burning old tally sticks.
Parliament burned because clerks were burning old wooden tally sticks in a furnace below it. Turner watched from among the crowds on the Thames and turned the disaster into light.
568: Salisbury Cathedral from the Bishop's Grounds
The bishop wanted less cloud. He got a sunnier copy, with himself in it.
The bishop who commissioned it disliked the dark cloud and asked for a clearer sky. Constable painted him a sunnier version, and the bishop and his wife stand in the corner.
569: All of architecture, Egypt to Gothic, in one dream. The client rejected it.
An architect commissioned it, a whole history of building from Egypt to Gothic piled into one dream. When it arrived, he rejected it.
570: A Bird's-Eye View of the Bank of England
An architect had his masterpiece painted as a ruin. Today only its outer wall survives.
The architect John Soane had his own masterpiece painted as a ruin, cut open like a model. A century later most of the real building was demolished, and only its outer wall remains.
571: No money to build after the wars, so Berlin's great architect painted his cathedral.
Schinkel was Berlin's great architect, but after the Napoleonic wars there was no money to build. So he painted the cathedral he dreamed of, still under scaffolding, with a rainbow.
572: A former porcelain painter, finishing every brick with a jeweller's patience.
Gaertner began as an apprentice painting porcelain at Berlin's royal factory. You can feel it here: an ordinary street, every brick and shutter finished with a jeweller's patience.
573: The train is a small dark smudge: the future, arriving quietly.
Prussia's first railway had opened only nine years earlier. Menzel painted the train as a small dark smudge cutting through the fields, the future arriving quietly.
574: Unter den Linden after the Rain
Decades of Berlin's wet night streets, by a Jewish painter the city would soon turn against.
Lesser Ury, a Jewish painter from Prussia, spent decades painting Berlin's wet streets at night. He died in 1931, two years before the city turned on people like him.
575: Moscow, eleven years before the fire that burned most of it.
Alekseyev was nicknamed the Russian Canaletto. This is Red Square in 1801, eleven years before the fire of 1812 burned most of Moscow.
576: Venice from a height no human could reach in 1500.
Printed in 1500 from six huge woodblocks, it shows Venice from a bird's-eye view that no human could have had. It took about three years to make.
577: He painted it young, kept coming back for decades, and lived to 92.
Rudolf von Alt painted this cathedral as a young man and kept returning to it for decades. He lived to 92 and was still painting Vienna when the 20th century began.
578: A palace burned, politicians bickered for twenty years, and silence moved in.
Copenhagen's royal palace burned in 1884, and for over twenty years politicians could not agree on a new one. Hammershøi, the painter of silent rooms, found the same hush outdoors.
579: Ludgate Hill: A Block in the Street
Traffic jams are not modern. Doré drew London in 1872 choked with carts and horses under a new railway bridge, with St Paul's dome floating above the mess.
580: How the London poor lived, glimpsed from a passing train.
This is how the poor of Victorian London lived, seen from a passing train: back-to-back houses, each with a tiny yard. Van Gogh admired Doré's London so much he copied one of its prints.
581: London at the height of its power, drawn as a ruin.
In 1840 the historian Macaulay imagined a traveller from New Zealand sketching the ruins of St Paul's from a broken London Bridge. Doré drew the fantasy at the height of London's power.
583: The pit Penn Station rose from. Its demolition helped birth New York's landmark law.
Bellows painted the giant pit from which Penn Station rose. The station was demolished in the 1960s, and the outrage helped give New York its landmark preservation law.
584: There is no such corner. It is the whole city, squeezed into one street.
There is no such corner in New York. Bellows built a composite of the whole city's rush into one winter street: trams, carts, crowds and towers fighting for the same space.
585: Cold so well painted you can almost hear the crunch underfoot.
Snow at the southern tip of Manhattan, where the city meets the harbour. Bellows painted cold so well that you can almost hear the crunch underfoot.
586: A month into the war, Fifth Avenue hung out the flags of its allies.
A month after America entered the First World War, Fifth Avenue hung out the flags of Britain, France and the US. Hassam painted about thirty flag pictures in the years that followed.
587: The violet hour when New York stops working and starts going home.
Snow, dusk and the first streetlights: Hassam caught the violet hour when New York stops working and starts going home, and the whole city almost dissolves.
588: The wet street is a mirror, doubling every carriage and lamp.
Before he discovered Impressionism in Paris, Hassam was already painting Boston in the rain. The wet street works as a mirror, doubling every carriage and lamp.
589: One rule since 1854: no women. It took a court order in 1970.
McSorley's opened in 1854 and stood firm on one rule: no women. It only let them in in 1970, after a court ordered it to.
590: From the rooftops, the glowing towers downtown still looked like a promise.
Sloan painted the night city from the roofs of the Village, with an elevated train curving through. The glowing towers downtown were still new enough to feel like a promise.
591: Meant to stand for only twenty years. Artists petitioned against it.
The tower was built in just over two years and was meant to stand for only twenty. Artists signed a petition against it, and today it is hard to imagine Paris without it.
592: The Great East River Suspension Bridge
Her husband was bedridden, so Emily Roebling carried his orders to the site for years.
Its engineer was bedridden by the bends, so his wife Emily Roebling carried his instructions to the site for years. When it opened in 1883, she was the first to cross.
593: The wind swirled around its corner, and so, the story goes, did the onlookers.
Its sharp corner made the wind swirl, and a story says police shooed away men who loitered to watch women's skirts blow up, with the words '23 skidoo'.
594: Head of the Statue of Liberty in Paris
Before she had a body, her head went on a fundraising tour.
Before Liberty had a body, she went on a fundraising tour. Her torch arm stood in New York, and her head was shown in Paris, waiting for money to finish the rest.
595: The camera saw only black and white. The color was added by hand.
This was Little Italy around 1900. The color was not in the camera: it was added by hand in the photochrom process, which turned black and white into a painted postcard.
596: The world's tallest building, paid for in cash made of nickels and dimes.
Frank Woolworth paid for his tower in cash, built on nickels and dimes from his five-and-ten stores. From 1913 to 1930 it was the tallest building in the world.
597: The 'airship' was a chain of kites, lifting a huge camera over the burned city.
The 'airship' was a chain of kites. Lawrence lifted a huge camera about 450 metres above the burned city, six weeks after the 1906 earthquake.
598: Chicago after the Great Fire of 1871
100,000 homeless, and within fifteen years, the first skyscrapers.
The fire left about 100,000 people homeless. Chicago rebuilt so fast and so boldly that within fifteen years it was raising the first skyscrapers.
599: Straight down from a balcony: a bench, a tree grate, a few hats.
Caillebotte leaned out of a balcony and painted straight down: a bench, a tree grate, a few hats. It looks like a modern photograph, decades before cameras saw cities this way.
600: The Eiffel Tower at Night, Exposition Universelle
A city still lit by gas, swept by electric searchlights from above.
In 1889 most of Paris was still lit by gas. At the World's Fair, electric searchlights swept the city from the top of the world's tallest structure.
601: Stars are being born inside. This light left when the first cities were rising.
The tallest pillar is about four light-years long, and stars are being born inside it. The light you see left it some 6,500 years ago, when the first cities were just rising.
602: A whole Earth, fully lit. Only those who flew to the Moon have seen it with their own eyes.
603: They flew to study the Moon. The photo everyone remembers is of home.
Apollo 8 flew to study the Moon, and the photo everyone remembers is of home. Anders grabbed a roll of color film when the Earth suddenly rose over the horizon.
604: That speck, smaller than a pixel, is everyone you have ever loved.
That speck in the band of light, smaller than a pixel, is Earth seen from six billion kilometers. Carl Sagan: 'Everyone you love, everyone you know... lived out their lives there.'
605: Almost every dot here is a galaxy.
Hubble stared for about a million seconds at a speck of sky a tenth the width of the full Moon, and found some 10,000 galaxies. Almost every dot here is a galaxy.
606: Ten days staring at an empty patch of sky. It held about 3,000 galaxies.
In 1995 Hubble stared for ten days at a speck of sky near the Big Dipper that looked empty, a gamble some feared would waste its time. It held about 3,000 galaxies.
607: Armstrong held the camera, so he is barely in the photos. Except here, in the visor.
Neil Armstrong held the camera for most of the moonwalk, so the first man on the Moon barely appears in its photos. He is here, though: the small figure reflected in Aldrin's visor.
608: From the station, auroras ripple beneath your feet.
Auroras glow about 100 to 300 km up, and the space station orbits at around 400. Astronauts look down on them from above, like a curtain of light rippling beneath their feet.
609: A six-sided jet stream wider than Earth, and no one fully knows why.
A six-sided jet stream wider than Earth circles Saturn's north pole, and has been there at least since Voyager first glimpsed it in 1981. No one fully knows why it holds its shape.
610: More than 1,400 km per second. Earth would be a speck beside that arc.
On 31 August 2012 a long filament of solar material erupted into space at more than 1,400 km per second. The whole Earth would be a speck beside that glowing arc.
611: Before cameras could see nebulae, astronomy needed an artist's eye.
Before cameras could capture faint nebulae, astronomy depended on artists' eyes. Trouvelot drew the Orion Nebula through a telescope; the first photograph of it came only in 1880.
612: A star seen in daylight in 1054. At its heart, a dead star spins 30 times a second.
In 1054 Chinese astronomers recorded a new star bright enough to see in daylight for weeks. This is its wreckage, and at the center a dead star still spins 30 times a second.
613: No wind, no rain: a print like this could last millions of years.
Aldrin photographed his own bootprint as an experiment, to see how the lunar soil packs down. With no wind or rain to erase it, a print like this could last for millions of years.
614: Almost every light is ours: cities, highways, gas flares, fishing fleets.
Half of Earth is always in daylight, so this is a mosaic of cloud-free nights a satellite gathered in 2012. Almost every light is ours: cities, highways, gas flares and fishing fleets.
615: A world of gas with no surface, lighter than water on average.
Cassini reached Saturn in 2004 and stayed for 13 years. Saturn is so light for its size that its average density is less than water's: a world of gas with no surface at all.
616: 400 times smaller, 400 times closer: a perfect fit, for a few minutes.
The Moon is about 400 times smaller than the Sun and about 400 times closer, so it covers it almost exactly. For a few minutes the corona, over a million degrees hot, comes out.
617: He let loose a moth that still ravages American forests. Then he looked up.
Trouvelot is also remembered for a disaster: experimenting with silk moths in Massachusetts, he let loose the gypsy moth, which still ravages American forests. Then he looked up.
618: A galaxy that looks like a hat, hiding a black hole of a billion suns.
Seen almost exactly edge on, this galaxy looks like a hat. Its bright core hides a black hole of about a billion suns, and its light set out some 30 million years ago.
619: Every human then alive is said to be in the frame, except the one holding the camera.
Michael Collins took this from lunar orbit: Eagle returning from the surface, with Earth behind it. It is often said that every human then alive, except Collins himself, is in the frame.
620: Staring down into its eye was chilling, even from space.
Hurricane Florence from the space station, September 2018. Astronaut Alexander Gerst wrote that staring down into its gaping eye was chilling, even from space.
621: Fountains from a hidden ocean. Some fall as snow, the rest feeds a ring of Saturn.
These fountains spray from an ocean hidden under the ice of a moon only about 500 km wide. Some of the spray falls back as snow; the rest feeds one of Saturn's rings.
622: The ISS Crossing the Eclipsed Sun
Six people crossing the face of the Sun, in less than a second.
During the 2017 eclipse, a NASA photographer caught the space station crossing the Sun with six people aboard. The whole crossing took less than a second.
623: Thomas Edison went west for this same eclipse, to measure the corona's heat.
Trouvelot watched this eclipse on 29 July 1878 from the Wyoming Territory. Thomas Edison went west for the same eclipse, hoping to measure the corona's heat with an instrument he had invented.
624: The first nebula anyone saw as a spiral. Now watch the small galaxy tugging an arm.
In 1845 Lord Rosse saw arms curling in this smudge of light, the first time anyone realized a nebula could be a spiral. Hubble shows the smaller galaxy tugging at one of them.
625: About 13 tonnes of fuel and oxygen, burned every second.
At liftoff, the Saturn V that carried Apollo 11 burned about 13 tonnes of fuel and oxygen every second. Roughly a million people watched from the roads and beaches around it.
626: A clear ring around the plume, perhaps punched open by the shock wave.
Astronauts happened to pass over the Kuril Islands just as this volcano erupted in June 2009. The ring of clear sky around the plume may have been punched open by the eruption's shock wave.
627: From the Moon's surface Earth barely moves. Only from orbit does it rise.
In October 2015 a robotic orbiter, about 134 km above the Moon's far side, caught Earth rising. Only an orbiting craft sees this: from the lunar surface, Earth hangs almost still in the sky.
628: A dark smudge sliding over the clouds, and beneath it, sudden twilight.
From the space station, a total solar eclipse is a dark smudge sliding across the clouds. On 29 March 2006 this one crossed Africa and Turkey, where people below stood in sudden twilight.
629: Rings about 270,000 km wide, and in most places around ten meters thick.
Saturn's main rings span about 270,000 km, yet in most places they are only around ten meters thick. Trouvelot drew them in 1874, long before anyone knew they were mostly water ice.
630: This may be how our Sun ends, in about five billion years.
Astronomers expect the Sun to end much like this in about five billion years: a dying star shedding its outer layers into a glowing shell. Some call it the Eye of God.
631: The last time anyone walked on the Moon, under a small and distant Earth.
December 1972, the last time anyone walked on the Moon. Harrison Schmitt, the only geologist ever to go there, stands by the flag beneath a small and distant Earth.
632: At night from orbit, Egypt is a glowing lotus.
From orbit at night, Egypt is a glowing lotus: the Nile and its delta, where almost all Egyptians live, lit up against a black desert. Cairo shines where the stem meets the flower.
633: Days later, someone noticed a plume: the first active volcano found beyond Earth.
Voyager 1 swept past Jupiter in March 1979. Days later, engineer Linda Morabito spotted a plume rising from the moon Io in its images: the first active volcano ever found beyond Earth.
634: A loop of glowing helium over 45 Earths across.
In December 1973 Skylab's crew recorded one of the most spectacular solar eruptions seen until then: a loop of glowing helium spanning more than 580,000 km, over 45 Earths across.
635: He had to draw fast: a day on Jupiter lasts less than ten hours.
Trouvelot drew Jupiter in 1880, just after the Great Red Spot had turned startlingly vivid. He had to work fast: a day on Jupiter lasts less than ten hours, and the view keeps turning.
636: Butterfly wings of gas hotter than 20,000°C, fleeing a dying star.
The wings of this butterfly are gas hotter than 20,000°C, fleeing a dying star at more than 950,000 km/h. From tip to tip it spans over two light-years.
637: He felt God's presence on the Moon, and came home a preacher.
Jim Irwin salutes beside the first car ever driven on another world. He later said he felt God's presence on the Moon, and he spent the rest of his life as a preacher.
638: The side of the Moon we never see, passing in front of us.
From Earth we never see this side of the Moon. To catch it passing in front of us you need a camera 1.5 million km away, like the one aboard NASA's DSCOVR in July 2015.
639: Some 400 active volcanoes, kept molten by Jupiter's squeeze.
Io is the most volcanic world known, with some 400 active volcanoes. Jupiter's gravity squeezes and stretches it with every orbit, and the friction keeps its insides molten.
640: Flames taller than several Earths stacked up, visible only in an eclipse or a spectroscope.
These flames of gas rising from the Sun's edge can only be seen during an eclipse, or with a spectroscope. Trouvelot drew them with one; many of them are taller than several Earths stacked up.
641: Not a nebula, but a flash still spreading through dust: an echo made of light.
In 2002 an obscure star suddenly flared to 600,000 times the Sun's brightness. The 'nebula' you see is that flash still spreading through the dust around it: an echo made of light.
642: They landed within walking distance of a robot, and brought pieces of it home.
Apollo 12 landed within walking distance of a robot that had sat on the Moon for two and a half years. Pete Conrad and Alan Bean cut off pieces of it and brought them home.
643: That pale dot below the rings is us, waving.
On 19 July 2013 people were invited to go outside and wave at Saturn while Cassini, 1.4 billion km away, took a picture. We are the pale dot below the rings, at lower right.
644: Under the cracked ice, perhaps twice the water of all Earth's oceans.
Under this cracked shell of ice, scientists believe, lies a salty ocean holding about twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans. It is one of the best places to look for life.
645: Most of his names faded. The lunar Alps and Apennines survived.
Hevelius observed the Moon for years and engraved these maps himself for his Selenographia of 1647. Most of his names faded, but a few survived, like the lunar Alps and Apennines.
