646: A pillar three light-years tall, with newborn stars firing jets from its peaks.
This pillar of gas and dust is three light-years tall, and newborn stars are firing jets of gas from its peaks. Hubble made it to celebrate its own 20th birthday.
647: At a sixth of his weight, a salute turns into a leap.
On the Moon John Young weighed a sixth of what he did at home, so his salute turned into a leap. Nine years later he commanded the first Space Shuttle flight.
648: Every layer of sky that keeps us alive, seen as one thin glowing line.
Behind Endeavour lies every layer of sky that keeps us alive: orange near the ground, then white, blue and black. Seen edge on from orbit, our whole atmosphere is a thin glowing line.
649: A planet on its side: 42 years of sunlight, then 42 of darkness.
Uranus rolls around the Sun on its side, probably knocked over long ago by a giant impact. Each pole gets about 42 years of sunlight in a row, then 42 years of darkness.
650: The sky drawn as if seen from outside, published by his wife after his death.
Hevelius drew the constellations mirror-reversed, as if seen from outside the sky. His wife Elisabeth, who observed beside him, published this atlas in 1690, three years after his death.
651: Two galaxies colliding, and their stars almost never touch.
Two galaxies have been colliding for hundreds of millions of years, and the crash is lighting up billions of new stars. Their stars almost never hit each other: there is too much space between them.
652: He traced his daughter's initials in the lunar dust. They may still be there.
Gene Cernan named this boulder for his daughter Tracy, and said he traced her initials in the lunar dust before leaving. With no wind on the Moon, they may still be there.
653: The first photo of Earth from space survived the crash in a steel case.
On 24 October 1946 a camera aboard a captured German V-2 rocket, launched from New Mexico, took the first photo of Earth from space, about 105 km up. The film survived the crash in a steel case.
654: One visitor, ever, and winds of over 2,000 km/h.
Only one spacecraft has ever visited Neptune: Voyager 2, in 1989, twelve years after launch. Its winds are the fastest measured in the Solar System, over 2,000 km/h.
655: Three rival universes side by side, as if the debate were still open.
In 1660 Cellarius published a celestial atlas that set the rival models of the universe side by side, Ptolemy's, Tycho's and this one, with the Sun at the center, as if the debate were still open.
656: A bubble seven light-years wide, blown by a single star.
A star about 45 times the mass of the Sun is blowing this bubble, seven light-years wide, with a stellar wind of more than six million km/h.
657: Ordered back inside, he called it the saddest moment of his life.
Ed White was the first American to walk in space. Ordered back inside after about 20 minutes, he called it the saddest moment of his life. Less than two years later he died in the Apollo 1 fire.
658: The Milky Way from the ISS
Our galaxy and our weather, in one frame.
From orbit, the Milky Way rises over Earth's night side while a thunderstorm flashes below. Our galaxy and our weather, in a single frame: the faraway and the close at hand.
659: One of the coldest surfaces ever measured, and it erupts.
At about minus 235°C, Triton is one of the coldest surfaces ever measured, yet Voyager 2 saw dark plumes erupting from it. It also orbits Neptune backward, likely a captured wanderer.
660: A beautiful wrong idea that led to the right laws.
Young Kepler was sure God had built the Solar System from perfect solids nested between the planets' orbits. He was wrong, but the hunt led him to the true laws of planetary motion.
661: About 3,000 stars, and Earth is more than two thousand times older.
For its 25th birthday Hubble photographed a cluster of about 3,000 stars only some two million years old. For a star that is infancy: Earth is more than two thousand times older.
662: Two crewed ships in orbit, at times about 30 cm apart.
December 1965: for the first time, two crewed spacecraft met in orbit, at times only about 30 cm apart. Without learning this, no one could have landed on the Moon and come back.
663: The Moon only looks bright: it reflects about as much light as worn asphalt.
On its way to Jupiter, the Galileo probe looked back from about 6 million km and caught Earth and the Moon together. The Moon is darker than it looks at night: about as reflective as worn asphalt.
664: A faint dot for 85 years, then a heart of ice. Its discoverer's ashes flew along.
For 85 years Pluto was a faint dot. In 2015 New Horizons flew past and found a vast heart of nitrogen ice; aboard was a pinch of the ashes of Clyde Tombaugh, who discovered it.
665: It looks medieval. It first appeared in 1888, and no one knows who made it.
It looks medieval, but it first appeared in 1888, in a popular science book by Camille Flammarion. No one knows who made it, and it has become an emblem of the urge to look beyond the sky.
666: More than 3,000 stars, and some of the youngest may be growing planets.
Hubble's sharpest view of the nearest big star factory, some 1,350 light-years away, holds more than 3,000 stars. Some of the youngest are wrapped in dusty disks that may become planets.
667: No crew in Earth orbit went higher for the next 58 years.
In 1966 Gemini 11 climbed 1,369 km above Earth and photographed India curving away below. No crew in Earth orbit went higher for the next 58 years.
668: Even a world this small and cold has a blue sky.
Looking back as it sped away, New Horizons saw Pluto lit from behind: some twenty layers of blue haze above mountains of water ice. Even a world this small and cold has a sky.
669: One night in 1833 the sky fell, and people woke their neighbors for the end of the world.
On the night of 12 November 1833, meteors fell over North America at an estimated tens of thousands an hour. Many people woke their neighbors, sure the world was ending.
670: Inside lives a giant star that flared once, and is expected to explode one day.
This cloud is home to Eta Carinae, a giant star that flared up in the 1840s and became, for a while, the second-brightest star in the night sky. Astronomers expect it to explode one day.
671: No line tying him to the ship. Just a jetpack and 100 meters of nothing.
February 1984: Bruce McCandless became the first person to fly free in space, with no line tying him to his ship. He drifted about 100 meters away, steering with a jetpack.
672: The most distant world ever seen up close: two lumps that touched gently and stuck.
On New Year's Day 2019 New Horizons flew past Arrokoth, 6.6 billion km from the Sun, the most distant world ever explored up close: two lumps that touched gently and stuck long ago.
673: He thought he was watching a solar system being born. It was a whole galaxy.
In 1888 Isaac Roberts, a Welsh builder turned astronomer, made the first photographs to reveal Andromeda's spiral form. He thought he was watching a new solar system being born.
674: A grain of sand held at arm's length, and thousands of galaxies inside it.
This whole image covers a patch of sky the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length. Thousands of galaxies are in it, and some of their light has traveled for over 13 billion years.
675: Only hours before reentry, they finally saw what had nearly killed them.
Apollo 13's crew saw what nearly killed them only hours before reentry, when they cast off the service module: a whole side panel blown out by an exploding oxygen tank.
676: A moon falling in slowly: one day a crash, or a ring.
Mars's moon Phobos is spiraling slowly inward, a couple of meters closer every century. In tens of millions of years it will either crash into Mars or break up into a ring.
677: The dark rifts are not holes. They are dust.
Barnard grew up poor in Nashville and started working in a photo studio as a child. His long exposures of the Milky Way helped show that its dark rifts are clouds of dust, not empty holes.
678: These are not mountains. They are the edge of a cloud, hiding newborn stars.
These are not mountains: they are the edge of a gas cloud in the Carina Nebula, with peaks about seven light-years high. Webb's infrared eye found hundreds of hidden newborn stars inside.
679: First View of Earth from the Moon
Developed on board, scanned, and radioed home strip by strip.
Two years before Earthrise, a robot took the first picture of Earth from the Moon's vicinity. The film was developed on board, scanned, and radioed home strip by strip.
680: Who took this photo on Mars? Curiosity did.
Who took this photo of Curiosity on Mars? Curiosity did, with a camera on its arm, in dozens of frames stitched together. The arm was left out, so it looks as if someone else was there.
681: Earth at the center, and for some 1,400 years, scholars agreed.
Earth at the center, wrapped in the zodiac: for some 1,400 years this was the shape of the universe for most scholars in Europe and the Islamic world. Cellarius still drew it in full glory in 1660.
682: The bright star in the middle is not the one that made this.
The bright star at the center is not the one that made this nebula. Its dimmer partner did, shedding shells of gas for thousands of years, and Webb was the first to show it wrapped in dust.
683: If she says the numbers are good, Glenn said, I'm ready to go.
Before this launch in 1962, John Glenn asked that mathematician Katherine Johnson personally check the computer's orbit figures. If she said they were good, he said, he was ready to go.
684: On Mars, sunsets are blue. Fine dust lets blue light through near the Sun's direction, the reverse of Earth, where sunsets glow red. The rover Spirit watched this one in 2005.
685: He gave up the law for the sky, and built his own observatory.
Lewis Rutherfurd gave up a law career for the sky and built his own observatory in New York. This 1865 photograph of the Moon was hailed as one of the finest yet made.
686: Five galaxies, but one is only pretending: it is seven times closer.
Four of these galaxies are locked in a slow collision some 290 million light-years away. The fifth, at left, only seems to belong: it is about seven times closer to us.
687: Launched with a flawed mirror, repaired in orbit, and set free one last time.
The telescope behind so many of these images, set free over Earth in May 2009 after its last repair. Astronauts visited Hubble five times, and launched it with a flawed mirror they later fixed.
688: Planned for five short hops, it flew 72 times, carrying a scrap of the Wright Flyer.
The first powered flight on another world was planned as five short test hops. Ingenuity flew 72 times, carrying a scrap of fabric from the Wright brothers' first airplane.
689: The First Photograph of the Moon
Twenty minutes on a rooftop, and one of the oldest faces of the Moon.
In March 1840, on the roof of New York University, John W. Draper exposed a plate to the Moon for about twenty minutes. This damaged daguerreotype is among the oldest photographs of it.
690: Red jets from some 50 young stars: this is how our own Sun began.
The nearest stellar nursery to us, about 390 light-years away. The red jets burst from some 50 young stars, most the size of the Sun or smaller: this is how our own Sun began.
691: First Photo from the Surface of Mars
The first photo from Mars's surface, seven years to the day after Apollo 11.
The first photograph ever taken on the surface of Mars, minutes after Viking 1 landed on 20 July 1976: seven years to the day after Apollo 11 touched down on the Moon.
692: Hold the card up to a lamp, and the constellation shines through.
Urania's Mirror was a set of 32 constellation cards from 1824, with holes punched where the stars are. Hold one up to a lamp, and the constellation shines through.
693: Its light reached us about 340 years ago, and no one clearly wrote it down.
Light from this star's explosion reached Earth about 340 years ago, yet no one clearly recorded it. Webb shows the wreckage still spreading, seeding space with the stuff of future planets.
694: Built to last 90 Martian days, it kept driving for almost 15 years.
The rover Opportunity, built to last 90 Martian days, spent about two years exploring this crater, some 750 meters wide. In all it kept driving for almost 15 years.
695: The first comet ever photographed, and many called it the century's most beautiful.
Donati's Comet of 1858, with its sweeping curved tail, was the first comet ever photographed. Many who saw it called it the most beautiful comet of the century.
696: Auroras on both poles, faint rings, tiny moons. Even the astronomers were surprised.
In Webb's infrared, auroras glow over both of Jupiter's poles, and its faint rings appear with two tiny moons. One of the astronomers admitted they hadn't expected it to be this good.
697: Days hot enough to melt lead, and ice hiding in the shadows.
Mercury, closest to the Sun, has days hot enough to melt lead, yet MESSENGER confirmed water ice in polar craters that sunlight never reaches. The colors here are enhanced.
698: Visible to the naked eye as a faint smudge. Up close, a young star is carving it.
On a dark night you can see the Lagoon Nebula without a telescope, as a faint smudge in Sagittarius. Up close, a young star at its heart is blasting the surrounding gas into these shapes.
699: A canyon that on Earth would stretch from New York to Los Angeles.
The scar across Mars is Valles Marineris, a canyon system some 4,000 km long and up to 7 km deep. On Earth it would stretch from New York to Los Angeles.
700: The golden arcs are galaxies far behind, bent by gravity just as Einstein said.
The thin golden arcs are not galaxies of this cluster. They are galaxies far behind it, their light bent and stretched by its gravity, exactly as Einstein predicted.
701: One man, a circle and a square: the body as the measure of the universe.
Leonardo wrote the notes in mirror script, around a man who fits a circle and a square at once. The idea: the human body as the measure of the universe.
702: Does a galloping horse ever fly? Twelve cameras said yes.
Does a galloping horse ever leave the ground entirely? No eye could tell. Muybridge set up twelve cameras, and the answer, yes, was a first step toward cinema.
703: A flea bigger than the page, and Pepys reading until two in the morning.
In 1665 no one had ever seen a flea like this. Hooke's engraving folded out of the book, larger than the page, and Samuel Pepys sat up till two in the morning reading it.
704: Mountains on a body everyone believed was perfect.

Left, what Galileo drew in 1609 through a telescope he built himself; right, a photograph. He saw mountains and craters on a body everyone believed was perfect, and the heavens were never perfect again.
705: Sea anemones, drawn by a biologist, copied by architects.
These are sea anemones, drawn by a biologist. Haeckel's plates argued that nature is a better designer than any of us, and Art Nouveau architects copied them into buildings.
706: Studies of the Fetus in the Womb
The baby is human. The placenta around it comes from a cow.
The baby is human, but the placenta around it is drawn from a cow. Leonardo, dissecting whatever he could get, joined two bodies in one of the most tender drawings in science.
707: A skull opened like a house, searching for the seat of the soul.
Leonardo was 37 when he drew this skull, opened like a house with its front wall removed. He hoped to find inside it the point where all the senses meet: the seat of the soul.
708: Behind the skeleton stands a celebrity: a rhinoceros who toured Europe for 17 years.
Behind the skeleton stands a celebrity: Clara the rhinoceros, who toured Europe for 17 years. Wandelaar drew her from life in Leiden and gave anatomy an unexpected co-star.
709: Drawn through string grids for perfect accuracy. The rhino is just for pleasure.
Albinus wanted a perfect, distortion-free skeleton, so Wandelaar drew through string grids set at two distances. Clara the rhinoceros, seen from behind, was added for the pleasure of the eye.
710: A body squatting like a frog, drawn one inner system at a time.
Around 1390 a Persian physician drew the body squatting like a frog, one inner system at a time. It is one of the earliest full-body anatomy atlases of the Islamic world.
711: They could barely read the Dutch book, but they could see it was right.
In 1771 three Japanese doctors watched a dissection holding a Dutch anatomy book they could barely read. The book was right and the old Chinese charts wrong, so they spent three years translating it.
712: Too bloody for the art show. Only the woman hiding her eyes reacts like us.
It was judged too bloody for the art show of the 1876 Centennial and hung in the army medical exhibit instead. The woman covering her eyes is the only one in the room who reacts like us.
713: Anatomy in full colour from stacked plates, looking like Surrealism two centuries early.
Gautier d'Agoty was one of the first to print anatomy in full colour, stacking mezzotint plates inked in different hues. Two centuries early, the result looks like Surrealism.
714: At 52 she sailed to Suriname for insects, paying her way with paintings.
In 1699, at 52, Maria Sibylla Merian sailed from Amsterdam to Suriname with her daughter to study insects, paying her way by selling her paintings. This pineapple opens the book she brought back.
715: Critics called her bird-eating spider a fantasy. Then someone saw one do it.

Merian painted a tarantula eating a bird, and critics called it fantasy. In 1863 the naturalist Henry Walter Bates reported seeing one do it in the Amazon, and 'bird-eating spider' entered the language.
716: Small Emperor Moth on a Damson Plum
When many believed insects came from rotting mud, she showed them hatching from eggs.
In 1679, when many still believed insects were born from rotting mud, Merian showed caterpillars on the exact plants they eat, from egg to moth. This is plate 13 of that book.
717: A whole life on one branch: egg, caterpillar, cocoon and wings.

Merian put each insect's whole life on a single branch: egg, caterpillar, cocoon and wings together. Showing nature as a cycle rather than a pinned specimen put her decades ahead of the science of her day.
718: The planters mocked her for looking for anything but sugar.
In Suriname, Merian wrote, the plantation owners mocked her for looking for anything in their land except sugar. She stayed two years, raising caterpillars and drawing them alive.
719: He painted roses for Marie Antoinette, survived the Revolution, then painted for Joséphine.
Redouté, 'the Raphael of flowers', painted for Marie Antoinette and then for Empress Joséphine, surviving the Revolution in between. Many of his roses grew in Joséphine's garden at Malmaison.
720: One plate, several colours inked by hand at once, then a brush to finish.
Les Liliacées ran to eight volumes and nearly 500 plates. Each print came from one engraved plate inked by hand in several colours at once, then finished with a brush.
721: A newcomer from the Americas, filling an entire giant page.
Sunflowers reached Europe from the Americas only in the 1500s, and here one fills an entire giant page. Besler's 1613 book recorded a bishop's garden in Eichstätt, season by season.
722: A flower that opens for a single night, painted under the moon.
This cactus flower opens for a single night, so it was painted under the moon, a church tower in the distance. The book it appeared in cost Robert Thornton his fortune.
723: 500 plants to pay her husband's debts and get him out of prison. It worked.
Elizabeth Blackwell drew, engraved and coloured 500 plants to pay her husband's debts and free him from prison. It worked; years later he was executed in Sweden for conspiracy.
724: Painted for a Byzantine princess, annotated centuries later in Arabic and Hebrew.
This cannabis plant was painted around 512 for the Byzantine princess Anicia Juliana. Later owners wrote plant names in its margins in Arabic and Hebrew, a sign it stayed in use for centuries.
725: Life-size or nothing, so the flamingo had to bow its neck to fit.
Audubon insisted every bird be printed life-size, so even on the biggest paper he could get, the flamingo had to bow its neck to fit the page.
726: Once in noisy flocks across the East. The last one died in a zoo in 1918.
These were the only parrots native to the eastern United States, once seen in noisy flocks. Audubon painted them on cocklebur; the last known one died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1918.
727: So lifelike, because he wired the fresh bodies into place.
Two snowy owls glow against a night sky. To get poses like these, Audubon shot his birds and wired the fresh bodies into position on a gridded board before painting.
728: Plate 1 of a book that has sold for over 11 million dollars.
Plate 1 of The Birds of America, a book whose copies have sold for over 11 million dollars. Audubon opened it with the wild turkey, a bird Benjamin Franklin once praised over the eagle.
729: Eleven years of hand colouring, and this heron needed a page a metre tall.
All 435 plates of Audubon's birds were engraved in London and coloured by hand, sheet by sheet, for eleven years. The heron alone needed a page about a metre tall.
730: A bill once traded far and wide. The last widely accepted US sighting: 1944.
Its bill was so prized that Native Americans traded it far beyond the bird's range. Audubon printed this plate in 1829; the last widely accepted US sighting was in 1944.
731: Gold leaf under glaze to fake a shimmer he had never seen alive.
John Gould painted hundreds of hummingbirds from dead skins, layering gold leaf under glazes to fake their shimmer. He saw his first living one only in 1857, in Philadelphia.
732: 1,500 stuffed hummingbirds, and Queen Victoria came to look.
Gould showed some 1,500 stuffed hummingbirds in cases at London Zoo during the Great Exhibition of 1851. Tens of thousands came to see them, among them Queen Victoria.
733: Darwin barely noticed these finches. Someone else saw what they meant.
Darwin barely noticed these finches and labelled them poorly. The ornithologist John Gould saw they were separate species, and his wife Elizabeth drew the plates.
734: She sailed to Australia for its birds and died soon after coming home. Another hand finished.
John and Elizabeth Gould sailed to Australia in 1838 to collect its birds. Elizabeth died in 1841, soon after their return, and Henry Richter took over the drawing, including this western rosella.
735: Across the world, Audubon had a rival.
The Birds of America had a rival across the world: Gould's Birds of Australia, seven volumes and some 600 hand-coloured plates, many showing species new to science.
736: Before the Owl and the Pussy-cat, an 18-year-old drawing live parrots.
Edward Lear, later famous for 'The Owl and the Pussy-cat', began at 18 by drawing living parrots at London Zoo. His parrot book was one of the first in Britain devoted to a single family of birds.
737: Dürer never saw it, and Europe believed him for over 200 years.
Dürer never saw this rhinoceros. He worked from a letter and sketch sent from Lisbon, added armour plates and a small horn on its back, and Europe trusted his version for over 200 years.
738: The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands
Birds painted with the plants they live among, etched by his own hand to save money.
Mark Catesby was among the first to paint American birds with the plants of their habitat. To save money, he learned etching and made most of the plates himself.
739: This jellyfish carries the name of his late wife. Its tentacles recalled her hair.
The jellyfish with long trailing tentacles here bears the name of Haeckel's first wife, Anna Sethe, who died on his 30th birthday. He said its tentacles recalled her hair.
740: It looks like one animal. It is a colony of many, acting as one.
It looks like one animal, but a siphonophore is a colony: many tiny bodies, each specialised to swim, sting, eat or breed, acting as one creature.
741: Single cells, smaller than a grain of sand, that build skeletons of glass.
Radiolarians are single cells, smaller than a grain of sand, that build skeletons of glass. Haeckel described thousands of new species from the Challenger expedition's ocean samples.
742: One cell in a glass box, and a fifth of the oxygen you breathe.
Each diatom is one cell living in a glass box made of two halves. These tiny algae produce roughly a fifth of the oxygen we breathe; Haeckel laid them out like jewellery.
743: Humans at the crown of the tree. Today biologists see a bush with no top.
Haeckel drew evolution as a mighty tree with humans at its crown. Biologists now picture a branching bush with no top, but this image carried Darwin's idea to a wide public.
744: A glimpse of deep time, sold as prints to help the fossil hunter who found its creatures.
The first painting of a scene from deep time, full of creatures Mary Anning had dug up. De la Beche sold prints of it and gave the money to Anning, who was struggling.
745: Leaping dinosaurs in 1897. Science took about 70 years to catch up.
Painted in 1897, these two dinosaurs leap and fight, while most images of the time showed sluggish lizards. It took science about 70 years to catch up with Knight's lively guess.
746: A neck so impossible that Cuvier at first suspected a fake.
Mary Anning, a working-class fossil hunter, found the first complete plesiosaur and sketched it in a letter. The neck looked so impossible that Cuvier at first suspected a fake.
747: Little empty rooms in a slice of cork, and the word that now names all life.
Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork and saw rows of little rooms, which he called 'cells'. They were empty walls of dead plant tissue, but the word went on to name the unit of all life.
748: A giant portrait of a creature living on the reader's own head.
Hooke drew the louse gripping a human hair, on a fold-out plate bigger than the book. In 1665 readers met, at giant scale, a creature that lived on their own heads.
749: A forest of tiny globes, growing on a book cover.
Hooke found blue mould on the sheepskin cover of a small book and drew it as a forest of stalks topped with tiny globes. It is often called the first picture of a microscopic fungus.
750: About 14,000 lenses, and in each one, Hooke's own window.
Hooke estimated about 14,000 tiny lenses in the eyes of a drone fly and drew its head like a helmet of beads. In each bead, he noticed, his own window was reflected.
751: The ant wouldn't sit still, so Hooke got it drunk on brandy.
The ant would not keep still under the lens, so Hooke gave it brandy until it lay dead drunk, then drew it. After about an hour, he reported, it got up and walked away.
752: A draper with no degree, and the first look at bacteria.
A draper with no university training, Leeuwenhoek ground lenses that magnified some 270 times. His letters to London introduced the world to bacteria and to the tiny creatures on pond weed seen here.
753: His father wanted a doctor, not an artist. He became both.
Cajal wanted to be an artist, but his father pushed him into medicine. He did both, drawing neurons so precisely that his sketches are still used to teach how the brain is wired.
754: More than 5,000 snowflakes, and he never found two alike.
A Vermont farmer, Wilson Bentley, photographed more than 5,000 snowflakes through a microscope, starting in 1885. He never found two alike, and helped make that phrase famous.
755: She saw her own bones and reportedly said: I have seen my death.
Days after discovering X-rays, Röntgen photographed his wife Anna Bertha's hand, ring and all. Seeing her own bones, she reportedly said: 'I have seen my death.'
756: Two Goldfish and a Sea Fish (X-ray)
Josef Maria Eder and Eduard Valenta
Weeks after X-rays were announced, someone was already making art with them.
Within weeks of Röntgen's announcement in 1896, two Viennese photographers were X-raying fish and frogs and printing the results as fine-art photogravures.
757: Josef Maria Eder and Eduard Valenta
A spine like a necklace, from a time when no one knew X-rays could hurt.
The snake's spine curls like a necklace, every vertebra sharp. In 1896 X-rays were a public sensation, and their dangers were not yet known.
758: Josef Maria Eder and Eduard Valenta
Inside a body without cutting it. Doctors understood at once.
Two frogs, one on its back and one on its belly, show the same skeleton from both sides. Doctors grasped at once what it meant: seeing inside a body without cutting it.
759: Sailors could steer by ruler, and Greenland grew to the size of Africa.
Mercator made lines of constant compass bearing straight, so sailors could steer by ruler. We still pay the price: Greenland looks as big as Africa, which is about 14 times larger.
760: The birth certificate of 'America'. One copy of about a thousand survives.
The first map to use the name 'America'. Of about 1,000 printed copies only one is known to survive, bought by the Library of Congress for 10 million dollars.
761: A Venetian monk mapped the world from travellers' tales, with south at the top.
A Venetian monk drew the known world from travellers' accounts, with south at the top and nearly 3,000 written notes. For Asia he drew on Marco Polo.
762: An Arab geographer, a Norman king, 15 years, and south at the top.
In 1154 the Arab geographer al-Idrisi completed a great atlas of the world for Roger II, the Norman king of Sicily, after some 15 years of work. Like many maps of the time, it puts south at the top.
763: An admiral's map drawn partly from a chart he said was Columbus's, then forgotten for centuries.
An Ottoman admiral drew this in 1513 from about twenty older charts, including one he said was by Columbus. It lay forgotten until its rediscovery in Topkapı Palace in 1929.
764: The whole world in one book, and beneath it: what is great, to one who sees eternity?
The first modern atlas gathered the world into one standard book in 1570. Beneath it Ortelius placed a line of Cicero: what can seem great in human affairs to one who sees all eternity?
765: A king of Mali holding a gold nugget: Europe learns where the wealth is.
Made in Majorca by the Jewish cartographer Abraham Cresques, it shows Mansa Musa of Mali holding a gold nugget. Europe was learning that Africa had the world's richest king.
766: Jerusalem at the centre, Paradise at the top: a map of faith as much as roads.
The largest surviving medieval map puts Jerusalem at the centre and Paradise at the top, in the east. It was a map of faith and history as much as of roads.
767: A careful map of a place no one has ever found.
A Jesuit scholar placed Atlantis in the middle of the Atlantic, with south at the top, following Plato's story. No trace has ever been found; the map records a legend, not a place.
768: He reportedly had himself lowered into Vesuvius to see for himself.
Kircher pictured the Earth with a fiery core feeding volcanoes through hidden channels. He reportedly had himself lowered into the crater of Vesuvius in 1638 to see for himself.
769: The map that changed the world, by a man who ended up in debtors' prison.
A canal surveyor with no degree mapped the rocks beneath England and Wales, colouring each layer by hand. He later landed in debtors' prison; today it is called the map that changed the world.
770: A whole town seen straight from above, centuries before anyone could fly.
Drawn for Cesare Borgia, it is one of the first accurate town plans seen straight from above, likely measured with a compass and a wheel that counted distance. Leonardo was 50.
771: The Sun takes the centre, and the planets ride around it.
Cellarius's atlas of the heavens gave equal glory to rival theories. In this one, from 1660, the Sun takes the centre as Copernicus proposed, and the planets ride around it.
772: A compromise universe: everything circles the Sun, except Earth.
Tycho Brahe's compromise: the planets circle the Sun, and the Sun circles a motionless Earth. It fit the observations without moving the Earth, so many astronomers preferred it for decades.
773: A mountain sliced open to show what grows at every height.
Humboldt climbed most of Chimborazo in 1802 and drew the mountain as a slice of life, showing which plants grow at each height. It is often called the founding image of ecology.
774: The winds blow on a world that does not yet include America.
A world map built from rules written about 1,300 years earlier: Ptolemy's Geography, printed in Ulm in 1482. The wind-faces blow on a world that does not yet include America.
775: The oldest surviving map of the Americas, drawn by the owner of Columbus's flagship.
The oldest surviving map to show the Americas, drawn in 1500 by Juan de la Cosa, the owner of Columbus's flagship, the Santa María.
776: Smuggled out of Lisbon, carrying Portugal's secrets.
Smuggled out of Lisbon in 1502 by an Italian agent, this chart revealed Portugal's secrets: the line dividing the world with Spain, and the newly found coast of Brazil.
777: Minard's Map of Napoleon's Russian Campaign
422,000 men march on Moscow. About 10,000 come back.
One band tells it all: 422,000 men march on Moscow in tan, and about 10,000 return in black. Charles Minard, a retired engineer, drew it at 88.
778: Diagram of the Causes of Mortality in the Army in the East
The blue is not wounds. It is disease that could have been prevented.
Each wedge is a month of the Crimean War, and the blue is soldiers dying of preventable disease, far more than from wounds. Nightingale drew it to make politicians see.
779: He invented the line chart, and here a gap between two lines tells a whole economy.
William Playfair invented the line chart and the bar chart, and later the pie chart. Here, in 1786, the gap between two lines shows a trade balance at a glance.
780: The deaths cluster around one pump. Remove its handle, and an old theory cracks.
Each black bar is a death from cholera, and they cluster around one water pump on Broad Street. John Snow persuaded officials to remove its handle, and the old idea of 'bad air' began to crack.
781: Two words in a private notebook, 22 years before the book: 'I think'.
In a private notebook in 1837, 22 years before On the Origin of Species, Darwin wrote 'I think' and drew life as a branching tree.
782: He drew the atoms in circles, and lent his name to his own colour blindness.
John Dalton gave each element its own circle and tried to show how atoms join. He was also colour-blind, and studied it so well that the condition was long called 'Daltonism'.
783: A crossbow 24 metres across, perhaps built to impress rather than to fire.
Leonardo designed a crossbow some 24 metres across in Milan in the 1480s. It was never built, and may have been meant to impress a patron more than to fire.
784: Calm reading inside a lightning storm. It is a double exposure.
Tesla sits calmly reading as lightning fills the room, but it is a double exposure: the sparks were shot first and he was added later. A publicity photo that still works.
785: A clock dressed as an elephant, with a bird that sings on cue.
In 1206 al-Jazari described a water clock dressed as an elephant, with a driver and a bird that sings on cue. He used symbols he linked to India, China, Persia and Egypt.
786: Twelve seconds of flight, photographed by a man who had reportedly never used a camera.
Twelve seconds, 37 metres: the first powered flight, December 17, 1903. The man who took the photo, John T. Daniels, had reportedly never used a camera before.
787: The king reportedly suggested sending prisoners. The pilot insisted on going himself.
On 21 November 1783 two men rose over Paris in this balloon, the first humans ever to fly. The king reportedly suggested sending condemned prisoners; Pilâtre de Rozier insisted on going himself.
788: Thousands of materials tested, and the winner was bamboo.
Patent 223,898, granted January 27, 1880. Edison's team tested thousands of materials for the filament; carbonised bamboo later burned for more than a thousand hours.
789: A giant bridge explained with three men and a few sticks.
To explain the Forth Bridge, engineers made a living model: two men's arms and sticks form the cantilevers, and the man in the middle is the Japanese engineer Kaichi Watanabe.
790: The first programmers, and for decades their names were left out of the captions.
ENIAC's first programmers were women, and for decades their names were left out of photo captions. They programmed it by plugging cables and setting switches by hand.
791: Sixteen milliseconds old, and already about 200 metres high.
Sixteen milliseconds after the first atomic explosion, on July 16, 1945, the fireball was already about 200 metres high. A special high-speed camera caught it.
792: Deck Scene of the Great Eastern
The biggest ship ever built, and a photographer who died the next year at 27.
Robert Howlett photographed the Great Eastern, then the biggest ship ever built, while it was being finished. He died the next year at 27.
793: Twitching frog legs started a quarrel, and the quarrel produced the battery.
Galvani saw dissected frog legs twitch when touched with metal and believed he had found 'animal electricity'. His rival Volta disagreed and, to prove it, built the first battery.
794: An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump
The bird lives only if he lets the air back in. What will we sacrifice to know?
A scientist pumps the air out of a glass globe, and the cockatoo inside will die unless he lets it back in. Wright painted a question we still face: what will we sacrifice to know?
795: He boiled urine looking for gold, and found a light in the dark.
In 1669 Hennig Brand boiled down urine looking for gold and instead found an element that glows in the dark: phosphorus. Wright painted the moment a century later.
796: Euclid with colours instead of letters. The Victorians found it strange.
Oliver Byrne taught Euclid with colours instead of letters: red, yellow and blue shapes carry the proofs. Victorians found it strange; designers now call it far ahead of its time.
797: Faraday's Laboratory at the Royal Institution
The basement where the idea behind every power station was found.
This is the basement laboratory where Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831, the principle behind every power station today. Harriet Moore painted it while he still worked there.
798: About 2,000 flights, and reportedly his last words: sacrifices must be made.
Otto Lilienthal made about 2,000 glider flights and was photographed in the air, inspiring the Wright brothers. He died after a crash in 1896, reportedly saying 'sacrifices must be made'.
799: Chronophotograph of a Man on a Bicycle
A photographic gun turns a cyclist into a ripple in time.
Marey, a physiologist, built a 'photographic gun' and stacked moments of motion on one plate. A cyclist becomes a ripple in time, and the idea fed the birth of cinema.
800: A brass pocket computer that told time by the stars.
An astrolabe was a brass pocket computer: it told time by the stars, found latitude and set prayer times. This one was made in Iran in 1654 by Muhammad Zaman.
801: He ran for the one plate he had left.
Stieglitz saw this scene on deck, ran to his cabin for the one plate he had left, and made the picture he believed turned photography from record into art.
802: Her face stirred a nation. She received nothing.
Dorothea Lange made a few exposures in about ten minutes and never asked the woman's name. Florence Owens Thompson's face stirred a nation's conscience; she herself received nothing.
803: The street was crowded, but only the man getting a shoeshine stood still long enough.
The street was full of carriages and people, but the exposure took minutes, so they all vanished. Except one man who stood still to have his boots shined: the first person ever photographed.
804: The Valley of the Shadow of Death
Cannonballs on the road, then off it, or the other way round? The argument is 150 years old.
Fenton photographed this road twice, once with cannonballs on it and once without. People have argued for 150 years over whether he moved them, which may make it the first staged war photograph.
805: Power House Mechanic Working on Steam Pump
After years exposing child labor, he went looking for the dignity of work.
Lewis Hine spent years photographing children in factories to get child labor banned. Then he set out to show the dignity of work, and made this: a man and a machine that need each other.
806: View from the Window at Le Gras
An exposure so long that the sun lights both sides of the courtyard.
The oldest surviving photograph taken with a camera needed an exposure so long, perhaps days, that the sun lights both sides of the courtyard. Then it was lost for half a century, until 1952.
807: A humble broom, defended by pointing to the Dutch masters.

Talbot invented the negative, which let one picture be printed again and again. In the first commercial book illustrated with photographs, he defended this humble broom by pointing to the Dutch painters.
808: A painter would have tidied it up. The camera cared about every stray straw.
A painter would have tidied it up. Talbot's camera recorded every stray straw with the same care, and he realized that this indifference to importance was photography's new power.
809: No camera at all: real seaweed laid on paper, and the sun did the rest.
No camera at all: Anna Atkins laid real seaweed on light-sensitive paper and let the sun do the rest. Her privately made volumes are often called the first book illustrated with photographs.
810: That blue is pure chemistry, and in her hands botany turned into poetry.
The blue is the chemistry of the cyanotype, invented in 1842 by Sir John Herschel, a friend of Atkins' father. Within a year she was using it to turn botany into something close to poetry.
811: She sold fish, held still for long seconds, and became one of the first faces of working people on film.
Elizabeth Johnstone sold fish in Edinburgh. Around 1845 she held still in the sun for long seconds, and her face became one of the first photographs ever made of working people.
812: A break from painting 457 ministers on one canvas, a job that took 23 years.
The painter David Octavius Hill took up photography to help him paint 457 ministers on one canvas, a task that took him 23 years. Here he relaxes with two friends over a jug of ale.
813: Self Portrait as a Drowned Man
Robbed of credit for his invention, he photographed himself dead in protest.
Bayard invented his own process, but France rewarded Daguerre instead. In protest he photographed himself as a suicide: the first staged photograph, and perhaps the first photographic hoax.
814: On the back he wrote: 'The first light Picture ever taken'. He may have been right.

In 1839 a Philadelphia lamp maker held still for minutes in front of his own camera. On the back he wrote 'The first light Picture ever taken', and it may be the first photographic portrait ever made.
815: No negative, no copies, no name. Just one silver mirror, and she still seems ready to answer.
A daguerreotype has no negative: each one is a single mirror-polished silver plate. We do not know her name, but the Boston studio of Southworth & Hawes made her look as if she could still answer.
816: A hand raised as if swearing an oath, more than a decade before Harpers Ferry.
A Black photographer made this portrait of the abolitionist John Brown, hand raised as if swearing an oath, more than a decade before his raid on Harpers Ferry. Washington later emigrated to Liberia.
817: She would become the mother of Virginia Woolf.
Cameron got her first camera at 48, a gift from her daughter. Four years later she photographed her niece Julia Jackson, who would become the mother of Virginia Woolf.
819: The man who coined 'negative' and 'positive', his wild white hair catching the light.
Herschel coined the words 'negative' and 'positive' for photographs and was Cameron's friend for thirty years. She draped him in black and moved in close, so his wild white hair caught the light.
820: Critics called her blur clumsy. She kept it, and it became her signature.
Cameron titled this portrait of the writer 'Carlyle like a rough block of Michael Angelo's sculpture'. Critics mocked her blur as clumsy; she kept it, and it became her signature.
821: The real Alice from Wonderland, now twenty, playing a goddess of fruit.
The girl who inspired Alice in Wonderland, now twenty, poses as Pomona, goddess of fruit. Cameron photographed her the year after Through the Looking-Glass came out.
822: Twenty, unknown, wrapped in velvet. Within a decade the whole world knew her.
Sarah Bernhardt was about twenty and not yet famous when she sat for Nadar, wrapped in velvet. Within a decade she would be the most celebrated actress in the world.
823: He called photography art's most mortal enemy, then kept sitting for it.
Baudelaire called photography 'art's most mortal enemy'. Yet he kept returning to sit for his friend Nadar, and this is how the poet of Paris still looks at us.
824: A mime pretending to be a photographer, when photography was barely fifteen.
The mime Charles Deburau plays Pierrot pretending to be a photographer: a joke about the medium when it was barely fifteen years old. The series won a gold medal at the 1855 Paris Exposition.
825: Exposures took up to 18 minutes, so the worker among the bones is a mannequin.
Nadar was among the first to photograph underground by artificial light. Exposures in the catacombs took up to 18 minutes, so the 'worker' resting among the bones is a mannequin.
826: This sea made him famous. He died in Cairo, far from it, fleeing his debts.
Le Gray's seascapes dazzled Paris and London. A few years later he fled his debts, left his family, and died in Cairo, teaching drawing, far from the sea that made him famous.
827: 800 copies ordered in two months: photography had its first hit.
A lone ship, a band of light and a dark sea: after it was shown in London in 1856, a dealer advertised 800 copies ordered in two months. Photography had its first hit.
828: Painters came to this forest with easels. He came with a camera.
The painters of Barbizon came to this forest to paint trees from life. Le Gray, trained as a painter himself, came with a camera, and showed that light on bark could be enough.
829: Still Life with Fruit and Decanter
From the Crimean War to a bowl of grapes, and then he quit photography for good.
Five years after photographing the Crimean War, Fenton was arranging grapes. Two years later he sold his cameras and went back to the law, leaving photography for good at 43.
831: Victorians were outraged. They didn't know the dying girl was a healthy model.
Victorians were outraged that a camera would intrude on a girl dying of tuberculosis. They did not know it was assembled from five negatives, and the 'dying' girl was a healthy model.
832: An empty London house, two teenage daughters, and nearly 800 pictures.
Lady Hawarden turned the empty rooms of her London house into a studio and photographed her teenage daughters in nearly 800 pictures. She died at 42, less than ten years after she began.
834: Photographed so it could be remembered, then torn down for a boulevard.
Paris hired Marville to photograph its medieval lanes before Baron Haussmann tore them down for wide boulevards. Many of the streets he recorded vanished within a few years.
835: A record made for city planners, before the bulldozers, that became art.
Glasgow hired Annan to photograph its worst slums before they were demolished. A record made for city planners became one of the first great works of social documentary.
836: The dead were already buried. Historians believe the bones were dug up for the picture.
Beato arrived months after the 1857 battle in Lucknow, when the dead had been buried. Historians believe he had bones dug up and scattered for the picture, one of the first images of war's carnage.
837: The tiny man on the pharaoh's crown is there just to show the scale.
In 1850 Du Camp traveled up the Nile with his friend Gustave Flaubert and photographed Abu Simbel half buried in sand. The man perched on the pharaoh's crown is there to show the scale.
838: The Great Pyramid and the Great Sphinx
Developed in a desert tent where the chemicals could boil.
Frith coated and developed his glass plates in a dark tent in the desert heat, where the chemicals could boil. For most Victorians, these prints were the first true sight of the pyramids.
839: Lincoln reportedly said this photograph helped make him president.
Taken the day of Lincoln's New York speech in 1860 and copied endlessly during the campaign. Lincoln reportedly said that Brady and the Cooper Union speech made him president.
840: The body was dragged 40 yards for a better shot. No one noticed for 112 years.
Gardner's team dragged this dead soldier about 40 yards into a better setting and propped a rifle beside him. The staging went unnoticed until a historian proved it in 1975.
841: Barthes looked at him and wrote: 'He is dead and he is going to die.'
Lewis Powell, 21, in irons after the plot to kill Lincoln, weeks before his hanging. Roland Barthes wrote of this photograph: 'He is dead and he is going to die.'
842: The man listed as 'E. J. Allen' is really the Union's spymaster.
The man listed as 'E. J. Allen' is really Allan Pinkerton, the Union's spymaster, under his alias. Lincoln, towering in his stovepipe hat, had come to push his generals to fight.
843: The blank horror of war, against all its pageantry.
Gettysburg, July 1863. Gardner's book printed it with a lesson: such a picture shows 'the blank horror and reality of war, in opposition to its pageantry'.
844: Ancient Ruins in the Cañon de Chelle
After the Civil War dead, he drove his darkroom wagon west, toward silence.
After photographing the Civil War dead, O'Sullivan took his darkroom wagon west with government surveys. Here the streaked cliff dwarfs an ancestral Pueblo ruin and the tiny figures at its foot.
845: Giant glass plates hauled in by mule, and Congress was persuaded to save the valley.
Watkins hauled a camera taking glass plates 18 by 22 inches into Yosemite by mule. His prints are credited with helping persuade Congress to protect the valley in 1864.
846: Before the galloping horse, he signed his work 'Helios', after the sun god.
Years before he froze a galloping horse, Muybridge made his name in Yosemite, signing his work 'Helios', the Greek sun god. His 1872 views of the valley won a gold medal in Vienna the next year.
848: He fought for photography as art, then publicly declared it dead.
Emerson, a doctor, fought fiercely for photography as an art equal to painting. Then, a year after his manifesto, he published 'The Death of Naturalistic Photography' and renounced it.
849: Lodgers in a Crowded Bayard Street Tenement
Five cents for a spot on the floor, lit by exploding flash powder at night.
Five cents a spot on the floor. Riis, a police reporter, burst into rooms like this at night with exploding flash powder, and his book How the Other Half Lives shook New York.
850: Three hours in a blizzard, waiting for one coach.
Stieglitz stood for three hours in a February blizzard, waiting for one coach to come through the snow, using a hand camera serious photographers then looked down on.
851: A driver watering his steaming horses, and a lonely man felt less alone.
Back in New York after years in Europe, Stieglitz felt lost. Then he saw a driver tenderly watering his steaming horses in the cold, and later wrote that the sight made him feel less alone.
852: New Yorkers called it ugly. He saw the bow of a monster steamer.
New Yorkers thought the new Flatiron Building was ugly. Stieglitz saw it through snowy branches and wrote that it seemed to move toward him 'like the bow of a monster ocean steamer'.
853: More than 300 pictures of one woman: a portrait, he believed, had to be a life.
Stieglitz photographed Georgia O'Keeffe more than 300 times over two decades, often just her hands. He believed a true portrait could not be one picture; it had to be a life.
854: A small-town bookkeeper who shot his family before and after work.
White was a bookkeeper in a small Ohio town who photographed his family before and after work. He became one of the great teachers of photography; among his students was Dorothea Lange.
855: A mother sending her daughter out into the world, by a woman who started art school at 37.
Käsebier raised three children before she went to art school at 37. This mother sending her daughter out into the world became one of the most admired photographs of its time.
856: White on white, and reportedly the highest price yet paid for an art photograph.
White on white, in a whitewashed stable. In 1899 a print of The Manger sold for $100, reported as the highest price yet paid for an art photograph.
857: A violinist at 22, who would co-write the first Native American opera.
Zitkala-Ša, a Yankton Dakota violinist and writer, was 22 here. She went on to co-write the first Native American opera and fight for her people's citizenship and voting rights.
858: A cigarette, a beer stein, petticoats showing: every rule for a lady, broken on purpose.
A cigarette, a beer stein, petticoats showing: one of America's first women photojournalists posed herself breaking every rule for a lady, in 1896.
859: Louis Firetail in American History Class
Staged to show 'progress' in Paris. Today it reads very differently.
A Sioux student in full traditional dress stands among classmates in suits. The school staged the scene to show 'progress' at the 1900 Paris Exposition; today it reads very differently.
860: The title said these people were disappearing into the dark. They were not.
Curtis opened his twenty-volume North American Indian with this picture, and its title announced his belief that these people were disappearing into the dark. They were not.
861: Seven riders, cliffs a thousand feet high, and a project that nearly ruined him.
Seven Navajo riders cross the canyon floor beneath cliffs that tower a thousand feet above them. Curtis spent three decades on a project that nearly ruined him financially.
862: A chief's daughter who dug clams for a living, paid a dollar per picture.
Kikisoblu, daughter of the chief Seattle was named after, earned a living digging clams and doing laundry. Curtis recalled paying her a dollar per picture; she died the same year.
863: The original negative shows an alarm clock between them. He erased it.
Between these two Piegan men, the original negative shows an alarm clock. Curtis erased it before publishing, to keep his subjects in a timeless past that never quite existed.
864: Italian Family in the Baggage Room, Ellis Island
He hoped his students would see these newcomers as they saw the Pilgrims.
Hine was a schoolteacher when he began photographing Ellis Island, hoping his students would regard these newcomers as they did the Pilgrims who landed at Plymouth Rock.
865: 48 inches high. He measured children against his coat buttons so no one could lie.
Hine's caption: 'Sadie Pfeifer, 48 inches high, has worked half a year.' He measured children against his own coat buttons, so no mill owner could claim they were older.
866: Newsies at Skeeter's Branch, St. Louis
Monday, eleven in the morning, no school. The note says: 'They were all smoking.'
Eleven in the morning on a Monday, and these newsboys should be in school. Hine's note says simply: 'They were all smoking.'
867: To get past the guards, the photographer sometimes posed as a Bible salesman.
These boys picked slate out of coal by hand, in clouds of black dust. To get past the guards at mines and mills, Hine sometimes posed as a Bible salesman or a fire inspector.
868: Swung out in a basket above Fifth Avenue to catch an ironworker he nicknamed Icarus.
To photograph the Empire State Building going up, Hine, in his mid-fifties, was swung out in a basket high above Fifth Avenue. He named this ironworker after the boy who flew too close to the sun.
869: A former sailor and failed actor, turning his camera on the street trades of Paris.
Atget had been a sailor and a struggling actor before he took up the camera. Among his first subjects were the street trades of Paris, like this organ grinder and the girl who sang beside him.
870: The Surrealists adored it. He insisted: 'These are simply documents.'

The Surrealists loved Atget's shop windows, where mannequins mingle with reflections of the street. When Man Ray published his work, Atget asked that his name be left off: 'These are simply documents.'
871: An empty park at dawn, sold to painters as a 'document for artists'.
Atget walked out early, before people filled the park, and photographed it in near silence. He sold such pictures to painters as 'documents for artists', and lived in poverty most of his life.
872: Without one young American who bought his negatives, he might be forgotten.
After Atget died in 1927, a young American, Berenice Abbott, bought thousands of his prints and negatives and spent decades making the world see him. Without her, he might be forgotten.
873: Around 10,000 photographs of old Paris, and hardly a person in them.
Atget made around 10,000 photographs of old Paris with a heavy wooden view camera he used to the end, long after lighter cameras arrived. Few people appear; the city itself is the subject.
874: This blaze of color is from 1911. Nine years later the Emir fled the Red Army.
This blaze of color is from 1911, made from three black-and-white exposures through red, green and blue filters. Nine years later the Emir fled the Red Army into Afghanistan.
875: Tolstoy at 79, in what is considered Russia's first color portrait photograph.
In May 1908 Prokudin-Gorsky traveled to Yasnaya Polyana to photograph Tolstoy, then 79. The result is considered the first color photographic portrait made in Russia.
876: They look like our contemporaries, but the tsar himself sent the photographer.

Three girls offer berries in front of a log house in 1909. They look like our contemporaries, but Tsar Nicholas II had lent the photographer a railway car fitted as a darkroom to capture his empire in color.
877: Eighty-four years old. Sixty-six years of service. In color.
The caption reads: 'Pinkhus Karlinskii. Eighty-four years old. Sixty-six years of service.' A Jewish floodgate keeper, photographed in color more than a century ago.
878: Each color was once three black-and-white plates, fused only decades later.

Each of these colors was once three black-and-white glass plates. The Library of Congress bought them from Prokudin-Gorsky's heirs in 1948, and only digital scans decades later fused them into this summer day of 1909.
879: Scott's ship, framed by ice. Fourteen months later, Scott was dead.
Ponting framed Scott's ship, Terra Nova, from inside an ice cave in January 1911. Fourteen months later, Scott and four companions died on their way back from the South Pole.
880: Stone stairs worn by centuries of feet into soft waves.
Evans, a London bookseller, saw the stairs of Wells Cathedral worn by centuries of feet into soft stone waves. He called it 'a sea of steps' and waited for the light to prove it.
881: The Soul of the Blasted Pine
Naked women, often herself, merged with storm-twisted trees. In 1907.

Anne Brigman carried her camera into the Sierra Nevada and photographed nude women, often herself, merged with storm-twisted trees. In 1907 it was radical; Stieglitz made her a Photo-Secession fellow.
882: Looking Down Sacramento Street, San Francisco
People in their best clothes, watching the fire come up the street toward them.
The earthquake wrecked Genthe's studio, so he borrowed a camera from a shop and went out. People in their best clothes watch the fire come up the street toward them.
883: A plant stem, magnified up to 30 times, until it becomes a tower.
Karl Blossfeldt, an art teacher, photographed plants magnified up to 30 times as models for his students. His 1928 book made him famous at 63, and this horsetail stem looks like a tower.
884: Pledge of Allegiance, Raphael Weill School
They pledge allegiance weeks before the camps. The Army hid these photographs.
Children of Japanese descent pledge allegiance in San Francisco, weeks before being sent to camps. The Army impounded many of Lange's internment photographs, and few were seen for decades.
885: The furrows run right up to the door. Nobody lives here anymore.
Tractor furrows run right up to the door of an empty farmhouse in the Texas Panhandle. Machines let one man farm what tenant families once worked, and Lange titled it 'Tractored Out'.
886: The book sold a few hundred copies. Twenty years later her face was an icon.
Evans and the writer James Agee lived among sharecroppers in Alabama in 1936. Their book about them sold only a few hundred copies; twenty years later it was a classic, and her face an icon.
887: The mill, the houses, the graves: a whole life in one frame.
A cross in the graveyard, the workers' houses, the mill chimneys behind: Evans stacked a whole life in a steel town into one frame, from the job to the grave.
888: Farmer and Sons Walking in the Face of a Dust Storm
The fence is nearly buried. The photographer was 20.
Arthur Rothstein was 20 when he photographed farmer Arthur Coble and his sons in Oklahoma. The fence is nearly buried, and the picture became the face of the Dust Bowl.
889: The Bleached Skull of a Steer
He moved the skull a few steps, and critics cried that the drought was faked.
Rothstein moved this skull a short distance to improve the picture. When newspapers found out, critics used it to accuse the government of faking the drought.
890: A town named for a man who sold pies, caught on rare early color film.
Pie Town was named for a man who sold pies to travelers. In 1940 Russell Lee found Dust Bowl families homesteading there and photographed them on early color film, a rarity then.
891: Segregation, made visible in a single staircase.
On a Saturday afternoon in Belzoni, Mississippi, a man climbs the outside stairs to the movie theater's 'colored' entrance. Marion Post Wolcott made segregation visible in a single staircase.
892: A mop, a broom, and a pose his boss warned could get them all fired.
Stung by segregation in Washington, Gordon Parks posed Ella Watson, a government cleaner, with her mop and broom like Grant Wood's farmers. His boss warned it could get them all fired.
893: Of some 175,000 government pictures, only about 1,600 are in color.
In wartime Chicago, Delano photographed the railroads on color film, still rare. Of the roughly 175,000 FSA and OWI pictures, only about 1,600 are in color.
894: Women at Work on a Bomber, Long Beach
The color looks modern. So do the women, in jobs once closed to them.

Taken for the Office of War Information in 1942, when millions of American women went into factories. The color looks modern; so do the women, doing factory jobs most had been shut out of before the war.
895: The Tetons and the Snake River
In 1977 this view set off on Voyager, to show strangers what Earth looks like.
896: Made for giant murals the war cancelled. The pictures stayed.
In 1941 the Interior Department hired Adams to make huge photomurals for its new building. The war ended the project within a year, but left the public these pictures.
897: The same cliff ruin, seventy years after another government photographer.
Nearly seventy years after Timothy O'Sullivan photographed this same cliff ruin for a government survey, Adams came on a government job too, and found the light moving across it.
898: In the wilderness master's hands, even concrete looks like a canyon wall.
The great wilderness photographer was also asked to show what people had built, and he turned his lens on Boulder Dam. Even concrete, in his hands, looks like a canyon wall.
899: His photographs helped create this park. Then he came back to shoot it.

Adams' 1938 book of Sierra photographs reached Interior Secretary Harold Ickes and helped persuade Washington to create Kings Canyon National Park in 1940. Then he came back to photograph it for them.
901: Crowds came to stare at the empty wall. That is when she became famous.
For four centuries she was simply a fine painting. In 1911 she was stolen from the Louvre, and crowds came to stare at the empty wall. That is when she became the most famous painting in the world.
902: He is not hiding the wound. He is showing he is back at work.
Painted weeks after he cut off his ear, in a fur cap, with a Japanese print on the wall behind him. He is not hiding the wound; he is showing that he is back at work.
903: 1,900 years old, laid over the face of the dead, and still looking right at us.
Painted on wood about 1,900 years ago and laid over the face of the dead, these are the oldest portraits that still look back at us as if we had just met.
904: One strap slipped off her shoulder, and Paris was scandalized.
In the original, one strap had slipped off her shoulder. Paris was scandalized; Sargent repainted the strap, moved to London, and later called it the best thing he had ever done.
905: He wanted you to see grey and black. The world saw his mother.
Whistler titled it 'Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1'; he wanted you to see shapes and tones, not his mother. The world ignored him, and she became an icon of motherhood.
906: Her left eye was never inlaid. 3,300 years later, no one knows why.
Found in 1912 in the ruins of the sculptor Thutmose's workshop. Her left eye was never inlaid, and 3,300 years later no one knows whether he simply never finished.
907: Only the lips and chin survive, and the mouth alone is enough.
Only the lips and chin survive, carved in yellow jasper, a stone so hard it was rarely sculpted. No one knows which queen she was, and the mouth alone is enough to stop you.
908: After her death her statues were smashed and dumped in a quarry. This one came back.
A woman who ruled Egypt as pharaoh for some twenty years. After her death her statues were smashed and dumped in a quarry; archaeologists pieced this one back together in the 1920s.
909: Three centuries too old for Agamemnon, but the name never came off.
Schliemann was sure he had found the face of Homer's king. The gold mask is roughly three centuries too old for Agamemnon, but the name he gave it in 1876 never came off.
910: A scroll and writing tablets: a Pompeii couple, proud that they could read.
A couple from Pompeii chose to be painted holding a scroll and writing tablets, proud that they could read. Vesuvius buried their wall in 79 AD and kept their faces for us.
911: Father, mother, two sons. One face has been rubbed out by his brother's order.
Father, mother, two sons. One face has been rubbed out: after Caracalla had his brother Geta murdered in 211, Geta's image was erased across the empire, even here.
912: Cover one half of the face, then the other: gentle, then stern.
Cover one half of the face, then the other: one side looks gentle, the other stern. Painted in the 6th century, it survived because it hung far from Constantinople, at the foot of Mount Sinai.
913: Worn at a king's hip, it is believed to show the queen mother who raised armies.
Carved in ivory for a king of Benin to wear at his hip, it is believed to show Idia, the queen mother who raised armies for her son. British troops took it in the looting of 1897.
914: Some faces return at different ages, like a family album in clay.
Moche potters in ancient Peru shaped portraits of real people as vessels, and some of the same faces appear again at different ages, like a family album in clay.
915: 'Jan van Eyck was here, 1434.' And in the mirror, maybe he is.
Above the mirror the painter wrote 'Jan van Eyck was here, 1434'. Look into the convex mirror and you find two tiny figures in the doorway; one of them may be him.
916: Portrait of a Man in a Red Turban
'As I can', says the frame. Many believe he painted his own face in a mirror.
On the original frame he wrote 'Als ich can', as I can, a modest motto and a pun on his own name. Many believe the man in the red turban is van Eyck himself, looking into a mirror.
917: Nobody knows who she was, but that wary sideways glance still reaches us.
No one knows who she was. Christus was among the first to set a sitter in a real room instead of a flat background, and her wary sideways glance still reaches us.
918: A veil so thin you can see her forehead through it.
Her name is lost; only the lowered eyes and tightly folded hands remain. Rogier painted the starched veil so thin that you can see her forehead through it.
919: An Old Man and His Grandson
The painter refused to hide the swollen nose. The child doesn't even notice it.
The grandfather's nose is swollen by a skin disease, and the painter refused to hide it. The child does not notice; he looks up only at the face he loves.
920: There is no angel here. Whoever stands in front of it takes his place.
There is no angel in this Annunciation. Mary raises her hand toward the space in front of her, so whoever stands before the painting takes the angel's place.
921: She was about sixteen, and the ermine is a double pun.
Cecilia Gallerani was about sixteen. The ermine is a double pun: its Greek name echoes her surname, and a court poet called her lover, the Duke of Milan, 'the white ermine'.
922: Face-on, a pose reserved for Christ, 'in everlasting colours'. He was 28.
At 28, Dürer painted himself face-on, a pose until then reserved for images of Christ, and wrote that he made himself 'in everlasting colours'. Few artists ever claimed so much.
923: A thistle that hints at faithfulness, a year before an arranged marriage.
At 22, far from home, Dürer painted himself holding a thistle whose German name hints at a man's faithfulness. A year later he married the bride his father had chosen for him.
924: Portrait of the Artist's Mother at the Age of 63
No flattery at all. Two months later he added the night she died.
Dürer drew his mother at 63, gaunt and ill, without a trace of flattery. About two months later he added a note on the same sheet recording the night she died.
925: Rembrandt sketched it at an auction, then painted himself in the same pose.
In 1639 the painting came up for auction in Amsterdam. Rembrandt sketched it on the spot, and a year later painted himself in the same pose.
926: He never confirmed she was his lover, but he signed her arm.
Her armband bears Raphael's own name. Tradition says she was Margherita, a baker's daughter and his lover; he never confirmed it, but he signed her arm.
927: Portrait of a Man with a Quilted Sleeve
The real star is the sleeve, pushing out of the frame toward you.
Titian was barely twenty, and the real star is the sleeve: a great quilted blue mass pushing out of the frame toward you. Who the man is remains an open argument.
928: Under 30 centimetres tall, yet it shaped how history sees a king.
The image of Henry VIII that history remembers was shaped by Holbein. This panel, under 30 centimetres tall, is the only portrait of the king by Holbein's own hand known to survive.
929: Christina of Denmark, Duchess of Milan
If she had two heads, she reportedly said, one would be at the king's service.
Henry VIII sent Holbein to paint the 16-year-old widowed duchess as a possible bride. She is said to have answered that if she had two heads, one would be at the king's service.
930: A woman at the easel, when that was almost unheard of.
A woman painter was almost unheard of when Sofonisba painted herself at the easel. She later served the Spanish court, and in her nineties was visited by the young Van Dyck, who sketched her.
931: Raised as a court curiosity, painted as a girl in a fine dress, not a monster.
Antonietta was born with hair covering her face and grew up as a curiosity at European courts. Lavinia painted her holding a note that tells her story, as a girl in a fine dress, not a monster.
932: An emperor, built from pears, peas, corn and flowers.
This is Emperor Rudolf II, built from pears, peas, corn and flowers. In 1648 Swedish troops took it from Prague as war loot, and it still hangs in a castle in Sweden.
933: Venice sent its finest painter to the conqueror of Constantinople. Six months later he was dead.
In 1479 Venice sent its finest painter to the sultan who had conquered Constantinople. Bellini dated this portrait November 1480; Mehmed died six months later.
934: 'With time', says her note. Not a portrait so much as a warning to you.
She points to herself and holds a note that reads 'Col tempo', with time. It is not a portrait of an old woman so much as a warning to whoever is looking.
935: Bankrupt, house sold, painted without pity. Tired, but not defeated.
Three years after his bankruptcy, with his house and collection sold, Rembrandt painted himself without pity. The face is tired, but it is not defeated.
936: No one has ever explained the two great circles behind him.
No one has ever explained the two great circles behind him. Old and in debt, Rembrandt stands with his palette and brushes, as if to say that this, at least, is still his.
937: At first he held a brush. In the end he simply folded his hands.
Painted in the year he died, after he had buried his wife and his son Titus. X-rays show he first held a brush; in the end he simply folded his hands.
938: 'Too true,' the pope reportedly murmured. Centuries later Bacon made him scream.
The pope is said to have looked at it and murmured 'Troppo vero', too true. Three centuries later Francis Bacon painted it again and again, turning the pope's silence into a scream.
939: Enslaved in the painter's workshop, freed the same year, and then a painter himself.
Juan de Pareja was enslaved in Velázquez's workshop. The painter portrayed him with dignity in Rome in 1650, signed his freedom papers that year, and Pareja became a painter himself.
940: He isn't laughing, and nobody called him a cavalier in his lifetime.
He is not laughing, only half smiling, and no one called him a cavalier in his lifetime. The title was invented in the 19th century, after a bidding war in Paris made him famous.
941: Mad Babs was real, a woman locked in the same workhouse as the painter's son.
'Malle Babbe' means Mad Babs, and she was a real woman of Haarlem: a 1653 record places her in the city's workhouse, where Hals's own son had also been confined.
942: Probably no one at all: no beauty to hide behind, only light and a shy look.
Like the Girl with a Pearl Earring, she is probably no one: a 'tronie', a study of a face. Vermeer gave her no beauty to hide behind, only light and a shy, open look.
943: Barely bigger than a postcard, with an upside-down man hidden underneath.
One of Vermeer's smallest paintings, barely bigger than a postcard. X-rays reveal another face beneath it: an upside-down portrait of a man that he painted over.
944: For two centuries her work was sold as a Hals, until her monogram turned up.
For two centuries her paintings were sold as works by Frans Hals. In 1893 her monogram was found under a false Hals signature, and the woman at the easel got her name back.
945: Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting
Men could only paint Painting as a woman. She simply painted herself.
Male painters could only show Painting as a woman. Artemisia was a woman, so she painted herself as Painting itself, hair loose, arm raised, lost in her work.
946: A guide for a sculptor who never met the king. The marble burned; this survived.
Painted so that Bernini, in Rome, could carve the king's bust without ever meeting him. The marble bust was lost in a fire; the three faces painted to guide it are what remains.
947: Portrait of a Cardinal (Niño de Guevara)
The Grand Inquisitor, in rare spectacles, and behind them a gaze that judges you.
Cardinal Niño de Guevara was the Grand Inquisitor of Spain. El Greco gave him something rare in a portrait of the time, spectacles, and behind them a gaze that seems to judge you.
948: A few fast strokes he never sold. She stayed in his house until he died.
Hogarth painted a London street seller in a few fast strokes and never sold it. The girl with a basket of shrimp on her head stayed in his house until he died.
949: 90,000 people came to say goodbye, and someone pencilled 'Au revoir' on the back.
When an American bought it in 1922, some 90,000 people came to say goodbye at the National Gallery. Its director pencilled 'Au revoir' on the back; it returned once, on loan, a century later.
950: Convinced spirits were tormenting him, he pinched himself and carved the faces.
Messerschmidt left Vienna convinced that spirits were tormenting him. Pinching himself in front of a mirror, he carved more than sixty grimacing heads; this is one of them.
951: Critics were shocked by one detail: you can see her teeth.
When it was shown in Paris in 1787, critics were shocked by one detail: her parted lips show her teeth. A smile like that broke the rules of portraits of the time.
952: Same pose, proper silk: the first version looked to Paris like underwear.
The first portrait of the queen, in a simple muslin dress, caused a scandal in 1783, as if she had been shown in her underwear. Vigée Le Brun quickly painted this one, same pose, in proper silk.
953: Only four women allowed in the Academy, so she painted herself teaching two more.
The Royal Academy allowed only four women members at a time. Labille-Guiard painted herself with two of her students, a quiet manifesto for training women to paint.
954: A dignified gaze of her own, and a name recovered only in 2019.
Painted six years after France abolished slavery, it gave a Black woman a rare dignified gaze of her own. Her name, Madeleine, was only recovered in 2019.
955: Portrait of Antoine Lavoisier and His Wife
She drew the plates for his chemistry book. After the guillotine, she published his last.
Marie-Anne Lavoisier worked beside her husband in the lab and drew the plates for his chemistry book. Six years after this portrait he was guillotined; she published his last work.
956: The Athenaeum Portrait of George Washington
Unfinished on purpose: he reportedly called the copies his hundred-dollar bills.
Stuart never finished it; he kept the original to paint dozens of copies, which he reportedly called his hundred-dollar bills. The face ended up on the one-dollar bill.
957: A glass of medicine, a thank-you note, and how close he came.
Goya painted his doctor holding a glass of medicine to his lips, and wrote beneath it his thanks for saving his life in 1819. It is a portrait of gratitude, and of how close he came.
958: Leaning forward, hands on his knees, mid-argument: the face of a new ruling class.
Ingres struggled with the pose until he saw Bertin leaning forward, hands on his knees, in the middle of a conversation. That impatient body became the face of a new ruling class.
959: The Woman with a Gambling Mania
Painted for a doctor who read madness on faces. What remains is simply a person.
Géricault painted ten asylum patients for a doctor who believed madness could be read on the face. Five portraits survive, and in this one what remains is simply a person.
960: Chopin at the piano, George Sand beside him. Then the canvas was cut in two.
Delacroix painted Chopin at the piano with George Sand listening beside him. After the painter's death the canvas was cut in two, and the lovers now hang in different countries.
961: Tearing at his hair, staring straight out, and kept by him until he died.
Courbet was in his early twenties when he painted himself tearing at his hair and staring straight out. He never sold it, and it was still with him when he died.
962: Berthe Morisot with a Bouquet of Violets
Green eyes painted dark. She married his brother and kept her own name.
