Manet painted fellow painter Berthe Morisot in black, her green eyes turned dark. Two years later she married his brother Eugène, and kept painting under her own name.
963: He never said who she was, and Russia has been guessing ever since.
Kramskoi never said who she was, and Russia has been guessing since 1883. Some see Tolstoy's Anna Karenina in her; the painter simply called her 'Unknown'.
964: Four days in a hospital gown, eyes wandering. Ten days later he was gone.
Repin painted his friend in a military hospital over four days in March 1881, in a hospital gown, eyes wandering. Mussorgsky died about ten days later.
965: Two months sitting still to catch the freshness of a single moment.
Vera Mamontova was eleven and had to sit still for nearly two months. Serov, just 22, was chasing one thing: the freshness of a single moment, and he caught it.
966: The Daughters of Edward Darley Boit
Four sisters, each a little farther from the light.
Four sisters in a dim Paris apartment, each a little farther from the light. None of them married, and the two huge vases beside them now stand next to the painting in Boston.
967: His friend's wife, the woman he loved, trapped in the underworld by a pomegranate.
The model was Jane Morris, his friend's wife and the woman he loved. He painted her as Proserpine, trapped in the underworld for tasting a pomegranate, and began it at least eight times.
968: Dressed in red to soften her father's image. A year later he fell.
The daughter of Argentina's ruler Juan Manuel de Rosas, painted in Federalist red to soften his image. A year later her father fell, and she followed him into exile in England.
969: Twenty years old and crowned a king. Three years later he was dead.
Maurycy Gottlieb, a Jewish painter from Galicia, painted himself wearing a crown as Ahasuerus when he was twenty. Three years later he was dead at 23, a talent the world barely met.
970: Born into slavery, now seated in the pose of art's most famous mother.
Tanner posed his mother like Whistler's Mother, the most famous mother in art. Sarah Tanner was born into slavery and sent north by her parents; here she takes that same seat of honour.
971: The background swirls like a starry night. His face stays perfectly still.
Perhaps the last self-portrait he painted, in the asylum at Saint-Rémy. The background swirls like the sky of The Starry Night, but his face stays perfectly still.
972: He wanted 'the heartbroken expression of our time'. Two months later he was dead.
Van Gogh wanted to paint 'the heartbroken expression of our time'. Dr Gachet, who looked after him in his final weeks, was a melancholic himself; within two months Vincent was dead.
973: Portrait of the Postman Joseph Roulin
A postman who stood by him after the ear, and was painted six times.
Joseph Roulin, a postal worker in Arles, became one of Van Gogh's few true friends. He stood by Vincent after the ear crisis, and Vincent painted him six times.
974: Madame Cézanne in a Red Armchair
He wanted her as still as an apple. Her patience became the subject.
Hortense Fiquet sat for Cézanne some 29 times, and for years he hid her and their son from his father. He wanted her as still as an apple; her patience became the subject.
975: Vahine no te tiare (Woman with a Flower)
She refused, then came back in her best dress.
Gauguin's first portrait in Tahiti. In his own telling, the woman first refused, then came back in her best dress with a flower behind her ear, ready to be painted.
976: A gift to Van Gogh, weeks before Arles, and the ear.
Gauguin painted himself as Jean Valjean, Victor Hugo's hunted outlaw, and sent it to Van Gogh as a gift. Weeks later he joined Vincent in Arles; their months together ended with the ear.
977: Her parents hung it with the servants. The Nazis stole it. She got it back.
Her parents disliked it and hung it in the servants' quarters. Decades later the Nazis seized it and murdered Irène's daughter and grandchildren; after the war she got it back, and sold it.
978: Little Girl in a Blue Armchair
Sprawled, bored, and posing for no one.
The American jury of the 1878 Paris World's Fair rejected it, which Cassatt never forgot. Her friend Degas had helped paint the background, and the sprawled, bored girl is posing for no one.
979: A customs clerk who painted himself taller than the Eiffel Tower.
A customs clerk who taught himself to paint made himself taller than Paris and its new Eiffel Tower. On his palette are the names of his first wife and, added later, his second.
980: Renamed 'The Lady in Gold' to hide that she was Jewish.
The Nazis stole her and renamed her 'The Lady in Gold' to hide that she was Jewish. In 2006 her niece Maria Altmann won her back from Austria after an eight-year legal fight.
981: His last words, it is said, were 'Send for Emilie'.
Emilie Flöge ran one of Vienna's leading fashion houses and was Klimt's closest companion all his life. His last words, it is said, were 'Send for Emilie'.
982: Twelve years in legal limbo before she could go home.
On loan to New York in 1998, Wally was seized as suspected Nazi loot. She stayed in legal limbo for twelve years, until a $19 million settlement let her go home to Vienna.
983: Looking back over his shoulder, wary and defiant, the year he went to jail for his drawings.
Painted at 22 as a pair to his portrait of Wally, in the same year he spent 24 days in jail over his drawings. He looks back over his shoulder, wary and defiant.
984: Jeanne Hébuterne with Hat and Necklace
A painter herself. The day after he died, she fell from a fifth-floor window.
Jeanne Hébuterne was Modigliani's partner and a painter herself. The day after he died in 1920, she fell to her death from her parents' fifth-floor window, heavily pregnant with their second child.
985: A doctor-to-be called it proof he was abnormal. He painted himself for fifty more years.
Munch emerges from blue darkness in a cloud of his own smoke. In 1895 a medical student cited this painting as proof that he was abnormal; Munch kept painting himself for another fifty years.
986: Self-Portrait on Her Sixth Wedding Anniversary
She painted herself pregnant when she was not. A year later she was.
Possibly the first nude self-portrait by a woman painter. She painted herself pregnant when she was not, having just left her husband; a year later she was, and died weeks after giving birth, at 31.
987: His hand was never cut off. He painted it that way anyway.
Kirchner's hand was never cut off. After a breakdown during military training he painted himself maimed: a painter who could no longer paint, with a nude model behind him.
988: One green line down the nose, and a face built from colour alone.
A green line runs straight down Amélie Matisse's nose and splits her face into warm and cool halves. Her husband showed that a face could be built from colour alone.
989: His dentist and his sister, who never posed side by side.
The farmer is Grant Wood's dentist, the woman his sister Nan, and they never posed side by side. Wood meant a father and daughter; most of the world has seen a married couple.
990: Her name lettered across the top like a sign, before decades of growing barer.
Commissioned by the Finnish Art Society, she lettered her own name across the top like a sign. For thirty more years her self-portraits grew barer, until the last ones were almost a skull.
991: Ten silent years for her partner's career, then blazing red eyes and no apology.
Marianne von Werefkin stopped painting for ten years to promote the career of her partner, Alexej von Jawlensky. When she returned, she painted herself with blazing red eyes, and no apology.
992: Self-Portrait with Hand on the Forehead
Four years before her son was killed, she already looks braced for grief.
Käthe Kollwitz portrayed herself about a hundred times over fifty years. In this etching, four years before her son Peter was killed in the First World War, she already looks braced for grief.
993: Seventeen, in Paris, about to help invent modern Indian art.
Amrita Sher-Gil, half Hungarian and half Sikh, was a 17-year-old art student in Paris when she painted herself. Within a decade she was a founding figure of modern Indian art, and dead at 28.
994: Her famous brother predicted he'd be remembered as Gwen John's brother.
Her famous brother Augustus predicted that in fifty years he would be known as Gwen John's brother. She painted herself at 26, steady and unsmiling, and lived much of her life quietly in France.
995: The bush behind her is a pun on her name. Her hands were probably cut away.
The only Leonardo painting in the Americas. The juniper bush behind her puns on her name, Ginevra, and the panel was later cut down, probably taking her hands with it.
996: No money for models, so he became his own, more than twenty times.
In Paris Van Gogh could not afford models, so he painted himself, more than twenty times in two years. Here the new lessons of colour turn his own face into a field of strokes.
997: 'The straw hat', they call it. The hat is black felt.
Le Chapeau de Paille means 'the straw hat', yet the hat is black felt. The name stuck long after Rubens's death; the woman is thought to be Susanna Lunden, sister of his future wife.
998: He refused to paint her, then took twelve years to finish.
Ingres at first refused to paint her, then took twelve years to finish. Her pose, a finger at her temple, is borrowed from an ancient Roman fresco found at Herculaneum.
999: Shirtsleeves, a silver teapot, and seven years until a famous midnight ride.
Copley painted Paul Revere as a craftsman, in shirtsleeves, holding a silver teapot he might have made himself. Seven years later this silversmith rode through the night to warn of British troops.
1000: The Greek painter who, legend says, died laughing. Rembrandt laughs with him.
Legend says the Greek painter Zeuxis died laughing while painting an ugly old woman. Near the end of his life, Rembrandt cast himself as Zeuxis, laughing at the edge of the dark.
1001: Hundreds of channels, frozen seven months a year, until May sets them loose.
The Lena splits into hundreds of channels on its way to the Arctic Ocean. Its delta, about 32,000 square km, lies frozen some seven months a year, then in May it bursts back into wetland.
1002: It looks like a crater, but no meteorite made it.
It looks like an impact crater, but no meteorite made it. The 40 km Eye of the Sahara is a dome of rock layers that wind and time wore into rings, so big it is easiest to see from orbit.
1003: Astronauts say the island looks like it is bleeding into the sea.
Astronauts say Madagascar looks as if it is bleeding into the sea. Forests cleared for farming let rain wash red soil into the Betsiboka, and its delta now fills more than half of the estuary.
1004: A glacier spreading like batter on a pan, its stripes folded by every surge.
Malaspina pours out of the mountains and spreads like batter on a pan, about 3,900 square km of ice. The zigzag stripes are rock debris, folded each time one of its feeder glaciers surges.
1005: Each circle is one sprinkler arm, drinking an aquifer that refills far too slowly.
Each circle is a field watered by one sprinkler arm turning around a pivot, often about 800 m across. Much of the water comes from the Ogallala Aquifer, which refills far slower than it is pumped.
1006: The floor of a vanished ice age lake, now a racetrack for speed records.
The Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah are the dry floor of a vast ice age lake. They are so flat and hard that drivers have chased land speed records on them for more than a century.
1007: A lake with no outlet: its water can only leave by vanishing into the air.
Gas Hure Lake on the Tibetan Plateau has no outlet, so its water leaves only by evaporating. The angular ponds beside it harvest potash, salts rich in potassium, for fertilizer.
1008: Cold air over a warm sea, and the clouds tile the ocean to the horizon.
Cold air flowing over a warmer sea east of Japan breaks into stratocumulus, cells of cloud that tile the ocean all the way to the horizon.
1009: A glacier floating on the sea, shedding icebergs from its jagged edges.
The Erebus Ice Tongue juts about 11 km into McMurdo Sound, a glacier floating on the sea. Its jagged edges mark where pieces break away and drift off as icebergs.
1010: The paint is alive: countless microscopic algae, blooming as the sea warms.
In June 2025 the sea around the Shetland Islands turned milky green and turquoise. The paint is alive: countless microscopic algae blooming as northern waters warm.
1011: A meteorite's crater, where souls are believed to say goodbye to Earth.
Ghana's only natural lake fills a crater left by a meteorite about a million years ago. The Asante believe souls come here to bid farewell to Earth before the afterlife.
1012: Winter on top, mild weather by the river 1.8 km below.
Snow outlines the rims of the Grand Canyon and leaves its depths bare. The canyon drops about 1.8 km, enough for winter on top and mild weather by the river below.
1013: Where ice once stood, more than 20 km of seawater now fills the fjord.
Alaska's Columbia Glacier has retreated more than 20 km since the 1980s, one of the fastest glacier retreats ever measured. Seawater now fills the fjord where the ice once stood.
1014: Earth's spin coils the clouds like a seashell.
A low pressure system spirals off Iceland. In the Northern Hemisphere, Earth's spin turns the winds rushing toward a low counterclockwise, coiling the clouds like a seashell.
1015: About 9 km tall from the sea floor, and in 2022 it woke after 38 years.
Mauna Loa is the largest volcano on Earth, rising about 9 km from the sea floor. In 2022 it erupted for the first time in 38 years, starting in this summit caldera.
1016: Scientists chase dust devils here because Mars has them too.
Oregon's Alvord Desert is the dry bed of an ice age lake, so flat that dust devils race across it. Scientists study them here because similar whirlwinds sweep the plains of Mars.
1017: A famed canoe trip at the top of the world, with a dozen visitors a year.
The Thomsen River on Banks Island in the Canadian Arctic is a famed canoe trip at the top of the world. In a typical year only about a dozen people visit the park around it.
1018: A volcano hides under this ice, and when it erupts, the ice floods.
Iceland's Skeiðarárjökull flows from the ice cap above Grímsvötn, a volcano hidden under the ice. When it erupts, meltwater can burst out in sudden floods called jökulhlaups.
1019: Redrawn every day by currents, wind and melt, like a sketch that never ends.
Off Russia's Anzhu Islands, sea ice changes from day to day as currents, winds and melting redraw it. The lines across the ice may be pressure ridges where floes collided.
1020: Fed by melting glaciers, it swelled until it became Tibet's largest lake.
Fed by melting glaciers, Siling Co has swelled so much in recent decades that around 2014 it overtook Nam Co as the largest lake in Tibet.
1021: Green where the water is fresher, red where it is saltier.
Iraq's Razazah Lake, called the Sea of Salt, is drying into pools of red and green. The colors are algae: green where the water is fresher, red where it is saltier.
1022: Ancient seabeds crumpled as Africa pushed into Europe, with no plants to hide the folds.
These swirls are rock layers laid down in ancient seas, then crumpled as Africa pushed into Europe. With no plants to hide them, the Anti-Atlas shows its folds like a textbook.
1023: A turquoise sea around the biggest northern fur seal colony on Earth.
Off Alaska's Pribilof Islands, a phytoplankton bloom swirled the Bering Sea turquoise and green. The islands host the largest northern fur seal colony on Earth.
1024: Iceland's largest eruption in over 200 years, glowing orange in false color.
In false color, fresh lava glows orange at Holuhraun, Iceland's largest eruption in more than 200 years. In six months of 2014 and 2015 it covered about 85 square km.
1025: A forest harvested since 1902, and still standing.
In false color, Malaysia's Matang mangroves glow green along the coast. Managed since 1902, it is one of the oldest examples of a mangrove forest harvested sustainably.
1026: The lowest dry land on Earth, and the water drops about a meter a year.
The Dead Sea shore is the lowest dry land on Earth, more than 430 m below sea level, and the water drops about a meter a year. The green squares in the south are evaporation ponds.
1027: Green paint that once left 400,000 people unable to drink from the tap.
Almost every summer, cyanobacteria paint western Lake Erie green. In 2014 a bloom here poisoned the water supply of Toledo, Ohio, and some 400,000 people could not drink from the tap.
1028: Snow in summer above, and enough heat below to power a plant.
Mutnovsky on Kamchatka is a volcano with figure-eight craters and ridges lined with snow even in summer. Its underground heat also powers a geothermal plant.
1029: A hurricane churned the seabed, and the sea turned chalk white.
After Hurricane Frances in 2004, the sea around Andros Island in the Bahamas turned chalk white. The storm had churned up fine carbonate mud from the shallow bank below.
1030: The 'New' River may be one of the oldest on the continent.
Despite its name, West Virginia's New River is thought to be one of the oldest rivers on the continent. In December 2020 its gorge became the newest US national park, the state's first.
1031: Inside this bend, women made quilts that now hang in major museums.
Sunglint lights up the loops of the Alabama River. Inside its great bend lies Gee's Bend, a small community whose women's quilts now hang in major American museums.
1032: Long taken for meteorite craters, they may be magma that cooled underground.
The rings of Jabal Arkanu in the Libyan Sahara were long taken for meteorite craters. Fieldwork suggests they are rings of magma that cooled underground and were later bared by erosion.
1033: Still frozen in May, and about 614 m deep: North America's deepest lake.
In May 2015 ice still covered much of Great Slave Lake, the deepest lake in North America at about 614 m. The Mackenzie River begins at its western end.
1034: A river that flows 2,330 km, and in most years never reaches the sea.
The Colorado River flows some 2,330 km from the Rockies, yet in most years it no longer reaches the sea. Its delta in Mexico is now a ghost of channels, salt and dry mud.
1035: When the tide goes out, the table is set for hundreds of thousands of birds.
At low tide the Bijagós Archipelago bares sand and mudflats full of worms and shellfish, a vital feeding stop for hundreds of thousands of migrating shorebirds.
1036: Tides and currents brushing broken ice across a canvas 400 km wide.
In July, the Arctic's warmest month, currents and tides stir broken ice in Canada's Foxe Basin into patterns like brushwork on a canvas some 400 km wide.
1037: A ring of reefs where manta rays gather, barely above the sea.
This ring of reefs in the Maldives, also called Baa Atoll, is a UNESCO biosphere reserve where manta rays gather. Like most of the country, its land sits barely above the sea.
1038: Cliffs 240 m high, thousands of seabirds, and walrus waiting on the ice.
Akpatok Island in Quebec's Ungava Bay rises from the sea in cliffs up to about 240 m high. Thousands of seabirds nest on them, and walrus and whales haunt the ice floes around it.
1039: Calderas nested inside each other: a mountain that collapsed more than once.
On Simushir in the Kuril Islands, the Zavaritskogo volcano cradles a lake inside calderas nested one within another, the record of the mountain collapsing more than once.
1040: An astronaut looked straight down into the eye, with winds still over 200 km/h.
Astronaut Ed Lu looked straight down into the eye of Hurricane Isabel in September 2003. The storm had just eased from Category 5 to Category 4, with winds still over 200 km/h.
1041: Rectangles tended by women at low tide, ending up in cosmetics worldwide.
The rectangles along Pemba's shore are seaweed farms. Off Tanzania they are tended mostly by women at low tide, and the harvest ends up in food and cosmetics worldwide.
1042: Sea Ice in the Denmark Strait
Ice drifting south past the largest fjord system on Earth.
In July 2020, sea ice drifted south along Greenland's east coast past the mouth of Scoresby Sound, the largest fjord system on Earth.
1043: Two rivers were once one, until lava split them 8,700 years ago.
Iceland's two largest rivers once flowed as one. About 8,700 years ago the Great Þjórsá lava, the country's largest lava flow, split them, and they still run on either side.
1044: A round lake flashing in the sun, and smoke showing which way the wind blew.
Round Lake Iro, about 12 km across, flashes in the sunlight in southeastern Chad. The smoke plumes from nearby fires show the wind was blowing west that day.
1045: Striped rock holding giant dinosaurs above, and oil and gas below.
Bands of red and white rock in Argentina's Neuquén Basin hold some of the richest dinosaur fossils on Earth, including the giant Argentinosaurus. Deeper down lie big oil and gas reserves.
1046: A delta shaped like a bird in flight, built from the river's own silt.
The Ebro Delta, shaped like a bird in flight, is the fourth largest delta on the Mediterranean. Its wetlands and rice fields sit barely above the sea, built from the river's silt.
1047: Jewel-blue ponds that can vanish through a crack and speed the ice to sea.
Each summer, meltwater gathers on Greenland's ice sheet in jewel-blue ponds. Some drain suddenly through cracks to the bedrock, lubricating the ice and speeding its slide to sea.
1048: Great Sand Dunes, Colorado from Space
Dunes 230 m high, dropped where the wind meets the mountains.
North America's tallest dunes, about 230 m high, are piled against Colorado's Sangre de Cristo Mountains, where the wind drops the sand it carried across the valley.
1049: A pink heart on the plains, probably colored by salt-loving microbes.
From orbit, an astronaut caught a pink heart in the Argentine plains. It is Salinas Las Barrancas, a salt flat whose pink is a color often given by salt-loving microbes.
1050: A fan blossoming at the desert's edge: blue where water still flows.
A vast alluvial fan blossoms between the Kunlun and Altun mountains at the edge of China's Taklimakan Desert. Its blue side is where streams still flow; the rest is dry.
1051: A volcano under the sea threw ash some 57 km high.
A day after the undersea volcano Hunga Tonga exploded in January 2022, astronauts saw its plume spread over the Pacific. The blast had thrown ash some 57 km high.
1052: The Thousand Islands of Sinan, Korea
More than 1,000 islands, and twice a day the tide ties them together.
Sinan County in South Korea holds more than 1,000 islands, about a quarter of the country's total. Twice a day the tide pulls back and bares the mudflats that link them.
1053: A lagoon so wide that from one shore you cannot see the other.
Rangiroa in French Polynesia is one of the largest atolls on Earth, a ring of reef about 80 km long. Its lagoon is so wide that from one shore you cannot see the other.
1055: A thin dark thread of water now. In flood, the whole bed runs to the sea.
In the dry season the Rio Lúrio in Mozambique is a pale bed of sand with a thin dark thread of water. In floods the river fills its whole width and carries the sand to sea.
1056: One cloud, one long shadow across the whole desert.
A single towering cloud rises over the Arabian Peninsula and throws a long shadow across the desert. Qatar's coast and Doha lie in view along the Persian Gulf.
1057: Ships sail into the heart of a volcano, and visitors bathe there.
Deception Island is the flooded caldera of a volcano that blew apart about 4,000 years ago. Ships slip through a narrow gap into its heart, and visitors bathe in volcanic hot springs.
1058: Iron and aluminum paint the soil; the lake itself is human-made.
Soils rich in iron and aluminum paint the land around Brazil's Três Marias Reservoir red and yellow. The lake itself is human-made, a dam on the São Francisco River.
1059: The volcano sank long ago. The coral kept climbing and left a necklace.
A ring of reef and islets in French Polynesia marks where a volcano once stood. The volcano sank long ago, but the coral kept building upward and left this thin necklace.
1060: A time machine in stripes: an ocean, rivers and a shallow sea, folded together.
These Xinjiang ridges are a time machine: green sandstone from a Silurian ocean, red sandstone from Devonian rivers and cream limestone from a shallow sea, folded together.
1061: A new satellite that can tell kinds of plankton apart just by their color.
Off Argentina, a phytoplankton bloom spread across the South Atlantic in November 2024. NASA's PACE satellite, launched that year, can tell kinds of plankton apart by color.
1062: About 30 active volcanoes, and these peaks pierce straight through the clouds.
Volcanic peaks of Kamchatka pierce a sea of cloud in this oblique view from the space station. The peninsula has about 30 active volcanoes, one of the densest clusters on Earth.
1063: Water from eight countries, turning the coast milky green far out to sea.
The Zambezi, Africa's fourth largest river, gathers water from eight countries before reaching the Indian Ocean. Its silt turns the coast milky green for tens of km out to sea.
1064: Clouds, the thin blue skin of the air, and black space, in one frame.
Looking toward the horizon over the Philippine Sea, an astronaut caught towering clouds, the thin blue skin of the atmosphere and the black of space in a single frame.
1065: The lights stop exactly where the river's water ends.
Greater Cairo, home to more than 20 million people, glows on both banks of the Nile. Beyond the lights the dark desert begins abruptly, exactly where the river's water ends.
1066: Algae armored in tiny chalk plates, scattering sunlight like milk.
Each late spring, parts of the Black Sea turn turquoise. The color comes from coccolithophores, algae armored in tiny chalk plates that scatter sunlight like milk.
1067: An iceberg twice the size of Chicago, and a research station moved just in time.
In February 2021 Antarctica's Brunt Ice Shelf finally calved an iceberg about twice the size of Chicago, named A-74. A British research station had been moved inland ahead of the break.
1068: Tides sloshing between two countries, stirring silt into swirls of tan and green.
In Solway Firth, between Scotland and England, strong tides slosh water in and out, stirring silt and dissolved plant matter into swirls of tan, green and blue.
1069: The island erupted and all 1,250 residents fled. The lava paths are still there.
Sangeang Api, an island volcano 13 km wide in Indonesia, erupted from 1985 to 1988 and all 1,250 residents fled. The lava channels running west from its summit are still easy to trace.
1070: Brushstrokes wiped out and repainted with every rise and fall of the sea.
At the mouth of Sumatra's Rokan River, the tides push silt back and forth into long brushstrokes. The pattern is wiped out and repainted with every rise and fall of the sea.
1071: Red Beds of the Bighorn Basin, Wyoming
Rust from monsoons over a supercontinent, still glowing 220 million years later.
These red stripes in Wyoming are about 220 million years old. Giant monsoons over the supercontinent Pangea rusted the sediments, and the iron oxide still glows today.
1072: Liquid silver at 3,810 m, written over with the wind.
Sunglint turns the southern end of Lake Titicaca into liquid silver, revealing wind streaks and currents. At about 3,810 m, it is one of the highest large lakes on Earth.
1073: Two icebergs still wear the stripe of rock they carried on the glacier.
Icebergs calve from Argentina's Upsala Glacier into Lago Argentino. Two of them carry a dark stripe of rock debris, the moraine they once wore on the glacier's back.
1074: A tide up to 10 m high, carving swirls twice a day.
In Broad Sound, Queensland, the tide can rise as much as 10 m, the largest on Australia's east coast. Twice a day it floods the mudflats, drains them again and carves these swirls.
1075: No forest to hide them, so the water's old paths lie open to the sky.
On Severny Island in the Russian Arctic, a braided river spreads fans of gravel across bare ground. With no forest to hide them, the water's old paths lie open to the sky.
1076: Islands about 2 m above the sea, and a neighbor offering visas to leave.
Tuvalu's nine coral islands average about 2 m above sea level. As the sea rises, Australia agreed in 2023 to offer visas to Tuvaluans who want to move, a first for climate.
1077: A few meters above the sea, and running almost entirely on sunlight.
Atafu in Tokelau is a ring of coral islets around a lagoon, its land only a few meters above the sea. In 2012 Tokelau became one of the first territories to run almost entirely on solar power.
1078: After about 800 years of quiet, Iceland's lava came back.
In 2021, after about 800 years of quiet, lava returned to Iceland's Reykjanes Peninsula at Fagradalsfjall. In this May view, fresh lava glows red as it spills into the valleys.
1079: More than 2,000 stone arches, all cracked open by buried salt.
Arches National Park in Utah holds more than 2,000 natural stone arches, the densest collection on Earth. Salt layers deep underground flexed the rock and cracked it into fins.
1080: A river that writhes in loops, carrying the silt that built a rice bowl.
The Irrawaddy, Myanmar's largest river, runs about 2,170 km to the Andaman Sea. Near its delta it writhes in loops, heavy with the silt that built the country's rice bowl.
1081: A near perfect circle of forest, drawn not by nature but by law.
The near perfect circle around Mount Taranaki was drawn by law. Since 1881 forest within 9.6 km of the summit has been protected, while dairy farms grew right up to the line.
1082: Legend says a wrecked canoe; geology says sunken land. Both agree the sea came in.
Māori tradition says these drowned valleys are the prow of a canoe, wrecked by a storm god and turned to stone. Geology agrees on one thing: the land sank and the sea flowed in.
1083: Water so clear that satellites can see the seafloor.
In the clear shallows around the Florida Keys, satellites can see the seafloor: sandbars, seagrass and, along the edge, the only living coral barrier reef in the continental US.
1084: From space, Greenland's tip is almost colorless: ice, cloud, snow and a band of blue.
From the Space Shuttle, the southern tip of Greenland looks almost colorless: ice, cloud and snow against black space, with deep fjords notched into the coast and a band of blue sea.
1085: Tomales Bay on the San Andreas Fault
Two shores, two tectonic plates, sliding past each other.
Tomales Bay in California lies right on the San Andreas Fault. Its forested west shore rides the Pacific Plate, its grassy east shore the North American Plate, sliding past each other.
1086: Greenhouses of the Cayambe Valley, Ecuador
Inca fields of corn, now glittering greenhouses full of roses for America.
Where Inca farmers once grew corn and quinoa, Ecuador's Cayambe Valley now glitters with greenhouses. Most are full of roses, cut and flown to the United States.
1087: The river moved on; the state border still follows its old loops.
South of Memphis the Mississippi swings in loops, and every loop it abandons becomes an oxbow lake. The state border still follows channels the river left long ago.
1088: Clockwise here, counterclockwise there: the weather map draws itself.
Over the Bering Sea, clouds circle clockwise around a high and counterclockwise around a low, with the Aleutian Islands in between. Here the weather map draws itself.
1089: The oil smooths the waves, so the slick shines in the sun.
Sunlight glints off the Deepwater Horizon oil slick in May 2010. Oil smooths the waves, so the slick shines brighter or darker than the sea. About 4.9 million barrels spilled in all.
1090: Japan's second largest lake, drained and turned into rice paddies.
In 1957 Japan began draining Lake Hachirō, then its second largest lake, to grow rice. Two decades later most of it had become paddy fields, ringed by an oval dike.
1091: Visitors dig here for crystals with an hourglass hidden inside.
On Oklahoma's Great Salt Plains, visitors dig for selenite crystals with an hourglass shape inside them, a form said to be found nowhere else on Earth.
1092: When high tide comes, barriers now rise from the seabed to guard Venice.
Venice sits on islands in a lagoon at the top of the Adriatic, the Grand Canal tracing an S through it. Since 2020, mobile barriers called MOSE rise from the seabed to hold back high tides.
1093: Europe's tallest dune is walking inland, burying a forest as it goes.
Europe's tallest sand dune rises more than 100 m above the Atlantic near Bordeaux. It is walking inland 4 to 5 m a year, slowly burying the pine forest behind it.
1094: Mountain meltwater runs into the desert to feed a lake.
The Ili River carries meltwater from the Tian Shan into the desert and supplies most of Lake Balkhash. In March its delta still holds ice while the lake breaks into swirls.
1095: Corals that survive some of the hottest seawater on Earth may hold a clue.
Pale green coral reefs fringe the islands of the United Arab Emirates. Gulf corals endure some of the hottest seawater of any reef, a clue for reefs facing a warming ocean.
1096: Sediment paints currents the eye normally cannot see.
Sediment turns the sea off western Italy into a painting, tracing eddies and currents the eye normally cannot see. Each swirl is a body of water turning on itself.
1097: A chain of islands built one by one over a single hot spot.
The Hawaiian Islands trail across the Pacific, each built over a hot spot as the ocean plate slides past. The youngest and largest, the Big Island, is still growing.
1098: A lake gone dry, and on its shore, people buried 40,000 years ago.
Lake Mungo in Australia dried up thousands of years ago. On its old shore lay Mungo Lady and Mungo Man, buried some 40,000 years ago, among the oldest humans known on the continent.
1099: A lake on an island in a lake, weeks before the volcano woke.
Taal is a volcano on an island in a lake, and the island holds a lake of its own. Weeks after this image, in January 2020, it erupted and many thousands of people had to flee.
1100: Storms march to the horizon, and beyond them the thin blue edge of the air.
Over the Amazon basin, thunderstorms march toward the horizon, some leaving rings of cloud as they die. Beyond them a thin blue line marks the edge of the atmosphere.
1101: A river so muddy it is named for its color, and it keeps building new land.
Few rivers carry as much silt as China's Yellow River, named for its muddy water. It builds new land into the Bohai Sea so fast that its delta changes shape within a few years.
1102: It survived a ferocious battle in 1943. Now it faces a rising sea.
Tarawa, the capital atoll of Kiribati, saw a ferocious battle between US and Japanese forces in 1943. Today its people face a slower threat: a sea that keeps rising.
1103: Named for turtles and for having no fresh water, with a brick fort in the middle.
About 110 km west of Key West, the Dry Tortugas were named for their turtles and their lack of fresh water. Garden Key holds Fort Jefferson, one of the largest brick forts in the Americas.
1104: Andros and the Tongue of the Ocean, Bahamas
A few meters deep, then more than a kilometer: a second coastline under water.
Beside Andros Island, turquoise banks only a few meters deep end at the Tongue of the Ocean, a trench more than a kilometer deep. From orbit the drop looks like a second coastline drawn under water.
1105: One mountain's shadow falls across the border of two countries.
Cerro San Lorenzo, about 3,700 m tall, casts a long shadow on the Argentine and Chilean border. The lakes around it were dug by glaciers that once filled these valleys.
1106: Orange streets, white downtown, and at the lake the city's light simply stops.
Chicago's street grid glows orange with sodium lamps, whiter where LEDs light downtown. Navy Pier juts into the black of Lake Michigan, where the city's light simply stops.
1107: An island of rainbow rock, where people cook with the red soil as a spice.
Hormuz Island is a salt dome that rose through the crust like a bubble, carrying red, yellow and orange rocks with it. Locals even cook with its red soil as a spice.
1108: Folded when Africa crashed into North America, gilded every November.
The ridges of central Pennsylvania were folded when Africa collided with North America some 300 million years ago. In November the forests paint them copper and gold.
1109: Beach Ridges of the James Bay Lowlands
Lines in the snow: old beaches, left as the land rises out of the sea.
Snow traces lines across Canada's James Bay Lowlands. They are old beaches, left behind as the land, freed from the weight of Ice Age glaciers, keeps rising out of the sea.
1110: A leftover of the ice sheet that once buried all of Patagonia.
The Northern Patagonian Ice Field, about 4,200 square km, is a leftover of the ice sheet that once buried Patagonia. Its glaciers flow out on every side, two almost to the Pacific.
1111: Long and narrow in the valleys, broad squares on the plains: fields that follow the land.
In eastern Kazakhstan the fields follow the land: long and narrow up the valleys, broad squares on the plains. By early September many were already harvested and bare.
1112: An atoll that almost vanishes at high tide, and has wrecked many ships.
Bassas da India, between Madagascar and Mozambique, is a lonely atoll that almost vanishes at high tide. Its hidden reef has wrecked many ships over the centuries.
1113: Shrimp Farms of the Guayas, Ecuador
Red mangroves, dark rectangles between them: the ponds of a shrimp superpower.
In false color, mangroves glow red along Ecuador's Guayas River, and the dark rectangles between them are shrimp ponds. Ecuador is now the world's largest shrimp exporter.
1114: Mackenzie River Meets the Beaufort Sea
A river flowing north paints the Arctic sea with milky brushstrokes.
The Mackenzie, North America's longest north-flowing river, pours fresh water and silt into the Beaufort Sea, painting it with milky brushstrokes every summer.
1115: Plankton with chalk shells turned the sea milky green.
In August 2016 the waters off British Columbia turned milky green with coccolithophores, plankton with chalk shells. Local scientists said they had never seen blooms this bright there.
1116: The astronauts watched Etna erupt; its ash fell in Libya.
In October 2002 the space station crew watched Mount Etna erupt. The ash plume curved toward Africa, and ash fell in Libya, more than 550 km away.
1117: So remote that about 100,000 giant tortoises still rule it.
Aldabra is one of the largest raised coral atolls on Earth, so remote that about 100,000 giant tortoises still rule it. Twice a day the tide drains and refills its lagoon.
1118: A new satellite's first look at the Himalaya, and lakes swelling as the ice melts.
Landsat 9, launched in September 2021, captured the Himalaya north of Kathmandu weeks later. Glacial lakes glint among the peaks, swelling as the ice above them melts.
1119: One cold winter, Great Britain became a map drawn in chalk.
In January 2010, during one of Britain's coldest winters in decades, snow covered almost the whole island. From orbit Great Britain looked like a map drawn in chalk.
1120: Cloud Coils over the Kuril Islands
Too little wind and nothing happens; too much and the coils break apart.
Winds over the Kuril Islands set the clouds spinning into coils. Such vortex streets need just the right wind: too weak and air slides around, too strong and the swirls break apart.
1121: Mining Mud Reaches the Atlantic, Brazil
A dam burst inland; weeks later its mud reached the ocean.
In November 2015 a mining dam burst at Bento Rodrigues, Brazil. Weeks later its iron-laden mud reached the Atlantic, in what is counted among Brazil's worst environmental disasters.
1122: A red amphitheater whose rocks hold flying reptiles.
This red amphitheater in Argentina's Sierra de las Quijadas was carved over millions of years. In its rocks, scientists have found fossils of pterosaurs, the flying reptiles.
1123: Stone born from sea life, carved into temples older than the pyramids.
Malta grew from the sea floor: its limestone formed from ancient marine life, and the same honey-colored stone built its temples, which are older than the pyramids of Giza.
1124: About 90 percent of the lake is gone, and it still sustains millions.
Lake Chad has shrunk by about 90 percent since the 1960s. Ancient dunes now rise from its shallows as islands, and the water that is left still sustains millions of people.
1125: People farm and live inside the volcano.
Fogo in Cape Verde is a volcano whose eastern wall collapsed into the sea long ago. Inside its 9 km caldera people farm and live, beside the young cone of Pico, 2,829 m tall.
1126: Swirls of turquoise that end up feeding penguins and whales.
Off Argentina's Santa Cruz province, phytoplankton swirl in turquoise and green. Blooms like this feed a food web that runs from tiny grazers to fish, penguins and whales.
1127: An asteroid came in at a shallow angle and gouged a canoe-shaped trough.
About 600 million years ago an asteroid struck this Australian range at a shallow angle. It gouged a canoe-shaped trough 5 km long and bent the ridges for some 10 km.
1128: Salt Works of Shark Bay, Australia
A place called Useless Loop, where seawater turns to salt pond by pond.
At Useless Loop in Shark Bay, seawater flows through more than 50 ponds, growing saltier in each until salt crystals form. The ponds shift color as the brine concentrates.
1129: Frozen meters deep for eight months, then a flood that stains the sea almost black.
The Kolyma River is frozen meters deep for about eight months a year. Each June it thaws and flushes soil and plant matter into the Arctic, staining its gulf almost black.
1130: Mount Everest from the Space Shuttle
From orbit, the roof of the world looks like crumpled paper.
Everest, 8,849 m, seen from the Space Shuttle in October 1993 with its north and south faces in shadow. From orbit, the roof of the world looks like crumpled paper.
1131: The crater wore away; a ring of lakes still remembers the asteroid.
About 380 million years ago an asteroid slammed into what is now central Sweden. Erosion has worn the crater down, yet a ring of lakes still traces the largest known impact in Europe.
1132: Turned upside down on purpose, so the mountains do not look like holes.
Mount Damavand, Iran's highest peak at about 5,600 m, is a dormant volcano that last erupted some 7,300 years ago. The photo is turned north-down so the relief does not look inverted.
1133: A stream hits flat ground, drops its gravel, and over ages draws a fan.
When a mountain stream bursts onto flat ground it slows, drops its gravel and splits into braided channels. Over ages that spill builds a fan like this one.
1134: A sixth of Australia drains toward it, and it is still usually dry.
Lake Eyre is usually a dry salt pan, even though a sixth of Australia drains toward it. In 2025, Queensland floods traveled hundreds of km across the outback and filled it again.
1135: Its name means nine eyes, after nine narrow channels.
Mataiva in French Polynesia means nine eyes, after nine narrow channels on its south side. Inside, ridges of old reef divide the lagoon into a net of small basins.
1136: So like Mars that rovers are tested here, yet polar bears come for the grass.
Much of Canada's Devon Island is a polar desert so like Mars that scientists test rovers there. Yet the Truelove Lowlands turn green with arctic grasses and draw muskoxen and polar bears.
1137: The Last Drift of Iceberg A-23A
Stuck on the seabed for over 30 years, then one last drift.
Iceberg A-23A broke from Antarctica in 1986 and stayed stuck on the seabed for over 30 years. Once the largest iceberg on Earth, by September 2025 it was crumbling in the South Atlantic.
1138: A glacier few people ever see, so satellites watch it retreat.
Deep in Alaska's Glacier Bay National Park, Grand Plateau Glacier is thinning and pulling back, leaving lakes where ice stood. Few people ever see it, so satellites keep watch.
1139: An entire island built by one volcano, dotted with hundreds of small cones.
Jeju Island off South Korea was built by eruptions of Hallasan, the volcano at its center. Its lava tubes and hundreds of small volcanic cones are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
1140: A glacier that lurches forward, then retreats leaving a painter's palette of lakes.
Múlajökull is a surging glacier in Iceland that lurches forward every few years. As it pulls back it leaves lakes in an artist's palette of colors, each tinted by its own silt.
1141: December, and Fuji stood almost bare.
Mount Fuji's snowcap is usually visible all through December, but at the end of 2020 the mountain stood almost bare, with one of its smallest December snow covers in 20 years.
1142: It looked like an oil spill. It was alive.
Dark threads off the coast of São Paulo in 2017 looked like an oil spill. They were in fact a bloom of plankton, probably dinoflagellates, spread over more than 100 km.
1143: Lightning that shoots up, from the top of a storm toward space.
Above a storm over northern Mexico, astronaut Nichole Ayers caught a gigantic jet, a rare bolt that shoots upward from the top of a thundercloud toward the edge of space.
1144: Everything that breathes lives beneath these thin bands of light.
At sunset from the space station, the atmosphere appears as thin glowing bands of color above a dark Earth. Everything that breathes on the planet lives beneath this thin veil.
1145: Dark round islands in a sea of sand, born from collapsing magma chambers.
The dark round domes of Niger's Aïr Mountains rise from the Sahara like islands. They are ring dikes, formed when magma filled circular cracks above collapsing magma chambers.
1146: Lava so sticky it piled up in wrinkles, like honey cooling on a plate.
Chao, in the Chilean Andes, is the largest known flow of its kind: sticky dacite lava that crept out about 14 km and piled up in wrinkles, like honey cooling on a plate.
1147: In 30 years, a forest became a grid.
In Argentina's Salta province, dry Chaco forest is giving way to crops and cattle. In 30 years a grid of huge fields has replaced almost all of the forest in this scene.
1148: In a dry land, a river that flows all year.
Hingol National Park in Pakistan spans about 6,200 square km of rocky hills, caves and beaches by the Arabian Sea. Its river, the longest in Balochistan, flows all year in a dry land.
1149: Von Kármán Vortex Street off Chile
The same swirls form behind a stick in a stream, only thousands of times smaller.
Wind flowing past Alejandro Selkirk Island, off Chile, sheds whirlpools on alternating sides. The same pattern forms behind a stick in a stream, only thousands of times smaller.
1150: Spring sun cracks the sea ice into marble.
In April 2018, spring sun began breaking the ice of the Beaufort Sea into marbled patterns. It came after one of the smallest winter ice maximums ever recorded in the Arctic.
1151: Snow on the Gulf Coast, the heaviest some places had ever recorded.
In January 2025 a rare winter storm buried the Gulf Coast in snow, the heaviest some places there had ever recorded. Days later astronauts saw the Mississippi Delta still dusted white.
1152: Towers that grew underwater, bared when a distant city took the streams.
Mono Lake in California is at least 760,000 years old and saltier than the sea. Its tufa towers grew underwater and were bared after Los Angeles began diverting its streams in 1941.
1153: The Brown Waters of Rupert Bay, Quebec
Peat and forest soil turn a whole bay the brown of strong tea.
Several large rivers pour into Rupert Bay at the southern end of James Bay. Their water, stained by peat and forest soils, turns the bay the brown of strong tea.
1154: About twice as deep as the Grand Canyon.
Cotahuasi Canyon in Peru is about twice as deep as the Grand Canyon, up to 3.5 km from rim to river, cut by water and ice into a plateau of volcanic rock.
1155: Growing Lakes of the Tibetan Plateau
While lakes elsewhere shrink, these keep growing.
While lakes in much of the world shrink, those on the northern Tibetan Plateau keep growing in number and size. Melting glaciers and more rain are filling the roof of the world.
1156: Rub' al Khali, the Empty Quarter
Half as much sand as the whole Sahara, and dunes taller than 250 meters.
The Empty Quarter of Arabia is the largest sand sea on Earth, about 583,000 square km, holding roughly half as much sand as the whole Sahara. Some of its dunes top 250 m.
1157: An island hidden in fog most of the year, caught on a rare clear day.
Umnak Island in Alaska's Aleutians hides under cloud and fog most of the year. On a rare clear day in May 2014 its snowy volcanoes stood out against a dark sea.
1158: Mine workers scratched one of the earliest alphabets here.
Southwest Sinai hides traces of one of the earliest alphabets ever written, scratched by workers at the ancient Egyptian turquoise mines of Serabit el-Khadim.
1159: Salton Sea and Imperial Valley, California
A sea born by accident, when a river broke through a canal.
The Salton Sea was born by accident in 1905, when the Colorado River broke through an irrigation canal and flooded a desert basin. Today it is saltier than the ocean.
1160: Two cities blaze, joined by threads of light, while the Himalaya barely glimmer.
On a long night exposure from orbit, New Delhi and Lahore blaze below, linked by threads of light, while the snowy Himalaya glimmer faintly to the north.
1161: The remnant of an ice age lake, swirling green almost every autumn.
Swirls of cyanobacteria fill Nevada's Pyramid Lake almost every autumn. The lake, on Paiute land, is a remnant of Lake Lahontan, an ice age lake that once flooded the region.
1162: The child of Krakatau, born from the sea inside its parent's crater.
Anak Krakatau, the child of Krakatau, rose from the sea in 1927 inside the caldera left by the 1883 blast. In September 2026 it erupted for more than a day, disrupting thousands of flights.
1163: A capital built from scratch in under four years, shaped like a bird or a plane.
Brasília was built from scratch in under four years and became Brazil's capital in 1960. Its plan, often likened to an airplane or a bird, curves around an artificial lake.
1164: Tides sculpt the sand, and in the water swim some of the last dugongs.
Off Mozambique, tides and currents sculpt the sand around the Bazaruto islands into ripples and tongues. The park shelters dugongs, among the last in the western Indian Ocean.
1165: Too small to block the wind, but tall enough to stir it.
Winds flowing past Hallasan, the 1,950 m volcano of Korea's Jeju Island, spin the clouds downwind into eddies. The island is too small to block the wind, but tall enough to stir it.
1166: Dunes up to 460 meters, lakes between them, and no one knows where the water comes from.
The Badain Jaran in China holds some of the tallest dunes on Earth, up to 460 m, and between them dozens of lakes. Where their water comes from is still a mystery.
1167: Once the fourth largest lake on Earth, given away for cotton.
Once the fourth largest lake on Earth, the Aral Sea had shrunk to a fraction of its size by 1997, after its rivers were diverted to grow cotton. Here it is already splitting apart.
1168: One dam turned a maze of lakes into a single many-armed reservoir.
A dam begun in 1916 flooded a maze of Quebec lakes into one many-armed reservoir, Réservoir Gouin. The dark patches beside it are recent burn scars, the pale ones logged forest.
1169: A river of ice about 77 km long, fed by its tributaries.
Fedchenko in Tajikistan's Pamirs is one of the longest glaciers outside the polar regions, about 77 km. It starts at 5,200 m and gathers ice from tributaries as it flows.
1170: Mounds built by microbes about 3.4 billion years ago.
In these ancient rocks of Western Australia lie stromatolites about 3.4 billion years old, mounds built by microbes and among the oldest widely accepted traces of life on Earth.
1171: Meltwater on the Amery Ice Shelf
Blue streaks of meltwater on a floating shelf of ice.
In January 2025, meltwater streaked the Amery Ice Shelf in East Antarctica with blue. The Lambert, the largest glacier on Earth, is among those feeding this floating shelf.
1172: Tyndall Glacier's Trail of Icebergs, Chile
A glacier sheds icebergs, and the wind herds them into a line.
Chile's Tyndall Glacier sheds icebergs into Lago Geikie, and the wind herds them into a long drifting trail. The glacier flows from the Southern Patagonian Ice Field.
1173: A volcano that collapsed into itself again and again: craters inside craters.
Ksudach on Kamchatka is a volcano that has collapsed into itself again and again, leaving calderas nested inside calderas. Its last eruption, in 1907, blasted out a new crater.
1174: Red and green ponds, colored by microbes that change with the salt.
Red and green salt ponds stain the south end of San Francisco Bay. Their colors come from microbes and algae that change with salinity, and many are now being returned to marsh.
1175: If the debris dam breaks, a whole lake can empty in hours.
At the ends of Bhutan's Himalayan glaciers, lakes have been forming fast in recent decades. If a natural dam of debris gives way, a lake can empty in hours into the valleys below.
1176: A 145 km wall holding back the dunes, until a river slips through.
Locals call it the red and white mountain. The Mazartagh ridge runs 145 km across the Tarim Basin like a wall, holding back the dunes until a river slips through it.
1177: Nearly fresh at one end, salty at the other.
Lake Balkhash in Kazakhstan is nearly fresh in the west and salty in the east, the two halves joined by a narrow strait. It is the largest lake in Central Asia.
1178: Drifting cells too small to see, feeding one of the richest fisheries on Earth.
In August 2025 phytoplankton bloomed around Bear Island, halfway between Svalbard and Norway. These drifting cells feed the Barents Sea, one of the richest fishing grounds on Earth.
1179: Folds of the Labrador Trough, Quebec
Glaciers scraped the land clean, exposing a mountain belt nearly 2 billion years old.
In northern Quebec, Ice Age glaciers scraped the land clean and laid bare rock folded nearly two billion years ago. Each band is a layer of an ancient mountain belt.
1180: Two rivers carve a maze and meet at its heart.
The Green and Colorado rivers carved Canyonlands into a maze of mesas and gorges, and they meet at its heart. Here a Landsat image is draped over elevation data.
1181: Legend says dragon children spat jewels that became islands. Geologists say rain.
Vietnamese legend says a mother dragon landed in Ha Long Bay and her children in Bai Tu Long, spitting jewels that became islands. Geologists credit limestone and rain.
1182: Shackleton's men waited here for months for rescue, and every one survived.
After losing their ship Endurance to the ice, Shackleton's 28 men reached Elephant Island in 1916. Most waited there for months while he sailed for help, and every one survived.
1183: A salt lake 4,700 meters up, its blues changing with the stirred sediment.
At 4,700 m above the sea, Ngangla Ringco is one of the highest salt lakes on Earth. Its milky and deep blues depend on how much sediment is stirred into the water.
1184: A ring lake 70 km across, and under the snow, the scar of an asteroid.
This ring lake in Quebec, about 70 km across, fills a crater left by an asteroid some 214 million years ago. Under winter snow the ancient scar stands out sharply.
1185: Spring Ice in the Bering Strait
Where Asia and North America almost touch, the Arctic ice squeezes through.
In May 2000, ice from the Arctic Ocean squeezed south through the Bering Strait, about 82 km wide, where Asia and North America almost touch.
1186: Days later, Antarctica hit 18.3°C, and the island's snowcap turned to slush.
Days after this image, on February 6, 2020, Antarctica's Esperanza Base recorded 18.3°C, a record for the continent. The heat wave turned much of Eagle Island's snowcap to slush.
1187: Clouds spun off an island drift away like smoke rings.
Wind passing Peter I Island off Antarctica spun the clouds into a vortex street, a chain of eddies turning in alternate directions, drifting away like smoke rings.
1188: Red Sandstone near the Rainbow Mountains, China
Neighbors of the Rainbow Mountains, carved into ridges instead of stripes.
These rust-red Cretaceous sandstones lie about 150 km from China's Zhangye Danxia, the famous Rainbow Mountains. Different erosion here carved ridges instead of painted stripes.
1189: To fill this lake, ancient temples were cut apart and moved uphill.
Lake Nasser stretches about 500 km along the Nile behind Egypt's Aswan High Dam, finished in 1970. To fill it, the temples of Abu Simbel were cut apart and moved uphill.
1190: A current carries the sea ice around Greenland's tip in white whorls.
In February 2025, sea ice swirled in white whorls along Greenland's southern coast, carried by the East Greenland Current around the island's tip.
1191: A Turkish lake whose white shores helped NASA rehearse for Mars.
Turkey's Lake Salda helped NASA prepare for Mars. Its white shores are made of minerals much like those at Jezero Crater, where the Perseverance rover landed in 2021.
1192: Thames Estuary and Offshore Wind Farms
Muddy river water inshore; offshore, a forest of wind turbines.
Silt clouds the Thames Estuary, and offshore stand wind farms including the London Array, the largest offshore wind farm in the world when it opened in 2013.
1193: An earthquake dropped a mountainside, and behind it grew a lake 500 m deep.
In 1911 an earthquake brought down a mountainside in Tajikistan's Pamirs and dammed a river. The lake that formed behind it, Sarez, is now 61 km long and up to 500 m deep.
1194: A lagoon ringed by a reef about 1,500 km long.
Off New Caledonia lies one of the largest lagoons on Earth, ringed by a barrier reef some 1,500 km long. Pale water marks reef and sand, deep blue the open ocean.
1195: Green marble, cut by the thin straight lines of passing boats.
Nearly every summer, algae turn the Baltic Sea into green marble. The thin straight lines cutting through the swirls are the wakes of boats crossing the bloom.
1196: One unusually hot, sunny spring, and the sea burst into bloom.
A sunny, unusually hot spring in 2020 set off large plankton blooms around Britain. Here a bloom swirls through the sea off the southwest coast of England.
1197: A fire so hot it built its own cloud, complete with a veil on top.
Montana's Sand Creek Fire threw up so much heat and smoke that it built its own cloud, a pyrocumulus, capped by a thin veil called a pileus. A NASA ER-2 jet shot it from about 20 km up.
1198: Sunbeams through storm clouds, seen from above instead of below.
An astronaut caught towering storm clouds over southern Asia at sunset, their shadows cutting dark shafts through the glowing haze. These are crepuscular rays, seen from above.
1199: The highest peak in the Sahara, with a dried salt lake inside.
Emi Koussi in Chad, 3,415 m tall, is the highest peak in the Sahara: a volcano about 70 km wide. Inside its caldera lies the white bed of a dried salt lake.
1200: Picked for one reason only: it is beautiful.
High winds spun this cloud into a giant whirlpool over the sea between Spain and Morocco. The image is part of the USGS Earth as Art series, chosen purely for its beauty.
1201: A cliff that poured lava into the sea like a firehose for weeks.
For weeks in early 2017 a lava tube on Kīlauea opened in a sea cliff and poured a steady stream of molten rock into the Pacific. This is how Hawaii grows, one blast of steam at a time.
1202: NPS / L. Law, Katmai National Park
A bear may eat 30 salmon a day, and the internet votes for the fattest.
Every July sockeye salmon leap up Brooks Falls in Alaska, and brown bears wait at the top with open jaws. A big bear may eat 30 salmon a day, and each fall the internet votes for the fattest one.
1203: A thunderstorm that spins, kilometers wide, for hours.
A supercell is a thunderstorm that spins. Its whole updraft rotates like a slow tornado kilometers wide, which is why these storms can last for hours and breed the most violent tornadoes.
1204: Ice turns this blue after centuries of squeezing. The tiny dots are penguins.
Glacier ice turns this deep blue when centuries of pressure squeeze out its air bubbles and it starts to absorb red light. The tiny dots on the slope are chinstrap penguins, for scale.
1205: Almost twice as tall as Niagara, and sketches of it helped create a national park.
At 94 meters the Lower Falls is almost twice as tall as Niagara. Thomas Moran's sketches of this canyon in 1871 helped persuade Congress to create Yellowstone, the world's first national park.
1206: A crack in a neighborhood that buried 700 homes and made new land.
In 2018 a crack opened in a Hawaiian neighborhood and fountained lava for over two months. Fissure 8 buried more than 700 homes and added about 3.5 square km of new land to the island.
1207: While its neighbors retreat, this glacier advances, and twice it sealed off a fjord.
Hubbard is the largest tidewater glacier in North America, and unlike most of its neighbors it has been advancing for over a century. Twice, in 1986 and 2002, it sealed off a whole fjord with ice.
1208: Lionesses often nurse each other's cubs.
Lions are the only truly social cats. Lionesses in a pride often give birth around the same time and nurse each other's cubs, and a roar can carry about 8 km across the open bush.
1209: Cloud Inversion in the Grand Canyon
On rare mornings the canyon fills with cloud like a bowl of milk.
On a few rare mornings cold air sinks into the Grand Canyon and is trapped under warmer air above, so the canyon fills with cloud like a bowl of milk while the rim stands in sunshine.
1210: It flaps its fins like ears, almost 7 km below the surface.
Dumbo octopuses are named after Disney's flying elephant for the fins they flap like ears. They live deeper than any other octopus: one was filmed almost 7 km down in the Java Trench.
1211: Most clouds rise. These are pouches of cold air sinking from a storm.
Most clouds form where air rises. Mammatus do the opposite: they are pouches of cold, wet air sinking from the underside of a storm's anvil, and they often hang in the sky after the worst has passed.
1212: About 2,200 years old, and each year it still grows a good-sized tree's worth of wood.
By volume General Sherman is the largest single-trunk tree on Earth, about 1,487 cubic meters of wood. It is roughly 2,200 years old and still adds enough wood each year to make a good-sized tree.
1213: Polar Bears on the Beaufort Sea Coast
Hunters of the sea ice, stranded on land as the ice retreats.
Polar bears hunt seals from sea ice, so on Alaska's Beaufort coast, where the ice now retreats farther each summer, more of them are stranded on land. In 2008 the US listed them as threatened.
1214: After a storm: hundreds of waterfalls that soon vanish.
Despite its name, Milford Sound is a fjord carved by glaciers. It gets nearly 7 meters of rain a year, and after a storm hundreds of short-lived waterfalls pour down its cliffs.
1215: It was once deep blue, until visitors' coins clogged its vents.
Morning Glory was once a deep blue. Visitors threw in so many coins, rocks and trash that they clogged its vents; the water cooled, and orange and yellow bacteria crept in around the rim.
1216: Wisdom, the Oldest Known Wild Bird
Banded as an adult in 1956, and at about 74 she laid another egg.
Wisdom the Laysan albatross was banded on Midway in 1956, already an adult. Scientists believe she is the oldest known wild bird, and in late 2024, at about 74, she laid yet another egg.
1217: Delicate Arch under the Milky Way
The sky here is protected too, so the Milky Way still blazes above the arch.
Delicate Arch stands 16 meters tall on a bare sandstone rim, and Utah puts it on license plates. Arches became an International Dark Sky Park in 2019, so the Milky Way still blazes above it.
1218: That green is oxygen glowing some 100 km up, struck by the Sun.
The green of the northern lights is oxygen glowing some 100 to 300 km up, struck by particles from the Sun. Lofoten lies under the auroral oval, so on clear winter nights its sky often comes alive.
1219: NOAA / Antarctic Marine Living Resources Program
It waits at the ice edge, exactly where penguins jump in.
A leopard seal can be 3.5 meters long, and it hunts by waiting at the ice edge just where penguins jump into the sea. Apart from orcas, it is the top predator in Antarctic waters.
1220: Seeds that waited underground for years, all sprouting at once.
In spring 2017, after heavy rains ended California's five-year drought, seeds that had waited underground for years sprouted at once, and the Carrizo Plain turned yellow and purple.
1221: It can go a year or more without drinking.
A desert tortoise spends up to 95 percent of its life in burrows, hiding from heat and cold. It stores water in its bladder, can go a year or more without drinking, and may live 50 years or longer.
1222: For decades, no one knew how these rocks moved on their own.

For decades nobody knew how these rocks crossed a dry lake bed on their own. In 2014 scientists finally saw it: thin sheets of ice, nudged by light wind, shoved the stones along a few meters a minute.
1223: NOAA / Channel Islands National Marine Sanctuary
Not a plant at all, yet it grows half a meter a day and builds a forest.
Giant kelp is an alga, not a plant, yet it builds a forest: in good conditions it can grow about half a meter a day and reach 45 meters, a canopy that shelters hundreds of species.
1224: A rainbow almost always, and, legend says, a Viking's gold behind the water.
Skógafoss drops 60 meters and throws up so much spray that on sunny days a rainbow almost always hangs at its foot. Legend says a Viking hid a chest of gold behind the falling water.
1225: 31 wolves came back, and scientists still argue over how far the ripples went.
Wolves were wiped out of Yellowstone by 1926. In 1995 and 1996, 31 wolves from Canada were set free here, and scientists still debate how far their return rippled through elk, willows and beavers.
1226: A cave dissolved not by rain but by acid rising from oil below.
The Big Room covers about 3.3 hectares, the largest cave chamber by volume in North America. Unlike most caves it was dissolved not by rainwater but by sulfuric acid rising from oil deposits below.
1227: Most waterspouts here are born under ordinary fair-weather clouds.
At its peak this waterspout was about 30 meters wide. The Florida Keys see more waterspouts than almost anywhere on Earth, and most are born under ordinary fair-weather clouds, not storms.
1228: From millions to fewer than 2,000, and then, partly, back.
Western monarchs fly hundreds of kilometers to spend the winter clustered in coastal trees like these. Counts fell from millions in the 1980s to fewer than 2,000 in 2020, then partly bounced back.
1229: Dead for some 600 years, and too dry to ever rot.

The trees of Deadvlei died some 600 to 700 years ago, when dunes cut this clay pan off from its river. The air is so dry they never rotted; they still stand beneath some of the tallest dunes on Earth.
1230: For ten years a lake of molten rock churned here. Then it drained within days.
From 2008 to 2018 a lake of molten rock churned in Kīlauea's summit crater, its crust cracking into glowing plates. In May 2018 it drained within days as magma rushed off to the lower Puna eruption.
1231: Among these deer, the females grow antlers too.
Denali rises about 5,500 meters from its base, a greater vertical rise than Everest's. Caribou graze below it, and they are the only deer in which females grow antlers too.
1232: NOAA / NZ-American Submarine Ring of Fire 2005
Undersea chimneys where life runs on chemistry instead of sunlight.
These chimneys on an undersea volcano north of New Zealand vent water hotter than 300°C, black with metals. Around such vents, whole ecosystems run on chemical energy instead of sunlight.
1233: A calf's first moment in the world: a two meter drop.
A giraffe gives birth standing up, so her calf's first experience is a drop of about 2 meters to the ground. Within an hour it is on its feet, already taller than most adult humans.
1234: A sand dune turned to stone, and only 64 people a day may walk it.
The Wave is a frozen sand dune: Navajo Sandstone laid down by wind about 190 million years ago, then carved into stripes by water and wind. Only 64 people a day win a permit to walk here.
1235: Sun Halo at the South Pole
Millions of tiny ice crystals, each bending sunlight by 22 degrees.

At the South Pole the air glitters with tiny ice crystals, and each six-sided one bends sunlight by 22 degrees. Together, millions of them paint a ring around the Sun with bright sundogs at its sides.
1236: A mother and two kits: the first breeding wolverines seen here in a century.
In 2020 cameras on Mount Rainier caught a wolverine mother with two kits, the first breeding wolverines seen in the park in about a century. Wolverines can cover dozens of kilometers a day over snow.
1237: 16 lakes held in place by dams that moss and algae build.
Plitvice's 16 lakes step down a valley, held in place by dams that living things build: moss and algae trap calcium carbonate, and the travertine barriers grow about a centimeter a year.
1238: NOAA / Hawaiian Islands Humpback Whale NMS
Why throw 40 tons into the air? No one is quite sure.
Each winter about 10,000 humpbacks swim nearly 5,000 km from Alaska to Hawaii to mate and give birth, eating almost nothing until they return. Why they hurl 40 tons into the air is still debated.
1239: Castle Geyser and the Milky Way
A geyser that built its own castle, perhaps over thousands of years.
Castle Geyser has built one of the largest cones in Yellowstone, a silica mound perhaps thousands of years old. It erupts about every 10 to 14 hours, here under a sky dark enough for the Milky Way.
1240: No leaves, a floating flower, and nectar only a few moths can reach.
The ghost orchid has no leaves: its green roots, glued to a tree do the photosynthesis. Its flower floats in the swamp, and its nectar lies so deep only a few long-tongued sphinx moths reach it.
1241: George Murray Levick, Terra Nova Expedition
What he saw shocked him so much his notes stayed hidden for a century.
Levick spent a season with these penguins in 1911 to 1912 and saw behavior so shocking to Edwardian eyes that his notes on it went unpublished. They were rediscovered and printed only in 2012.
1242: Light bounces up from the canyon and sets the arch glowing from below.
Mesa Arch sits right on the lip of a cliff about 150 meters high. At sunrise, light bounces up off the canyon below and sets the arch's underside glowing red, as if lit from within.
1243: It walked to Iceland over the sea ice at the end of the Ice Age.
The Arctic fox is Iceland's only native land mammal; it arrived over sea ice at the end of the Ice Age. Its winter coat is so warm that it reportedly does not start shivering until about minus 70°C.
1244: One of dozens of tornadoes spun off in a single day.
This tornado was one of dozens spun off on 23 May 2008 by storms stretching from Colorado to Oklahoma. The United States gets more tornadoes than any other country, about 1,200 in an average year.
1245: Trees standing in a row, along a log that vanished centuries ago.
In the Hoh, where about 3.5 meters of rain fall a year, moss so crowds the forest floor that seedlings sprout on fallen trees instead. Centuries later the trees stand in a row along a vanished log.
1246: Older than the dinosaurs, and their blue blood still tests our medicines.
Horseshoe crabs were already crawling ashore to spawn long before the dinosaurs. Their blue, copper-based blood is still harvested to test vaccines and medicines for bacterial toxins.
1247: Hillary trained here for Everest. In one night the peak lost 10 meters.
Aoraki is New Zealand's highest mountain, where a young Edmund Hillary trained for Everest. In 1991 its summit collapsed in a huge rock avalanche, and the peak lost about 10 meters overnight.
1248: Explorers found ten thousand smokes. Today almost all are cold.
The 1912 eruption of Novarupta was the largest of the 20th century, filling this valley with up to 200 meters of ash. Explorers in 1916 found thousands of steam vents; today almost all are cold.
1249: The biggest fish alive lives on some of the smallest food in the sea.
The whale shark is the biggest fish alive, reaching about 18 meters, yet it lives on some of the smallest food in the sea, filtering plankton and fish eggs through its gaping mouth.
1250: Down to 20 or 30, until eight pumas from Texas came to the rescue.
By the early 1990s only 20 to 30 Florida panthers were left, so inbred many had kinked tails and heart defects. Eight female pumas from Texas came in 1995; today there are about 120 to 230.
1251: No river flows in or out; rain and snow alone filled it.
About 7,700 years ago the volcano Mount Mazama blew out its insides and collapsed. Rain and snow alone filled the hole, making the deepest lake in the US, 594 meters, with no river flowing in or out.
1252: Nearly 2,000 islands: the drowned tops of an ancient landscape.
Hạ Long means 'descending dragon', and legend says dragons spat out jewels that became these islands. In fact there are nearly 2,000 limestone islets, the drowned tops of an ancient karst landscape.
1253: Two summers a year, and more daylight than any other creature.

Arctic terns fly from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back every year, about 70,000 km, the longest migration of any animal. They live two summers a year and see more daylight than any other creature.
1254: Five times hotter than the Sun's surface, for a few millionths of a second.
A lightning bolt heats the air around it to about 30,000°C, five times hotter than the surface of the Sun, in a few millionths of a second. That sudden explosion of air is the thunder we hear.
1255: Thin blades of stone, and a cave that breathes.
Wind Cave holds most of the world's known boxwork, thin blades of calcite left standing when the rock around them dissolved. The cave also breathes: air rushes in or out as outside pressure changes.
1256: The lava crept toward the island's main highway, then stopped 2.7 km short.
In November 2022 Mauna Loa, the largest active volcano on Earth, erupted for the first time since 1984. Its rough 'a'ā lava crept toward the island's main highway, then stalled 2.7 km short.
1257: Nearly every wild musk ox in Alaska descends from 31 animals.

Musk oxen had vanished from Alaska by the early 1900s. In the 1930s a small herd was brought from Greenland and 31 were freed on Nunivak Island; nearly every wild musk ox in Alaska descends from them.
1258: Two shrimp move in young and grow too big to leave: a wedding gift.
These deep-sea sponges build skeletons of pure glass. A pair of tiny shrimp moves in young and grows too big to leave, so in Japan the sponges were given as wedding gifts, a symbol of lasting love.
1259: Seven men reached the top. On the way down, a rope broke.
The Matterhorn was one of the last great Alpine peaks to be climbed. Edward Whymper's party reached the top in July 1865; on the way down a rope broke and four of the seven men fell to their deaths.
1260: Fewer than two dozen were left in 1902. Today about 5,000 plow the snow.
Bison swing their huge heads like snowplows to reach the grass beneath. In 1902 fewer than two dozen wild bison were left in Yellowstone, the last in the US; today the park holds about 5,000.
1261: The hottest place ever measured, covered in golden flowers.
Death Valley holds the record for the hottest air temperature ever measured, 56.7°C in 1913. Yet after a rare wet winter, as in 2005, its floor bursts into a carpet of golden desert flowers.
1262: Explorers mistook the chicks for another species: the woolly penguin.
King penguin chicks wear thick brown down for over a year, and early explorers took them for a separate species, the 'woolly penguin'. Their parents can raise at most two chicks every three years.
1263: Most of a species, crowded onto one stretch of one river.
Every March hundreds of thousands of sandhill cranes, most of the species, crowd onto one stretch of Nebraska's Platte River to rest and fatten up, a gathering whose roots go back millions of years.
1264: Monsoon Storm over the Grand Canyon
Almost every summer afternoon, the storms come back.
From July to September moist air flows north from the Gulf of California, and almost every afternoon storms like this build over the Grand Canyon, bringing much of its yearly rain and lightning.
1265: A park made just for them, and still fewer than 100 were left.
In 1937 South Africa created a national park just for these zebras, but by the 1950s fewer than 100 were left. Careful protection worked: there are now several thousand Cape mountain zebras.
1266: No brain, no heart, no bones, and to a turtle it looks like a plastic bag.
A sea nettle has no brain, no heart and no bones, and is about 95 percent water, yet it hunts with stinging tentacles meters long. To a sea turtle, a drifting plastic bag looks just like one.
1267: One woman's cry of delight named this place.
Paradise got its name in 1885, when Martha Longmire saw these meadows and cried out what a paradise it was. Snow lies here most of the year, so the flowers rush to bloom in a few summer weeks.
1268: In a good lemming year, a dozen eggs. In a bad one, none.
Snowy owls hunt in the 24-hour daylight of the Arctic summer. Their families rise and fall with the lemmings: in a boom year a female may lay a dozen eggs, in a bust year none at all.
1269: A glacier that ends among rainforest, barely 300 m above the sea.
Fox Glacier falls about 2,600 meters on its 13 km journey from the Southern Alps, ending among rainforest barely 300 meters above sea level. Few glaciers anywhere reach so low, so close to the coast.
1270: A fire so fierce it spun whirlwinds, and 1.3 million Joshua trees burned.
In August 2020 a lightning fire swept the Cima Dome in the Mojave, one of the densest Joshua tree forests on Earth. Its heat spun up whirls like this, and about 1.3 million Joshua trees burned.
1271: It spends all summer making hay, and a warm afternoon can kill it.
The pika, a tiny cousin of rabbits, does not hibernate. All summer it dries grass and flowers in hay piles among the rocks, and its fur is so warm that a few hours at 25°C can kill it.
1272: Steam that skips the liquid stage and freezes into feathers of ice.
Warm water from hot springs keeps Tangled Creek steaming even in deep cold. On still nights the steam skips the liquid stage and freezes straight onto every twig, growing feathers of ice.
1273: It sneezes out salt, and Darwin called it an imp of darkness.
The marine iguana is the only lizard on Earth that feeds in the sea, grazing algae off underwater rocks. It sneezes out the extra salt, and Darwin, unimpressed, called them 'imps of darkness'.
1274: Each family speaks its own dialect, learned from the mothers.
Orcas are the largest dolphins. Each pod speaks its own dialect of calls, passed down from mothers, and some families eat only fish while others hunt only seals and whales.
1275: 93 meters long and under 2 meters thick at its thinnest.
