Landscape Arch spans 93 meters, the longest natural arch in North America, and at its thinnest it is under 2 meters thick. In 1991 a large slab fell from it, and the trail beneath was closed for good.
1276: Its pounces work best facing north-east. A compass in a fox?
A fox can hear a mouse under a meter of snow, then dive in nose first. One study found pounces succeed far more often when the fox faces north-east, hinting it may sense Earth's magnetic field.
1277: Rock ground to dust by glaciers turns the lake this milky blue.
Lake Tekapo's milky turquoise comes from 'rock flour', rock ground to dust by glaciers and suspended in the water. Its skies are so dark that in 2012 it became one of the first dark sky reserves.
1278: Its sibling from the same storm set the fastest winds ever measured.
This tornado formed on 3 May 1999 from the same storm that went on to produce the Bridge Creek to Moore tornado, where a mobile radar clocked winds of about 480 km/h, the fastest ever measured.
1279: Over 7,000 species, and a quarter of them live nowhere else.
The reefs of the remote Northwestern Hawaiian Islands shelter over 7,000 marine species, a quarter found nowhere else. They lie inside Papahānaumokuākea, one of the largest protected areas on Earth.
1280: A mountain so big it makes its own weather, and hides on most days.
At 6,190 meters this is the highest peak in North America. Its Koyukon Athabascan name, Denali, means 'the high one', and it is so big that it makes its own weather; clouds hide it on most days.
1281: Roosevelt said he would never have been president without his years here.
These horses descend from ranch and Native horses left loose in the badlands where young Theodore Roosevelt ran cattle in the 1880s. He said he would never have been president without his years here.
1282: A path leads behind the falling water, to watch the curtain from inside.
Seljalandsfoss drops about 60 meters over an old sea cliff, left behind when the coast retreated after the Ice Age. A path runs into the cave behind it, to watch the falling curtain from inside.
1283: The warmth of the nest decides if the baby is male or female.
An alligator's sex is decided by the warmth of its nest: warmer eggs tend to hatch males, cooler ones females. The mother guards the nest for two months and gently carries hatchlings in her jaws.
1284: Once a swampy coast where dinosaurs walked; their bones still weather out.
About 70 million years ago this was a swampy coast where dinosaurs walked. Now wind and rain carve its layers into hoodoos and 'cracked eggs', and fossils of those dinosaurs still weather out.
1285: Weddell Seal at Its Breathing Hole
It saws its breathing hole with its teeth, and wears them down over the years.
Weddell seals live farther south than any other mammal. To breathe under winter sea ice they keep holes open by sawing at the ice with their teeth, which wears them down over the years.
1286: Not the biggest geyser, just the most dependable.
Old Faithful is not the biggest geyser, just the most dependable. Rangers predict each eruption from the length of the one before, usually within ten minutes, and it goes off about 17 times a day.
1287: A parrot at home in the snow, with a habit of taking cars apart.
The kea is the world's only alpine parrot, at home in the snow of New Zealand's Southern Alps. It is famously clever and curious, and has a habit of pulling apart cars, tents and backpacks.
1288: Gentle sea cows whose closest living relatives are elephants.
Manatees cannot survive long in water colder than about 20°C, so in winter hundreds crowd into springs like these, which stay near 22°C all year. Their closest living relatives are elephants.
1289: Every few years it dams a lake, and the ice dam bursts with a roar.
Perito Moreno is one of the few Patagonian glaciers that held steady for a century while most retreated. Every few years it dams a lake arm, water builds behind the ice and the dam bursts in a roar.
1290: Look at the outer bow: its colors run backwards.
In a double rainbow the outer bow's colors are reversed, because its light bounces twice inside each raindrop. The sky between the two bows is darker, a strip called Alexander's band.
1291: Born while their mother sleeps, each weighing about half a kilo.
Grizzly cubs are born in the winter den while their mother sleeps, each weighing about half a kilogram. By the time they come out in spring her rich milk has made them many times heavier.
1292: Bigger than any dinosaur, with a heart the size of a small car.
The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived, bigger than any dinosaur, up to about 30 meters long. Its heart is the size of a small car, and its calls carry hundreds of kilometers.
1293: Dunes turned to stone and twisted, with tiny shrimp in the puddles.
White Pocket's swirls are ancient sand dunes that hardened into stone and were twisted while still soft. Rain collects in its hollows, so tiny shrimp and plants live in pools amid the desert.
1294: The fastest land animal cannot roar, only purr and chirp.
The cheetah is the fastest land animal, reaching about 100 km/h in a few seconds. It pays for speed: it cannot roar, only purr and chirp, and bigger predators often steal its kills.
1295: Meltwater carved this cave, and an ice-dammed lake here bursts almost every summer.
Meltwater carves caves like this through the glacier above Juneau, Alaska. Since 2011 a lake dammed by the ice has burst almost every summer; the floods of 2024 and 2025 were the biggest on record.
1296: 50 to 70 years before the first arm.
A saguaro may not grow its first arm until it is 50 to 70 years old, and it can live past 150. After a storm it swells with water like an accordion, and a big one can hold well over a ton.
1297: A brief side show beside a volcano that erupted for 35 years.
The cone in the background, Puʻu ʻŌʻō, erupted almost without pause for 35 years, from 1983 to 2018. These fountains were a brief side show in March 2011, when a new fissure split open beside it.
1298: There were never twelve. They used to be the Sow and Piglets.
There were never twelve. The stacks were known as the Sow and Piglets until a 1920s rebranding for tourists, and in July 2005, two months before this photo, one of them collapsed into the sea.
1299: Thousands of kilometers from any city, and the chicks are fed plastic.
Midway lies thousands of kilometers from any city, yet albatross parents bring back plastic from the sea and feed it to their chicks, by one estimate about 5 tonnes a year on this atoll alone.
1300: Mountain Goat Kid, Glacier National Park
Hours after birth, the kid follows its mother up a cliff.
Mountain goats are not true goats but cousins of antelopes. Their hooves have hard rims and soft, grippy pads, and kids follow their mothers up near-vertical cliffs within hours of birth.
1301: A rainbow of fog, with droplets so tiny the colors melt into white.
A fogbow is a rainbow made of fog. Its droplets are so tiny, under a twentieth of a millimeter, that light diffracts around them and the colors smear together into a ghostly white arc.
1302: Born into deep frost, it doubles its weight in about two weeks.
A Weddell seal pup is born on the ice into temperatures far below zero. Its mother's milk is so rich that the pup roughly doubles its weight in about two weeks, and soon follows her into the sea.
1303: A tree and a moth that cannot survive without each other.
The Joshua tree is a giant yucca, and it depends on a single partner: only the yucca moth pollinates its flowers, and only in its seeds can the moth's larvae grow. Neither survives without the other.
1304: A darker mane is an honest ad, and the lionesses notice.
A lion's mane is an honest advertisement. Researchers in the Serengeti found that darker manes go with higher testosterone and better health, and that lionesses prefer males who wear them.
1305: It slept for years at a time, then woke up and erupted 48 times in one year.
Steamboat is the tallest active geyser in the world, throwing water over 90 meters high. For decades it slept for years at a time; in 2018 it woke up, and in 2019 it erupted a record 48 times.
1306: One of the rarest seals on Earth, simply sharing the sand with a turtle.
Hawaiian monk seals are among the rarest seals on Earth, about 1,600 left, and Hawaii's green turtles are among the few that bask on beaches. On this remote atoll the two simply share the sand.
1307: Almost no rain, so the beetles drink the fog off their own backs.
The Namib may be the oldest desert on Earth, dry for tens of millions of years. Almost no rain falls, so some beetles drink the morning fog, facing the wind to catch drops on their backs.
1308: In 1941 only 15 or 16 were left. Now there are over 800.
Whooping cranes are the tallest birds in North America, about 1.5 meters. In 1941 only 15 or 16 were left in the wild; decades of protection and captive breeding have brought them back to over 800.
1309: Declared 'perfectly inaccessible'. Ten years later, someone drilled his way up.
In 1865 a California survey declared Half Dome 'perfectly inaccessible', never to be trodden by human foot. Ten years later George Anderson drilled his way up the smooth granite with iron bolts.
1310: Two million eggs a year, and almost nothing here eats them.

Lionfish belong in the Indo-Pacific, but since the 1980s, likely freed from aquariums, they have spread across the Atlantic. A female can spawn two million eggs a year, and few local predators eat them.
1311: Here the summer sun barely sets, so the lights belong to autumn and winter.
In Denali the summer sun barely sets, so the northern lights belong to autumn and winter. Auroras tend to peak around the equinoxes, when Earth's magnetic field lines up best with the solar wind.
1312: Boulders that grew like pearls, layer by layer, in the seabed mud.
The Moeraki boulders grew in the seabed mud about 60 million years ago, layer by layer around a core, much like pearls. As the cliffs behind the beach erode, new ones keep tumbling out.
1313: Young Mountain Lion, Santa Monica Mountains
Freeways trapped them, so a bridge is being built for wildlife.
Mountain lion kittens are born spotted, and the spots fade as they grow. Around Los Angeles freeways trap the cats, so in 2022 work began on the world's largest wildlife bridge, over the 101.
1314: Mexico on the left wall, the United States on the right, a river in between.
The Rio Grande has cut a canyon about 460 meters deep through limestone here. The left wall is in Mexico and the right wall in the United States, and the river between them is the border.
1315: The orange bill is only a summer costume.
A tufted puffin's bright orange bill and golden plumes are only a summer costume for the breeding season. In winter it sheds the outer bill plates and heads far out to sea, rarely seen until spring.
1316: Millions of tiny ice mirrors draw a column of light above the Sun.
A sun pillar is sunlight bouncing off millions of flat ice crystals that drift down nearly level. Each is a tiny mirror, and together they draw a column of light above the rising Sun.
1317: NOAA / Linda Snook, Cordell Bank NMS
Three hearts, blue blood, and a mother who starves guarding her eggs.
The giant Pacific octopus is the largest octopus, often over 15 kg, with three hearts and blue blood. Clever as it is, it lives just three to five years, and a mother starves guarding her eggs.
1318: Each winter leaves a ring on his horns: count them like a tree.
Dall sheep are the only wild white sheep in the world. A ram's curling horns never stop growing, and each winter leaves a ring on them, so you can count his age like the rings of a tree.
1319: Lawrence called it godlike. Filmmakers use it as Mars.
T. E. Lawrence rode through Wadi Rum and called it vast, echoing and godlike. Its red sand and sandstone towers look so unearthly that filmmakers have used it to stand in for Mars.
1320: A venomous lizard whose saliva led to a diabetes drug.
The Gila monster is one of very few venomous lizards. A hormone in its saliva led to exenatide, a diabetes drug approved in 2005, the first of the class that now includes popular weight-loss drugs.
1321: Yosemite Falls in a Drought Year
One of the continent's tallest falls, shrunk to a thread.
At 739 meters Yosemite Falls is among North America's tallest falls, but it runs on snowmelt. In autumn of a dry year like 2014 it can shrink to a thread, leaving a dark stain on the cliff.
1322: For two months the father balances the egg on his feet and eats nothing.
Emperor penguins breed in the dark Antarctic winter. The father balances the egg on his feet under a fold of skin for about two months, eating nothing, while the mother feeds at sea.
1323: Only 27 were left, so the last wild one was captured to save them all.
By 1987 only 27 California condors were left, and the last wild one was captured to save the species. Bred in zoos and set free again, they now number over 500, about half of them flying wild.
1324: Bristlecone Pine at Night, Great Basin
He cut it down, counted the rings, and found the oldest tree known.
Bristlecone pines are among the oldest living things on Earth. In 1964 a researcher cut one down here, later nicknamed Prometheus, then counted almost 4,900 rings: the oldest tree known at the time.
1325: Hunted almost to the last one, now back on beaches they had abandoned.
In the 1800s sealers killed New Zealand fur seals almost to the last one for their pelts. Protected since, they are back to about 200,000 and spreading to beaches they had not used for generations.
1326: Emperor Penguins at the Ice Edge
More than 500 meters down on one breath, then home on their bellies.
Emperor penguins are the deepest-diving birds, reaching over 500 meters and holding their breath for more than 20 minutes. On land they walk or toboggan on their bellies, the tallest penguins alive.
1327: When the lake froze solid, about 138,000 people walked out to these caves.
Waves have hollowed caves into the sandstone of Lake Superior's shore, and in hard winters they fill with icicles. When the lake froze solid in 2014, about 138,000 people walked out to see them.
1328: At home everywhere, even in suburbs, yet almost no one sees one.
The bobcat is named for its short, 'bobbed' tail. It is the most widespread wild cat in North America, at home in forests, deserts, swamps and suburbs, yet so secretive that few people ever see one.
1329: Stacked like pancakes, and no one fully knows why.
These limestone stacks began 30 million years ago as shells of sea creatures settling on the seabed. Why they weathered into neat layers like stacked pancakes is still not fully understood.
1330: California sea lions can swim at about 40 km/h and turn on a dime among the kelp. Unlike seals, they 'walk' on land on rotating rear flippers, which is why they became stars of aquariums.
1331: Lightning lit a fire that burned for weeks and took a 1913 stone lodge.
The Sprague Fire, started by lightning in August 2017, burned through Glacier's forests for weeks. It destroyed the main building of Sperry Chalet, a stone backcountry lodge from 1913, since rebuilt.
1332: From 11 elephants to more than 600, and many females have no tusks at all.
When Addo Elephant Park was founded in 1931, only 11 elephants were left in the area, hunted almost to the end by farmers. Today more than 600 live here, and many of the females have no tusks at all.
1333: 900 meters of sheer granite, climbed alone and without a rope.
El Capitan rises about 900 meters of nearly sheer granite from the valley floor. In 2017 Alex Honnold climbed it alone and without a rope in 3 hours 56 minutes, a feat many thought impossible.
1334: A tooth growing through the lip, sold in Europe as a unicorn horn.
A narwhal's tusk is a tooth that spirals out through its upper lip, up to about 3 meters long, laced with millions of nerve endings. Medieval traders sold these tusks in Europe as unicorn horns.
1335: Thought extinct, until a ranch dog brought one home.
Black-footed ferrets were thought extinct until a ranch dog in Wyoming brought one home in 1981. Every ferret alive today descends from a handful of survivors, and in 2020 one was even cloned.
1336: Once on the back of Canada's 20 dollar bill.
Moraine Lake gets its blue from rock flour, dust ground by glaciers that scatters sunlight in the water. The view was printed on the back of Canada's 20 dollar bill in the 1970s.
1337: The wind races through it, yet the cloud hangs still. Often mistaken for a UFO.

A lenticular cloud forms where wind flowing over a mountain rises in a standing wave and cools. The air races through it, yet the cloud seems to hang still, so lenticulars are often mistaken for UFOs.
1338: To keep from drifting apart, they sometimes hold paws.

Sea otters have no blubber; they keep warm with the densest fur of any animal, up to a million hairs per square inch. Resting in groups called rafts, they sometimes hold paws so as not to drift apart.
1339: Trees from the dawn of the dinosaurs, their wood slowly turned to quartz.
These logs were trees about 220 million years ago, when dinosaurs were just appearing. Buried in ash and mud, their wood was slowly replaced by quartz, colored by traces of iron and other minerals.
1340: Wings over 3 meters wide, gliding for hours without a single flap.
The wandering albatross has the longest wingspan of any living bird, over 3 meters. It can glide for hours without a single flap, and one bird may fly hundreds of thousands of kilometers in a year.
1341: In 1850 the area of today's Glacier National Park held around 150 glaciers. By 2015 only 26 were big enough to count as active glaciers, and Grinnell, like the rest, keeps shrinking into its lake.
1342: The biggest brain ever, diving 2 km into the dark for squid.
The sperm whale has the biggest brain of any animal that has ever lived. It dives more than 2 km into the dark to hunt squid, and off Kaikōura a deep canyon brings them close to shore all year.
1343: Trolls caught by the dawn, says the legend, above a beach of sneaker waves.
Icelandic legend says these basalt sea stacks are trolls who tried to drag a ship ashore and turned to stone at dawn. The beach below is known for sudden 'sneaker waves' that sweep people away.
1344: Their alarm calls may even describe the color of your shirt.
Prairie dogs greet family members with a kind of kiss. Their alarm calls are remarkably rich: studies suggest they can signal a predator's type, size and even the color of a person's shirt.
1345: Here, legend says, a demigod lassoed the Sun to slow it down.
Haleakalā means 'house of the sun': legend says the demigod Māui lassoed the Sun here to make it cross the sky more slowly. Its vast summit valley was carved by erosion, not by an eruption.
1346: Tens of thousands of geese lift off almost together, in seconds.
Each winter tens of thousands of snow geese gather at this refuge in New Mexico. At dawn they often lift off almost together, a roaring 'blast-off' that fills the sky in seconds.
1347: A lake at the bottom of the sea, with its own shore and waves.
A kilometer down in the Gulf of Mexico, water several times saltier than the sea sinks into hollows and forms lakes with their own shores and waves. Animals that swim in can die of the shock.
1348: Ice almost on the equator, and more than 80 percent of it gone since 1912.
Kilimanjaro, 5,895 meters, is the highest mountain in Africa and the tallest free-standing mountain on Earth. Its ice, almost on the equator, has shrunk by more than 80 percent since 1912.
1349: Brown now, white only when the snow arrives.
In a good lemming year an Arctic fox mother can raise more than a dozen kits, among the largest litters of any wild carnivore. Their summer coats are brown and gray, turning white only with the snow.
1350: To reach this stone tube you wade, swim cold pools and sometimes rope down.
A creek in Zion has carved this tube-shaped canyon into the sandstone, and hikers named it the Subway. Reaching it takes a permit, wading, swimming through cold pools and sometimes a rope.
1351: Touch one hair and nothing happens. The plant counts before it eats.
Venus flytraps grow wild only in a small area of the Carolinas. A trap shuts only if two trigger hairs are touched within about 20 seconds, so in a sense the plant counts before it eats.
1352: Up to 20,000 km a year, and close enough to shore to watch.

Gray whales make one of the longest migrations of any mammal, some 16,000 to 20,000 km a year between Mexico's lagoons and the Arctic. Mothers and calves hug the coast, close enough to see from shore.
1353: These towers were molten rock underground, until glaciers stripped them bare.
These granite towers are magma that cooled underground about 12 million years ago, then were stripped bare by glaciers. 'Paine' is thought to mean 'blue' in the language of the Tehuelche people.
1354: Mothers guard so fiercely that in Alaska, moose hurt more people than bears.

Moose are the largest deer on Earth. Calves born at about 14 kg gain over a kilogram a day and swim within days, and mothers guard them so fiercely that in Alaska moose hurt more people than bears do.
1355: A turtle that eats so many plants its fat turns green.
Adult green sea turtles are the only sea turtles that eat almost only plants, and their diet tints the fat under their shells green. Protected since 1978, Hawaii's honu have come back strongly.
1356: Northern Lights over Bear Lake, Alaska
The same storm that paints the sky can knock out satellites.
An airman took this photo in January 2005, during a burst of strong solar storms. The same particles that light the sky can induce currents in power lines and disturb satellites and radio.
1357: Iceland's most photographed peak may look familiar: it played the 'Arrowhead'.
Kirkjufell, 'church mountain', is a lone peak of layered rock shaped by Ice Age glaciers. It may be the most photographed mountain in Iceland, and it appeared in Game of Thrones as the 'Arrowhead'.
1358: Down the bank, again and again. Scientists think it is mostly play.
A river otter can close its ears and nostrils underwater and stay down for several minutes. Otters slide down muddy and snowy banks again and again, and scientists think much of it is simply play.
1359: In 1794 this bay was a wall of ice.
When George Vancouver sailed past in 1794, Glacier Bay was a wall of ice. When John Muir came in 1879 the ice had retreated about 77 km, opening the bay where Margerie Glacier still calves today.
1360: A pancake-flat octopus that became Pearl in Finding Nemo.
The flapjack octopus flattens itself like a pancake on the seafloor, here 814 meters down off the US West Coast. Its round body and ear-like fins inspired the character Pearl in Finding Nemo.
1361: Pink granite, 420 million years in the making.
Acadia's pink granite cooled from magma about 420 million years ago, then glaciers scraped it bare. Nearby Cadillac Mountain is, for part of the year, the first place in the US to see the sunrise.
1362: Three grams of bird, flying from Mexico to Alaska and back.
A rufous hummingbird weighs about 3 grams, yet it flies from Mexico to Alaska and back each year. Measured in body lengths, that is one of the longest migrations of any bird on Earth.
1363: A century ago this lagoon did not exist.
This lagoon did not exist a century ago. It began forming in the 1930s as the glacier Breiðamerkurjökull retreated, and it is now one of Iceland's deepest lakes, full of icebergs drifting out to sea.
1364: A whale that builds a net out of bubbles.
A humpback blows a spiral of bubbles underwater, and the rising curtain traps a school of fish like a net. Then the whale lunges up through the middle, mouth wide open. Some hunt this way in teams.
1365: The yellow was there all summer, hiding. Only the red is new.
The yellow and orange of autumn leaves are there all summer, hidden under green chlorophyll; when it breaks down they show through. The reds are different: trees make them fresh in the fall.
1366: Faster than any predator here. Maybe still fleeing a cheetah gone 10,000 years.
The pronghorn is the fastest land animal in the Americas, near 90 km/h, faster than any predator here. Some biologists think it gained that speed to escape the American cheetah, gone 10,000 years.
1367: A rainbow made of moonlight: white to the eye, colored to the camera.
A moonbow is a rainbow lit by the Moon. To the naked eye it usually looks white, because moonlight is too dim for our color vision; a long camera exposure, as here at 1:30 a.m., reveals the colors.
1368: Every manta's belly carries a fingerprint of spots.
No two manta rays have the same pattern of spots on their bellies, so researchers identify each one like a fingerprint. Mantas also have one of the largest brains for their body size of any fish.
1369: Brad Benter / U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
As the ice shrinks, thousands crowd the beaches, and one stampede can kill.
Walruses rest on floating ice between dives for clams on the shallow seafloor. As summer ice retreats, they crowd onto Alaskan beaches by the thousands, where a single stampede can crush calves.
1370: Two winds fight over this sand, and both keep piling it higher.
The tallest dunes in North America rise here, about 230 meters, against the snowy Rockies. Winds from opposite directions keep piling the sand back up, and a creek at their base recycles it.
1371: Pink from shrimp, and nearly wiped out to make fans.

Spoonbills are pink for the same reason flamingos are: pigments from the shrimp and crustaceans they sweep up. In the 1800s they were nearly wiped out in Florida for their feathers, used to make fans.
1372: The lowest dry land on Earth, and it drops another meter every year.
The Dead Sea's shore is the lowest dry land on Earth, 430 meters below sea level, and drops over a meter a year as the Jordan is diverted. Its water is nearly ten times saltier than the sea.
1373: Up to 2,700 km a year, always coming home to the same coast to give birth.

The Porcupine caribou herd may travel up to about 2,700 km a year, one of the longest land migrations on Earth. Each spring it returns to the Arctic Refuge's coastal plain, where most calves are born.
1374: Those horns are nostrils. And there is a second set of jaws in its throat.
The 'horns' of the dragon moray are tube-shaped nostrils that help it smell prey in the dark of the reef. Morays also have a second set of jaws in the throat that shoots forward to drag food in.
1375: They call it the Mist Trail: you climb through rainbows and come out soaked.
Vernal Fall drops about 97 meters, and the trail beside it is called the Mist Trail for good reason: in spring hikers climb through clouds of spray and rainbows and come out drenched.
1376: It keeps fishing with a beak already full. The record is 62 fish at once.
A puffin's tongue and spiny palate let it hold a row of fish crosswise while it keeps catching more; the record is 62 in one beakful. It beats its wings up to about 400 times a minute.
1377: Fed by hidden springs, this waterfall rarely runs dry.
Multnomah Falls drops about 189 meters in two tiers, the tallest waterfall in Oregon. It is fed by underground springs as well as rain and snowmelt, so unlike many falls it rarely runs dry.
1378: A penguin that nests alone in the forest, out of sight of its neighbors.
The hoiho, or yellow-eyed penguin, lives only in New Zealand and may be one of the rarest penguins on Earth. Unlike most penguins it nests alone in coastal forest, out of sight of its neighbors.
1379: Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes, Death Valley
Footprints vanish with the next wind. Star Wars filmed its Tatooine here.
These dunes rise from one of the hottest places on Earth, and Death Valley's desolate scenery stood in for the planet Tatooine when Star Wars was filmed in 1976. Footprints vanish with the next wind.
1380: Its tendons are springs: hopping faster costs it almost nothing.
A kangaroo's leg tendons work like springs, storing energy on each landing and releasing it on the next hop. Thanks to that, hopping faster costs a kangaroo almost no extra energy.
1381: These black peaks are the roots of a volcano, 60 million years old.
The Black Cuillin of Skye are the roots of a volcano active about 60 million years ago, made of gabbro, a rough, grippy rock climbers love. Ice Age glaciers carved this valley between them.
1382: NOAA / Hawaiian Islands Humpback Whale NMS
Up to seven twists in a single leap.
Spinner dolphins can twist up to seven times in a single leap. In Hawaii they feed offshore at night and rest by day in calm bays, which is why disturbing them there is now restricted.
1383: This whole forest is one tree.
This whole grove in Utah is a single aspen, about 47,000 stems rising from one root system. Called Pando, Latin for 'I spread', it weighs some 6,000 tonnes and may be many thousands of years old.
1384: Thousands of four-second naps add up to 11 hours of sleep.
Nesting chinstrap penguins sleep in thousands of tiny naps, each only about four seconds long, so they can keep watch over eggs and chicks. Added up, they still get around 11 hours of sleep a day.
1385: From above, the lake is shaped like a wolf's head.
Peyto Lake is named after Bill Peyto, an eccentric mountain guide of the early 1900s. In summer, glacial rock flour turns it a vivid turquoise, and from above its outline looks like a wolf's head.
1386: One mother swam nine days straight, almost 700 km. Her cub did not make it.
Polar bears are classified as marine mammals, at home in the sea. One tracked female swam for nine days straight across the Beaufort Sea, almost 700 km, though she lost her cub along the way.
1387: Fur Seal Rookery, St. Paul Island
She took this photo while counting seals with her daughter.
The tiny Pribilof Islands host about half of the world's northern fur seals each summer. A member of the island's Tribal Government took this photo while counting them with her daughter.
1388: The face of the American West, on Navajo land.
Monument Valley lies within the Navajo Nation and is run as a Navajo tribal park. Its sandstone buttes became the face of the American West in John Ford's westerns, starting with Stagecoach in 1939.
1389: Markers along the path show where the ice stood each decade.
The Athabasca Glacier has retreated more than 1.5 km in about 125 years, and it now loses roughly 5 meters a year. Markers along the path to its toe show where the ice stood in each decade.
1390: They called it the smoking mountain, for the cloud trailing from its top.
The Tehuelche called this granite spire Chaltén, the 'smoking mountain', for the cloud that often trails from its summit. Sheer walls and violent winds make it one of the hardest big peaks to climb.
1391: Not one waterfall but about 275. 'Poor Niagara!', Eleanor Roosevelt is said to have cried.
Iguazú is not one waterfall but about 275, strung along almost 3 km of the border between Argentina and Brazil. On seeing it, Eleanor Roosevelt is said to have exclaimed, 'Poor Niagara!'
1392: Halfway to the North Pole, and warming several times faster than the world.
About 60 percent of Svalbard is covered by glaciers, halfway between Norway and the North Pole. The archipelago is warming faster than almost anywhere else on Earth, several times the global average.
1393: Carved by ice: on 200-plus nights a year, freezing water pries the rock apart.
Bryce is not really a canyon but a row of amphitheaters. Its hoodoos are carved mostly by ice: on more than 200 nights a year meltwater freezes in cracks, expands and pries the rock apart.
1394: White is not a color here. It is what a starving coral looks like.
When seawater stays too warm, corals expel the algae that feed them and turn white. If the heat lasts, they die and seaweed takes over, as on this reef in one of the most remote places on Earth.
1395: Inside them, scientists have found license plates and tires.
Tiger sharks will eat almost anything: fish, turtles, birds and, in their stomachs, scientists have found license plates and tires. Young ones wear tiger stripes that fade as they grow.
1396: It does not chase. It waits, dangles a lure, and snaps.
This goosefish, a kind of anglerfish, lies still about 640 meters down and dangles a fleshy lure from a spine on its head. When curious prey comes close, its huge mouth snaps shut in an instant.
1397: Down to 417 pairs in 1963. Off the endangered list by 2007.
In 1963 only 417 nesting pairs of bald eagles were left in the lower 48 states, poisoned by DDT. After DDT was banned in 1972 they recovered so well that they left the endangered list in 2007.
1398: Glaciers grind rock into powder, and the powder paints the lake milky blue.
Lake Pukaki sits behind a dam of rubble left by an Ice Age glacier, and it is fed by the Tasman and Hooker glaciers, whose finely ground rock gives it this milky blue. Aoraki rises at its head.
1399: A tongue of the biggest ice field south of the equator, outside Antarctica.
Los Perros spills from the Southern Patagonian Ice Field, the largest ice field in the Southern Hemisphere outside Antarctica. Hikers on the Torres del Paine circuit pass it before John Gardner Pass.
1400: In summer you hear it before you see it: ice avalanches thundering off its face.
Mount Sefton, 3,151 meters, towers over Hooker Valley, and in summer the thunder of ice avalanches off its face echoes. It was first climbed in 1895 by Edward FitzGerald and Matthias Zurbriggen.
1401: A virus 100 nanometers wide, painted with red spikes so we could finally see it.
Two CDC medical illustrators built this portrait in January 2020 and painted the spikes red to make a virus 100 nanometers wide feel real. It became one of the most seen images of the pandemic.
1402: Every plant's pollen is a fingerprint, and forensic scientists read it.
Sunflower, morning glory, hollyhock, lily: each plant's pollen has its own shape, spikes and pits, as distinct as a fingerprint. Forensic scientists use it to tie a suspect to a crime scene.
1404: Photographed the year it was shown to cause AIDS. Today it can be made undetectable.
The green dots are new HIV particles budding from a human immune cell, photographed in 1984, the year the virus was shown to cause AIDS. Today treatment can make it undetectable and untransmittable.
1405: MRSA and a White Blood Cell
The red mass is a white blood cell. It tried to eat the bacteria, and died.
The yellow balls are drug-resistant staph bacteria; the red mass is a human white blood cell that tried to eat them and died. Antibiotic resistance already kills over a million people a year.
1406: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Thousands of tiny lenses, and a world of ultraviolet we cannot see.
Each of the thousands of tiny facets in this bee's compound eye is a separate lens with its own narrow view. The bee sees a mosaic, and it also sees ultraviolet patterns on flowers that we cannot.
1407: A Cell Overrun by the Coronavirus
Every yellow speck is a new virus. One cell can release thousands.
Every yellow speck is a coronavirus particle, pouring from a cell grown from a patient's sample in 2020. A single infected cell can release thousands of new copies before it dies.
1408: A pinhead of blood holds about five million of these discs.
A drop of blood the size of a pinhead holds about five million red cells like these smooth discs, plus white cells that hunt intruders and tiny platelets that seal a cut.
1409: Harmless, mostly. But one cell could become billions overnight.
Most E. coli are harmless residents of your gut, and in ideal conditions a cell can divide every 20 minutes. Left unchecked, a single cell could become billions overnight.
1410: A numbing straw and a drinking straw. Most victims sleep right through it.
The purple beak is a bedbug's drinking kit: one channel injects saliva that numbs the skin and stops blood from clotting, another draws the blood up. Most victims sleep right through it.
1411: Graupel: Snow in a Coat of Ice
USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
There is a snowflake hidden inside this lump of ice.
A snowflake is hidden inside this lump. It fell through a cloud of supercooled droplets that froze onto it until the crystal vanished, becoming the soft pellets known as graupel.
1412: Living cells in glass houses, piling up into seafloor layers hundreds of meters thick.
This diatom is a living chain of single cells, each sealed in a shell of glass. When diatoms die, their shells sink and pile up on the seafloor, and some deposits are hundreds of meters thick.
1413: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
She never builds a nest. She borrows one, and her larva kills the owner's young.
This bee never builds a nest. Nomada females slip into other bees' burrows and lay an egg there, and their larva kills the host's offspring and eats the pollen stored for it.
1414: First seen in 1681, in a sample of the discoverer's own diarrhea.
This parasite grips the lining of the gut with a disk that works like a suction cup. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first saw its human cousin in 1681, in a sample of his own diarrhea.
1415: A crown of spikes gave the family its name, and each spike is a key to our cells.
Captured in early 2020 from a patient's sample, these particles wear the ring of spikes that named the family: corona is Latin for crown. The spikes are the keys the virus uses to enter our cells.
1416: Hundreds of billions of soldiers, each trained to recognize one enemy.
This is one of the immune system's soldiers, a T cell from a healthy donor. Your body holds hundreds of billions of them, and each carries a receptor tuned to recognize one particular enemy.
1417: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
Much of what we know about genes, we learned from a humble gut bacterium.
E. coli is one of the most studied living things on Earth. Much of what we know about genes, from how they switch on to how DNA is copied, was first worked out in this humble gut bacterium.
1418: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
There is no blue pigment here. The color is made of light.
This metallic blue has no pigment in it. The color comes from microscopic layers in the shell that reflect light, and when attacked, many cuckoo wasps curl up into an armored ball.
1419: A tiny catapult with legs, and a carrier of the Black Death.
A flea can leap many times its own length, powered by a pad of rubbery protein that snaps like a catapult. Fleas also spread the Black Death, which killed perhaps a third of Europe.
1420: A Dying Cell Covered in Virus
The cell is dying on purpose, a last sacrifice to slow the virus.
The green cell is dying, and the purple beads on it are coronavirus particles. Infected cells often trigger their own death, a last act of sacrifice that can slow the virus down.
1421: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Thirteen or 17 years underground, almost always red-eyed. This one came up blue.
Periodical cicadas spend 13 or 17 years underground and almost always have red eyes. Blue eyes like these are a rare mutation, and in 2021, a 17-year emergence year in Maryland, the lab found one.
1422: Macrophages Close In on a Cancer Cell
The big eaters have caught a cancer cell, and are poisoning it.
Immune cells called macrophages, whose name means big eaters, have latched onto this cancer cell and are injecting toxins into it. It is already rounding up and losing its invasive spikes.
1423: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
To see a snowflake without melting it, they kept it colder than minus 170.
To image snowflakes without melting them, USDA scientists kept them colder than minus 170 degrees Celsius and scanned them with electrons, revealing steps and facets no ordinary camera could show.
1424: It can slip inside an egg before the shell even forms.
These rods are Salmonella Enteritidis, a bacterium that can infect a hen's ovary and end up inside an intact egg before the shell forms. That is why eggs should be cooked through.
1425: The Surface of a Tobacco Leaf
Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
To a tiny insect, this leaf is a field of sticky traps.
These hairs are trichomes, and on this flowering tobacco many end in glands that ooze sticky chemicals. To a tiny insect, the leaf is a field of traps.
1426: Up each night, down at dawn: the largest daily migration on Earth.
These drifting crustaceans link microscopic algae to fish, seabirds and whales. Many rise toward the surface each night and sink at dawn, the largest daily migration on Earth.
1427: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
Find the rust-colored oval: beekeepers' worst enemy, hiding in the hairs.

The rust-colored oval is a varroa mite hiding between a honeybee's hairs. It feeds on the bee's fat tissue and spreads viruses, and since reaching the US in 1987 it has become beekeepers' worst enemy.
1428: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Part male, part female, and about five in 400,000 bees examined.
This sweat bee is a gynandromorph, part male and part female in one body. The lab's head says he has seen only about five among some 400,000 bee specimens he has examined.
1429: A Red Blood Cell Taken by Malaria
Spot the rough one: a red cell taken over by malaria.

The blue cell in the center is a red blood cell infected with malaria parasites, its surface turned rough and bumpy, beside smooth healthy cells. Malaria still kills over half a million people a year.
1430: A virus shaped like a shepherd's crook.
Ebola is a long thread, often hooked at one end like a shepherd's crook. The 2014 to 2016 epidemic in West Africa infected more than 28,000 people and led to the first approved Ebola vaccine.
1431: He won the Nobel for finding these cells. He had died three days earlier.
Ralph Steinman discovered dendritic cells, the immune system's scouts, and won the 2011 Nobel Prize for it. The committee announced the award not knowing he had died three days earlier.
1432: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
He collects perfume from flowers and blends his own scent to win a mate.
Male orchid bees collect perfumes from flowers and store them in pockets on their hind legs, blending a personal scent to win females. This species turned up in Florida around 2003 and stayed.
1433: The bacteria make the cell swallow them, then hide inside.
The red rods are Salmonella injecting proteins into a human cell that make its surface ruffle up and swallow them. Once inside, the bacteria hide from much of the immune system.
1434: Ebola's cousin, discovered nine years before Ebola.
Marburg was the first filovirus ever identified. In 1967 it sickened lab workers in Germany and Yugoslavia who had handled monkeys from Uganda, nine years before its cousin Ebola appeared.
1435: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
The size of a grain of salt, and dressed like a peacock.
This citrus pest, about the size of a grain of salt, carries fans of feathery bristles like a tiny peacock. USDA scientists froze it in place to capture it at 260 times magnification.
1436: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
Every branch of a snowflake records the air it fell through.
A snowflake's shape is a diary of its fall. Near minus 15 degrees Celsius crystals grow feathery arms, near minus 5 they grow needles and columns, so every branch records the air it passed through.
1437: Shaved away one layer at a time, then rebuilt in 3D.

This image was built by shaving a melanoma cell away layer by layer with an ion beam and photographing each new surface. Stacked together, the slices reveal its inner architecture in three dimensions.
1438: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
An emerald with wings, from a bee family found nowhere but Australia.
Its name comes from smaragdus, Latin for emerald. It belongs to a family of bees found nowhere but Australia, an old lineage that evolved in isolation.
1439: Maybe the most numerous animal on Earth, and it glows.
This tiny copepod glows green and yellow under blue light, thanks to proteins related to the one that makes jellyfish shine. Copepods may be the most numerous animals on Earth.
1440: Plague Bacteria in a Flea's Gut
The bacteria starve the flea, so it bites again and again.
Plague bacteria build a sticky mass in a flea's gut that blocks its food from passing. Starving, the flea bites again and again, and each time it spits bacteria into a new victim.
1441: It does not just make you sick: it can erase your immune memory.
Measles is among the most contagious diseases known: up to nine in ten unvaccinated people near an infected person catch it. It can also erase the immune system's memory of past infections.
1442: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
So fast it goes blind mid-chase and has to stop and look again.
Tiger beetles sprint so fast that their eyes cannot keep up, and they go briefly blind mid-chase, stopping to look again before they lunge. For its size, it is one of the fastest runners alive.
1443: Tunneling through a mosquito's gut, on their way to the next bite.
These purple shapes are bird malaria parasites tunneling through a mosquito's gut wall. Inside the insect they multiply, then move to its salivary glands, ready for the next bite.
1444: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
A quarter of a millimeter long, with a back like woven lace.
This citrus mite is about a quarter of a millimeter long, yet its back is patterned like woven lace. Freezing it instantly let scientists see it as it was in life, without drying it out.
1445: Henrietta Lacks's cells were taken without her knowledge. They never stopped dividing.
HeLa cells come from Henrietta Lacks, whose tumor cells were taken without her knowledge in 1951. They never stopped dividing, and helped create the polio vaccine and countless other discoveries.
1446: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Beautiful, and eating its way across America.
Beautiful and destructive, this planthopper from Asia was first found in Pennsylvania in 2014 and has spread to many US states, sucking sap from grapevines, fruit trees and maples.
1447: Declared eliminated in the US in 2000. It came back.
In 2000 the United States declared measles eliminated. Falling vaccination rates have brought it back, with large outbreaks in 2025 and the first US measles deaths in a decade.
1448: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
Why six arms? Because frozen water locks into hexagons.
Every snowflake has six arms because water molecules lock into hexagonal rings when they freeze. That hidden molecular geometry is magnified here into a crystal you can see.
1449: A quarter of humanity carries it without knowing.
Tuberculosis is once again the deadliest single infectious disease, killing about 1.2 million people in 2024. Roughly a quarter of humanity carries the bacterium silently.
1450: Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
These stripes are behind every move you make.
These stripes power every move you make. Each segment is a sarcomere, a couple of thousandths of a millimeter long, where protein filaments slide past each other to contract the muscle.
1451: Scientists photographed it, and could not even name it.
Scientists could not even name this jelly-like drifter, photographed in the Gulf of Mexico in 2005. A large share of the open ocean's tiny creatures has never been formally described.
1452: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
A jewel-green beetle that has killed hundreds of millions of trees.
This jewel-green beetle from Asia was discovered near Detroit in 2002. Its larvae tunnel under ash bark, and it has since killed hundreds of millions of North American ash trees.
1453: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
Four legs instead of eight, and light enough to ride the wind.
Eriophyid mites like this one have only four legs instead of the usual eight and are among the smallest arthropods known, light enough to ride the wind from plant to plant.
1454: 300 million dead in one century. Then, in 1980, it was gone.
Smallpox killed an estimated 300 million people in the 20th century alone. In 1980 it became the first human disease ever eradicated, thanks to vaccination.
1455: Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Tom Kirn, Ron Taylor, Louisa Howard
The year a London pump was blamed for cholera, this microbe was first described.
The bundled threads are pili, which cholera bacteria need to settle in the gut. In 1854 John Snow traced a London outbreak to one pump, the year Filippo Pacini first described the microbe.
1456: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
No sting, no food gathering, and he dies the moment he succeeds.
A drone has no sting and gathers no food. His huge eyes help him spot a queen in flight, and if he manages to mate with her, he dies within moments.
1457: A Red Cell in a Capillary
Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
So narrow that red cells fold to squeeze through.
Capillaries are so narrow that red blood cells pass almost single file, sometimes folding to squeeze through. By a common estimate, an adult's vessels laid end to end would circle the Earth twice.
1458: A Malaria Parasite Ready to Burst
A cell about to burst. In this species, it is why the fever returns every 72 hours.

Inside this red cell a malaria parasite has split into a cluster of new parasites. When the cell bursts they invade fresh cells; for this species the cycle takes three days, so fevers recur every 72 hours.
1459: A Snowflake a Third of a Millimeter Wide
USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
Smaller than a grain of sand, and one breath would erase it.
This crystal is about 300 micrometers across, smaller than many grains of sand. Kept frozen in an electron microscope, it shows ridges and terraces that would vanish in a single breath.
1460: CDC / William L. Nicholson, Cal Welbourn
One of its relatives lives at 85 degrees south, in Antarctica.
Mites of this genus are champions of survival. One species lives in Antarctica as far as 85 degrees south, among the southernmost animals ever found living on land.
1461: Eight pieces of genes, and when two strains swap them, pandemics can start.
Inside this flu virus lie eight separate pieces of genetic material. When two strains infect the same cell they can swap pieces, and that reshuffle has sparked several pandemics.
1462: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Barbed, so it tears free, and the bee dies defending her hive.
A worker honeybee's sting is barbed. In a mammal's skin it anchors so firmly that the sting, venom sac and all, tears free, and the bee dies defending her hive.
1463: Named after a convention it struck in 1976.
Legionnaires' disease got its name in 1976, when an outbreak at an American Legion convention in Philadelphia sickened more than 180 people. The bacteria thrive in warm water systems.
1464: Underside of a Black Walnut Leaf
Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
A single leaf can breathe through hundreds of thousands of tiny mouths.
Among these hairs sit stomata, tiny mouths that open to let carbon dioxide in and water vapor out. A single leaf can carry hundreds of thousands of them.
1465: A mother carrying her eggs, and a hidden pillar of the world's fisheries.
The blue clusters are eggs this female copepod carries until they hatch. Copepods graze on algae and feed fish such as herring and young salmon, a hidden pillar of the world's fisheries.
1466: Our eyes are wired backward, and they still work beautifully.
Light passes through all these layers of nerve cells before it reaches the photoreceptors, shown here in green. The vertebrate eye is wired backward, yet it works astonishingly well.
1467: Its close relative can recognize its nestmates by their faces.
A close relative of this paper wasp can recognize individual faces of its nestmates, a skill once credited only to big-brained animals. It builds its nest from chewed wood pulp.
1468: To learn why it killed tens of millions, scientists rebuilt it.
In 2005 CDC scientists rebuilt the 1918 flu virus from genes recovered from victims, one of them buried in Alaskan permafrost, to learn why it killed tens of millions.
1469: Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
Born already pregnant: one female can found a colony of thousands.
Many aphids give birth to live young that are already carrying the next generation inside them, so one female can found a colony of thousands within weeks without ever mating.
1470: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Dressed as a wasp, with no sting at all.
Hoverflies dress like wasps but cannot sting. Their larvae devour aphids, and the adults are among the most important pollinators after bees.
1471: The green glow is glue. Cancer cells that lose it break loose.
The green outlines are E-cadherin, a protein that glues cells together. When cancer cells lose it they can break loose and spread, so this glow maps cells still holding on.
1472: They have learned to resist nearly every antibiotic thrown at them.
These paired bacteria cause gonorrhea, and they have learned to resist nearly every antibiotic used against them. For years doctors have relied mainly on a single injected drug.
1473: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
It started as a column, then grew a plate on each end, like a Japanese drum.
This crystal is named after the tsuzumi, a Japanese hourglass drum. It began as a column, then drifted into air where flat plates grow, and sprouted a plate on each end.
1474: Its larvae burrow through skin in fresh water, and the adults can live in veins for years.
This worm's larvae burrow through human skin in fresh water. Schistosomiasis affects more than 200 million people, mostly in Africa, and adult worms can live in the veins for years.
1475: A bird virus that, in 2024, turned up in American dairy cows.
H5N1 first jumped from birds to people in Hong Kong in 1997. In 2024 it surprised scientists again by spreading through American dairy cattle.
1476: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Garnets the size of sand, carrying a record of the deep crust where they grew.
These garnets are about a millimeter across, glued to an insect pin. Garnets grow deep in the crust under heat and pressure, and geologists read the conditions of their birth from their chemistry.
1477: A baby crab or shrimp, looking nothing like its parents.
Many crabs and shrimp begin life as see-through larvae like this one, drifting with the plankton and molting through stages that look nothing like their parents.
1478: Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
About 800 domes, and a lesson in how genes build an organ.
Each dome is one unit of a fruit fly's eye, roughly 800 in all, separated by tiny bristles. Working out how this tidy pattern forms has taught biologists how genes build an organ.
1479: A rare cancer that strikes mostly teenagers, often while they grow.
In this osteosarcoma cell, DNA glows blue, mitochondria yellow and the actin skeleton purple. Osteosarcoma is rare and strikes mostly teenagers, often during growth spurts.
1480: Penicillin still cures it, and yet cases are climbing again.
These green corkscrews cause syphilis, which still yields to penicillin, the drug that first cured it in 1943. Cases have been climbing again in many countries.
1481: From bats to pigs to people, and it kills up to three in four it infects.
Nipah virus jumped from fruit bats to pigs to people in Malaysia in 1999. It kills 40 to 75 percent of those it infects, and no vaccine is licensed yet, though candidates are in trials.
1482: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Each pearl is a caterpillar waiting to eat maize, now on three continents.
Each of these pearls holds a caterpillar that will chew through crops. Native to the Americas, the fall armyworm reached Africa in 2016 and Asia two years later, and now threatens maize worldwide.
1483: USDA ARS Electron and Confocal Microscopy Unit
Each bump is a frozen cloud droplet that hit it in midair.
The bumps on this hexagonal plate are frozen cloud droplets that struck it as it fell. Add enough of them and the crystal disappears inside, becoming graupel.
1484: Grown from a patient's own cells, to give back their sight.
These retinal support cells were grown from a patient's own stem cells on a biodegradable scaffold. NIH has begun testing such patches in people losing their sight to macular degeneration.
1485: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
It sneaks into other nests, wearing armor that shrugs off stings.
Cuckoo wasps lay their eggs in the nests of other bees and wasps. Their hard, deeply pitted armor shrugs off the stings of angry hosts.
1486: Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
Tens of thousands of species, many of which eat only one kind of plant.
Leaf beetles are among the most diverse animals on Earth, with tens of thousands of species described, many of them specialists that eat only one kind of plant.
1487: It reaches people from camels, and kills about a third of those known to be infected.
MERS was identified in Saudi Arabia in 2012 and passes to people from dromedary camels. It kills roughly a third of the people known to be infected.
1488: Every time the body catches it, it changes disguise, and the fever returns.
These spiral bacteria swim among red blood cells and keep changing their surface coat. Each time the immune system catches up, a new disguise appears and the fever comes back.
1489: A single spore that makes wheat smell of rotten fish.
This fungal spore, magnified about 2,000 times, causes a wheat disease that makes grain smell of rotten fish. Its discovery in Arizona in 1996 led to quarantines and halted some US wheat exports.
1490: A Larva and a Sea Butterfly
A snail that flies through water, its shell slowly dissolving in a souring sea.
Beside the crustacean larva floats a pteropod, a tiny snail that swims with wing-like flaps. Its thin shell dissolves more easily as the ocean absorbs carbon dioxide and turns more acidic.
1491: Three millimeters long, with a back like a stained glass window.
This bug is only 3 millimeters long, and its back is a lattice of see-through cells, like a stained glass window without the color. Lace bugs feed on the undersides of leaves.
1492: A Mini Brain in a Dish
Smaller than a pea, it built itself into layers like a growing brain.
This organoid, smaller than a pea, grew from human stem cells and arranged itself into layers like a developing brain. They let researchers study disorders that cannot be studied in a living brain.
1493: Up to 300,000 infections a year, and most people never get very sick.
Lassa virus reaches people from the droppings of a common rat in West Africa. It infects an estimated 100,000 to 300,000 people a year, most of whom never become seriously ill.
1494: Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
A beak of needles, and a smell often compared to coriander.
The long groove down the middle holds the stink bug's beak, a bundle of needles it drives into plants to suck their juices. When threatened it releases a smell often compared to coriander.
1495: Wrapped in slime inside a catheter, safe from antibiotics.

Staph bacteria found inside a catheter tube have wrapped themselves in biofilm, a sticky slime that shields them from antibiotics. Biofilms make infections of medical devices notoriously hard to cure.
1496: No pigment at all: the colors are light bouncing between scales.
No pigment makes these colors. The scales of Madagascar's sunset moth are curved and layered so that light bouncing between them emerges as shimmering green, gold and violet.
1497: USDA ARS Electron and Confocal Microscopy Unit
Crystals like this one are weak, and can bring down an avalanche.
The same snow crystal from the bottom of a Wyoming snowpack, seen by video camera and by electron microscope. Layers of crystals like this are weak and can set off avalanches.
1498: The cell's power plants carry their own DNA, and it comes only from your mother.
The branching threads are mitochondria, the cell's power plants, spread in a web around the nucleus. They carry their own small loop of DNA, which we inherit only from our mothers.
1499: Under early microscopes, its insides looked like sand. Hence its family's name.
Inside Lassa particles sit grains of borrowed ribosomes that looked like sand under early microscopes. That gave the family its name: arenavirus, from the Latin word for sand.
1500: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Up close, a butterfly wing is shingled like a roof.
The silver dots on this Peruvian butterfly's underside are clusters of scales that work like tiny mirrors. Seen this close, a butterfly wing turns out to be shingled like a roof.
1501: Lace Bug under the Electron Beam
Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
A honeycomb of tiny windows: the same trick engineers use for light, strong panels.
Under the electron beam, a lace bug's wings become a honeycomb of tiny windowpanes. The lattice is light yet stiff, the same trick engineers use to build strong, lightweight panels.
1502: USDA ARS / De Wood, Christopher Pooley
A corkscrew built to drill through the lining of your gut.
These corkscrew bacteria are a leading cause of food poisoning in the US, usually from undercooked poultry. Their spiral shape helps them drill through the mucus that lines the gut.
1503: Dartmouth College EM Facility / Louisa Howard
Tough enough to last thousands of years in mud, and tell us what grew there.
Pollen walls are made of sporopollenin, one of the toughest natural materials known. Grains like these survive in lake mud for thousands of years, letting scientists reconstruct ancient landscapes.
1504: Thousands of eggs, and only a tiny few will grow up.
These fish larvae, lined up above a ruler, are only days or weeks old. Of the thousands of eggs a female may spawn, usually only a tiny fraction survive to adulthood.
1505: Soybean Cyst Nematode and Its Egg
A microscopic worm costing farmers over a billion dollars a year.
This microscopic worm is the most damaging pest of soybeans in the US, costing farmers well over a billion dollars a year. Its eggs can wait in the soil for years for a host.
1506: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Those tiny dots by its mouth? Those are its eyes.
This green face belongs to the caterpillar of the northern pearly eye butterfly. The tiny dots near its mouth are its eyes: most caterpillars see with six simple eyes on each side of the head.
1507: A deadly mystery in 1993, and its virus was named 'without a name'.
In 1993 a mysterious lung disease struck the Four Corners region of the US. The virus behind it, carried by deer mice, was named Sin Nombre, Spanish for without a name.
1508: Swollen power plants that help explain a rare disease in children.
These swollen, misshapen mitochondria come from the liver of a mouse with a rare inherited disease, methylmalonic acidemia. They help explain what goes wrong in children with the same condition.
1509: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
The bubbles trapped in this snow are samples of ancient air.
Firn is snow on its way to becoming glacier ice. Over years the grains fuse and trap the air between them in bubbles, samples of ancient atmosphere that scientists drill out of ice sheets.
1510: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
It makes tiny hollow balls inside its body and powders itself with them.
Leafhoppers coat themselves in brochosomes, microscopic hollow balls they make inside their bodies and spread like powder. The coating repels water and may help hide them from predators.
1511: Breathe in just a handful of these and you may get sick.
This cell has been cracked open to reveal a cavity crowded with Coxiella, the bacteria behind Q fever. Breathing in just a handful of them can be enough to make a person sick.
1512: Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
Almost cold light, and every species flashes its own code.
A firefly's light is nearly cold, wasting far less energy as heat than an old incandescent bulb. Each species flashes its own code, a language of light for finding mates.
1513: Its name means 'that which bends up', after the patients' stooped backs.
Chikungunya comes from a word in the Kimakonde language of Tanzania meaning that which bends up, after the stooped posture of patients in severe joint pain.
1514: Every red spot is a break in the DNA, and a sign the drugs are working.
These colorectal cancer cells were treated with two drugs that stop them from repairing their DNA. The red spots mark breaks in the DNA, signs that the treatment is hitting home.
1515: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Those feathery antennae are ears, tuned to the hum of her wings.
Those feathery antennae belong to a male midge and work as ears, picking up the hum of a female's wings. Midge larvae are a staple food for fish in ponds and streams.
1516: In open water there is nowhere to hide, so it became see-through.
This young fish, see-through except for its eyes and gut, was netted along with the plankton. Transparency is a common disguise in open water, where there is nowhere to hide.
1517: A Protozoan from a Sheep's Stomach
USDA ARS / Sharon Franklin, Stephen Ausmus
A sheep cannot digest grass alone. Cells like this do it for her.
This single cell, up to 200 micrometers long, lives in the rumen of sheep. Countless microbes like it help ruminants digest grass that their own enzymes cannot break down.
1518: Pneumonia Bacteria Meet a White Cell
A white cell on the attack, against a leading cause of pneumonia.
The yellow balls are Streptococcus pneumoniae, a leading cause of pneumonia, and the red shape is a white blood cell attacking them. Vaccines now protect children from its most dangerous strains.
1519: Proving mosquitoes spread it helped make the Panama Canal possible.
In 1900 Walter Reed's team in Cuba proved that mosquitoes spread yellow fever, confirming Carlos Finlay's idea. Mosquito control then helped make the Panama Canal possible.
1520: Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
The snout is a drill, made for boring into seeds.
Weevils form one of the largest families of animals, with over 80,000 described species. The long snout is a drill: females bore into seeds and stems to lay their eggs.
1521: Face of a Phantom Crane Fly
USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Its feet are filled with air, so it floats on the breeze.
Phantom crane flies drift through forest clearings with their banded legs spread wide. Their swollen feet are filled with air, helping them float on the breeze.
1522: The chatter behind memory may run on its own energy feedback loop.
NIH researchers tracked energy levels as these neurons signaled to each other, and found that the intense chatter behind learning and memory may be fueled by an energy-sensing feedback loop.
1523: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
Rings like a tree: each one is another trip through the storm.
Split open, this small hailstone shows layers like the rings of a tree. Each shell of ice formed on another trip through the storm cloud before it finally fell.
1524: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Eight eyes, and the front two work like telephoto lenses.
Jumping spiders have eight eyes and some of the sharpest vision of any small animal. The big front pair works like telephoto lenses, letting them judge distance before they pounce.
1525: Most adults carry it for life, unaware it can trigger multiple sclerosis.
Most adults carry this virus for life without knowing it. In 2022 a study of over ten million US soldiers found that infection with it is the leading known trigger of multiple sclerosis.
1526: The first microbe ever proven to cause a specific disease.
In 1876 Robert Koch showed that these rod-shaped bacteria cause anthrax, the first time any microbe was proven to cause a specific disease.
1527: Three quarters of our disease genes have a match in this fly.
About three quarters of human disease genes have a match in the fruit fly. In this fly brain, NIH scientists traced how an overactive immune system may harm nerve cells as brains age.
1528: Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
Claws for rough surfaces, oily hairs for glass.
Leaf beetles walk up glass on thousands of tiny hairs on their feet, each tipped with a film of oily fluid. The claws grip rough surfaces; the hairs stick to smooth ones.
1529: Curled around their yolk, and on their own from the very start.
Inside these clear eggs, fish embryos are curled around their yolk. Many ocean fish release eggs that drift with the plankton, leaving each one to fend for itself from the very start.
1530: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
So small it needed a microscope. In a few months it will walk out of the water.
This tadpole, probably a spring peeper, is only days out of the egg and so small it needed a microscope lens. In two or three months it will grow legs, lose its tail and leave the water.
1531: Usually just a cold. But in 2014 its spread came with a wave of paralysis in children.
This cousin of poliovirus usually causes a cold. But its spread in 2014 coincided with a wave of sudden paralysis in children, and it is now seen as a leading cause of that condition.
1532: Dartmouth EM Facility / Elizabeth Smith, Louisa Howard, Erin Dymek
One alga, and the same tube pattern as the cilia in your airways.
This single-celled alga swims with two whip-like flagella, built on the same nine-plus-two pattern of tubes as the cilia in our airways and the tail of a sperm.
1533: USGS / B.W. Hallett, V.F. Paskevich, L.J. Poppe et al.
Slice granite thinner than paper, and it lights up in colors.
Slice granite thinner than a sheet of paper and shine polarized light through it, and its crystals light up in colors that reveal each mineral and the order in which they grew.
1534: The first responder of an infection, swallowing drug-resistant staph.
The green shape is a neutrophil, our most common white blood cell, engulfing purple drug-resistant staph. Neutrophils are the first responders of an infection, arriving within hours.
1535: Tiny feet that grip and dissolve the tissue around them.
The yellow dots are podosomes, tiny feet rich in actin that these melanoma cells use to grip and dissolve the tissue around them. Blocking them is one strategy for stopping cancer from spreading.
1536: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Pinned in 1867, and still the yardstick for naming new species.
The label pinned under this Mexican bee reads 1867, yet it has kept its shape and color. Old museum specimens like it are still the yardsticks against which new species are named.
1537: A clear wing that hides a rainbow, maybe a signal for mates.

A mosquito's wing looks clear, but on a dark background it shows rainbow patterns. The colors come from the varying thickness of the membrane, and some insects may use such patterns to recognize mates.
1538: It infects few people, but about a third of those who get brain inflammation die.
Spread by mosquitoes in the eastern US, this virus infects few people but is among the deadliest: about a third of those who develop brain inflammation from it die.
1539: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Its antennae split each eye in two: four eyes, as its Latin name says.
This beetle's antennae split each eye in two, so in effect it has four eyes; its name, Tetraopes, means four eyes. Its red warns predators of the milkweed toxins stored in its body.
1540: Normal cells stop when they touch. These keep piling on.

Lit from the side so that only scattered light reaches the lens, these cancer cells glow against black. Unlike normal cells, they keep piling on top of one another instead of stopping when they touch.
1541: CDC / Janice Haney Carr, Matthew Arduino
Ordinary-looking staph, with walls thick enough to trap a last-line drug.
These look like ordinary staph, but they came from a strain that resists vancomycin, a last-line antibiotic. Their secret is a cell wall thick enough to trap the drug before it reaches its target.
1542: Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
The groove is an exit: after landing, a tube breaks out and races to deliver.
Each lily pollen grain is netted with ridges and has a long groove where the pollen tube breaks out after landing on a flower, then races down to deliver the sperm.
1543: Harpoons that fire in under a millionth of a second.
This jellyfish, small enough to need a microscope, has caught a crustacean larva. Even jellies this small hunt with stinging cells that fire like harpoons in less than a millionth of a second.
1544: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Its larvae eat their hosts alive. The idea troubled Darwin.
Ichneumon wasps lay their eggs in or on other insects, and the larvae eat their hosts alive. The idea troubled Darwin, yet these wasps are vital natural controllers of pests.
1545: Found in a monkey in 1947. Nearly 70 years later it swept through Brazil.
Zika was discovered in 1947 in a monkey in Uganda's Zika Forest. Nearly seven decades later it swept through Brazil and was linked to babies born with unusually small heads.
1546: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
A mite that carries a virus that can bring down whole citrus trees.
This citrus pest, magnified 600 times, carries leprosis, a virus disease that scars citrus leaves and fruit and can make whole trees decline.
1547: USGS / B.W. Hallett, V.F. Paskevich, L.J. Poppe et al.
A crystal that cracked deep underground, and healed with quartz.
This rock began as granite and was squeezed and heated deep underground until its minerals recrystallized. Here a single feldspar crystal has cracked and healed with veins of quartz.
1548: The First Picture of a Tardigrade
A pastor drew a little water bear. It turned out to survive even outer space.
In 1773 pastor Johann Goeze drew this tiny creature and called it a little water bear. Tardigrades can survive drying out, deep freezing, and even exposure to outer space.
1549: Bristling and frightening in 1980. Today, found early, it can usually be cured.
Photographed by a scanning electron microscope in 1980, this cancer cell bristles with projections. Today most breast cancers found early can be cured, thanks to screening and better treatment.
1550: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
She shivers to warm up, and buzzes flowers until they let go of their pollen.
Bumblebees shiver their flight muscles to warm up, flying in weather too cold for most bees. They also buzz flowers to shake loose pollen, a trick tomato flowers need.
1551: Bacteria that cannot live outside a cell, and arrive in flea droppings.
These bacteria cause murine typhus, which reaches people when infected flea droppings are scratched into the skin. They can live only inside cells, borrowing much of what they need from their host.
1552: In 2022 it reached more than a hundred countries, and lost its old name.
In 2022 mpox, long confined mostly to Central and West Africa, spread to more than a hundred countries. That year the WHO renamed the disease, retiring the old name monkeypox.
1553: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
Too small to see, and its damage is often mistaken for disease.
Broad mites are too small to see without magnification, yet they attack hundreds of crops, from peppers to cotton. Their feeding twists and bronzes young leaves, damage often mistaken for disease.
1554: The queen builds the first rooms alone, from chewed wood.
Each paper cell holds a growing wasp. The queen builds the first cells alone in spring from chewed wood pulp, and her daughters take over the work as the colony grows.
1555: A newborn already able to change color in a blink.
This hatchling octopus or squid is already dotted with color cells it can open and close in a blink, using tiny muscles wired directly to its brain.
1556: Dartmouth EM Facility / Louisa Howard, Michael Binder
Nine pairs around two: the pattern sweeping dust out of your lungs.
Each circle is a cilium cut across, showing nine pairs of tubes around a central two. Countless cilia beat in waves along your airways, sweeping out dust and germs.
1557: Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
Bacteria living inside a root, trading fertilizer for sugar.
The dark ovals are bacteria living inside a soybean root cell, turning nitrogen from the air into fertilizer for the plant. In return the plant feeds them sugar.
1558: A two-millimeter crystal that remembers how deep the magma sat.
The brown crystal at the center, about two millimeters long, is amphibole; the white rectangles are plagioclase; blue marks empty space. Such crystals reveal how deep magma sat before erupting.
1559: Descendants of the 1918 flu are still going around.
Descendants of the 1918 flu virus still circulate as H1N1. In 2009 a new H1N1 strain mixing pig, bird and human genes swept around the world within weeks.
1560: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Its eyes wrap around its antennae and peek out on top.
This longhorn beetle's eyes wrap around the base of its antennae and peek out on top of its head. Longhorn larvae can spend years tunneling inside wood before they emerge.
1561: These are the neurons ALS kills. In mice, researchers found a way to protect them.
These are healthy mouse spinal cord neurons, the kind that die in ALS. NIH researchers found a way to rein in Cdk5, an overactive enzyme that kills them in mice with an ALS mutation.
1562: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
A quarter of a millimeter long, it swept the Caribbean and reached Florida.
This invasive mite, about a quarter of a millimeter long, swept through the Caribbean in the 2000s and reached Florida in 2007, threatening coconut palms and bananas.
1563: One mushroom, billions of spores, each one a possible new fungus.
These are budding spores of the common button mushroom. A single mushroom can release billions of spores, each one able to start a new fungus wherever the air sets it down.
1564: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
To this fly, a movie would look like a slide show.
This fly's head is about the size of a pinhead, yet its eyes hold hundreds of facets. Flies process images so fast that a movie would look to them like a slide show.
1565: It arrived in 1968 and never left.
H3N2 arrived in 1968 as the Hong Kong flu pandemic and never left. It changes so quickly that flu vaccines must be updated almost every year to keep up.
1566: In wet weather these threads break into swimming spores.
These branching threads cause rain scald, a skin disease of cattle and horses. In wet weather the filaments break up into swimming spores that spread from animal to animal.
1567: It may live about a year: grow fast, spawn once, and die.
This squid hatchling already has its full set of arms and tentacles. Many squid live only about a year, growing at astonishing speed before they spawn once and die.
1568: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
A one-millimeter seed, and up close, a honeycomb.
A poppy seed is about a millimeter long, but up close its surface is a honeycomb of ridges. A single poppy pod can hold more than a thousand of them.
1569: A body so clear you can watch its organs form, live.
Magenta blood cells flow through yellow vessels on the yolk of a two-day-old zebrafish embryo, about the size of a grain of rice. Its transparent body lets scientists watch organs form live.
1570: A rock from 1,600 meters under a buried crater, with a hot past locked inside.
This schist came from more than 1,600 meters down a drill core sunk into the buried Chesapeake Bay impact crater. Its sillimanite crystals form only at high temperatures, recording a hot past.
1571: USDA ARS / Ronald Ochoa, Gary Bauchan, Chris Pooley
Head-on, this tiny pest looks like a cartoon.
Seen head-on, the mouthparts of this tiny cassava pest look like a cartoon creature. Spider mites suck plant cells dry, and many species spin fine silk webs like spiders.
1572: Something rare happened: tracing and isolation stamped it out.
