SARS emerged in China in 2002 and infected about 8,000 people in 29 countries. Then something rare happened: isolation and contact tracing stamped it out by mid 2003.
1573: CDC / Janice Haney Carr, Margaret Williams
It lives in tap water, and once infected over a hundred nail salon customers.
This relative of the tuberculosis bacterium lives in soil and tap water. In 2000 it infected more than a hundred customers of a single California nail salon through its footbaths.
1574: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Let the lawn grow wild, and creatures like this move in.
This planthopper's long nose is a hollow extension of its head. It feeds on grasses, part of the hidden diversity that thrives wherever lawns are left to grow wild.
1575: The brain's guards remember a past meningitis, and are weaker for it.
These macrophages patrol the membranes around a mouse brain. NIH researchers found that meningitis leaves a lasting mark on them, which can weaken the defense against later infections.
1576: Swarming the very cell they destroy. Two shots a year can now prevent it.
The yellow dots are HIV particles swarming a human T cell, the very immune cell the virus destroys. A daily pill, or now an injection just twice a year, can prevent infection.
1577: Glowing red under UV, and capable of poisoning a lake.
Under ultraviolet light, the filaments of this lake cyanobacterium glow red from chlorophyll. Blooms of such microbes can release toxins dangerous to pets, livestock and people.
1578: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
It sings by drumming on stems, songs we hear only with sensors.
Treehoppers talk by drumming vibrations through the stems they sit on, songs people can hear only with special sensors. This tiny one sips sap from tick-trefoil plants.
1579: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
It lays its eggs inside maggots, and its young eat them from within.
This tiny wasp, Tachinaephagus zealandicus, lays its eggs inside fly maggots, and its young eat them from within. It has been studied as a natural way to control filth flies.
1580: From sink drains to ventilators: a germ the WHO most wants new drugs for.
This bacterium thrives almost anywhere wet, from sink drains to hospital ventilators, and shrugs off many antibiotics. The WHO counts drug-resistant strains among the germs most in need of new drugs.
1581: Female Flower of a Black Walnut
USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Walnut trees do bloom. Almost nobody notices.
Black walnut trees do bloom, though few people notice. These fuzzy stigmas catch pollen drifting on the wind, and the swelling beneath them will grow into a walnut.
1582: Shells of single cells, and a thermometer for ancient oceans.
Each of these shells, magnified 255 times, was built by a single-celled organism. Their fossils fill seafloor mud, and the chemistry of their shells is a key record of past ocean temperatures.
1583: A teaspoon holds thousands of these, each with its own sharp edges.
Table sugar is made of crystals like these, each a stack of sucrose molecules in a repeating pattern. A single teaspoon holds thousands of them, each with its own flat faces and sharp edges.
1584: Your body does this millions of times every second.
This hamster cell is caught in anaphase, the moment its doubled chromosomes are pulled to opposite ends. Your body carries out this split millions of times every second.
1585: Safe to release because it eats only one plant: the one we wanted gone.
This weevil, about a millimeter and a half long, was brought from Asia to fight mile-a-minute weed, an invasive vine. It eats only that plant, which is what made it safe to release.
1586: It can turn a sheep's tongue blue, and it moves north as winters soften.
Spread by biting midges, bluetongue sickens sheep and cattle and can turn a sheep's tongue blue for lack of oxygen. It has been spreading north through Europe as winters grow milder.
1587: Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
Jaws that slice sideways, like scissors.
A grasshopper's jaws move side to side, not up and down, slicing leaves like scissors. Under the right conditions some species swarm as locusts that can strip crops across whole regions.
1588: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Dozens of photos, each a hair deeper, stacked into one sharp picture.
Images like this are made by stacking dozens of photos, each focused a hair deeper, into one picture that is sharp from front to back. A single shot would be in focus only in a thin slice.
1589: Each whip is spun by a motor: one of nature's few true wheels.
A special stain reveals the whip-like flagella these Bordetella bacteria use to swim. Each flagellum is spun by a rotary motor in the cell wall, one of nature's few true wheels.
1590: Specks of gold inside a cell, being tested as couriers for cancer drugs.
The bright specks are gold nanoparticles inside a cell, lit with dark-field illumination. Because they are nontoxic and easy to load with drugs, they are studied as carriers for cancer treatment.
1591: CDC / C. S. Goldsmith, A. Balish
A first look, days after it was found. Two months later, a pandemic.
This is one of the first images of the new H1N1 virus, taken at CDC in April 2009, days after it was identified. Within two months the WHO declared the first flu pandemic in 41 years.
1592: A parasite that cycles between cattle and people, by way of a rare steak.
The purple ovals are cysts of Sarcocystis, a parasite that cycles between cattle and people. Eating raw or undercooked beef can infect us; thorough cooking kills it.
1593: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
No web. It hunts by sight and leaps.
Lynx spiders do not build webs to catch prey. They hunt on plants by sight, leaping onto insects, and this one was so small it took a microscope lens to see it clearly.
1594: A single glassy cell, nicknamed rock snot.
This glassy cell, Didymosphenia geminata, can carpet riverbeds in thick mats nicknamed rock snot. Its blooms surged in rivers from New Zealand to Chile in the 2000s.
1595: A reef built by algae in a lake, 50 million years ago.
This polished slice is a reef built by algae in a lake some 50 million years ago, from the Green River Formation of the western US. Its bands alternate between layers of life and layers of mud.
1596: Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility / Louisa Howard
Smaller than a grain of rice, and shaped like a polished seed.
Shining flower beetles are smaller than a grain of rice and spend their lives in flower heads, eating pollen and fungal spores. Their smooth, domed backs make them look like polished seeds.
1597: USDA ARS / Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley
Its thick capsule is a cloak that hides it from a cow's defenses.
To see this bacterium's thick capsule, scientists coated a freeze-dried sample with metal and imaged the replica. The capsule helps it hide from a cow's immune defenses and cause udder infections.
1598: Labs have grown tons of these, far more than her body ever held.
These two cells have just split from one. HeLa cells divide roughly once a day, and since 1951 laboratories have grown tons of them, vastly more than Henrietta Lacks's body ever held.
1599: Almost always fatal once symptoms show, and almost always preventable before.
Once symptoms appear, rabies is almost always fatal. Yet a vaccine given soon after a bite, first used by Louis Pasteur in 1885, prevents the disease nearly every time.
1600: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
Some of its desert cousins drink fog, tilting their backs into the wind.
Darkling beetles include desert species that drink fog by tilting their backs into the wind and letting droplets roll down to their mouths. This one came from a light trap on the Georgia coast.
1601: The Navy wanted yellow and black stripes. The architect loved the primer.
The bridge's color began as the red primer on its steel. Architect Irving Morrow loved it against the fog and hills and chose 'International Orange'. The Navy had wanted yellow and black stripes.
1602: Main Reading Room, Library of Congress
After the British burned the Capitol, the library was reborn from Jefferson's own books.
The Library of Congress was reborn from Thomas Jefferson's own books, bought in 1815 after the British burned the Capitol. This room, under a dome 49 meters high, opened in 1897.
1603: Sixteen years of work, and he died six months before it opened.
Frank Lloyd Wright spent 16 years on this spiral, a single long ramp you walk down past the art. He died in April 1959, six months before the museum opened.
1604: Built in secret inside the tower, hoisted in 90 minutes, tallest for under a year.
In the race for the world's tallest building, the Chrysler's spire was assembled in secret inside the tower, then hoisted into place in about 90 minutes in 1929. It held the title for under a year.
1605: Walt Disney Concert Hall, Los Angeles
Shaped with fighter-jet software, then too shiny: it cooked the neighbors.
Frank Gehry shaped these steel sails with software made for designing fighter jets. Soon after the 2003 opening, the shiniest panels beamed heat onto neighbors and had to be dulled.
1606: Not one wall but many, and no, you cannot see it from the Moon.
The Great Wall is not one wall but many, built and rebuilt over some 2,000 years. Despite the famous myth, it cannot be seen with the naked eye from the Moon.
1607: Exactly as wide as it is tall, climbed in tiny egg-shaped capsules.
Eero Saarinen's arch is exactly as wide as it is tall, 192 meters each way. Visitors ride to the top in tiny egg-shaped capsules that tilt to stay level as they climb the curve.
1608: For nearly 500 years, ordinary people could not walk in.
For nearly 500 years ordinary people could not enter the Forbidden City without permission. Its roughly 980 buildings were home to 24 emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties.
1609: He built the house on top of the waterfall, not facing it.
Frank Lloyd Wright put the house on top of the waterfall, not facing it, so the family would live with it. Its daring terraces sagged for decades until hidden steel cables saved them in 2002.
1610: Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, Beijing
28 pillars and not one nail: a building that is also a calendar.
This hall stands on 28 wooden pillars and no nails: 4 for the seasons, 12 for the months and 12 for the traditional hours of the day. After lightning burned it in 1889, it was rebuilt exactly.
1611: It looks like marble. It is 4,000 tonnes of painted cast iron.
The Capitol dome looks like stone but is cast iron, about 4,000 tonnes of it, painted to match the marble. It was built during the Civil War, because Lincoln insisted the work go on.
1612: Thirteen stories and over 1,000 rooms, at 3,700 meters.
The Potala Palace climbs 13 stories up a hill in Lhasa, at about 3,700 meters, with more than 1,000 rooms. It was the Dalai Lama's winter home until the 14th fled to India in 1959.
1613: One column for every state, and the steps where a dream was spoken aloud.
The memorial has 36 columns, one for each state in the Union when Lincoln died. In 1963 Martin Luther King Jr. stood on these steps and told the crowd, 'I have a dream'.
1614: It faces west, toward death, so some thought it was a tomb.
Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument on Earth, and it appears on Cambodia's flag. Unusually it faces west, the direction linked with death, which led some to think it was built as a tomb.
1615: Look a quarter of the way up: the marble changes shade.
Look about a quarter of the way up and the marble changes shade. Work stopped for over two decades from 1854, and when it resumed the stone came from a different quarry.
1617: The zodiac on the ceiling is backward, and one dark patch was left dirty on purpose.
The zodiac on the concourse ceiling is painted backward, as if seen from outside the heavens. Restorers in the 1990s left one dark patch uncleaned to show how much grime once covered it.
1618: Bullet marks up top: Bedouins believed the urn hid a pharaoh's treasure.
Al-Khazneh was not built but carved straight into the cliff by the Nabataeans some 2,000 years ago. Bullet marks on its top urn come from Bedouins who believed it hid a pharaoh's treasure.
1619: A whole tower whose center of gravity sits just 1.5 meters above the ground.
Built in about 400 days for the 1962 World's Fair, the Space Needle stands on a foundation so heavy that the whole tower's center of gravity sits just 1.5 meters above the ground.
1620: Its dome seemed to hang from heaven on a golden chain.
When Hagia Sophia was finished in 537 its dome seemed to float, and a writer of the time said it hung from heaven on a golden chain. It was the largest church on Earth for almost 1,000 years.
1621: One continuous ramp across four floors, so the catalog never breaks apart.
Rem Koolhaas stacked this library like shifted boxes in a glass net. Inside, the Books Spiral is one continuous ramp across four floors, so the shelves never break the catalog apart.
1622: Six minarets caused a scandal; the sultan settled it by paying for a seventh in Mecca.
The Sultan Ahmed Mosque was given six minarets, a number then matched only by the holy mosque in Mecca. Legend says the sultan ended the scandal by paying for a seventh minaret in Mecca.
1623: Mocked as a dunce cap, it tapers so more light reaches the street.
San Franciscans hated the pyramid when it rose in 1972, and critics mocked it as a dunce cap. It tapers to let more light reach the streets, and its top 65 meters are a hollow spire.
1624: Willem van de Poll / Nationaal Archief
Some 4,000 buildings, many drawn by architects trained in Europe.
Tel Aviv has some 4,000 buildings in the International Style, many designed in the 1930s by architects trained in Europe. In 2003 UNESCO declared its White City a World Heritage Site.
1625: His followers hid his remains for nearly 60 years before laying them here.
Nineteen garden terraces run down Mount Carmel around the Shrine of the Báb, a prophet executed in Iran in 1850. His followers hid his remains for nearly 60 years before laying them here in 1909.
1626: Nine square tubes bundled together, each stopping at a different height.
When it opened in 1973 the Sears Tower was the world's tallest building, and it kept the title for 25 years. It is nine square tubes bundled together, each ending at a different height.
1627: Gaudí joked that his client was in no hurry. The work began in 1882.
Construction began in 1882, and Gaudí, who joked that his client was in no hurry, gave the rest of his life to it. Builders set out to top its tallest tower in 2026, a century after his death.
1628: Corn cobs with a bowling alley, an ice rink and a marina: a city within a city.
Bertrand Goldberg's 'corn cobs' opened in 1964 as a city within a city, with flats stacked above a spiraling car park, a bowling alley, an ice rink and a marina on the river.
1629: A mosque's golden mihrab, and centuries later, a cathedral built in its heart.
The mihrab of Córdoba's great mosque, finished in the 960s, glows with gold mosaics made with help from a Byzantine craftsman. Centuries later a cathedral was built in the mosque's heart.
1630: Roofs that float six meters past the walls, held up by hidden steel.
Wright's Robie House, finished in 1910, hugs the ground like the prairie that gave his style its name. Its roofs reach about six meters past the walls, carried by hidden steel.
1631: A bridge replaced the causeway so the sea could surround it once more.
The tides around Mont-Saint-Michel are among the strongest in Europe, with a range of up to 14 meters. In 2014 a causeway was replaced by a raised bridge so the sea could surround it once more.
1632: Desert boulders for walls, stretched canvas for a roof, apprentices for builders.
Wright built his winter home in the Arizona desert from local boulders set in concrete, with canvas stretched for a roof. His apprentices raised it with their own hands.
1633: Its oak roof was so dense they called it 'the forest'. In 2019 it burned.
On 15 April 2019 fire brought down Notre-Dame's spire and its medieval oak roof, a lattice so dense it was called 'the forest'. Rebuilt largely by hand, the cathedral reopened in December 2024.
1634: Some 150 rooms in a cliff, found by two cowboys looking for stray cattle.
About 800 years ago, Ancestral Puebloans built some 150 rooms into this cliff alcove, then left within a few generations. Two cowboys hunting for stray cattle came upon it in 1888.
1635: 357 mirrors, made while Venice still guarded the secret of mirror-making.
The Hall of Mirrors has 357 mirrors, made when Venice still guarded the secret of mirror-making. The German Empire was proclaimed here in 1871, and the treaty ending World War I signed in 1919.
1636: Jefferson kept tearing it down and rebuilding it for 40 years.
Thomas Jefferson designed Monticello himself and kept tearing down and rebuilding it for 40 years. Its dome, one of the first on an American house, crowns a room that was rarely used.
1638: 250 rooms with electric light, when most homes nearby had none.
Biltmore, finished in 1895 for George Vanderbilt, has 250 rooms and is still the largest privately owned house in the United States. It had electric light when most homes nearby had none.
1639: Over 50 km, the water drops only about 12 meters.
The Pont du Gard carried water to Roman Nîmes, part of an aqueduct 50 km long that drops only about 12 meters over its entire length. Its stones were laid some 2,000 years ago, mostly without mortar.
1640: Cadet Chapel, US Air Force Academy
17 aluminum spires like fighter jets in formation, and many faiths under one roof.
The Air Force Academy chapel's 17 aluminum spires recall fighter jets in formation. Inside, under one roof, separate chapels for different faiths are stacked on two levels.
1641: A century of war paused the work, and probably saved the tower.
Pisa's tower began to lean in 1178, before its third floor was done. Wars paused the work for nearly a century, letting the soil settle, which probably saved it. Engineers trimmed the lean by 2001.
1642: Four million bricks in a herringbone pattern, and no wooden frame holding them up.
Nobody knew how to roof Florence Cathedral, so Brunelleschi invented a way: a double dome of some four million bricks, laid in a herringbone pattern, built without a wooden frame beneath it.
1643: A bare courtyard, and a thin line of water that seems to pour into the sunset.
Jonas Salk asked Louis Kahn for a laboratory fit to welcome Picasso. Kahn left the courtyard bare, split by a thin channel of water that runs toward the Pacific and seems to pour into the sunset.
1644: Michelangelo took charge at 71 and never saw his dome finished.
St. Peter's Basilica took 120 years to build, and Michelangelo took charge at 71 and designed its dome. He did not live to see it: the dome was completed in 1590, 26 years after his death.
1645: Split the stone open and fossil leaves and feathers appear.
The Getty Center is clad in about 16,000 tonnes of travertine from quarries near Rome that also supplied the ancient city. Some blocks were split to show fossil leaves and feathers.
1646: The king lived here about 172 days. Seven weeks after his death, tourists paid to enter.
King Ludwig II lived in Neuschwanstein for only about 172 days before he was declared insane, and he died in 1886. Seven weeks later it opened to paying visitors, and later it inspired Disney.
1647: Drawn by a draftsman with no degree, reportedly inspired by a novel about the year 2000.
This 1893 office building was designed by a draftsman with no architecture degree, reportedly inspired by a novel about the year 2000. Its atrium of iron and light later starred in Blade Runner.
1648: A crane stood on the unfinished tower for some 400 years.
Work on Cologne Cathedral began in 1248 and stopped around 1473, leaving a crane on the unfinished tower for some 400 years. Rediscovered medieval plans let builders finish it in 1880.
1649: Spanish Mission meets Art Deco, in one of America's last grand stations.
Opened in 1939, Los Angeles Union Station was among the last grand railway stations built in America. It blends Spanish Mission style with Art Deco, and has played a role in dozens of films.
1650: 28 years stranded in no man's land, then Berliners climbed on top of it.

The Brandenburg Gate, finished in 1791, stood in the no man's land of the Berlin Wall for 28 years. When the wall opened in 1989, Berliners climbed onto it here, and the gate became a symbol of unity.
1651: The Las Vegas Strip is mostly not in Las Vegas.
The Las Vegas Strip is mostly not in Las Vegas at all: it lies in unincorporated towns such as Paradise. City limits end near the Strat tower, and the casinos chose to stay outside.
1652: Citizens climb a spiral ramp and stand above their representatives.
Norman Foster's glass dome lets visitors climb a spiral ramp above Germany's parliament, so citizens stand over their representatives. A cone of mirrors throws daylight into the chamber below.
1653: One man, 33 years, no welds, no bolts, no scaffolding: just rods, bottles and seashells.
Simon Rodia, an Italian immigrant tile setter, built these towers alone over 33 years, with no welds, no bolts and no scaffolding. He used steel rods, mortar, broken bottles and seashells.
1654: The death strip was raked smooth so guards could spot footprints.
The Berlin Wall ran some 155 km around West Berlin from 1961 to 1989. Its death strip was raked smooth so guards could spot footprints, and at least 140 people died there.
1655: Too scared to cross? Staff will drive your car over for you.
The Mackinac Bridge joins Michigan's two peninsulas across 8 km of water. In extreme wind its deck may sway about 10 meters sideways, and nervous drivers can ask staff to drive their car across.
1656: The first stone, reportedly at 5:31 on 9 July 1357: a palindrome in time.
Charles IV laid the bridge's first stone in 1357, reportedly at 5:31 on 9 July, a moment that reads as a palindrome: 1357 9 7 5 31. Legend says eggs were mixed into the mortar for strength.
1657: A freighter brought the old bridge down, so the new one wears giant bumpers.
The old bridge here fell in 1980 when a freighter hit a pier in a storm, and 35 people died. Its replacement, opened in 1987, guards each main pier with huge concrete bumpers.
1658: Ivan blinded the architects, says the legend. One is recorded at work years later.
Legend says Ivan the Terrible blinded the architects of St. Basil's so they could never build anything as beautiful again. It is almost certainly false: one of them is recorded at work years later.
1659: The bridge began to open with a bus still on it. The driver floored it and jumped.
In 1952 Tower Bridge began to open with a double-decker bus still on it. The driver, Albert Gunter, accelerated and jumped the widening gap, and his passengers escaped with minor injuries.
1660: New River Gorge Bridge, West Virginia
267 meters above the river, and one day a year you may parachute off it.
When it opened in 1977 this was the world's longest single-span arch bridge, 267 meters above the river. One day a year, on Bridge Day, people are allowed to parachute off it.
1661: Its Altar Stone traveled over 700 km, from northern Scotland.
Some of Stonehenge's smaller stones were moved about 225 km from the hills of Wales some 5,000 years ago. In 2024 scientists found that its Altar Stone came from northern Scotland, over 700 km away.
1662: The lake drowned a canyon so beloved that a writer dreamed of blowing up the dam.
Glen Canyon Dam created Lake Powell, which took 17 years to fill after 1963. The lake drowned a canyon so beloved that writer Edward Abbey dreamed, in a novel, of blowing up the dam.
1663: It looks curved, yet almost all its glass is flat.
London's Gherkin looks curved, but almost all of its glass is flat. The only curved pane is the lens at the very top, over the bar with a view across the city.
1664: Woody Guthrie was hired for one month to sing about the dams. He wrote 26 songs.
Grand Coulee on the Columbia is the largest power station in the United States. Woody Guthrie was hired for one month in 1941 to write songs about the river's dams, and wrote 26.
1665: Every shell cut from one imaginary sphere, and the architect never saw it finished.
Jørn Utzon finally solved the Opera House's shells by cutting them all from one imaginary sphere. He quit in 1966 amid fights over cost and never returned to see it finished.
1666: A railroad across the open sea, until a hurricane wrecked it in 1935.
Henry Flagler ran a railroad across the open sea to Key West in 1912, and a hurricane wrecked it in 1935. Its old bridges became a highway, and this new Seven Mile Bridge opened beside them in 1982.
1667: Before the premier could cut the ribbon, a horseman slashed it with a sword.
At the Sydney Harbour Bridge's opening in 1932, a man on horseback, Francis de Groot, charged forward and slashed the ribbon with his sword before the premier could cut it.
1668: One woman painted a slum pink, and her neighbors answered in color.
Charleston's Rainbow Row was a decaying waterfront slum in the 1920s. Dorothy Porcher Legge bought a stretch in 1931 and painted it pastel pink, and her neighbors followed with colors of their own.
1670: The French Quarter is mostly Spanish.
Most of New Orleans' French Quarter is really Spanish. Great fires in 1788 and 1794 burned the old French town, and it was rebuilt under Spanish rule with brick, tile roofs and courtyards.
1671: The skybridge is not rigidly fixed, so each tower can sway on its own.
The Petronas Towers' floor plan is an eight-pointed Islamic star. The skybridge between them is not rigidly fixed, so each tower can sway on its own in the wind without tearing it apart.
1672: It stands on 4,500 wooden piles that rot unless they stay wet.
Trinity Church stands on Boston's Back Bay, once a tidal marsh. It rests on about 4,500 wooden piles that must stay soaked or they will rot, so the groundwater around it is closely watched.
1673: A park balanced on three rooftops, with one end jutting 67 meters into thin air.
Marina Bay Sands balances a 340-meter park across the roofs of its three towers, about 200 meters up. One end juts some 67 meters into thin air, among the longest public cantilevers on Earth.
1674: Gilded in 1874, then painted gray in wartime to hide from bombers.
The State House dome was sheathed in copper by Paul Revere's company in 1802 and gilded in 1874. In World War II it was painted gray so it would not catch the eyes of enemy bombers.
1675: Every car light turns red together, and up to 3,000 people step out at once.
At rush hour up to about 3,000 people cross Shibuya at once, when every car light turns red together. It is often called the busiest pedestrian crossing in the world.
1676: In 1945 a firebomb hit its top floor and never went off.
Himeji Castle has survived some 400 years of wars, earthquakes and fires. In 1945 a firebomb landed on its top floor and failed to go off, while much of the city around it burned.
1677: The Declaration and the Constitution, both born in one modest brick building.
Both the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution were debated and signed in this one modest brick building. In 1776 it was simply the Pennsylvania State House.
1678: A young monk burned the original, and Mishima turned it into a novel.
The Golden Pavilion that stands today dates from 1955. A young monk burned the original in 1950, an act Yukio Mishima turned into one of his most famous novels.
1679: Alone in a cell, under a skylight called the 'Eye of God'.
Opened in 1829, Eastern State tried to reform prisoners through total isolation, each alone in a cell lit by a skylight called the 'Eye of God'. About 300 prisons worldwide copied its wheel plan.
1680: Every gate is a wish for prosperity, the donor's name painted on the back.
Each of the thousands of gates at Fushimi Inari was donated by a person or company hoping for prosperity, the donor's name painted on the back. Inari is the god of rice, and of business.
1681: Every 11 September, the long skylight along its spine opens to the sky.
Santiago Calatrava's Oculus, opened in 2016, cost about $4 billion, among the priciest train stations ever built. Every 11 September the long skylight along its spine opens to the sky.
1682: Not anchored at all: 60 tonnes that stand by their own weight in the sea.
The great torii of Itsukushima is not anchored in the seabed: it stands by its own weight, about 60 tonnes, its top beam packed with stones. At low tide, people walk out to it.
1683: Philippe Petit walked a wire between them for 45 minutes, 400 meters up.
For about two years in the early 1970s the Twin Towers were the tallest buildings on Earth. In 1974 Philippe Petit walked a wire between them, more than 400 meters up, for 45 minutes.
1684: The Spanish never found it. Local farmers always knew.
The Spanish never found Machu Picchu. Built for an Inca emperor around 1450, it was known to local farmers but hidden from the wider world until Hiram Bingham publicized it in 1911.
1685: A newspaper gave the square its name, then dropped the first New Year's ball.
The square took its name in 1904 from The New York Times, which had just moved into a tower here. Three years later the newspaper lowered the first New Year's Eve ball from its roof.
1686: At the equinox, a serpent of light slides down the steps.
Near the equinoxes, the late sun casts a zigzag of light down the steps of El Castillo, like a serpent sliding toward the stone snake head at the bottom. Its four stairways total 365 steps.
1687: Nothing in Central Park is wild. Every hill was shaped by hand.
Nothing in Central Park is wild. From 1858 its lakes were dug and its hills shaped by thousands of workers, and Bethesda Terrace was built as the formal heart of this man-made countryside.
1688: Already a ruin when the Aztecs found it, they called it the birthplace of gods.
When the Aztecs found Teotihuacan it was already a ruin, and they named it the place where the gods were born. At its height, around 450 CE, it was one of the largest cities in the world.
1689: Rose Main Reading Room, New York Public Library
A reading room a city block long, with books rising from millions stored below.
The Rose Main Reading Room is nearly 90 meters long, about as long as a city block. Readers still order books that rise from millions stored in stacks below and under Bryant Park next door.
1690: 16 concrete columns, like hands raised toward the sky.
Brasília was built from scratch in about four years and became Brazil's capital in 1960. Oscar Niemeyer's cathedral is 16 curved concrete columns, like hands raised toward the sky.
1691: No long walk to the gate: rooms on wheels carried passengers to the planes.
Saarinen hung Dulles Airport's roof like a hammock between leaning concrete pillars. Instead of long walks to the gates, he had passengers carried out to the planes in rooms on wheels.
1692: 134 stone columns, the tallest about 21 meters, raised 3,200 years ago.
The Great Hypostyle Hall at Karnak holds 134 stone columns, the tallest about 21 meters high. It was built some 3,200 years ago under the pharaohs Seti I and Ramesses II.
1693: Alexander burned it, perhaps as revenge for Athens.
Darius the Great began Persepolis around 518 BCE as the ceremonial heart of the Persian Empire. Alexander the Great burned it in 330 BCE, perhaps in revenge for the Persian burning of Athens.
1694: It opened 16 months late, partly because the baggage robots mangled luggage.
Denver airport's white roof is fabric, Teflon-coated fiberglass stretched over masts to echo the snowy Rockies. It opened in 1995, 16 months late, partly because its baggage robots mangled luggage.
1695: Clap once under the main dome and it answers again and again.
Shah Abbas I began this mosque in 1611 as the jewel of his new capital, and covered it in some 475,000 tiles. Under its main dome, a single clap echoes back again and again.
1696: 28 km of corridors, yet any two points are about seven minutes apart.
Built in just 16 months during World War II, the Pentagon holds about 28 km of corridors. Yet its ring design lets someone walk between any two points in roughly seven minutes.
1697: Its oldest madrasa was built by a ruler who was also a great astronomer.
Registan means 'sandy place'. Samarkand's three great madrasas face each other across it, and the oldest, from the 1420s, was built by Ulugh Beg, a ruler who was also a great astronomer.
1698: High on the tower, among the gargoyles, sits Darth Vader.
Washington National Cathedral took 83 years to build, from 1907 to 1990. High on its northwest tower, among the gargoyles, sits Darth Vader, chosen in a children's design contest.
1699: Squeezed between mountains and sea, people live higher up than almost anywhere.
Hong Kong has more skyscrapers than any other city, by most counts. Squeezed between steep mountains and the sea, its people live higher above the ground than almost anyone on Earth.
1700: Its founder never set foot in America, but his remains rest inside.
James Smithson, a British chemist who never set foot in America, left his fortune to found the Smithsonian. In 1904 his remains were brought from Italy to a crypt inside this red sandstone Castle.
1701: Ai Weiwei helped design the nest, then turned against the Games.
Beijing's Bird's Nest, built for the 2008 Olympics, is a tangle of some 42,000 tonnes of steel. The artist Ai Weiwei helped design it, then turned against the Games as propaganda.
1702: For 146 years the highest court had no building of its own.
For 146 years the US Supreme Court had no building of its own and met in borrowed rooms, mostly in the Capitol. Its marble temple opened in 1935, a year after architect Cass Gilbert died.
1703: It leaves Sweden as a bridge and reaches Denmark as a tunnel.
The Øresund link leaves Sweden as a bridge, lands on an artificial island and dives into a tunnel to Denmark. The tunnel keeps the sky clear for Copenhagen's airport and the strait open to ships.
1704: The legionnaires were sculpted nude, so each was handed a shield.
Union Station's 46 Roman legionnaires were sculpted nude, which alarmed officials when it opened in 1908. Each was given a shield to hold in front, and they still guard the great hall.
1706: Paid for not in cash but with 3 million acres of land.
Texas paid for its capitol not in cash but in land, about 3 million acres that became one of the largest ranches on Earth. Finished in 1888, it stands a few meters taller than the US Capitol.
1707: An earthquake pushed its towers almost a meter apart, and the bridge grew.
In 1995, mid-construction, the Kobe earthquake pushed the Akashi Kaikyō Bridge's towers almost a meter apart, so the span grew. At 1,991 meters it held the suspension span record until 2022.
1708: That famous curved 'hump' was added by the US Army in 1850.
The Alamo was built as a Spanish mission church in the 1700s, long before the famous siege of 1836. Its familiar curved crown, the 'hump', was only added by the US Army in 1850.
1709: An iron crystal blown up 165 billion times, meant to last six months.
The Atomium is a crystal of iron blown up 165 billion times, built for the 1958 Brussels World's Fair. It was meant to stand for six months, and it is still there almost 70 years later.
1710: A student thesis that became 354 boxes, most with a garden on a neighbor's roof.
Habitat 67 began as the student thesis of Moshe Safdie, a young architect born in Haifa. Built for Expo 67, it stacks 354 concrete boxes so that most homes get a garden on a neighbor's roof.
1711: Eight people sealed in for two years, until oxygen had to be pumped in.
In 1991 eight people sealed themselves inside Biosphere 2 for two years, to see if a closed world could keep them alive. Oxygen fell so low that fresh air had to be pumped in.
1712: Walk around the outer rim, 356 meters up, tied to a rail overhead.
From 1976 to 2007 Toronto's CN Tower was the tallest freestanding structure on Earth, at 553 meters. Brave visitors can now walk around its outer rim, 356 meters up, tied to an overhead rail.
1713: Surplus Navy paint turned them gray, until one artist reached for bright colors.
After World War II many San Francisco Victorians were painted battleship gray with surplus Navy paint. In 1963 artist Butch Kardum painted his in bright colors, and the 'Painted Ladies' were born.
1714: A railway hotel where Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the war.
Château Frontenac was built in 1893 by a railway company to lure travelers. In 1943 and 1944 Churchill and Roosevelt met in Quebec City to plan the war, including the invasion of Normandy.
1715: So steep that the street had to be folded into eight hairpin turns.
This block of Lombard Street was so steep, a 27 percent grade, that in 1922 it was rebuilt with eight hairpin turns. Cars now creep down at the speed limit, about 8 km per hour.
1716: 'Kremlin' just means fortress. Italian architects built this one.
'Kremlin' simply means fortress, and many Russian cities have one. Moscow's red brick walls, built by Italian architects in the 1480s and 1490s, run about 2.2 km with 20 towers.
1717: A new skin of corn every year. Then the birds start eating it.
Every year the Corn Palace in Mitchell, South Dakota, gets a new skin: murals made of hundreds of thousands of ears of corn in natural shades. Then the birds start eating it.
1719: The trains faded; cartoon fans know it as the Hall of Justice.
Cincinnati Union Terminal opened in 1933 under what was then the largest half dome in the Western Hemisphere. Its trains faded, but cartoon fans know it as the Super Friends' Hall of Justice.
1720: They lean forward on purpose, so hoisted goods don't hit the windows.
Amsterdam's canal houses are narrow and deep, partly because taxes were tied to frontage. Many lean forward on purpose, so goods hoisted up by the hook at the top do not bang into the windows.
1721: Nicknamed the Cathedral of Finance, it glows in a brick made just for it.
Detroit's Guardian Building, finished in 1929, was nicknamed the Cathedral of Finance. Its glowing orange comes from a brick made just for it, and its halls shine with Pewabic and Rookwood tile.
1722: They pump water off land lower than the river, and millers' families still live inside.
The 19 windmills of Kinderdijk were built around 1740 to pump water off land that lies below the river. Some are still homes, lived in by families of millers.
1723: Thirty years empty, a symbol of decline, then a carmaker brought it back.
Michigan Central Station stood empty for three decades after its last train in 1988, a symbol of Detroit's decline. Ford bought it in 2018 and reopened it, restored, in 2024.
1724: The channel to the sea silted up, and the city froze in time.
Bruges was one of Europe's richest ports until its channel to the sea silted up in the 1500s. Trade left, money ran out, and the medieval city was frozen in place almost untouched.
1725: This museum has wings, and they fold shut when the wind blows too hard.
The Milwaukee Art Museum has wings. Santiago Calatrava's sunscreen, 66 meters across, opens each morning and folds shut at night, or whenever the wind blows too hard.
1726: Walls that held off attackers for centuries, then played King's Landing.
Dubrovnik's walls run nearly 2 km around the old town and rise up to 25 meters. They held off attackers for centuries, and in the 2010s they played King's Landing in Game of Thrones.
1727: Almost no straight lines, so it looks perfectly straight.
The Parthenon has almost no straight lines: its floor bows upward and its columns swell slightly, so it looks perfectly straight to the eye. In 1687 a Venetian shell ignited gunpowder stored inside.
1728: A California hotel that played a Florida resort for Marilyn Monroe.
The Hotel del Coronado, opened in 1888, is one of the largest wooden buildings in the United States. Marilyn Monroe's 'Some Like It Hot' was shot here, with the hotel playing a Florida resort.
1729: White houses clinging to the rim of a drowned volcano.
Oia's white houses cling to the rim of a drowned volcano. The eruption that formed this caldera, about 3,600 years ago, was one of the largest in human history.
1730: Built in 1916 to look centuries old, with a stone barge of mermaids out in the bay.
Industrialist James Deering built Vizcaya in Miami in 1916 to look like an Italian villa centuries old. Out in the bay, a stone barge carved with mermaids serves as its breakwater.
1731: A national disgrace in the 1950s, a European Capital of Culture in 2019.
Matera's cave homes have been lived in for thousands of years. In the 1950s Italy called them a national disgrace and moved their people out; in 2019 the town was a European Capital of Culture.
1732: So vast that on humid days clouds can form under its ceiling.
NASA's Vehicle Assembly Building is so vast, about 3.7 million cubic meters, that on very humid days clouds can form below its ceiling. Its high bay doors are the tallest in the world.
1733: Cliffs carved into terraces of dry stone, all for a sweet wine.

Manarola, one of Cinque Terre's five villages, clings to a cliff above the sea. Its farmers carved the slopes above it into terraces held by dry stone walls, to grow grapes for sweet Sciacchetrà wine.
1734: To escape the sea, the whole lighthouse was rolled 880 meters inland on rails.
In 1999 the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse, the tallest brick lighthouse in the United States, was rolled about 880 meters inland on rails, in one piece, to escape the advancing sea.
1735: The graveyard ran out of room, so skulls were dug up and painted.

Hallstatt is squeezed so tightly between lake and mountain that its graveyard ran out of room, so old bones were dug up and skulls painted and stored. In 2012 China built a full-size copy of the town.
1736: First lit in 1791, and still warning ships off the rocks.
Portland Head Light was first lit in January 1791, under George Washington's new federal government. It has warned ships off this rocky Maine coast ever since.
1737: Two stairways twist around each other: one only goes up, the other only down.
The Vatican Museums' spiral staircase, designed by Giuseppe Momo in 1932, is a double helix: two separate stairways twist around each other, one going up and one coming down.
1738: Ships climb a staircase of water, then step down into another ocean.
Ships crossing Panama climb a staircase of water: locks lift them 26 meters to a man-made lake, then lower them to the other ocean. The US finished the canal in 1914, after France had failed.
1739: When the tax man came, the story goes, owners just pulled off the roof.
Alberobello's trulli are built of dry stone without mortar. A local story says this let owners pull the roofs off quickly when the king's tax inspectors came, so the houses would not count.
1740: A log lobby 23 meters high, around 500 tonnes of local stone.
Old Faithful Inn, opened in 1904, is one of the largest log buildings in the world. Its lobby rises about 23 meters, around a stone chimney built from some 500 tonnes of local rhyolite.
1741: About 3,500 steps down, into the cool, away from the desert heat.
Chand Baori in Rajasthan drops about 30 meters into the ground in 13 levels and some 3,500 steps. Built in the 800s, it stored rainwater and gave people a cool place to escape the desert heat.
1742: That timber is concrete, stained brown, so this lodge would not burn.
The Ahwahnee hotel in Yosemite looks like timber, but much of it is concrete, poured into wooden forms and stained redwood brown. After earlier lodges burned, the park wanted one that would not.
1743: 953 windows, so royal women could watch the street without being seen.

Jaipur's Hawa Mahal, built in 1799, is almost all facade: 953 small windows let royal women watch street life without being seen. Its name means Palace of the Winds, for the breezes that flow through.
1744: Felice Beato / J. Paul Getty Museum
Free meals for some 50,000 people a day, of any faith, around the clock.
The Golden Temple's community kitchen serves free meals to some 50,000 people a day, often many more, to anyone of any faith. Volunteers cook, serve and wash up around the clock.
1745: Round Stone Barn, Hancock Shaker Village
One farmer at the center feeds 50 cows: efficient work as a form of prayer.
The Shakers built this round stone barn in 1826 so that one farmer standing at the center could feed some 50 cows at once. For them, efficient work was a form of prayer.
1746: 27 marble petals and nine doors, open to every faith.
Delhi's Lotus Temple, opened in 1986, is made of 27 marble-clad petals in groups of three. Like every Bahá'í house of worship it has nine doors, and it welcomes people of all faiths.
1747: 10,000 panes of glass built for a TV preacher, now a Catholic cathedral.
Philip Johnson's Crystal Cathedral, finished in 1980, is wrapped in more than 10,000 panes of glass. Built for a TV preacher, it was sold to the Catholic Church in 2012 and is now Christ Cathedral.
1748: Gods, demons and animals, some 33,000 of them by one count, all painted bright.
The towers of Madurai's Meenakshi Temple are covered in brightly painted gods, demons and animals, some 33,000 sculptures by one count. The tallest gopuram rises about 52 meters.
1749: Carol M. Highsmith / Library of Congress
No dome here: a 122-meter tower crowned by a farmer sowing seed.
Nebraska broke the mold of domed capitols: its statehouse, finished in 1932, is a tower 122 meters tall, crowned by a bronze farmer sowing seed. Locals call it the Tower of the Plains.
1750: Thousands of diamonds and rubies at the tip, crowned by one of 76 carats.
The Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon is covered in gold plates, and its tip is set with thousands of diamonds and rubies, crowned by a single diamond of 76 carats.
1751: The steel was meant to hide under stone, but people liked it bare.
The George Washington Bridge nearly doubled the world record for span when it opened in 1931. Its steel towers were meant to be covered in stone, but people liked the bare frame, and it stayed.
1752: Broken crockery from ships' ballast, it is said, now sparkling on the towers.
Wat Arun's towers sparkle with countless pieces of Chinese porcelain set into the plaster. Much of it is said to have come from broken crockery carried as ballast on trading ships from China.
1753: No piece bigger than two men could carry down a footpath, to spare the trees.
Fay Jones designed Thorncrown Chapel in the Arkansas woods so that no piece was larger than two men could carry along a footpath, to spare the trees. Its 425 windows make it almost all glass.
1754: Once said to be 2,000 years old; newer research says a few centuries.
The Ifugao carved these rice terraces into the mountains of Luzon by hand, and still farm them. Their age is debated: once said to be 2,000 years, newer research suggests a few centuries.
1755: It looks like stone, but it is wood coated in sand.
Mount Vernon looks like stone, but it is wood. George Washington had its pine boards beveled and coated with sand while the paint was still wet, to fake the look of masonry.
1756: Nearly 2,000 years without mortar, held up by its own weight.
The Roman aqueduct of Segovia has stood for nearly 2,000 years without mortar: its granite blocks hold together by their own weight. It kept carrying water to the city into modern times.
1757: A Gothic skyscraper for a university, with classrooms in the style of 30 homelands.
The University of Pittsburgh teaches in a 42-story Gothic tower. Inside, some 30 classrooms were each designed by a different immigrant community in the style of its homeland.
1758: A duke tired of the butchers' smell gave the bridge to goldsmiths.
In 1944 retreating German troops blew up every bridge in Florence except the Ponte Vecchio. Its butcher shops had been replaced by goldsmiths in 1593, by a duke tired of the smell.
1759: 30 km of lakefront kept 'forever open, clear and free'.
Chicago's lakefront is almost all open to the public, about 30 km of parks and beaches instead of private towers. Daniel Burnham's 1909 plan fought to keep it 'forever open, clear and free'.
1760: Shelled in 1993, rebuilt from the same quarry, and divers still leap from it.

Mostar's Old Bridge stood for 427 years until it was shelled and destroyed in 1993, in the Bosnian war. Rebuilt with stone from the original quarry, it reopened in 2004, and divers still leap from it.
1761: Three stones of about 800 tonnes each, and bigger ones still lie in the quarry.
The Roman temples of Baalbek in Lebanon rest on some of the largest stones ever moved by people: three blocks of about 800 tonnes each. Even bigger ones still lie in the ancient quarry nearby.
1762: In 1811 they drew streets across empty hills. Central Park came decades later.
In 1811, when most New Yorkers lived at the island's southern tip, planners drew a grid of streets far north across Manhattan's empty hills. Central Park was not in the plan; it came decades later.
1763: Maya temples above the jungle, which in 1977 played the rebels' hidden base.
Tikal's temples rise above the Guatemalan jungle, built by the Maya mostly between about 600 and 800 CE. In 1977 this skyline appeared in Star Wars as the rebels' hidden base.
1764: It opened before the Golden Gate and carries far more traffic.
The Bay Bridge opened in 1936, six months before the Golden Gate, and carries far more traffic. A piece of its upper deck fell in the 1989 earthquake, and its eastern half was rebuilt by 2013.
1765: Nearly 50,000 people were told to pack for three days. They never came back.
Pripyat was built in 1970 for the workers of the Chernobyl power plant. In April 1986 its nearly 50,000 people were told to pack for three days. They never came back.
1766: The building was largely rebuilt in 1850, but the parish goes back to 1720.
St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans is the oldest cathedral in continuous use in the United States, though the building itself was largely rebuilt in 1850. Its parish dates to 1720.
1767: Church of the Savior on Spilled Blood, St. Petersburg
Inside, a shrine keeps the exact stretch of street where the tsar was bombed.
The Church of the Savior on Spilled Blood stands where Tsar Alexander II was mortally wounded by a bomb in 1881. Inside, a shrine marks the exact stretch of street, cobblestones included.
1768: A dome taller than the US Capitol's, where DiMaggio married Marilyn Monroe.
San Francisco City Hall's dome, finished in 1915, rises higher than the US Capitol's. Joe DiMaggio and Marilyn Monroe were married here in 1954.
1769: A titanium skin under half a millimeter thick, and a city reborn.
Frank Gehry's museum opened in 1997 in a declining industrial port and drew so many visitors that cities everywhere hoped for a 'Bilbao effect'. Its titanium skin is under half a millimeter thick.
1770: Free since 1935, and more eyes have used its telescope than any other, it says.
Griffith Observatory has been free to enter since it opened in 1935, as its donor insisted. More people have looked through its telescope than through any other on Earth, the observatory says.
1771: Under one square kilometer, holy to three faiths.
Jerusalem's Old City walls were rebuilt by the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent between 1537 and 1541. Within them, under one square kilometer holds places sacred to three faiths.
1772: She loved hollyhocks, so Wright grew them into the walls, columns and chairs.
Oil heiress Aline Barnsdall loved hollyhocks, so Frank Lloyd Wright worked the flower into the walls, columns and furniture of her Los Angeles house, finished in 1921.
1773: Not the Temple itself but its retaining wall, with one hidden stone over 500 tonnes.
The Western Wall is not part of the Temple itself but of the retaining wall Herod built around the Temple Mount about 2,000 years ago. One stone hidden in its tunnels weighs over 500 tonnes.
1774: Inspectors doubted the columns, so Wright piled on five times the required weight.
Building inspectors doubted Wright's slender 'lily pad' columns, so in 1937 he piled weight on a test column until it held about 60 tonnes, five times what was required. Only then was it pulled down.
1775: Willem van de Poll / Nationaal Archief
A blocked sewer led to a whole Crusader city underneath.
Under Akko's Ottoman old city lies a whole Crusader city: vaulted halls of the Knights Hospitaller and a Templar tunnel to the port, found by chance in 1994 when a resident's sewer was blocked.
1776: By law, nothing nearby may rise above the columns at the base of its dome.
Wisconsin's capitol stands on a narrow isthmus between two lakes. By local law, nothing nearby may rise higher than the columns at the base of its dome, so the skyline stays bowed to it.
1777: A floating bridge between two worlds, and everyone who crossed paid a toll.
Around 1890 this floating bridge across the Golden Horn joined old Stamboul to the merchant quarter of Galata, where the Genoese tower of 1348 still rises. Everyone who crossed paid a small toll.
1778: A castle on an extinct volcano that fires a gun at one o'clock, except Sundays.
Edinburgh Castle sits on the plug of an extinct volcano, some 350 million years old. Every day except Sunday a gun fires from it at one o'clock, a time signal first used by ships in the harbor.
1779: Whisper into one end of the arch, and it is heard clearly at the other.
St. Louis Union Station opened in 1894 as one of the largest railway stations in the world. In its Grand Hall, a whisper spoken into one end of an arch can be heard clearly at the other.
1780: Two towers planned, over 250 years of work, and only one was ever built.
Toledo Cathedral was begun in 1226 on the site of the city's great mosque and took more than 250 years to finish. Only one of its two planned towers was ever built.
1781: A king's palace with electric light before the White House had it.
Iolani Palace, finished in 1882 for King Kalākaua, had electric light before the White House did. It is the only royal palace in the United States, home to Hawaii's last two monarchs.
1782: Stepping stones over the filth, and ruts left by carts before 79 CE.

Pompeii's streets have raised stepping stones so people could cross without wading through rainwater and waste. Cart wheels passed between them, wearing ruts still visible since the eruption of 79 CE.
1783: Bill Spindler / US Antarctic Program, NSF
Built on stilts so the wind sweeps the snow underneath instead of burying it.
The South Pole station stands on stilts so the wind can sweep snow underneath instead of burying it. It can be jacked up two floors, because about 20 cm of snow piles up there every year.
1784: For 1,500 years a Buddha stood here. Now only the shape of his absence remains.
For some 1,500 years two giant Buddhas stood carved into this cliff in Afghanistan, the taller one 55 meters high. In March 2001 the Taliban blew them up, and only their empty niches remain.
1785: Reinhart Piuk / US Antarctic Program, NSF
The largest settlement in Antarctica once ran its own small nuclear reactor.
McMurdo, run by the United States on Ross Island, is the largest settlement in Antarctica, with up to about 1,000 people in summer. From 1962 to 1972 it even ran a small nuclear reactor.
1787: The price of onions soared, so farmers cut out the middlemen.
Pike Place Market opened in 1907 after the price of onions soared, so farmers could sell straight to shoppers without middlemen. It is one of the oldest continuously running public markets in the US.
1788: Five joined towers, some 2,200 flats, and a wall of air conditioners.
The so-called Monster Building in Hong Kong's Quarry Bay is five joined towers with some 2,200 flats around a narrow courtyard. Its wall of windows and air conditioners draws photographers.
1789: No road up the cliff, so everything was hoisted from the water.
After a 1905 storm wrecked some 29 ships on Lake Superior, Split Rock Lighthouse was built atop a 40-meter cliff. There was no road, so materials were hoisted up from the water by derrick.
1790: A wooden tower that survives earthquakes by letting its floors sway.
Tō-ji's five-story pagoda, 55 meters tall, is the tallest wooden tower in Japan. Like other old pagodas it has survived centuries of earthquakes, helped by a central pillar and floors that sway.
1791: 634 meters, because in Japanese the digits read as the region's old name.
Tokyo Skytree is 634 meters tall, the tallest tower in the world. The height was chosen because in Japanese the digits can be read 'mu-sa-shi', the old name of the region around Tokyo.
1792: Red and yellow, Moorish and Gothic: a king's romantic dream on a monastery's ruins.
King Ferdinand II built Pena Palace in the 1840s on the ruins of a monastery, painting it red and yellow and mixing Moorish, Gothic and Manueline styles into one romantic dream on a hilltop.
1793: A mud-brick village that has played Jerusalem, Rome and a fantasy city.
Aït Benhaddou, a fortified mud-brick village on an old caravan route across the Sahara, has played Jerusalem, Rome and the fantasy city of Yunkai on screen, in films like Gladiator.
1794: 73 meters of brick, wrapped in bands of carved verses.
Delhi's Qutb Minar, begun around 1199, is the tallest brick minaret in the world at 73 meters. Bands of carved verses from the Quran wrap around it as it rises.
1795: Carved top-down from one rock: they removed 200,000 tonnes and left a temple.
The Kailasa temple at Ellora, from the 700s, was carved top-down out of a single mass of basalt. Workers removed an estimated 200,000 tonnes of rock and left a temple behind.
1796: The Ramayana, told around the walls like a stone comic strip.
Prambanan, built in the 800s, is the largest Hindu temple compound in Indonesia, its central tower 47 meters tall. Carved reliefs around it tell the Ramayana like a stone comic strip.
1797: A replica diamond in the floor marks kilometer zero for all of Cuba.
Havana's Capitolio, finished in 1929, echoes the US Capitol. A replica diamond set in its floor marks kilometer zero, the point from which road distances across Cuba are measured.
1798: A temporary cathedral of 98 cardboard tubes, designed to last about 50 years.
After the 2011 earthquake ruined Christchurch's cathedral, Shigeru Ban built a temporary replacement in 2013 from 98 giant cardboard tubes. It was designed to last for about 50 years.
1799: People live in the arch, and fruit and flowers cover the ceiling above the market.
Rotterdam's Markthal, opened in 2014, is an arch of 228 apartments around a food market. Its inner ceiling is one of the world's largest artworks, about 11,000 square meters of fruit and flowers.
1800: Ten times over budget, then sold out for years.
Hamburg's Elbphilharmonie, a wave of glass on top of an old brick warehouse, opened in 2017, years late. It cost about ten times the first estimate, then sold out its concerts for years.
1801: Offered a country's presidency, he said he lacked the aptitude to deal with people.
In 1952 Israel offered Einstein its presidency. He declined, writing that he lacked the natural aptitude and experience to deal with people, and that the offer moved and saddened him at once.
1802: Martin Luther King Jr., March on Washington
The dream was not in the script. A singer called out, and he set his notes aside.
The 'dream' was not in his written speech. Near the end, gospel singer Mahalia Jackson called out, 'Tell them about the dream, Martin,' and King set his notes aside and improvised.
1803: The other angle on the famous kiss. She later said it was not her choice.
Alfred Eisenstaedt's photo of this kiss became famous, but Navy photographer Victor Jorgensen caught the same seconds from another angle. The two were strangers; she later said it was not her choice.
1804: Four months later, she vanished over the Pacific without a trace.
March 1937, under the nose of the plane she hoped to fly around the world. Four months later she and navigator Fred Noonan vanished over the Pacific, and no confirmed trace has ever been found.
1805: Her notebooks are still radioactive, kept in lead-lined boxes.
She is still the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Her notebooks remain radioactive and are kept in lead-lined boxes in Paris.
1806: He posed more than Lincoln did, on purpose: dignity against caricature.
Douglass sat for more photographs than any other American of his century, Lincoln included. He did it on purpose: to replace racist caricatures with the dignity of a free Black man.
1807: Raised in workhouses, and ten years later recognized everywhere without a word.
Out of costume at 32. Chaplin grew up in London workhouses while his mother was in an asylum; a decade later he was the most famous face on Earth, recognised without a word.
1808: Boston sold him, then waited 86 years for another World Series.
Ruth began as one of baseball's best pitchers. Boston sold him to the New York Yankees in 1919, and Boston did not win the World Series again for 86 years.
1809: War Office official photographer / Imperial War Museums
The V sign began as chalk on occupied walls. He made it his own.
In January 1941 a Belgian broadcaster on the BBC proposed V for Victory as a sign that occupied Europe could chalk on walls. Churchill made it his own, here in Bradford in 1942, cigar and all.
1810: Back from holiday, he found mould killing bacteria in a dish he'd left out.
In 1928 he came back from holiday to find mould killing bacteria in a dish he had left out. In his 1945 Nobel lecture he already warned that misused penicillin would breed resistant germs.
1811: A lost photo, found in 2017, of the woman who freed hundreds.
This photo of Tubman in her forties came to light only in 2017, in a friend's album. She led about 70 people out of slavery, then guided a Union raid in 1863 that freed more than 700.
1812: He broke his neck doing a stunt and only found out years later.
Keaton did his own stunts. Filming Sherlock Jr. in 1924, a torrent from a water tower slammed him onto the rails and broke his neck, but he learned it only years later from an X-ray.
1813: Every 15 April, every player in the league wears his number.
On 15 April 1947 he broke baseball's colour line, enduring taunts and threats without hitting back. Every 15 April, every Major League player wears his number, 42.
1814: 'In fifty years everyone will know it,' he wrote. He was off by one.
After the first Zionist Congress in 1897 Herzl wrote in his diary: 'At Basel I founded the Jewish State... in fifty years everyone will know it.' Israel was declared fifty-one years later.
1815: Not even a doctor, he gambled on an untested vaccine, and the boy lived.
In 1885 a boy mauled by a rabid dog was brought to Pasteur, who was not even a doctor. He risked an untested vaccine; Joseph Meister lived, and later became caretaker of the Pasteur Institute.
1816: 'I sell the shadow to support the substance.'
She sold photos of herself to fund her work, printed with the words 'I sell the shadow to support the substance.' Born enslaved in New York, she grew up speaking Dutch.
1817: Sent to a boys' home for firing a pistol on New Year's Eve, he found the cornet.
Armstrong learned the cornet in a New Orleans home for troubled boys, sent there at 11 for firing a pistol into the air on New Year's Eve. He went on to change how the world sings and plays.
1818: He said no to the draft and lost three and a half years of his prime.
In 1967 Ali refused to be drafted for Vietnam and was stripped of his title, losing three and a half years of his prime. In 1971 the Supreme Court overturned his conviction unanimously.
1819: He declared the state, then left office to live in a desert hut.
He read out Israel's declaration of independence on 14 May 1948. In 1953 he left the prime minister's office to live in a hut at kibbutz Sde Boker, hoping others would follow him to the Negev.
1820: His current powers almost every grid on Earth. He died alone, in debt.
Tesla's alternating current won the 'war of the currents' and still runs almost every power grid on Earth. He died alone in a New York hotel room in 1943, deep in debt.
1821: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony
'I forged the thunderbolts, she fired them.' Neither lived to vote legally.
Stanton wrote the speeches and Anthony crossed the country to deliver them. 'I forged the thunderbolts, she fired them,' Stanton said. Neither lived to vote legally.
1822: Her label would not touch the song, so she closed her shows with it in the dark.
Strange Fruit, her 1939 song about lynching, was so raw that her record label would not touch it. She recorded it elsewhere and often closed her shows with it, the room dark, no encore.
1823: Wimbledon champion, and still refused hotel rooms.
In 1956 she became the first Black player to win a Grand Slam title, then won Wimbledon twice. Even as champion she was often refused hotel rooms; later she broke the colour line in pro golf too.
1824: Marion S. Trikosko / U.S. News & World Report
A Milwaukee schoolteacher, born in Kyiv, who came to lead a country.
Born in Kyiv and raised in Milwaukee, where she taught school, Golda Meir became Israel's prime minister in 1969, only the third woman in the modern world to lead a government.
1825: Nearly deaf, he reportedly bit into the wood of his machines to feel the music.
The first recorded words ever played back were Edison reciting 'Mary had a little lamb' in 1877. He was nearly deaf, and is said to have bitten into the wood of his machines to feel the music.
1826: She came to petition the King and left in a policeman's arms.
May 1914: a policeman lifts Emmeline Pankhurst off her feet outside Buckingham Palace, where she had come to petition the King. Four years later British women over 30 won the vote.
1827: William P. Gottlieb / Library of Congress
She came to dance, froze on stage, and sang instead.
At 17 she entered an amateur night at Harlem's Apollo Theater planning to dance, froze, and sang instead. She won, and went on to win 14 Grammy Awards.
1828: He knocked out the Nazis' symbol in two minutes. Later, that man paid for his funeral.
In 1938 Joe Louis knocked out Max Schmeling, held up by the Nazis as a symbol, in two minutes and four seconds. Years later they became friends, and Schmeling helped pay for Louis's funeral.
1829: Begin, Carter and Sadat at Camp David
When talks nearly collapsed, signed photos for Begin's grandchildren kept him there.
For 13 days in 1978 Carter kept Begin and Sadat at Camp David. When talks nearly collapsed, he brought Begin signed photos for each of his grandchildren, and Begin was moved to stay.
1830: Bell Opens the New York to Chicago Line
Gilbert H. Grosvenor Collection, Library of Congress
The telephone's inventor saw himself first of all as a teacher of the deaf.
18 October 1892: Bell makes the first call on the long-distance line from New York to Chicago. His mother and his wife were both deaf, and he saw himself first of all as a teacher of the deaf.
1831: A mob destroyed her newspaper. She kept writing.
After three friends were lynched in Memphis in 1892, Wells investigated hundreds of lynchings and published the facts. A mob destroyed her newspaper's office; she kept writing from the North.
1832: Someone fell on his trumpet at a party, and he loved the new sound.
His trumpet's bell points up because in 1953 someone fell on it at a party. Gillespie liked the new sound so much that he had his trumpets made that way from then on.
1833: Convicted for traveling with his girlfriend, pardoned 72 years after his death.
In 1908 he became the first Black world heavyweight champion. Convicted in 1913 for travelling with his white girlfriend, he received a presidential pardon in 2018, 72 years after his death.
1834: Decades of war, one reluctant handshake, and two years left to live.
13 September 1993: after decades of war, Rabin and Arafat shook hands on the White House lawn as Clinton spread his arms behind them. Rabin, visibly reluctant, was assassinated two years later.
1835: The Titanic's radio operators called almost to the end, and over 700 were saved.
When Titanic sank in 1912, her two Marconi radio operators kept calling for help almost to the end, and over 700 people were saved. The inventor of wireless became a hero overnight.
1836: He died on the eve of the March on Washington, and the crowd was told.
In 1895 Du Bois became the first African American to earn a Harvard PhD. He died in Ghana on the eve of the March on Washington in 1963, and the news was announced to the crowd.
1837: His chords sounded like mistakes, until everyone copied them.
Monk was house pianist at Minton's Playhouse in Harlem, where young musicians invented bebop in after-hours jam sessions. His odd, angular chords sounded like mistakes until everyone copied them.
1838: He paddled through heavy surf and pulled eight men from a capsized boat.
Olympic swimming champion in 1912, Duke brought surfing to Australia and California. In 1925 he paddled his board through heavy surf to rescue eight men from a capsized boat.
1839: A doctor who ended 2,000 years of emperors, honored by both Beijing and Taipei.
A doctor trained in Hong Kong, Sun Yat-sen led the movement that ended 2,000 years of imperial rule in China in 1912. Both Beijing and Taipei still honour him as father of the nation.
1840: She figured out the atom had split, on a snowy walk. He got the Nobel alone.
Thirty years of work together. In 1938, a refugee from the Nazis, Meitner worked out on a snowy walk in Sweden that Hahn's uranium atoms had split. He received the Nobel Prize alone.
1841: His entrance exam was to clean a room. He swept it three times.
Born into slavery, he arrived at Hampton Institute penniless, and his entrance exam was to clean a room; he swept it three times. In 1901 he was the first Black guest to dine at the White House.
1842: A drummer threw a cymbal at his feet. He went home and practiced.
As a teenager Parker was humiliated when a drummer threw a cymbal at his feet to end his solo. He went home and practised obsessively, and returned as Bird, the man who remade jazz.
1843: Too old, they said, at 30. She won four gold medals.
At 30, a mother of two, she was told she was too old. At the 1948 London Olympics she won four gold medals, and newspapers called her 'the Flying Housewife'.
1844: From prison, letters to his young daughter that became a history of the world.
Nehru spent nearly nine years in British prisons. There he wrote The Discovery of India, and letters to his young daughter Indira that became a history of the world.
1845: Unpaid because she was a woman, she lectured under a man's name.
For years Göttingen refused to pay her because she was a woman, so she lectured under David Hilbert's name. Einstein called her the most significant creative mathematical genius of her era.
1846: Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X
Marion S. Trikosko / U.S. News & World Report
Their only meeting lasted about a minute.
Their only meeting: 26 March 1964, in the US Capitol during the Senate debate on civil rights. It lasted about a minute. 'Now you're going to get investigated,' Malcolm joked.
1847: A fire took the use of two fingers. He reinvented the guitar with the rest.
At 18 Django was badly burned in a caravan fire and lost the use of two fingers on his left hand. He reinvented guitar playing with the two he had left and became Europe's first great jazz star.
1848: Told to quit in rough seas, she asked, 'What for?'
In 1926 she became the first woman to swim the English Channel, nearly two hours faster than any man before her. When her trainer urged her to quit in rough seas, she asked, 'What for?'
1849: Indira Gandhi at the White House
Party bosses called her the 'dumb doll'. They were badly mistaken.
March 1966, two months after becoming India's prime minister. Party bosses picked her thinking she would be easy to control, and nicknamed her the 'dumb doll'; they were badly mistaken.
1850: Two Nobel medals dissolved in a jar of acid, hidden in plain sight on a shelf.
When the Nazis invaded Denmark, a chemist at Bohr's institute dissolved two Nobel gold medals in acid and left the jar on a shelf. After the war the gold was recovered and the medals recast.
1851: 390 km on foot to pick up a handful of salt.
In 1930 Gandhi walked about 390 km to the sea to pick up a handful of salt, breaking a British law that taxed it. Some 60,000 Indians were jailed in the protests that followed.
1852: The Empress of the Blues lay 33 years in an unmarked grave.
The 'Empress of the Blues' was the highest-paid Black entertainer of the 1920s. She lay in an unmarked grave for 33 years, until Janis Joplin helped pay for a headstone in 1970.
1853: One fake pass, and a defender left facing the wrong way forever.
At the 1974 World Cup Cruyff faked a pass, dragged the ball behind his standing leg and left a Swedish defender facing the wrong way. The move is still called the Cruyff turn.
1854: Haile Selassie and John F. Kennedy
Robert L. Knudsen / The White House
'It is us today. It will be you tomorrow.'
In 1936, after Italy invaded Ethiopia, Emperor Haile Selassie warned the League of Nations: 'It is us today. It will be you tomorrow.' Kennedy received him in 1963, weeks before Dallas.
1855: He started quantum physics as 'an act of desperation'.
Planck launched quantum physics in 1900 almost against his will, calling it 'an act of desperation'. In 1945 his son Erwin was executed for his part in the plot to kill Hitler.
1856: Agence Rol / Bibliothèque nationale de France
Cinema's most famous man met a man who had reportedly never seen a film.
London, 1931: the most famous man in cinema asked to meet Gandhi, who had reportedly never seen a film. They talked about machines; Chaplin later made Modern Times, about men crushed by them.
1857: She left her honeymoon to sing for 100,000 soldiers in the cold.
February 1954, on her honeymoon with Joe DiMaggio, she flew off to entertain US troops in Korea and sang for some 100,000 soldiers in the cold. She later called it the best moment of her life.
1858: He died on New Year's Eve, flying relief supplies to an earthquake zone.
Clemente died on New Year's Eve 1972 when a plane carrying his relief supplies to earthquake-hit Nicaragua crashed. Months earlier he had made his 3,000th hit.
1859: The country stopped when she died. Then her embalmed body went missing.
Born poor and illegitimate, Evita helped win Argentine women the vote in 1947. When she died of cancer at 33 the country stopped; her embalmed body then went missing for 16 years.
1860: Under a football stadium, the atomic age began. 'The Italian navigator has landed.'
On 2 December 1942, under the stands of a Chicago football field, Fermi's team ran the first man-made nuclear chain reaction. The coded call to Washington: 'The Italian navigator has landed.'
1861: 'The only tired I was, was tired of giving in.'
She was not just a tired seamstress that December day in 1955. 'The only tired I was, was tired of giving in,' she wrote. She had been fighting for civil rights for over a decade.
1862: Elvis showed up at the gate asking to be made a federal agent.

December 1970: Elvis turned up at the White House gate with a handwritten letter asking to be made a federal agent in the war on drugs. Nixon met him. It is the National Archives' most requested photo.
1863: Stripped of his medals over baseball, restored 110 years later.
Thorpe won the pentathlon and decathlon in Stockholm in 1912, then lost his medals for having played semi-pro baseball. In 2022 the Olympic committee restored him as sole champion.
1864: Killed in 1919, yet villagers swore he still rode in the hills.
'Land and liberty' was Zapata's cry for Mexico's landless peasants. He was ambushed and killed in 1919, yet villagers long insisted he was alive and still riding in the hills.
1865: He built the bomb, lost his clearance, and 68 years later the verdict was reversed.
The man who led the building of the atomic bomb lost his security clearance in 1954 after a hearing on his loyalty. In 2022 the US government formally reversed that decision as flawed.
1866: Every teacher but one refused, so one taught her alone for a year.
Six years old, escorted by federal marshals past a jeering crowd into a New Orleans school. Every teacher but one refused to teach her, so Barbara Henry taught Ruby alone for a whole year.
1867: Born with Halley's Comet, he said he'd go out with it. He did.
Twain was born in 1835, when Halley's Comet was in the sky, and said he expected to go out with it. He died in April 1910, the day after the comet's closest approach to the Sun.
1868: Seventeen, two goals in a World Cup final, and tears on the keeper's shoulder.
Pelé was 17 when he scored twice in the 1958 World Cup final in Sweden, then wept on goalkeeper Gilmar's shoulder. He remains the only player with three World Cup winner's medals.
1869: Few heard the broadcast live. Today it is one of France's founding texts.
On 18 June 1940 de Gaulle, a little-known general, spoke on BBC radio from London and urged the French to keep fighting. Few heard it live; today it is one of France's founding texts.
1870: For fun, he cracked the safes holding the bomb's secrets.
His Los Alamos badge, taken when he was in his mid-twenties. To prove the security was weak, the young Feynman amused himself by cracking the safes that held the atomic bomb's secrets.
1871: Weeks earlier the Guard kept them out. Now soldiers walk them in.
September 1957: soldiers of the 101st Airborne escort nine Black teenagers into Little Rock Central High. Weeks earlier, the governor had sent the National Guard to keep them out.
1872: 'I have nothing to declare except my genius,' the story goes.
Wilde was 27 when Sarony took this in New York at the start of a year-long American lecture tour. A famous story says he told customs, 'I have nothing to declare except my genius.'
1873: Four Olympic golds, and at his own reception, the freight elevator.
Owens won four golds at the Berlin Olympics in 1936. Back home no invitation came from the White House, and at his own reception in a New York hotel he was sent up in the freight elevator.
1874: 'He savaged me.' Sixteen months later came the missile crisis.
Kennedy left the 1961 Vienna summit telling a journalist it had been the worst thing in his life: 'He savaged me.' Sixteen months later came the Cuban Missile Crisis.
1875: Genes that jump, said she. Colleagues scoffed; thirty years later, a Nobel.
In the 1940s she found that genes can jump from place to place in maize, and most colleagues dismissed her. More than thirty years later, in 1983, she won an unshared Nobel Prize.
1876: Warren K. Leffler / U.S. News & World Report
She told live TV how she was beaten in jail. The President hurried to pull the cameras.
Evicted for trying to register to vote, Hamer told the 1964 Democratic convention on live TV how she was beaten in jail. President Johnson hastily called a press conference to pull the cameras away.
1877: Fake beards, an invented prince, and a tour of the navy's flagship.
Woolf was 20 here. In 1910 she and friends wore fake beards and robes, posed as an Abyssinian prince and his court, and were given a tour of the Royal Navy's flagship, HMS Dreadnought.
1878: All four majors in one year, then retirement at 28.
In 1930 Bobby Jones won all four of golf's major titles of his day, the original Grand Slam, then retired at 28. An amateur all his life, he went on to found the Masters.
1879: His mother was 18, his father left when he was two.
His mother was 18 when he was born in Honolulu, and his father left when he was two. In 2008 he became the first Black president of the United States, and won again in 2012.
1880: To explain a nanosecond, she handed out wires 30 cm long.
