Hopper loved to tell how her team found a real moth in a relay of the Harvard Mark II in 1947 and taped it into the logbook. To explain a nanosecond, she handed out wires 30 cm long.
1881: His skull was fractured on this bridge. Fifty years later he crossed it again.
At 25 his skull was fractured by state troopers on Selma's Edmund Pettus Bridge in 1965. Fifty years later he crossed it again, as a congressman, beside the first Black president.
1883: Simone Biles Receives the Medal of Freedom
She stepped back mid-Olympics to protect her mind, then returned for bronze.
In 2022, at 25, Biles became the youngest person ever given the Presidential Medal of Freedom. A year earlier she withdrew mid-Olympics to protect her mind, then came back to win bronze on the beam.
1884: The Dalai Lama at the White House
Recognized at two, he fled his homeland disguised as a soldier.
Recognised at two as the reincarnation of the 13th Dalai Lama, he fled Tibet in 1959 disguised as a soldier. He has lived in exile in India for more than sixty years.
1885: A little scattered light changes color: a fingerprint of molecules.
Raman found that a little of the light scattered by any substance changes colour, a fingerprint of its molecules. In 1930 he became the first Asian to win a Nobel Prize in science.
1886: W-a-t-e-r, spelled into her hand under a pump, and the world opened.
Anne Sullivan spelled w-a-t-e-r into six-year-old Helen's hand under a pump, and the world opened. Helen went on to graduate from Radcliffe, the first deafblind person to earn a degree.
1887: He printed his own book, then wrote its glowing reviews anonymously.
Whitman paid to print Leaves of Grass in 1855, helped set the type, and wrote glowing anonymous reviews of it himself. He kept revising and expanding the book until he died.
1889: He founded the Red Cross, went bankrupt, vanished, and won the first Peace Prize.
Dunant founded the Red Cross after seeing the wounded left on the field at Solferino, then went bankrupt and vanished. Found in a Swiss hospice in 1895, he won the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.
1890: 'I can heartily recommend the Gestapo,' he is said to have added.
In 1938 the Nazis let Freud leave Vienna only if he signed that he had been treated well. Legend says he added, 'I can heartily recommend the Gestapo to anyone.'
1891: 'Mr. President, how long must women wait for liberty?'
From January 1917 women stood silently at the White House gates six days a week, holding banners: 'Mr. President, how long must women wait for liberty?' Many were arrested.
1892: Nearly 1,800 poems, and only about ten published in her lifetime.
This is the only authenticated photograph of Dickinson after childhood, taken at about 16. Of her nearly 1,800 poems, only about ten were published while she lived.
1893: His first marathon ever, and he won that too, grimacing every step.
At Helsinki in 1952 Zátopek won the 5,000 m and the 10,000 m, then entered the marathon, his first ever, and won that too. He ran grimacing, as if each step hurt.
1894: Eight days in a tsar's palace to shape postwar Europe. One of the three had two months to live.
February 1945, in a former tsar's palace in Crimea, three men spent eight days shaping postwar Europe. Roosevelt, visibly ill, had two months to live.
1895: His famous dogs mostly heard metronomes and buzzers. The bell came later, in the retellings.
Pavlov won the 1904 Nobel Prize for work on digestion, before the experiments that made him famous. And his dogs mostly heard metronomes and buzzers; the bell owes much to retellings.
1896: The day before the inauguration, crowds attacked the marchers while police looked on.
On 3 March 1913, the day before Wilson's inauguration, thousands of women marched down Pennsylvania Avenue. Crowds attacked them while police looked on; about 100 ended up in hospital.
1897: Bedridden after a bus crash, she painted with a mirror fixed above her bed.
Photographed by her father. At 18 a bus crash drove a steel handrail through her body; bedridden, she began to paint with a mirror fixed above her, and painted herself for life.
1898: Bare forearms, a short skirt, and leaps like a dancer: Wimbledon was shocked.
Lenglen shocked Wimbledon in 1919 with bare forearms and a calf-length skirt, and leapt about the court like a dancer. She won six Wimbledon singles titles and changed what women wore to play.
1899: Hours before D-Day, a note in his pocket took all the blame in case it failed.
5 June 1944: Eisenhower talks with paratroopers hours before the invasion of Normandy. In his pocket was a note he had written in case it failed, taking all the blame on himself.
1900: He left gaps in his table and described elements nobody had found yet.
Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table and described the missing elements before anyone found them. Within 17 years gallium, scandium and germanium turned up, close to his predictions.
1901: $1.50, five pupils, charcoal for pencils: the start of a university.
Bethune opened a school for Black girls in 1904 with $1.50 and five pupils, using charcoal for pencils and elderberry juice for ink. It grew into Bethune-Cookman University.
1902: Carl Van Vechten / Library of Congress
He refused to paint out Lenin, so Rockefeller Center destroyed his mural.
In 1934 Rockefeller Center destroyed Rivera's mural because he refused to paint out Lenin's face. He repainted it in Mexico City and added John D. Rockefeller Jr. drinking in a nightclub.
1903: Olympic golds, ten golf majors. Anything she didn't play? 'Yeah, dolls.'
She won two golds and a silver in track at the 1932 Olympics, then took up golf and won ten major titles. Asked if there was anything she did not play, she reportedly said, 'Yeah, dolls.'
1904: Robert F. Sargent / U.S. Coast Guard
Wading from the landing craft toward the guns, on D-Day's deadliest beach.
Omaha Beach, the morning of 6 June 1944. Coast Guard photographer Robert Sargent shot these soldiers wading from a landing craft toward German guns. Losses there were the heaviest of D-Day.
1905: Charles R. B. Claflin / Library of Congress
A bullet passed through her sleeve and killed the man she was tending.
At the battle of Antietam in 1862 a bullet passed through her sleeve and killed the man she was tending. She went on to found the American Red Cross, at 59.
1906: Carl Van Vechten / Library of Congress
Barred from a hall for being Black, she sang outdoors to 75,000 people.
In 1939 a patriotic women's society barred her from singing in its Washington hall because she was Black. So she sang outdoors at the Lincoln Memorial on Easter Sunday, to 75,000 people.
1907: A flop silenced him for three years. The concerto that followed went to his doctor.
His First Symphony flopped so badly in 1897 that Rachmaninoff could barely compose for three years. After treatment by Dr. Nikolai Dahl he wrote his Second Piano Concerto and dedicated it to him.
1908: New York World-Telegram and the Sun
A leg brace until about 12, then the fastest woman in the world.
As a child she had polio and wore a leg brace until she was about 12. At the 1960 Rome Olympics she won three gold medals and was called the fastest woman in the world.
1909: The First Flag on Iwo Jima
Louis R. Lowery / U.S. Marine Corps
The first flag on the mountain. Hours later a second one stole its fame.
This is the first flag raised on Mount Suribachi, on 23 February 1945. Hours later a larger flag replaced it, and that second raising became one of the most famous photographs of the war.
1910: He saved worn-out soil with peanuts, but no, he didn't invent peanut butter.
Born into slavery, Carver taught poor Southern farmers to rotate cotton with peanuts and sweet potatoes to revive worn-out soil. Contrary to legend, he did not invent peanut butter.
1911: 'From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever.'
'Hear me, my chiefs. I am tired. My heart is sick and sad. From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever.' Words reported from his surrender in 1877, after a flight of 1,900 km.
1912: Anna Pavlova as the Dying Swan
About 4,000 swan deaths, and reportedly a last wish for the costume.
Pavlova danced The Dying Swan around 4,000 times and took ballet to places that had never seen it. On her deathbed in 1931 she is said to have whispered, 'Prepare my swan costume.'
1913: He smashed the Boston record, then was twice wrongly reported dead in the trenches.
An Onondaga runner from Canada, Longboat smashed the Boston Marathon record in 1907. In World War I he carried messages between trenches and was twice wrongly reported dead.
1914: Japan's government tried to stop this photo. The occupation ordered it printed.
Their first meeting, September 1945. Japan's government tried to stop newspapers printing this photo of the emperor beside a tall, relaxed foreigner; the occupation ordered it published.
1915: In orbit she opened every shift with 'Hailing frequencies open.'
In 1992 she became the first African American woman in space, opening each shift with 'Hailing frequencies open.' A year later she was the first real astronaut to appear in Star Trek.
1916: A prisoner of war riding in a president's inaugural parade, asking to go home.
Geronimo surrendered to the US Army in 1886. Still a prisoner of war, he rode in Theodore Roosevelt's 1905 inaugural parade and asked to go home to Arizona; he died in captivity.
1917: She freed dance from corsets. A silk scarf in a car wheel ended her life.
She danced barefoot in loose tunics when ballet meant corsets and pointe shoes. In 1927 her long silk scarf caught in the wheel of an open car in Nice and killed her instantly.
1918: New York World-Telegram and the Sun
The man the phrase 'pound for pound, the best' was coined for.
Sportswriters coined the phrase 'pound for pound, the best' for Robinson. He won his first 40 professional fights and lost only once in his first 131 bouts.
1919: He signed the surrender leaning on a cane: a bomb years earlier had taken his leg.
2 September 1945, aboard USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay: Foreign Minister Shigemitsu signs Japan's surrender. He leaned on a cane; a bomb thrown at him in Shanghai in 1932 had cost him a leg.
1920: Reporters asked if she cried at work. Her partner of 27 years stayed private until her obituary.
Before her 1983 flight as the first American woman in space, reporters asked if she cried at work. Only her obituary in 2012 told the public of her partner of 27 years, Tam O'Shaughnessy.
1921: Nine years after Custer's defeat, Sitting Bull went on tour with a Wild West show.
Nine years after the defeat of Custer, Sitting Bull toured for four months with Buffalo Bill's Wild West show. He reportedly gave much of his pay to poor children he met in the cities.
1922: He left his wife a secret code from beyond. Ten years of séances, and it never came.
Houdini spent his last years exposing fake mediums. He left his wife a secret code so she would know if he ever reached her from beyond; for ten years of séances, the message never came.
1923: Five Olympic golds in the pool, then Hollywood handed him a jungle yell.
He won five Olympic swimming golds in the 1920s and is said never to have lost an official race. Then Hollywood made him Tarzan, in twelve films, yell and all.
1924: Second row from the bottom, seventh from the left: a 16-year-old future Nobel laureate.
Buchenwald, 16 April 1945, five days after liberation. In the second row from the bottom, seventh from the left, is 16-year-old Elie Wiesel, who would win the Nobel Peace Prize in 1986.
1925: She proved nature can tell left from right. The Nobel went to two men.
In 1956 her experiment showed that nature can tell left from right, overturning a law physicists thought sacred. The two men who proposed the idea won the Nobel Prize; she was left out.
1926: Her most famous line, about dancing and revolution, is one she never quite said.
Deported from the United States to Russia in 1919, Goldman soon turned against the Soviet regime too. She is credited with 'If I can't dance, it's not my revolution', words she never quite said.
1927: Carl Van Vechten / Library of Congress
A busboy left three poems beside a famous poet's plate. That night they were read aloud.

Working as a busboy in a Washington hotel in 1925, Hughes left three of his poems beside the plate of the poet Vachel Lindsay. Lindsay read them aloud that night, and the papers dubbed him the 'busboy poet'.
1928: Loose furs and dogs, learned from the Inuit: that is how he beat the British to the Pole.
Amundsen reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911, five weeks ahead of the British. He had learned from the Netsilik Inuit to dress in loose furs and travel with dogs, and it made the difference.
1929: A state's leaders on trial, and the court listening through headphones in four languages.

At Nuremberg the leaders of a state were tried before an international court for the first time, charged with crimes against humanity. Headphone interpreting in four languages was first used at scale here.
1930: To become an engineer, she first had to petition to sit in a whites-only classroom.
To take the classes an engineer needed, Jackson had to petition the city of Hampton to let her study at a whites-only school. In 1958 she became NASA's first Black female engineer.
1931: She watched a factory burn in 1911 and called it the day the New Deal was born.
The first woman in a US cabinet drove much of the New Deal, including Social Security. She had watched the Triangle factory fire in 1911, and called it the day the New Deal was born.
1932: Gordon Parks / Office of War Information
With his passport taken, he sang across the border to 40,000 people on the other side.
Football star, lawyer, singer and actor. For his politics the US took his passport in 1950, so in 1952 he sang across the Canadian border at Peace Arch Park to 40,000 people on the other side.
1933: 180 km from the Pole, he turned back: 'Better a live donkey than a dead lion.'
In 1909 Shackleton turned back about 180 km from the South Pole rather than let his men die. 'Better a live donkey than a dead lion,' he told his wife.
1934: Johnson Sworn In on Air Force One
Cecil W. Stoughton / The White House
Two hours after the shots, she stands there in the clothes she would not change.
Dallas, 22 November 1963, about two hours after Kennedy was shot. Jacqueline Kennedy stands beside Johnson in the clothes she wore that morning; she would not change them.
1935: Paid about 30 cents an hour, she found a ruler for the size of the universe.
Paid about 30 cents an hour to catalogue stars at Harvard, she found that a pulsing star's rhythm reveals its true brightness. It gave astronomers their first ruler for the size of the universe.
1936: Elected to Congress before most women could vote, she said no to both world wars.
In 1916, before most American women could vote, Montana elected her to Congress. She voted against entering both world wars, the only member to vote against the second.
1937: 13 years of money and 1,200 letters, on one condition: they must never meet.
For 13 years the widow Nadezhda von Meck paid Tchaikovsky an allowance on one condition: that they never meet. They exchanged over 1,200 letters.
1938: The ice crushed the ship, yet all 28 men lived. The wreck waited 3,000 m down.
Shackleton's ship was crushed by Antarctic ice and sank in 1915, yet all 28 men survived. In 2022 the wreck was found 3,000 m down in the Weddell Sea, remarkably intact.
1939: Nixon offered his hand first, to the man an American had once snubbed.
February 1972, Beijing. Nixon made a point of offering his hand first to Zhou Enlai, who had been snubbed by US Secretary of State Dulles at Geneva in 1954.
1940: New York World-Telegram and the Sun
Almost deaf, she sorted some 350,000 stars by hand. Students still recite her code.
Almost deaf from her twenties, she sorted some 350,000 stars by hand and set the O B A F G K M sequence still used today, remembered by students as 'Oh Be A Fine Girl, Kiss Me.'
1941: Thomas J. O'Halloran / U.S. News & World Report
When her segregationist rival was shot, she went to visit him in hospital.
The first Black woman in Congress, and in 1972 the first to seek a major party's nomination for president. When segregationist rival George Wallace was shot, she visited him in hospital.
1942: 39 endings for one novel. The problem? 'Getting the words right.'
Typing For Whom the Bell Tolls in Idaho, 1939. Hemingway said he rewrote the ending of A Farewell to Arms 39 times; asked what the problem was, he answered, 'Getting the words right.'
1943: Five men where Peary believed the Pole lay. Whether they truly reached it is still debated.
Peary photographed Matthew Henson and four Inuit, Ootah, Egingwah, Seegloo and Ooqueah, where he believed the North Pole lay. Whether they truly reached it is still debated.
1944: 'A nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.' The line is still quoted today.
Their first meeting, Geneva, 1985. They agreed that 'a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.' The words still appear in official statements of the nuclear powers.
1945: She wrote the book quietly fighting cancer. Industry called her hysterical; DDT was banned anyway.
Carson wrote Silent Spring in 1962 while quietly being treated for breast cancer. The chemical industry attacked her as hysterical; ten years later the US banned DDT on crops.
1946: Supreme Court of the United States
The dean asked her why she was taking a man's place. She ended up on the Supreme Court.
When she entered Harvard Law in 1956 she was one of nine women in a class of some 500, and the dean asked each why she was taking a man's place. She later sat on the Supreme Court for 27 years.
1947: The poet at the inauguration once went almost five years without speaking a word.
Reading 'On the Pulse of Morning' at the 1993 inauguration. As a child, after a trauma, she stopped speaking for almost five years and read every book she could find.
1948: 18 years beside Peary, then a customs clerk. Honour came at Arlington, decades later.
Henson spent 18 years at Peary's side and spoke the Inuit language. After the North Pole he worked as a clerk in a New York customs house; in 1988 he was reburied at Arlington with honours.
1949: A New Gap in the Berlin Wall
One of Europe's busiest squares, then a death strip for 28 years. Now, a gap.
November 1989: Berliners gather at a fresh opening in the Wall at Potsdamer Platz, once one of Europe's busiest squares and for 28 years a death strip.
1950: Who owns the vaccine patent? 'The people. Could you patent the sun?'
Asked in 1955 who owned the patent on his polio vaccine, Salk answered: 'Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?'
1951: Near the top of her class, offered only a secretary's job. Then the Supreme Court.
She finished near the top of her Stanford law class, yet the only job offer she got was as a legal secretary. In 1981 she became the first woman on the US Supreme Court.
1952: As a hungry teenager she danced at secret recitals to fund the resistance.
As a teenager in occupied Holland she danced at secret recitals to raise money for the resistance and nearly starved in the Hunger Winter. Later she gave her last years to UNICEF.
1953: He let his ship freeze into the ice on purpose, just to see where it would drift.
Nansen let his ship Fram freeze into the Arctic ice on purpose in 1893, to drift with it across the polar sea. Later he won the Nobel Peace Prize for a passport that let stateless refugees travel.
1954: Lech Wałęsa at the White House
An electrician climbed a shipyard fence. Ten years later he was president.
A Gdańsk shipyard electrician, Wałęsa climbed over the fence in 1980 to lead the strike that created Solidarity, the first free trade union in the Soviet bloc. In 1990 he became Poland's president.
1955: Four years after Hiroshima, Japan's first Nobel went to a physicist of the nucleus.
In 1949, four years after Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Yukawa became Japan's first Nobel laureate, for predicting the particle that binds the atomic nucleus. He later campaigned against nuclear weapons.
1956: Malala Yousafzai at the White House
Shot on a school bus at 15. At 17, a Nobel laureate.
At 15 she was shot in the head by the Taliban on her school bus for speaking up for girls' education. A year later she was in the Oval Office; at 17 she became the youngest Nobel laureate.
1957: Hollywood turned his samurai into cowboys. One copy came without permission, until he sued.
On the set of Seven Samurai, 1953. Hollywood remade it as The Magnificent Seven, and his Yojimbo became A Fistful of Dollars without permission, until he sued.
1958: Lindbergh and the Spirit of St. Louis
33 and a half hours to Paris, alone, in a plane with no front window.
The Spirit of St. Louis had no front window: a fuel tank filled the space, so Lindbergh used a small periscope or looked out the side. He flew 33 and a half hours alone from New York to Paris.
1959: Margaret Thatcher at the White House
Before politics and law, she was a research chemist.
Britain's first woman prime minister trained as a chemist at Oxford and worked in industrial research before turning to law and politics. She led Britain for eleven and a half years.
1960: Child-sized chairs and low shelves are everywhere now. They began in a Rome slum.
One of Italy's first women doctors, Montessori opened her first 'Children's House' in a Rome slum in 1907. Low shelves and child-sized furniture, now everywhere, began there.
1961: Years of breaking rock in a glaring quarry, and four years after release, president.
Mandela spent 27 years in prison, many of them breaking rock in a lime quarry on Robben Island whose glare damaged his eyes. Four years after his release he was elected president.
1962: One lantern slide made him quit medicine: minds needed healing more than bodies.

Lu Xun studied medicine in Japan, then quit after seeing a lantern slide of Chinese onlookers watching an execution unmoved. Healing minds mattered more, he decided, and became modern China's great writer.
1963: No American school would teach her to fly, so she learned French.
No American flight school would take a Black woman, so Bessie Coleman learned French and earned her pilot's licence in France in 1921, the first African American woman to hold one.
1964: Mother Teresa Receives the Medal of Freedom
She won the Nobel and asked them to cancel the banquet and feed the poor instead.
Mother Teresa was given the US Medal of Freedom in 1985. When she won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979, she asked that the banquet be cancelled and the money given to the poor of Calcutta.
1965: 29 people, 17 Nobel laureates. The only woman had already won two.
Of the 29 people in this photo, 17 were or would become Nobel laureates. Marie Curie, the only woman, was also the only one there who had already won two.
1966: A birthday diary, then a radio call, and she began rewriting it for readers.
She got the diary for her 13th birthday in June 1942, a month before going into hiding. In 1944, hearing a radio call to keep wartime diaries, she began rewriting it for publication.
1967: She was the star. He was 22, and she kept bringing him onstage.
At the March on Washington, 1963. Baez was already a star; Dylan, 22, was still little known, and she had been bringing him onstage at her concerts to introduce him.
1968: She crossed Arabia's deserts and helped draw a country's borders.
Bell crossed the deserts of Arabia, spoke Arabic and Persian, and helped draw the borders of modern Iraq after World War I. She also founded the museum in Baghdad now called the Iraq Museum.
1969: Zelenskyy Brings a Flag to Congress
Office of the Speaker, U.S. House
A battle flag signed in Bakhmut, carried by a man who once played a president on TV.
December 2022, on his first trip abroad since Russia's invasion, Zelenskyy gave Congress a battle flag signed by soldiers in Bakhmut. A former comedian, he had once played a president on TV.
1970: Ernest Edwards / National Library of Medicine
The students voted to admit her as a joke. She graduated top of the class.
The medical school let the students vote on admitting her in 1847, and they voted yes as a joke. In 1849 she graduated top of her class, the first woman to earn a medical degree in the US.
1971: Warren K. Leffler / U.S. News & World Report
He organized the march in about eight weeks, while some allies wanted him out of sight.
Rustin organized the March on Washington in about eight weeks. Because he was gay, some allies wanted him out of sight; in 2013 he was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, after his death.
1972: 'They cheer me because they understand me, and you because no one understands you.'

At the 1931 premiere of City Lights crowds cheered both men. As the story goes, Chaplin told Einstein: 'They cheer me because they all understand me, and they cheer you because no one understands you.'
1973: She raced a fictional 80 days, won in 72, and stopped to meet the author on the way.
In 1889 reporter Nellie Bly set out to beat the fictional 80 days of Jules Verne's novel, and circled the world in 72, stopping on the way to meet Verne himself.
1974: From a Bronx housing project to the Supreme Court, and first, a hug for her mother.
Raised in a Bronx housing project by a widowed mother who worked six days a week, Sotomayor became the first Hispanic justice of the US Supreme Court in 2009. Here she hugs her mother, Celina.
1975: She made glass invisible. Its descendants sit on your eyeglasses.
General Electric's first woman scientist, she invented non-reflective 'invisible' glass in 1938. Its descendants coat camera lenses and eyeglasses today.
1976: Two weeks after Bloody Sunday, they set out again, and about 25,000 reached the capitol.
March 1965, on the road from Selma. Two weeks after troopers beat the marchers on Bloody Sunday, they set out again under federal protection; about 25,000 reached Alabama's capitol.
1977: Agence Rol / Bibliothèque nationale de France
A Nobel poet who wrote two nations' anthems, and only began drawing at 60.
Tagore, in Paris in 1930 for a show of his paintings, began drawing at 60. He was the first non-European Nobel laureate in literature, and wrote the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh.
1978: Faster than sound, with two cracked ribs and a broom handle to shut the hatch.
On 14 October 1947 Yeager flew faster than sound with two ribs cracked in a riding fall days before. He hid the injury and closed the cockpit hatch with a sawn-off broom handle.
1979: It burned in about half a minute, yet most people aboard survived.
Lakehurst, New Jersey, 6 May 1937. The Hindenburg burned in about half a minute, yet 62 of the 97 people aboard survived, many by jumping as it neared the ground.
1980: Mealworms told her how sex is decided. Textbooks credited a man.
Studying mealworms in 1905, she discovered that sex is decided by chromosomes, the X and the Y. For decades textbooks gave the credit to a male colleague.
1981: The Civil Rights Act Is Signed
Cecil Stoughton / White House Press Office
Dozens of pens for one signature, each one a souvenir.
2 July 1964: Johnson signs the Civil Rights Act with dozens of pens and hands them out as souvenirs. One went to Martin Luther King, standing right behind him.
1983: Raised poor, she broke the sound barrier with Chuck Yeager flying alongside.
Raised in poverty in Florida, Cochran founded the WASP women pilots of World War II. In 1953 she became the first woman to fly faster than sound, with Chuck Yeager flying alongside.
1984: Some 15,000 Chinese workers built the line. Hardly any made it into the photo.
Promontory, Utah, 10 May 1869: the two halves of the first transcontinental railroad meet. Some 15,000 Chinese workers built much of the western line, yet hardly any appear in this photo.
1985: Barred as a Jew, she built a lab in her bedroom and dissected with sewing needles.
Barred from Italian universities as a Jew in 1938, she built a lab in her bedroom and dissected chick embryos with sewing needles. In 1986 she won the Nobel Prize; she lived to 103.
1986: U.S. Army Signal Corps / National Archives
17 million letters waiting. Motto: 'No mail, low morale.' Three months to clear it.
In 1945 this all-Black women's battalion faced a backlog of some 17 million letters to US troops in Europe. Its motto was 'No mail, low morale', and it cleared the pile in three months.
1987: One speech against apartheid cost her 31 years away from home.
After she spoke against apartheid, South Africa cancelled her passport, and she spent 31 years in exile. 'Mama Africa' sang to the UN and came home in 1990 at Mandela's urging.
1988: Fairfax Corporation / National Library of Australia
England to Australia, alone, in a second-hand biplane, with under 100 hours of experience.
In 1930 she flew solo from England to Australia in a second-hand biplane, with less than 100 hours of flying experience. She died in 1941, ferrying a plane for the RAF over the Thames Estuary.
1989: Months from becoming prime minister, and within a year, murdered.
January 1960, at the talks on Congo's independence. Months later Lumumba became its first prime minister; within a year he was overthrown and murdered, with Belgian involvement.
1990: Hired as her husband's assistant for a fraction of his pay, then a shared Nobel.
In 1947 Gerty Cori became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in medicine, shared with her husband Carl. For years universities had hired her only as his assistant, at a fraction of his pay.
1991: A First Lady took a flight to prove that Black men could fly.
The first Black military pilots in US history. In 1941 Eleanor Roosevelt flew with their instructor to show that Black men could fly, and the photo helped secure their funding.
1992: Piccard and Walsh in the Trieste
Almost 11 km down. Nobody went back for 52 years.
On 23 January 1960 Jacques Piccard and Navy lieutenant Don Walsh sank almost 11 km to the bottom of the Mariana Trench. No one went back down there for 52 years.
1993: A famous organist who went back to school at 30, to build a hospital in Gabon.
A famous organist and theologian, Schweitzer went back to school at 30 to become a doctor, then built a hospital in Lambaréné, Gabon. He used his 1952 Nobel Peace Prize money to expand it.
1994: Margaret Hamilton and the Apollo Code
Next to her, printed out on paper: the code that steered Apollo.
She stands beside printouts of the guidance software her team wrote for Apollo. She pushed the term 'software engineering' so that writing code would be taken as seriously as building hardware.
1995: He sometimes parked his airship outside his flat, and asked Cartier for a watch to read in flight.
The Brazilian aviator flew his own airships over Paris and sometimes parked one outside his flat. He asked his friend Louis Cartier for a watch to read in flight, one of the first men's wristwatches.
1996: Film star by night, inventor by day: her patent was meant to stop torpedoes being jammed.
A Hollywood star by night and inventor by day, in 1942 she and composer George Antheil patented frequency hopping to stop torpedoes being jammed. Related ideas later fed into Wi-Fi.
1998: Once around the Earth in 108 minutes, at 27. Then around the world on tour.
Gagarin was 27 when he became the first human in space, circling Earth once in 108 minutes in April 1961. Three months later he toured the world; here he is in Helsinki.
1999: Robert Goddard and His First Rocket
2.5 seconds of flight. The newspaper that mocked him corrected itself 49 years later.

16 March 1926: the first liquid-fuelled rocket flew 2.5 seconds above a Massachusetts farm. The New York Times had mocked Goddard in 1920; it printed a correction in 1969, as Apollo 11 flew to the Moon.
2000: She flew across the Channel, and the news was buried: Titanic had sunk the day before.
In 1911 she became the first American woman to earn a pilot's licence, and in April 1912 the first woman to fly across the English Channel. The news was buried: Titanic had sunk the day before.
2001: Air gets in, dust gets stuck in the bend, and the broth stays clear.
Pasteur boiled broth in a flask with a curved neck: air got in, but dust and microbes stuck in the bend, and the broth stayed clear. Decay is the work of microbes, and so, it turned out, is disease.
2002: Where the pattern broke he left gaps, and unknown metals came to fill them.
Mendeleev sorted the elements by weight and saw their properties repeat in rhythm. Where the pattern broke he left gaps and predicted unknown metals; gallium, scandium and germanium soon filled them.
2003: The ground under you is moving, about as fast as your fingernails grow.
The ground under you is moving. Earth's shell is cracked into plates that drift about as fast as fingernails grow, raising mountains where they collide and opening oceans where they part.
2004: General Relativity: Starlight Bent by the Sun
The Illustrated London News, 1919 / W. B. Robinson
An eclipse showed stars beside the Sun, shifted out of place, as he predicted.
Einstein said mass curves space, so starlight passing the Sun should bend. The 1919 eclipse let astronomers see stars beside the Sun, shifted as he predicted. GPS still corrects for relativity daily.
2005: Interest on your interest: 40 years turn 1,000 into nearly 15,000.
Earn interest on your interest and growth stops being a straight line and becomes a curve. At 7% a year money doubles about every ten years, so 40 years turn 1,000 into nearly 15,000.
2006: Carved in 876, one of India's oldest dated zeros, keeping a place empty.
Zero lets a digit's place carry its value: in 270, the 0 keeps the ones place empty so the 7 means seventy. This inscription in Gwalior, carved in 876, holds one of the oldest dated zeros in India.
2007: Pen against counting board, and Lady Arithmetic is smiling at the pen.
On the left, a man calculates with written Hindu-Arabic numerals; on the right, a rival pushes counters on a board. Lady Arithmetic favors the pen: with place value, the digits do the work.
2008: A student's clay tablet: the square root of two, off by under a millionth.
A student drew a square and its diagonal, then wrote their ratio: about 1.414213, off by under one part in a million. Later Greeks proved that no fraction can ever hit it exactly.
2009: A handful of obvious rules, and hundreds of theorems that follow by force.
Euclid started from a handful of self-evident rules and built hundreds of theorems, each forced by the ones before. This scrap, copied about 1,900 years ago, shows the method that made math certain.
2010: How fast is a falling stone at this very instant? Two men answered, and feuded.
How fast is a falling stone moving at this exact instant? Calculus answers by slicing change into ever smaller steps. Leibniz published it here in 1684; Newton had his own version, and they feuded.
2011: John Napier, Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio
A trick that turns multiplying into adding, said to double astronomers' lives.
Napier found a way to turn multiplying into adding: look up two numbers' logarithms, add them, look up the answer. Tedious calculations shrank so much that Laplace said it doubled astronomers' lives.
2012: He saw mystical beauty in 0 and 1. We got computers.
Leibniz showed that every number can be written with just 0 and 1, each place worth double the one before. He saw a mystical beauty in it; we got computers, since a switch has exactly two states.
2013: Ten flips, seven heads. Ten thousand flips, almost exactly half. Casinos thank Bernoulli.

Flip a coin ten times and you may get seven heads; flip it ten thousand times and you will land very near half. Bernoulli proved why, and casinos and insurers have lived off that certainty ever since.
2014: Each number is the two above it, added. Together they count your choices.
Each number is the sum of the two above it, and together they count choices: row 4 says four coin flips can land 1, 4, 6, 4 or 1 ways. Chinese and Persian scholars knew it long before Pascal.
2015: A geometry where triangles add up to less than 180 degrees, and these tiles don't shrink.

For 2,000 years, space was assumed to follow Euclid. Then Lobachevsky and Bolyai built a consistent geometry where triangles add up to less than 180 degrees. In it, these tiles do not shrink toward the rim.
2016: One tiny rule, repeated, and an edge that never runs out of detail.
Take a number, square it, add a constant, and repeat. That one rule draws the Mandelbrot set, whose edge never runs out of detail: zoom in forever and new spirals keep appearing, like this one.
2017: Hundreds of pages to prove 1 + 1 = 2: 'occasionally useful.'
Russell and Whitehead tried to derive all of mathematics from pure logic. It took them hundreds of pages to prove 1 + 1 = 2, and they dryly added: 'The above proposition is occasionally useful.'
2018: Four colors for any map. A computer had to check, and the post office celebrated.
Any map can be colored with four colors so no neighbors match. Suspected since 1852, it was proved only in 1976, the first great theorem checked by computer. Illinois stamped its mail with the news.
2019: Western Han counting rods (photo: Gary Todd)
Red rods for gains, black for debts, some 1,500 years before Europe.
A debt is a number below zero. Chinese mathematicians used rods like these, red for gains and black for debts, and the Nine Chapters gave rules for both some 1,500 years before Europe.
2020: Halve a string and it sings an octave higher: the first hint that nature speaks math.

Halve a string and it sounds an octave higher; two thirds of it gives a fifth. The Pythagoreans found that pleasing sounds follow simple number ratios, the first hint that nature might be written in math.
2021: A sentence that says 'I cannot be proved', and is true.
Gödel built a sentence that says, in effect, 'I cannot be proved.' If the system is consistent, the sentence is true and unprovable, so no set of rules for arithmetic can ever capture every truth.
2022: Pile up enough small random nudges and you always get the same shape: a bell.
Add up many small random nudges and the totals pile into the same shape every time, a bell. That is why heights, measurement errors and exam scores so often cluster around an average with thin tails.
2023: A 99% accurate test says you're sick. You're probably fine.
A 99% accurate test says you have a disease that strikes 1 in 1,000. You are probably fine: false alarms outnumber real cases about ten to one. Evidence must be weighed against how rare things are.
2024: Just 23 people in a room, and two probably share a birthday.
Put just 23 people in a room and the odds are better than even that two share a birthday. It feels wrong because we think of ourselves; but 23 people form 253 pairs, and each pair is a chance.
2025: Some infinities are bigger than others, and you can prove it.
Try listing every decimal number between 0 and 1. Cantor showed you always miss one: change the first digit of the first, the second of the second, and so on. Some infinities are bigger than others.
2026: Graph Theory: The Bridges of Königsberg
Seven bridges, one walk, each crossed once. Euler proved you can't.
Could you walk through Königsberg crossing each of its seven bridges exactly once? Euler reduced the city to dots and lines and proved it impossible. Networks are still drawn his way.
2027: One number slightly rounded, and the forecast became unrecognizable.
Lorenz reran a weather simulation with one number slightly rounded, and the forecast soon became unrecognizable. Simple rules can magnify tiny differences: weather beyond two weeks is unknowable.
2028: Very tall parents, tall children, but usually less tall. Luck rarely repeats.
Very tall parents tend to have tall children, but usually less tall. Extreme results mix skill with luck, and luck rarely repeats, so a star's record season is often followed by a duller one.
2029: Isaac Newton, A Treatise of the System of the World
An orbit is just falling, fast enough that the Earth keeps curving away.
Fire a cannonball from a mountain and it curves to the ground. Fire it faster and it lands farther. Fast enough, about 8 km a second, and the Earth curves away as fast as it falls: it is in orbit.
2030: The pendulum keeps its swing. It's the floor that turns, knocking over the pegs.
A heavy pendulum keeps swinging in the same direction while the floor turns under it, slowly knocking over the pegs in its ring. In 1851 Foucault used one to let Parisians watch the Earth rotate.
2031: Thomas Young, A Course of Lectures on Natural Philosophy
Light plus light can make darkness. Only waves do that.
Young shone light through two slits and saw stripes. Where crests from both meet, the light doubles; where a crest meets a trough, they cancel into darkness. Only waves behave like that.
2032: Two coils that never touched, and current jumped from one to the other.
Faraday wound two coils on one iron ring. Switching on current in one made current jump in the other, though they never touched: changing magnetism creates electricity. Transformers work this way.
2033: Faraday disk, drawing by Émile Alglave (1884)
A spinning copper disk, a magnet, and the first steady current from motion.
Spin a copper disk between a magnet's poles and a steady current flows from rim to axle. Faraday built this first generator in 1831; most power stations still make electricity by turning magnetism.
2034: A falling weight stirs a can of water, and the water warms: heat is motion.
A falling weight turns paddles inside a can of water, and the water warms slightly. Joule found that the same amount of work always made the same amount of heat: heat is not a substance but motion.
2035: Every element has its own barcode of light, even inside the stars.

Heat an element in a flame, pass its light through a prism, and you get bright lines unique to it. Bunsen and Kirchhoff found two new metals this way, and the same lines reveal what stars are made of.
2036: Gary Sheahan, Birth of the Atomic Age (1957)
Under a Chicago stadium, a pile of uranium and graphite kept the chain going alone.
A splitting uranium nucleus releases neutrons that can split more nuclei. Under a Chicago stadium on 2 December 1942, a pile of uranium and graphite first kept that chain going on its own.
2037: Woodcut of Archimedes in his bath (16th century)
Why does a steel ship float? It shoves aside more water than it weighs.
Anything in water is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the water it pushes aside. So a steel ship floats: its hull shoves away more water than the steel weighs. Eureka, says the legend.
2038: Engraving of Archimedes moving the Earth
'Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth.'
'Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth.' A lever trades distance for force: push the long end a meter and the short end moves a sliver, but with many times the strength.
2039: Horses couldn't pull two half spheres apart. Nothing held them but air.
Von Guericke pumped the air out of two metal half spheres, and teams of horses could not pull them apart. Nothing held them but the air outside, pressing about 10 tonnes on every square meter.
2040: 'We live at the bottom of an ocean of air.'
Fill a tube with mercury, upend it in a bowl, and the column drops to about 76 cm and stops: the weight of the air holds it up. 'We live at the bottom of an ocean of air,' Torricelli wrote.
2041: Boyle's Law: The Spring of the Air
Robert Boyle's air pump, Philosophical Works (1725)
Squeeze air into half the space and it pushes back twice as hard.
Squeeze a trapped bubble of air into half the space and it pushes back twice as hard. Boyle called it the spring of the air; it is why tires hold cars up and why divers must breathe out as they rise.
2042: Every wing leaves a spinning vortex, strong enough to keep planes minutes apart.
A wing flies by throwing air downward, and the air pushes back up. The price is a spinning vortex off each wingtip, shown here in colored smoke, so strong that airports space planes minutes apart.
2043: Faster than sound, the air gets no warning, and the pressure piles into cones.
Below the speed of sound, air senses a plane coming and slips aside. Faster than sound, the warning cannot outrun the jet, so pressure piles into sharp cones. On the ground, they arrive as a boom.
2044: F. B. Farquharson, University of Washington / HAER, Library of Congress
A steady wind tore it apart. Not resonance, as often told: each twist fed the next.
Four months after opening, this bridge twisted itself apart in a steady 64 km/h wind. It is often blamed on resonance, but the culprit was flutter: each twist caught the wind so as to feed the next.
2045: Carl D. Anderson, cloud chamber photograph
This curved trail is the first positron ever seen: the electron's mirror twin.
This curved trail is the first positron ever seen, a twin of the electron with opposite charge. Every particle has an antimatter partner; when the two meet, both vanish into energy. PET scans use it.
2046: Too small to see, they leave trails of bubbles, and every curve tells a story.

Particles too small to see leave trails of bubbles as they race through superheated liquid hydrogen. A magnet bends each path, and the curve reveals charge and speed. Such photos revealed dozens of particles.
2047: Nobody sees the same rainbow: each viewer's colors come from different drops.
Each raindrop bends sunlight, reflects it off its back and bends it again on the way out, sending each color at its own angle near 42 degrees. So every viewer sees a rainbow made of different drops.
2048: Ibn Sahl, On Burning Mirrors and Lenses (Milli Library, Tehran)
Drawn in Baghdad around 984, some 600 years before Europe credited Snell.
Light bends when it passes from air into glass, by an exact rule. Ibn Sahl drew it in Baghdad around 984 while designing lenses to focus sunlight, some 600 years before Europe credited Snell.
2049: Woodcut from Ganot's Cours de physique (1858)
A tiny hole in a dark room, and the world appears upside down on the wall.
Light travels in straight lines, so a tiny hole in a dark room throws an upside down image of the world onto the wall. Artists traced inside tents like this, and your eye uses the same trick.
2050: A squirt of cold water, a vacuum, and the air shoves the piston down.

Steam fills a cylinder, a squirt of cold water condenses it, and the vacuum lets the air shove the piston down. Newcomen's engine turned fire into work to pump out mines, and the industrial age began.
2051: National Institute of Standards and Technology
Cold enough, and atoms stop being separate: they merge into one wave.

Cool atoms to billionths of a degree above absolute zero and they stop acting as separate atoms, merging into one quantum wave. Predicted in 1925, first made in 1995; this simulation shows one spinning.
2052: US Air Force Starfire Optical Range
A laser that lights a fake star 90 km up, so telescopes can see better.
Hit an excited atom with a photon and it releases a twin, same color, same direction. Chain that in a mirrored tube and you have a laser. This one lights a fake star 90 km up to help telescopes see.
2053: Engraving of the Leyden jar's discovery (before 1886)
A jar of water that held electricity, and gave its discoverer a jolt he never forgot.

Charge a jar of water from a spinning glass globe and it holds the electricity, then releases it all at once. Its discoverer got a jolt he never forgot. The capacitors in your phone are its descendants.
2054: Double the distance, and the force drops to a quarter, just like gravity.
Coulomb hung a needle from a thin wire and measured how hard charged balls pushed it. Double the distance and the force drops to a quarter, the same rule as gravity. It binds electrons to every atom.
2055: Millikan's oil drop apparatus (Museum of Science and Industry, Chicago)
Floating oil drops revealed that electricity comes in indivisible pieces.

Millikan floated tiny oil drops between charged plates and measured each one's charge. It was always a whole multiple of one tiny amount: electricity comes in indivisible pieces, the electron's charge.
2056: Every point on a wave becomes a new little wave. That's enough to bend light.

Huygens pictured every point on a wave as the source of a new little wave; together they build the next front. That simple idea explains why light bends in glass and splits in two inside some crystals.
2057: Wide swing or narrow, the same time. Clocks went from losing minutes to seconds.
A pendulum's swing takes nearly the same time whether wide or narrow; only its length matters. Huygens put one inside a clock in 1656, and the best clocks went from losing minutes a day to seconds.
2058: The farther a galaxy, the faster it flees: the whole universe is expanding.
Each dot is a galaxy: across, how far it is; up, how fast it is flying away. The farther, the faster. Hubble's 1929 plot was the first strong evidence that the whole universe is expanding.
2059: The Afterglow of the Big Bang
Ripples of one part in 100,000, and they grew into every galaxy.
The whole sky glows with faint microwaves, light released when the universe was about 380,000 years old. Its spots differ by about one part in 100,000, and those tiny ripples grew into every galaxy.
2060: He carved a little Earth from lodestone to find out why compasses point north.
Why does a compass point north? Gilbert carved a little Earth out of lodestone and watched needles behave around it exactly as they do at sea. His answer: the planet itself is one giant magnet.
2061: By his own account, a key on a wet kite string sparked in the storm.
By Franklin's account, a kite in a storm drew sparks from a key on its wet string: lightning is the same electricity as a spark from a jar. He then invented the rod that still guards buildings.
2062: Mid-lecture, a compass needle swung, and two forces became one.
During a lecture in 1820, Ørsted saw a compass needle swing when current ran through a nearby wire. Electricity and magnetism, thought separate, were two faces of one force. Electric motors followed.
2063: The Speed of Light Never Changes
Michelson and Morley, American Journal of Science
A stone slab floating on mercury hunted for a difference, and found none.

Earth races around the Sun, so light should seem faster one way than another. Michelson and Morley floated this stone slab on mercury to catch the difference, and found none. Relativity built on that.
2064: Edison tinfoil phonograph, 1878 (National Museum of American History)
The first thing the machine said back: 'Mary had a little lamb.'

Sound is just air shaking. Edison let a needle shake with his voice and dent a groove in tinfoil, then ran it back through the groove, and the machine said 'Mary had a little lamb'. Sound became storable.
2065: Your drink will never refreeze the ice by itself. That's why time has a direction.

Ice melts in a warm drink, and the drink never refreezes it on its own. There are vastly more messy arrangements of energy than tidy ones, so things drift toward mess: that is why time has a direction.
2066: Not a flaw in our tools: at the smallest scale, nature itself is blurred.
The more precisely you pin down where a particle is, the less you can know how fast it moves, and the reverse. This is not a flaw in our instruments: at the smallest scale, nature itself is blurred.
2067: The siren that drops its pitch as it passes also times the stars.
A siren sounds higher as it rushes toward you and lower as it pulls away, because its waves bunch up in front and stretch out behind. Police radar uses it, and so do astronomers timing the stars.
2068: Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, plate for Traité élémentaire de chimie
He weighed everything before and after the fire. The total never changed.
Lavoisier weighed everything before and after it burned, gases included, in sealed glassware like this. The total never changed. Matter is not created or destroyed in chemistry, only rearranged.
2069: An ancient element, split by a battery into two gases.
Run current from a battery through water and bubbles rise at both wires: hydrogen on one side, oxygen on the other, twice as much hydrogen. Water, an ancient element, turned out to be H2O.
2070: From W. H. and W. L. Bragg, X Rays and Crystal Structure (1915)
A pattern of spots, read backward, tells you where every atom sits.

Shine X-rays through a crystal and they scatter into a pattern of spots, because its atoms stand in neat rows. Reading the spots backward reveals where every atom sits; that is how DNA's shape was found.
2071: Split it in two, and each half carries the recipe for rebuilding the other.

DNA is two strands wound together, held by letter pairs that always match, A with T and C with G. Split them and each strand carries the recipe for rebuilding its partner. That is how life copies itself.
2072: Bread from Air: The Haber-Bosch Process
The air is mostly nitrogen plants can't use. Locked into ammonia, it now helps feed half of us.
Air is mostly nitrogen, but plants cannot use it. Haber found how to lock it with hydrogen into ammonia, and Bosch scaled it up. The fertilizer made this way now helps feed roughly half of humanity.
2073: Spray cans tore a hole in the sky, and the world actually agreed to fix it.
Spray-can chemicals drifted up and tore open the ozone layer that shields us from ultraviolet light. Found in 1985, the hole led nations to ban the culprits in 1987, and it is slowly healing.
2074: Geoffrey Martin, illustration of a Carboniferous coal forest (1913)
Every lump of coal is a swamp forest that caught sunlight 300 million years ago.
Some 300 million years ago, giant swamp forests like this captured sunlight, died, and were buried and pressed into coal. Burning it releases that ancient energy, and ancient carbon, in a moment.
2075: A clock that starts ticking the moment life stops.
Every living thing absorbs a trace of radioactive carbon-14. After death it decays, halving every 5,730 years: a clock that starts when life stops. What remains dates things up to 50,000 years old.
2076: Water sinks in the North Atlantic and may take a thousand years to come back up.

In the far North Atlantic, cold salty water grows heavy and sinks, then creeps along the deep seafloor around the globe before rising again. One loop may take a thousand years, carrying heat as it goes.
2077: The trade winds weaken, and Peru floods while Australia dries out.

Every few years the trade winds weaken and warm Pacific water slides east toward South America. Rain worldwide reshuffles: floods in Peru, drought in Australia. Here, the giant El Niño of 1997 builds.
2078: Albert J. Myer, US Signal Service weather map (1873)
Storms are slower than the telegraph. That's all a forecast needed.

Storms travel, usually west to east, but slower than a telegraph signal. Gather readings taken at the same moment in many towns onto one map, and you see tomorrow's weather coming. That is a forecast.
2079: Seismometer at Lick Observatory (photo: Oleg Alexandrov)
No one has drilled through the crust, yet earthquakes have mapped the core.

No one has drilled even through the crust, yet we know Earth has a liquid outer core and a solid inner one. Earthquake waves bend and vanish passing through, and seismometers read the shadows they cast.
2080: Toomanina erratic boulder, Estonia (photo: Kurinurm, CC0)
A giant boulder, far from any rock like it. Who carried it here? Ice.
Giant boulders lie scattered across northern Europe, far from any rock like them. Agassiz argued that ice sheets kilometers thick once carried them there. Ice ages have come and gone many times.
2081: A London chemist gave the clouds Latin names, and every forecast still uses them.

Clouds seemed too fleeting to classify until a London chemist named them in Latin: cumulus for heaps, stratus for layers, cirrus for curls, nimbus for rain. His names are still used in every forecast.
2082: Survey of India, Great Trigonometrical Survey index chart (1870)
One perfect line, then only angles, and Everest got measured along the way.
Measure one line on the ground perfectly, then only angles: each triangle hands its sides to the next. This chain of triangles measured India over decades, and Mount Everest's height along the way.
2083: This stump remembers every fire from 1255 to 1930.
A tree adds one ring a year, wide in good years and thin in dry ones. Match the patterns between trees and you can date old beams and read past climate. This stump records fires from 1255 to 1930.
2084: Earnshaw chronometer from HMS Beagle (British Museum, CC0)
Longitude is just a clock comparison. The hard part was a clock that stayed true at sea.

Earth turns 15 degrees an hour. Keep a clock on home time, compare it with the Sun's noon at sea, and the gap tells how far east or west you are. The hard part: a clock that stayed true on a rolling ship.
2085: O. C. Marsh, in T. H. Huxley's Professor Huxley in America (1876)
Read upward: toes disappear and teeth grow taller as forests turn to grass.

Read from bottom to top: the fossil feet lose toes and the teeth grow taller as forests gave way to grassland. Marsh's horse fossils were so complete that Huxley called them direct proof of evolution.
2086: Charles Darwin, The Descent of Man (1874 edition)
Wings so heavy with eyespots they make survival harder. Why? Females choose.
Why would a pheasant grow wings so heavy with eyespots? Because females choose. Darwin saw that traits can evolve simply because they win mates, even when they make survival harder.
2087: Some of these butterflies taste foul. The others are just very good liars.
Some of these Amazon butterflies taste foul; others are harmless species that evolved to look just like them. Birds learn to avoid the pattern, so the fakes are spared. Natural selection at work.
2088: Abbott Handerson Thayer, Concealing-Coloration in the Animal Kingdom
Darker on the side facing the light, so its shadow cancels out. Flip it, and it pops.

This caterpillar is darker on the side facing the light, which cancels its shadow and makes it look flat. Turn it over and it pops out. Painter Abbott Thayer saw why so many animals have pale bellies.
2089: Richard Owen, description of the London Archaeopteryx (1862)
Feathers and wings, but also teeth, claws and a bony tail.

Two years after Darwin's book, a German quarry yielded a creature with feathers and wings but also teeth, clawed fingers and a bony tail: half bird, half reptile. Birds, we now know, are living dinosaurs.
2090: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Geographical Distribution of Animals
Kangaroos in Australia, none in nearby Borneo. Where an animal lives tells its history.
Why are there kangaroos in Australia but not in Borneo, so close by? Wallace split the world into realms of animals shaped by ancient seas and drifting land. Where a species lives tells its history.
2091: Threads appear, double, and split into two exact halves: our genes, dividing.
Flemming stained dividing cells and saw threads appear, double, and split into two exact halves, one for each new cell. He named it mitosis; those threads, the chromosomes, carry our genes.
2092: T. H. Morgan, in Popular Science Monthly (1914)
One white-eyed fly among red-eyed ones, and genes found their address.
In 1910 Morgan found a single white-eyed fruit fly among red-eyed ones. The trait passed from mothers to sons just as the X chromosome does, the first proof that a gene sits on a chromosome.
2093: Thousands of pea plants cracked heredity. The paper was ignored for 34 years.
Mendel crossed thousands of pea plants and found traits do not blend: they pass as separate units, and a hidden one can return in a quarter of the grandchildren. His paper was ignored for 34 years.
2094: Georges Cuvier, jaws of an Indian elephant and a mammoth
Two jaws side by side, and the shocking idea that a species can vanish.
People assumed no species could ever vanish. Cuvier compared these jaws and showed the mammoth matched no living elephant: it was a lost species. Life on Earth has had whole worlds that disappeared.
2095: Push the blood toward the heart and it moves. Push it away and tiny valves say no.
Press on a vein below a tourniquet and you can push blood toward the heart, never away: little valves block the way. Harvey showed the heart pumps the same blood around and around a closed loop.
2096: A two-part name for every animal, and in 1735, humans already filed among the apes.
Linnaeus sorted all known animals into nested boxes, class, order, genus, species, and gave each a two-part name like Homo sapiens. Boldly, this 1735 table already put humans among the apes.
2097: Santorio Santorio, De Statica Medicina (1703 edition)
30 years on a hanging scale, weighing himself, his food and his waste.
For some 30 years Santorio weighed himself, his food and his waste on a chair hung from a scale. Most of what he ate left without a trace, breathed or sweated away. The body burns its fuel invisibly.
2098: The Asteroid That Ended the Dinosaurs
A thin layer of clay, rich in a metal rare on Earth and common in asteroids.

In rocks like these, a thin clay layer marks the moment 66 million years ago when the dinosaurs vanished. It is rich in iridium, rare on Earth but common in asteroids: the clue that a space rock did it.
2099: Theodor Schwann, plate of animal and plant cells
Plant cells and animal cells, side by side: every living thing is built the same way.
Schleiden saw plants were built of cells; Schwann showed animals were too, drawing them side by side. Every living thing is made of cells, and every cell comes from another cell.
2100: Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins, frontispiece to Huxley's Man's Place in Nature
Line up the skeletons, bone for bone, and the family resemblance is plain.
Gibbon, orangutan, chimpanzee, gorilla, human: line up the skeletons and the family resemblance is plain, bone for bone. Huxley argued we differ from great apes less than they differ from monkeys.
2101: Not one organism but two, sharing a house on bare rock.
A lichen is not one organism but two: a fungus that builds the house and an alga or bacterium that makes food from sunlight. Together they live on bare rock. The word symbiosis was coined for them.
2102: Nectar 30 cm deep. Darwin predicted the moth; decades later it was named 'predicted'.
This Madagascar orchid hides its nectar at the bottom of a spur some 30 cm long. Darwin predicted a moth with a tongue that long must exist. In 1903 it was found and named praedicta: predicted.
2103: Charles Darwin, The Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication
Breeders made fantails from rock pigeons. Darwin, a pigeon fancier, saw nature doing it slower.

Breeders turned the wild rock pigeon into tumblers, pouters and fantails just by choosing which birds mated. Darwin, a pigeon fancier, argued that nature does the same, only slower and without a plan.
2104: Two copies cause disease. One copy protects against malaria.
Two copies of the sickle cell gene bend red blood cells into these crescents and cause disease. One copy protects against severe malaria. That trade explains why the gene is common where malaria is.
2105: Myograph, from Rosenthal's General Physiology of Muscles and Nerves (1881)
Nerve signals were thought instant. Timed in frogs, they crawled slower than sound.

People believed nerve signals were instant. Helmholtz timed twitching frog muscles with devices like this and found the signal crawls at about 30 meters a second, slower than sound. Thought takes time.
2107: The body is a machine, he said, but the mind is not. Where do they meet?

Light from an arrow enters the eyes and the hand points at it. Descartes said the body is a machine but the mind is not; they meet in a gland in the brain. How mind arises from matter is still unsolved.
2108: Stone 'tongues' grew in rock, people thought. A shark's head said otherwise.

Stone 'tongues' dug from hillsides were thought to grow inside rock. Steno dissected a shark's head, saw the same shapes in its jaw and concluded they were teeth: fossils are remains of living things.
2109: William Campbell / US Fish and Wildlife Service
Wolves came back, and in places the willows did too. How much is still debated.

A predator's effect ripples down the food chain. After wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995, elk numbers fell and habits shifted, and in places willows and aspens grew back. How much is still debated.
2110: Find the dark dots: sea otters, quietly holding a kelp forest together.

Look for the dark dots: sea otters resting in a kelp bed. Otters eat sea urchins, and urchins eat kelp. Remove the otters and urchins strip the forest bare. One species can hold an ecosystem together.
2111: After Charles and Francis Darwin, The Power of Movement in Plants
A root tip never grows straight: it circles and probes, too slowly for us to notice.

Darwin and his son traced a growing root tip on glass and found it never grows straight: it circles and probes, sensing gravity, touch and moisture. Plants move all the time, too slowly for us to notice.
2112: Hand of Sarah Nelmes, after Edward Jenner's Inquiry (1798)
Pus from a milkmaid's hand, scratched into a boy's arm. Vacca means cow.
Milkmaids who caught mild cowpox seemed spared from smallpox. Jenner took pus from this milkmaid's hand, scratched it into a boy's arm, and the boy resisted smallpox. Vacca is Latin for cow.
2113: A two-pronged needle and a killer of hundreds of millions, gone.

Smallpox killed hundreds of millions, then disappeared. Health workers found each case and vaccinated everyone around it with this two-pronged needle. In 1980 it became the first human disease wiped out.
2114: Chicago Department of Health poster (1936 to 1941)
Your shot shields babies too young for their own.

A virus spreads by jumping from person to person. When enough people are immune, the jumps run out and the outbreak dies, sparing even babies too young for the vaccine. Your shot shields your neighbors.
2116: She felt perfectly well. Wherever she cooked, people caught typhoid.

Mary Mallon felt perfectly well, yet wherever she cooked, people caught typhoid. She carried the germ without symptoms. 'Typhoid Mary' taught medicine that the sick are not the only spreaders of disease.
2117: Seattle police, 1918, with an answer that came back in 2020.

Influenza travels in droplets and fine particles we breathe out. In December 1918 Seattle's police wore Red Cross masks, an old answer that returned in 2020: put cloth between one breath and the next.
2118: Not bad air but one kind of mosquito, carrying the parasite from blood to blood.
Malaria is caught not from bad air but from the bite of one kind of mosquito, which carries the parasite from blood to blood. Ross proved it in 1897; malaria still kills about 600,000 people a year.
2119: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Water, salt and a little sugar: a surprise fix that has saved millions.

Cholera kills by draining the body of water. The surprise fix: clean water with salt and a little sugar, because sugar helps the gut pull salt, and water with it, back in. It has saved millions of lives.
2120: Transfusions once saved some and killed others. The clumped wells show why.
Early transfusions sometimes saved lives and sometimes killed. Landsteiner found why: blood comes in types, and the wrong mix clumps, as in some wells here. Matching types made transfusion safe.
2121: Breathing by Air Pressure: The Iron Lung
A machine that breathed for you by changing the air pressure around your body.
Polio could paralyze the muscles that breathe. The iron lung sealed the body in and lowered the air pressure around it, so the chest expanded and air flowed in. Vaccines later emptied these wards.
2122: Surgery once meant being held down wide awake. Then a patient slept through it.

Before 1846, surgery meant being held down while wide awake, and the best surgeons were the fastest. Then in Boston a patient inhaled ether and slept through an operation. Pain stopped being the price.
2123: A forgotten dish, a mold, and a ring of dead bacteria around it.

In 1928 Fleming saw that a mold on a forgotten dish had killed the bacteria around it. The mold, Penicillium, makes penicillin, which kills germs but spares us. Mass produced from 1943, it saved millions.
2124: Wash your hands, he told doctors, and deaths plunged. They mocked him.

In 1847 Semmelweis saw mothers dying far more often in a ward where doctors came straight from autopsies. He made them wash in chlorine, and deaths plunged. Colleagues mocked him; now it is basic medicine.
2125: Miasma: A Wrong Idea That Helped
Paul Fürst, Der Doctor Schnabel von Rom (after 1656)
A beak full of herbs against foul air: the wrong theory that still built sewers.

For centuries disease was blamed on foul air, and plague doctors stuffed their beaks with herbs against it. The theory was wrong, yet it drove cities to drain swamps and build sewers, which saved lives.
2126: Twelve sick sailors in pairs. The pair given oranges and lemons got well fastest.

To test a cure, give it to one group and not to an otherwise identical one, then compare. In 1747 Lind split twelve scurvy-stricken sailors into pairs; the pair given oranges and lemons recovered fastest.
2127: Joseph Jastrow's duck-rabbit, after Fliegende Blätter (1892)
Duck or rabbit? The lines never change. Your brain does.
Duck or rabbit? The lines never change, but your brain flips between two readings and cannot hold both at once. Perception is not a camera recording the world; it is a guess about what is out there.
2128: Electric currents made these faces smile. Look at the eyes, not the mouth.
Duchenne made faces smile with electric currents and saw what was missing: in a genuine smile, a muscle around the eyes tightens too, which few can do on purpose. Look at the eyes, not the mouth.
2129: Charles Darwin, The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals
Darwin wrote to explorers worldwide: how do your people show grief? The answers matched.
Darwin wrote to missionaries and explorers worldwide asking how people show grief, joy and anger. The answers matched: many expressions are inborn, shared across cultures and echoed in animals.
2130: A horse that did sums, as long as someone in the room knew the answer.
Hans the horse tapped out answers to sums and amazed Berlin. A psychologist found Hans was reading tiny, unconscious cues in his questioners' posture. If they did not know the answer, neither did he.
2131: Optical illusion from Popular Science Monthly (1899)
The two ends of the curve don't seem to line up. They do: your brain guessed wrong.
A bar hides the middle of a curve, and the two visible ends no longer seem to line up. The brain does not see the hidden part; it guesses where the line should run, and here it guesses wrong.
2132: Optical illusion from Popular Science Monthly (1899)
Stare long enough and the front face becomes the back.
Stare at a wireframe cube and it flips: the front face suddenly becomes the back. Flat lines fit two solid shapes equally well, so the brain keeps switching. What we see in depth is a hypothesis.
2133: A sound, food, again and again, until the sound alone was enough.
Pavlov's dogs drooled at food, naturally. After a sound was paired with feeding again and again, the sound alone made them drool. Much of what we feel toward places, smells and songs is learned so.
2134: Count the digits in 2222. Notice how the 2 gets in your way.
Count the digits in 2222. The answer is four, yet the 2 jumps out first and trips you up. Reading has become so automatic that it fights your intention. Some skills run whether we want them or not.
2135: The right line is obvious, until everyone else picks the wrong one.

Which line matches? The answer is obvious, until everyone else in the room confidently picks the wrong one. In Asch's tests about a third of answers went with the group, against the evidence of the eyes.
2136: Most forgetting happens in the first day. The fix is in the timing.
Ebbinghaus memorized nonsense syllables and tested himself for weeks. Most forgetting happens in the first day, then slows. Reviewing at growing intervals flattens the curve: that is how to study.
2137: Win 150 or lose 100 on a coin flip? Most people say no.
Offered a coin flip to win 150 or lose 100, most people refuse, though the odds favor them. Losing hurts about twice as much as winning pleases, a quirk that shapes markets, deals and politics.
2138: Plate on pin making, Diderot's Encyclopédie (1762)
One worker, 20 pins a day. Ten workers, about 48,000.
One worker alone might make 20 pins a day. Adam Smith described ten workers splitting the job into 18 steps and making about 48,000. Specialization is the hidden engine of modern wealth.
2139: Edward Matthew Ward, The South Sea Bubble
Shares bought in hope of a buyer who'd pay more, until the buyers ran out.
In 1720 South Sea Company shares rose about tenfold in months, bought less for profits than in hope of selling to someone else for more. When buyers ran out, the price collapsed, and so did fortunes.
2140: Luca Pacioli, Summa de arithmetica (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
Write everything down twice, and every mistake shows up as a gap.

Record every transaction twice, once where money came from and once where it went, and the two columns must always balance, so any mistake shows up as a gap. Pacioli printed the Venetian method in 1494.
2141: US Patent X1, signed by George Washington
The first US patent was for potash, and George Washington signed it.
A patent is a bargain: an inventor reveals exactly how something works and in return gets a monopoly for a limited time. The first US patent, for making potash, was signed by George Washington.
2142: The work moved past the workers, and 12 hours shrank to 90 minutes.

Instead of workers walking to the work, the work moved past the workers, each doing one task. At Ford in 1913, building a chassis fell from about 12 hours to about 90 minutes, and cars became affordable.
2143: One telephone is useless. A million make a world.

One telephone is useless; two make a line; a million make a world. Each new subscriber makes the network worth more to all the others, so phone systems, and later social networks, tend toward one winner.
2144: William Wyon (design), Penny Black stamps (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
Carrying a letter was cheap. Counting what to charge was the expensive part.

Rowland Hill saw that carrying a letter cost little; counting distances and collecting fees cost most. So: one penny, prepaid with a stamp, anywhere in Britain. Letters sent more than doubled in a year.
2145: Hendrik Gerritsz Pot, Flora's Wagon of Fools
Contracts for tulips still in the ground, promised for spring. Then February came.

In the Dutch tulip craze, people traded contracts for bulbs still in the ground, promising to buy at a set price in spring. When prices broke in February 1637, the deals collapsed. Futures work the same way.
2146: Job Berckheyde, The Stock Exchange in Amsterdam (c. 1675 to 1680)
A voyage too risky for one merchant, split into shares that anyone could buy.
A voyage to Asia was too risky for one merchant. The Dutch East India Company split ownership into shares anyone could buy and resell here. Pooling many small stakes built the modern corporation.
2147: UK ration book, 1918 (Warwickshire County Record Office)
Butter, meat and sugar that money alone could not buy.
Normally prices decide who gets scarce goods: whoever pays more. In wartime Britain that seemed unfair, so each person got coupons for a fixed share of butter, meat and sugar. Money was not enough.
2148: A bank works fine, until everyone wants their money back at once.

Banks lend out most of what you deposit and keep only a slice as cash. That works until everyone fears a collapse and rushes to withdraw at once; then it collapses. Deposit insurance aims to stop that.
2149: City of Trier, 10 million mark emergency note (Fritz Quant, 1923)
10 million marks, and soon it bought almost nothing.

Germany paid its bills by printing money, and money stopped meaning anything. By late 1923 prices doubled every few days and bread cost billions of marks. This 10 million note soon bought almost nothing.
2150: Ming dynasty banknote, Liaoning Museum (photo: Gary Lee Todd)
Paper, worth exactly as much as people trust it to buy.
Paper is worth whatever people trust it will buy. China issued state paper money in 1024, centuries before Europe; this note is from the Ming dynasty. Overprinting taught the other lesson: inflation.
2151: Knife coin, Zhao state, Shanghai Museum (photo: Gary Lee Todd)
Money shaped like a little bronze knife.
Barter needs a double coincidence: I want your grain exactly when you want my goat. Money solves it with a token everyone accepts. In ancient China the tokens were bronze shaped like little knives.
2152: It guides every ship, paid or not. So who pays for it?

A lighthouse guides every passing ship, whether or not it paid, and one more ship takes nothing from the rest. Things like that are hard to sell, so economists long said governments must provide them.
2153: Land damaged by overgrazing, Popular Science Monthly (1912)
One more cow is all gain to its owner, until the grass is gone.

On a shared pasture each herder gains the full benefit of one more cow but bears only a sliver of the harm, so cows multiply until the grass is gone. Elinor Ostrom showed communities can prevent this with rules.
2154: Thomas Rowlandson and Augustus Pugin, Lloyd's Subscription Room (1809)
A shipwreck that ruins one merchant can't ruin a hundred. It began over coffee.

One shipwreck can ruin one merchant, but not a hundred people who each paid a small share in advance. Insurance turns private disaster into a predictable cost. It began over coffee at Lloyd's in London.
2155: Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher, RAND
Each does better betraying the other, yet both do better staying silent.
Two suspects, held apart: each does better by betraying the other, whatever the other does, yet if both stay silent both do better. Arms races and overfishing follow this trap; trust can break it.
2156: Where two lines cross, a price settles that nobody set.

When a price rises, buyers want less and sellers offer more; when it falls, the reverse. Where the two lines cross, a price settles that no one set. A frost that kills orange trees shifts it: juice costs more.
2157: Why might a top lawyer still hire a typist?

Even if Portugal made both wine and cloth more cheaply than England, Ricardo showed both gain when each focuses on what it does relatively best and trades. That is why a top lawyer may still hire a typist.
2158: Hole or no hole: change the cards, and the same loom weaves something new.

Each card in this chain tells a loom which threads to lift: hole or no hole. Change the cards and the same machine weaves a new pattern. Jacquard split a machine from its instructions: the seed of software.
2159: US Naval Surface Warfare Center, Dahlgren
A real moth, taped into the log: 'First actual case of bug being found.'
In 1947 engineers found a moth stuck in a relay of the Harvard Mark II and taped it into the log: 'First actual case of bug being found.' The word was older, but the joke stuck to every error since.
2161: Two alphabets on spinning disks, so the same letter keeps changing its disguise.
A simple code swaps each letter for another, and the swaps betray themselves. Alberti put two alphabets on rotating disks and turned them mid-message, so the same letter keeps changing disguise.
2162: Al-Kindi, Risala fi istikhraj al-mu'amma (Süleymaniye Library)
Count the symbols in a secret message, and it starts to give itself away.
