In any language some letters show up far more than others. Al-Kindi realized that counting the symbols in a secret message reveals which stands for which. His 9th-century trick cracked codes for centuries.
2163: An astronomical number of settings, undone by flaws: no letter ever encoded as itself.

Enigma's rotors changed the cipher with every key press, giving an astronomical number of settings. It was broken through its flaws, such as no letter ever encoding as itself. Polish mathematicians led.
2164: Russell A. Kirsch, National Bureau of Standards
A baby son, scanned as 176 by 176 dots. Every digital image since is a grid like this.

In 1957 Russell Kirsch scanned a photo of his baby son into a computer as a grid of 176 by 176 dots, each black or white. Every digital image since, from phones to space telescopes, is a grid of numbers.
2165: GPS Block II test satellite, San Diego Air & Space Museum (photo: Blervis, CC0)
The satellites only tell the time. Your phone works out the rest.
Each GPS satellite simply broadcasts the exact time. Your phone hears several and notes how late each signal arrives; since light covers 300 km in a millisecond, the delays pin down where you are.
2166: A machine that could compose music, imagined in 1843, if only it were given the rules.
This table is a step-by-step plan for Babbage's unbuilt engine to compute Bernoulli numbers. Lovelace saw further: such a machine could handle any symbols, even compose music, if given the rules.
2167: Four computers, sketched by hand: the whole network.

Four computers, sketched by hand in December 1969: the whole network. Its idea: chop messages into small packets that find their own way and reassemble at the end, so no single broken line stops them.
2168: Nobody programmed it. It guessed, got it wrong, and rewired itself.
Instead of being programmed, the Mark I Perceptron learned: it guessed letters from a camera and adjusted its own wiring after each mistake. Its ideas, buried for decades, now drive modern AI.
2169: George B. Grant's difference engine, Centennial Exhibition (1876)
Tables full of human errors, and a simple insight: gears can add.

Tables of numbers were computed by hand and full of errors. Babbage saw that many could be built from repeated additions alone, the method of differences, and that gears can add. Grant built this in 1876.
2170: Morse telegraph register, Popular Science Monthly (1873)
Every message from just two signals, and the commonest letter got a single dot.
Any message can be built from two signals, short and long. The commonest letter, E, got the shortest: one dot. In 1844 'What hath God wrought' flashed from Washington to Baltimore in an instant.
2171: Hollerith tabulator replica, Computer History Museum (photo: Tomwsulcer, CC0)
One census took eight years to count. Then people became holes in a card.
The 1880 US census took about eight years to tabulate. For 1890, Hollerith punched each person's answers as holes in a card, and machines counted them electrically, far faster. His firm became IBM.
2172: Radio waves miss the curving Earth, so the signal was bounced off the sky.
Radio waves fly straight and miss the curving Earth. Put a relay in orbit and a signal can bounce across an ocean. In 1962 Telstar carried the first live television between America and Europe.
2173: A tape, a head and a few rules: enough to compute anything computable.

Turing imagined the simplest computer: a tape of symbols, a head that reads and writes, and a short list of rules. He showed it can compute anything computable, and that some questions none can answer.
2174: Whatever a message says, it can be weighed in yes-or-no answers.

Shannon showed that information can be measured in bits, yes-or-no answers, whatever it says, and that any noisy channel can carry messages almost error-free below a certain speed. Every phone relies on it.
2175: A padlock anyone can snap shut, but only you can open.

Imagine a padlock anyone can snap shut but only you can open. Hand out open padlocks freely and strangers can send you locked boxes. Two keys, one public and one private, protect secure websites today.
2176: About 2,300 transistors in 1971; tens of billions today. Now the pace is slowing.

In 1965 Gordon Moore predicted chips would hold twice as many components every year or two. It held for half a century: from about 2,300 transistors in 1971 to tens of billions today. The pace is slowing.
2177: Jan Saenredam after Cornelis van Haarlem (1604)
Chained to a wall of shadows, and sure it is reality. What are we mistaking for the real?
Prisoners chained in a cave see only shadows on the wall and take them for reality. One escapes into sunlight and returns, but no one believes him. Plato asks: what are we mistaking for the real?
2178: Abraham Bosse, frontispiece of Hobbes's Leviathan
Look closely: the giant king's body is made of hundreds of tiny people.

Look closely: the giant king's body is made of hundreds of tiny people. Hobbes argued that without government life is 'nasty, brutish, and short', so people hand power to a ruler in exchange for safety.
2179: Map of Utopia, first edition of Thomas More's book (Bibliothèque Mazarine)
A perfect island society, named in Greek for 'no place'.

More invented an island where property was shared and religions tolerated, and named it Utopia, Greek for 'no place'. Ever since, people have designed better societies on paper to criticize their own.
2180: Jean-Jacques-François Le Barbier, Declaration of the Rights of Man
The radical idea: rights are not a gift from kings. You are born with them.
'Men are born and remain free and equal in rights.' The radical idea of 1789 was that rights belong to every person by nature, not handed down by kings, so a government exists to protect them.
2181: Ostrakon from Athens, 482 BCE (Stoa of Attalos museum)
A name scratched on a pottery shard could send a man away for ten years.

Once a year Athenians could scratch a name on a pottery shard. If enough voted, the most named man was exiled for ten years, without trial or disgrace: democracy's way to cut down anyone too powerful.
2182: Magna Carta, British Library, Cotton MS Augustus II.106
The charter soon failed. Its idea did not: even a king is bound by law.
In 1215 English barons forced King John to put in writing that no free man could be jailed except by lawful judgment. The charter soon failed, but its idea outlived him: even a king is bound by law.
2183: All, none, some, some not: four little words that reasoning obeys like grammar.

'All', 'none', 'some', 'some not': Aristotle mapped how such claims constrain each other. If 'all swans are white' is true, 'some swans are not white' is false. Valid reasoning has rules, like grammar.
2184: Living or not? Animal or not? Split in two, again and again, until you reach 'human'.
Body or not? Living or not? Animal or not? Rational or not? Splitting each class in two, Porphyry's tree climbs from 'substance' to 'human'. Libraries and biology still sort the world this way.
2185: Frontispiece of Francis Bacon's Novum Organum
A ship sailing past the old edge of the world, and leaving the ancient books behind.

The ship sails past the Pillars of Hercules, once the edge of the known world. Bacon urged thinkers to stop trusting ancient books and learn by observation and experiment, so knowledge can keep growing.
2186: Jeremy Bentham, plan of the Panopticon (drawn by Willey Reveley)
The prisoner never knows when he is watched, so he acts as if always. Sound familiar?

Bentham designed a ring of cells around a central tower whose guards could see every prisoner, while no prisoner could tell when he was watched. So he must act as if always watched. Think of cameras today.
2187: Constitution of the United States, page 1 (National Archives)
Power tends to grow, so split it three ways and let each part block the others.

Power tends to grow, so split it: one branch makes laws, one carries them out, one judges, and each can block the others. 'We the People' on top says where authority comes from. It has governed since 1789.
2188: Most of its original timber is gone, yet it is still the same ship. Or is it?

If every plank of a ship is replaced one by one, is it still the same ship? USS Constitution, launched in 1797, keeps only a small share of its original timber, yet it is still the same vessel. Or is it?
2189: Benoît-Louis Prévost after Charles-Nicolas Cochin, frontispiece of the Encyclopédie
All knowledge, from philosophy to pin making, for anyone to read. Authorities tried to ban it.

Reason pulls a veil off Truth, who glows at the top. Diderot and d'Alembert set out to gather all knowledge, from philosophy to pin making, into volumes anyone could read. Authorities tried to ban it.
2190: Pull a lever to save five? Most say yes. Push a man? Most refuse. Same arithmetic.

A runaway trolley will kill five unless you pull a lever and send it toward one. Most say pull. Push a man off a bridge to stop it? Most refuse. Same arithmetic, different gut: morality is not just counting.
2191: Write the rules before you know if you will be rich or poor, healthy or sick.
Design the rules of a society without knowing who you will be in it: rich or poor, healthy or sick, which gender or faith. Rawls argued that what you would choose behind that veil is what justice is.
2192: Sumerian cuneiform tablet (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
The first writing was not poetry. It was a receipt for barley.

The first writing was not poetry but bookkeeping. Sumerian scribes pressed marks into clay to record who received how much barley, as on this tablet. Stories and laws came later, once the tool existed.
2193: Photograph from E. A. Wallis Budge, The Rosetta Stone (1922)
One decree carved three times, and one of the three could still be read.

The same decree carved three times: in hieroglyphs, in Demotic and in Greek, which scholars could read. With it as a key, Champollion showed in 1822 that hieroglyphs mix sound signs with picture signs.
2194: Gutenberg Bible, Bibliothèque nationale de France (photo: Zythème, CC0)
A year of a scribe's work, made by the hundreds. Ideas began to outrun censors.

Gutenberg cast thousands of separate metal letters that could be set into any page, printed, then reused. A book that took a scribe a year could be made by the hundreds, and ideas began to outrun censors.
2195: L. F. Labrousse, Usage des nouvelles mesures (1800)
Hundreds of local measures, replaced by one taken from the Earth itself.
Before 1795, France had hundreds of local measures. The Revolution replaced them with units based on the Earth and divided by tens: the meter was a ten-millionth of the distance from pole to equator.
2196: How many ploughs, how many pigs: a whole kingdom turned into data.
Twenty years after conquering England, William sent men to every village to record who held the land, how many ploughs, how many pigs. Domesday turned a kingdom into data, to tax and rule it.
2197: Hundreds of signs, or about two dozen you can learn in weeks.
Egyptian writing needed hundreds of signs; the alphabet needs about two dozen, one per sound, learnable in weeks. This Moabite stone, carved about 840 BCE, uses the same early alphabet as old Hebrew.
2198: Service géographique des colonies, map of the 24 time zones (1913)
Every town kept its own noon, until the trains arrived.
Every town once set its clocks by its own noon, which was fine until trains made timetables chaos. The fix: divide the globe into 24 zones, each an hour wide, counted from Greenwich, agreed in 1884.
2199: Armor the bombers where the holes are? No: where the missing planes were hit.
Bombers came home riddled with holes in the wings and tail, so armor them there? Abraham Wald said no: armor where returning planes had no holes. Planes hit there were the ones that never came back.
2200: Better for small cases, better for large ones, and somehow worse overall.
A treatment can do better for small kidney stones and for large ones, yet worse overall, because it was given mostly to hard cases. Pooled numbers can flip the truth; ask how the groups were mixed.
2201: Jacques-Louis David, The Death of Socrates (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
Sentenced to death for asking too many questions, he chose the cup over silence.
Socrates was sentenced to death for asking too many questions, and drank the hemlock rather than stop. 'The unexamined life is not worth living,' he told the jury.
2202: The boulder always rolls back down. 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy.'
Sisyphus pushes his boulder uphill forever, and it always rolls back. Camus saw all of us in him, asking 'why?' of a silent universe. His verdict: 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy.'
2203: He lived in a clay jar in the marketplace and called himself a citizen of the world.
Diogenes lived in a large clay jar in the Athens marketplace and owned almost nothing, to show how little a good life needs. Asked where he came from, he said: 'I am a citizen of the world.'
2204: Lu Zhi, Zhuangzi Dreaming of a Butterfly (16th century)
A man who dreamed he was a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming it is a man?
Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, flitting about happily. He woke and wondered: was he a man who had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming it was a man?
2205: At the hub, a pig, a snake and a rooster keep the whole wheel turning.
At the hub of this Tibetan wheel, a pig, a snake and a rooster stand for ignorance, hatred and greed, which keep us circling through birth and death. Buddhism's promise: the wheel can stop.
2206: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, French manuscript (15th century)
Written in a cell while awaiting execution: whoever rises will fall.
Jailed and awaiting execution, Boethius imagined Lady Philosophy visiting his cell. Fortune is a wheel, she told him: whoever rises will fall. Only what is inside you cannot be taken.
2207: For two thousand years, all existence was one ladder, from God down to stones.
For two thousand years many in the West pictured all existence as one ladder: God, angels, humans, beasts, plants, stones, each rung less perfect. Evolution replaced it with a branching tree.
2208: Robert Fludd, Utriusque Cosmi Historia, engraved by Johann Theodor de Bry
The head is its heaven, the heart its sun: the body as a tiny cosmos.
As above, so below: Renaissance thinkers saw the human body as a small copy of the cosmos, the head its heaven, the heart its sun. Wrong, but a beautiful way to feel at home in the universe.
2209: Achilles can never catch the tortoise. At least, that is what Zeno 'proved'.
Achilles gives a tortoise a head start. By the time he reaches where it was, it has moved on, and so on forever. Zeno 'proved' motion impossible; the math of infinite sums shows how Achilles wins.
2210: God as Architect, Bible moralisée (about 1220 to 1230, Austrian National Library)
Every cause has a cause. Can the chain run back forever?
Everything has a cause, and that cause has a cause. Can the chain run back forever? Aristotle said no: there must be an unmoved mover. Medieval art showed God measuring out the world with a compass.
2211: Alfred Stieglitz, photograph of Marcel Duchamp's Fountain (1917)
A store-bought urinal, signed 'R. Mutt'. Is art the object, or the choice?
In 1917 Duchamp signed a store-bought urinal 'R. Mutt' and entered it in an art show. It was hidden from view, photographed by Stieglitz, then lost. Is art the object, or the choice?
2213: Ramon Llull, Ars Magna, edition of 1517
Paper wheels meant to settle any debate by turning a dial.
Around 1300 Ramon Llull built paper wheels that combined basic concepts mechanically, hoping to settle any debate by turning dials. Leibniz later took up the dream: 'Let us calculate.'
2214: A skull among the treasures, not to depress you but to wake you up.
A skull, books, a seashell, a ray of light: Dutch vanitas paintings set life's treasures beside death. Not to depress you, but to wake you: remember you will die, so spend your days on what matters.
2216: One grain is not a heap, and one more never makes one. So when does it?
One grain of salt is not a heap, and adding one grain never makes a heap. Yet a million grains clearly are one. Eubulides' puzzle shows how vague words like 'heap' or 'old' break logic.
2217: Ludolf Bakhuizen, Dutch Merchant Ships in a Storm (1670s)
No sailor commands the storm. The sails, though, are his.
'Some things are up to us and some are not,' Epictetus opens his handbook. No sailor can command the storm, only the sails. The Stoics put all their effort into the second kind and let the first go.
2218: Perfect replies in Chinese, from a man who knows no Chinese. Does he understand?
A man who knows no Chinese matches Chinese symbols by a rulebook and passes out perfect replies. Outside, people think he understands. Searle asked: does a computer doing the same understand?
2219: Peter Paul Rubens, The Death of Seneca (about 1612 to 1615)
Ordered to kill himself, he kept dictating to his scribes to the very end.
Ordered by Nero to kill himself, Seneca kept dictating to his scribes to the end. To philosophize is to practise dying, the Stoics held: whoever has learned to die has unlearned how to be a slave.
2220: Bronze statue of Marcus Aurelius, Capitoline Museums (photo: Wilfredor)
The emperor of Rome, writing private notes on humility never meant to be read.
The ruler of the Roman Empire wrote private notes on humility: see the world from high above, cities like anthills, fame soon forgotten. Marcus Aurelius' Meditations were never meant to be read.
2221: The Ring of Gyges, Ferrarese painting (16th century)
If no one could ever see you, would you still be good?
A shepherd finds a ring that makes him invisible, then seduces the queen and seizes the throne. Plato asks: if no one could ever see you, would you still be just, or is goodness fear of being caught?
2222: Cham, Buridan's Ass Between Two Opinions (1859, LACMA)
Two identical bales of hay, exactly equal, and the donkey starves.
A donkey stands exactly between two identical bales of hay and, with no reason to prefer either, starves. The puzzle, pinned on Jean Buridan, asks: does a rational choice need a reason?
2223: The Best of All Possible Worlds
Jean-Louis Delignon after Jean-Michel Moreau, illustration for Voltaire's Candide (1787)
War, shipwreck, earthquake, and the tutor still insists: this is the best world.
Leibniz argued that a perfect God must have made the best of all possible worlds, evils included. Voltaire answered with Candide, whose tutor keeps saying so through war, shipwreck and earthquake.
2224: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792)
Teach girls as you teach boys, she wrote, and see what is left of the difference.
In 1792 Mary Wollstonecraft argued that women only seemed less rational because they were denied an education. Teach girls as you teach boys, she wrote, and see what is left of the difference.
2225: Henry David Thoreau, Walden, first edition (1854)
'I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately.'
In 1845 Thoreau built a cabin by Walden Pond for about 28 dollars and lived there two years. 'I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately': to learn how little a free life needs.
2226: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, first edition (1859)
Drugs, speech, seat belts: one line from 1859 still decides where we argue.
The only reason to force anyone against their will, Mill wrote in 1859, is to prevent harm to others. Their own good is not enough. Debates on drugs, speech and seat belts still run along this line.
2227: She knows every fact about color. Then she sees red for the first time.
Mary knows every physical fact about color but has lived all her life in a black and white room. Then she sees a red apple. Does she learn something new? If so, physics may not capture everything.
2228: Nicolaus Copernicus, manuscript of De revolutionibus (Jagiellonian Library)
What if space and time are not out there, but lenses inside us?
Copernicus explained the sky by moving the observer. Kant did the same for knowledge: space, time and cause may not be out there at all, but lenses through which any mind like ours must see.
2229: Ouroboros from the Chrysopoeia of Cleopatra (Byzantine copy, 10th to 11th century)
Your life again, exactly the same, forever. Curse or blessing?
Nietzsche's test: imagine living your life again, exactly the same, every joy and every pain, forever. Would you curse the thought or bless it? Live, he said, so that you could gladly say yes.
2230: Ma Yuan, The Waving Surface of the Autumn Flood, Water Album (about 1222)
Nothing is softer than water, and nothing is better at wearing down stone.
Nothing in the world is softer than water, says the Tao Te Ching, yet nothing beats it at wearing down the hard. Taoism's wu wei is strength without forcing: yield, flow around, keep going.
2231: The Blind Men and the Elephant
Hanabusa Itchō, Blind Monks Examining an Elephant (print of 1888, Library of Congress)
One feels a snake, one a wall, one a rope. Each is right, and all are wrong.
Blind men touch one elephant: one feels a snake, one a wall, one a rope. Each is right about his part and wrong about the whole. Jain thinkers used the tale to teach that truth has many sides.
2233: Roman writing tablet and stylus found in the City of London
Is a newborn mind a blank tablet, or does it come with ideas built in?
Aristotle compared a newborn mind to an unwritten tablet, and Locke to 'white paper': everything we know is written there by experience. Rationalists replied that some ideas come built in.
2234: Joseph Wright of Derby, A Philosopher Lecturing on the Orrery (about 1766, Derby Museum)
A mind that knows every particle would see the future like the past. Then where is free will?
Laplace imagined a mind that knew the position of every particle and every force. For it nothing would be uncertain: the future would lie open like the past. If so, where is free will?
2235: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
Ernst Haeckel, Chiroptera, Kunstformen der Natur (1904)
We could know every fact about a bat's brain, and still not know what it feels like.
A bat perceives the world by echoes. Thomas Nagel asked in 1974: what is it like to be one? We could learn every fact about its brain and still not know. Experience resists the view from outside.
2236: Every test you ran would come back normal. So how would you know?
How do you know you are not a brain in a vat, fed signals that fake a whole world? Every test you ran would come back normal. It is Descartes' evil demon, updated for the age of machines.
2237: Dew on a spider web (photo: Jonathon Coombes)
A jewel at every knot, each one reflecting all the others, endlessly.
In Indra's net a jewel hangs at every knot, and each jewel reflects all the others, endlessly. Huayan Buddhism used the image to say that nothing exists alone: each thing holds the whole.
2238: Aegidius Sadeler after Christoph Schwarz, Occasio (about 1595, Rijksmuseum)
The right moment had a forelock and a bald back: grab it coming, or never.
The Greeks had two words for time: chronos, the clock, and kairos, the right moment. Kairos wore a forelock and was bald behind: seize the chance as it comes, for once past it cannot be caught.
2239: Auguste Rodin, The Thinker / Cleveland Museum of Art
He doubted his senses, his body, even mathematics. One thing survived.
Descartes resolved to doubt everything: his senses, his body, even mathematics. One thing survived. To doubt is to think, and a thought needs a thinker: 'I think, therefore I am.'
2240: Historic American Buildings Survey, interior of Pantigo Windmill, East Hampton, New York
Walk inside a thinking machine the size of a mill. Where among the gears is the feeling?
Imagine a thinking machine enlarged to the size of a mill, said Leibniz, so you could walk inside. You would find only parts pushing parts, never a perception. Where among the gears is the feeling?
2241: Plato's Academy mosaic from Pompeii (National Archaeological Museum, Naples)
He claimed to know nothing, and asked until every certainty fell apart.
Socrates claimed to know nothing and only asked questions, each answer exposing a new contradiction, until a confident guest's certainty fell apart. Plato's Academy made the method a school.
2242: William England, Blondin Crossing the Niagara River (1859)
Courage sits between cowardice and recklessness. Virtue is a balancing act.
Aristotle saw each virtue as a balance between two vices: courage between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between meanness and waste. Goodness is less a rule than a skill, like rope walking.
2243: US Fish and Wildlife Service, North American porcupine, Seedskadee National Wildlife Refuge
Close enough for warmth, far enough not to get pricked.
On a cold day, Schopenhauer wrote, porcupines huddle for warmth, get pricked and pull apart, until they find a bearable distance. People do the same: close enough for warmth, far enough not to hurt.
2244: Jeremy Bentham's Auto-Icon, University College London (photo: Karmakolle)
He preached the greatest happiness, and his clothed skeleton still sits in London.
Bentham said the right act is the one that brings the greatest happiness to the greatest number. His preserved, clothed skeleton, with a wax head, still sits at University College London.
2245: What if your red is my green, and we would never find out?
What if the red you see is the green I see, and we both learned to call it 'red'? We would agree on every apple and traffic light and never know. Locke asked in 1690: can experiences be compared?
2246: Roman mosaic with theatre masks (National Archaeological Museum, Naples)
Why do we choose to watch tragedies? Every sad film you loved is part of the answer.
Why do we choose to watch tragedies? Aristotle's answer: by feeling pity and fear for the people on stage, we are cleansed of them, a catharsis. Every sad film you loved is part of the experiment.
2247: At the barber shop, Essex County (about 1900)
Who shaves the barber? A small riddle that shook the foundations of mathematics.
A barber shaves everyone who does not shave himself. Who shaves the barber? Either answer breaks the rule. In 1901 Russell found this trap in set theory, and it shook the foundations of mathematics.
2248: If a Tree Falls in a Forest
NPS / Jacob W. Frank, fallen trees in a forest
No one hears it fall. Does it make a sound? Depends what 'sound' means.
If a tree falls in a forest and no one hears it, does it make a sound? It depends what 'sound' means: waves in the air, or something heard. Berkeley went further: to be is to be perceived.
2249: US Fish and Wildlife Service, wild turkey
Fed every morning, the turkey grows surer each day. Until the day before Thanksgiving.
A turkey is fed every morning, so each day it grows surer breakfast will come, until the day before Thanksgiving. Hume showed that no number of past cases can prove the future will be like the past.
2250: Utagawa Hiroshige, Hooded Gulls and Cherry Blossoms (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
Cherry blossoms are loved because they fall within days.
Japanese has a phrase for the gentle sadness of passing things: mono no aware. Cherry blossoms are loved because they fall within days. In this view, beauty is sharpened because it cannot last.
2251: Manuscript of the Analects with Zheng Xuan's commentary (about 750)
One word to live by, and centuries later Hillel taught almost the same rule.
Asked for one word to live by, Confucius chose reciprocity: 'Do not impose on others what you do not wish for yourself.' Centuries later, in Jerusalem, Hillel taught almost the same rule.
2252: The world rests on an elephant, the elephant on a turtle. And the turtle?
If the world rests on an elephant, and the elephant on a turtle, what holds up the turtle? 'Turtles all the way down.' Every chain of explanation must stop somewhere, or never stop at all.
2253: Lucretius, De rerum natura, manuscript copied by Girolamo di Matteo de Tauris (1483)
Tiny uncuttable pieces in empty space: a guess, turned into a long poem.
Democritus guessed that everything is made of tiny uncuttable pieces moving through empty space. Lucretius turned the idea into a long poem, and a copy found in 1417 helped bring it back to Europe.
2254: A lie works only because most people tell the truth. What if everyone did it?

Before you act, Kant said, ask: what if everyone did this? A lie works only because most people tell the truth; if all lied, no one would believe anyone. Act only on rules you could will for everyone.
2255: Carlo Chiostri, cover of Le avventure di Pinocchio (1902)
What if Pinocchio says, 'My nose will grow now'?
'This sentence is false.' If true, it is false; if false, true. Pinocchio adds a twist: what if he says, 'My nose will grow now'? Gödel built his great theorem on a cousin of this paradox.
2256: Frans Francken I, Allegory: The Ship of State (Royal Museums Greenwich)
Would you let the passengers vote on who steers the ship?

Plato asked: would you let the passengers vote on who steers the ship, or hire someone who knows navigation? His 'ship of state' argued that ruling is a skill. Democracies have argued back ever since.
2257: Peter Van Dyck, teapot (about 1720, Metropolitan Museum of Art)
A china teapot orbiting the Sun, too small to see. Prove it isn't there.
Russell said no one could disprove him if he claimed a china teapot orbits the Sun between Earth and Mars, too small to see. That would not make it likely. The burden of proof lies with the claimant.
2258: Jacob van Ruisdael, Landscape with Cornfield (1660s)
'God, or Nature', as if the two were one word. At 23, he was expelled for it.
Spinoza wrote 'God, or Nature', as if the two were one word: God is not a king outside the world but the world itself and its laws. At 23, suspected of heresy, he was expelled by Amsterdam's Jews.
2259: Korean tea bowl with gold lacquer repairs, 16th century (Ethnological Museum, Berlin)
Mended with gold, the cracks become the most beautiful part.
In Japan a broken bowl may be mended with lacquer and gold, so the cracks become its most beautiful part. Wabi-sabi finds beauty in the worn, the imperfect and the passing: a history is not a flaw.
2260: Remains said to be Vaucanson's mechanical duck (photograph, 19th century)
Exactly like you, atom for atom, laughing and talking, and feeling nothing inside.
Picture a being exactly like you, atom for atom, that talks and laughs but feels nothing inside. If such a 'zombie' is even conceivable, consciousness is something more than the physical machinery.
2261: Robert Havell after John James Audubon, Raven (1831, National Gallery of Art)
By strict logic, a green apple is evidence that all ravens are black.
'All ravens are black' is logically the same as 'everything not black is not a raven'. So spotting a green apple supports the claim about ravens. Hempel's paradox shows how strange evidence can be.
2262: The king forbade it. She buried her brother anyway, by a higher law.
Antigone buries her brother against the king's command, saying the gods' unwritten laws outrank his. Sophocles staged the idea of natural law: some duties bind us even when the state says otherwise.
2263: An idea meets its opposite, they clash, and something new climbs out.

An idea meets its opposite, they clash, and something new emerges that keeps the best of both, then meets its own opposite. Hegel saw thought and history move like this: through contradiction, upward.
2264: Ford Madox Brown, Manfred on the Jungfrau (Manchester Art Gallery)
Terror felt from safety: why cliffs and storms make us feel small and alive.
Why do storms, cliffs and abysses thrill us? Burke called it the sublime: terror felt from safety. Unlike beauty, which charms, the sublime overwhelms, and makes us feel small and alive at once.
2265: Louis-Léopold Boilly, The Game of Billiards (1807, Hermitage Museum)
One ball hits another. You see two events, but never the cause.
One billiard ball strikes another and the second moves. Hume noticed that we never actually see the cause, only one event followed by another. Causation, he argued, is a habit of the mind.
2266: Michel de Montaigne, Bordeaux copy of the Essays with his handwritten additions
His motto was 'What do I know?', and he kept rewriting in the margins until he died.
Montaigne took 'What do I know?' as his motto and kept rewriting his Essays in the margins until he died. He invented the essay: not a verdict but an attempt, a mind testing itself in public.
2267: They came to ask about the future. The words at the door turned them inward.
'Know thyself' was inscribed at Apollo's temple at Delphi, where Greeks came to ask the oracle about their future. The words at the entrance turned them inward first. Socrates made them his task.
2268: Plaster cast of Michelangelo's Bearded Slave (Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen)
A knife is designed before it is made. We are made first, and design ourselves later.

A paper knife is designed before it is made. Sartre said humans are the reverse: we exist first and define ourselves by what we do. Like Michelangelo's half-carved slave, we are always still emerging.
2269: Limestone chariot model, Cyprus, 5th century BCE (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
Two winged horses, one noble, one unruly, and reason holding the reins.
Plato pictured the soul as a charioteer driving two winged horses, one noble, one unruly. Reason holds the reins but must win the passions over, not just whip them. Freud's map of the mind echoes it.
2270: Lisbone abysmée, French print of 1755 (Bibliothèque nationale de France)
An earthquake struck Lisbon while many were at Mass. How could a good God allow it?
On 1 November 1755 an earthquake, a tsunami and fires destroyed Lisbon, killing tens of thousands, many at Mass. How could a good, all-powerful God allow it? The question shook Europe's faith.
2271: Jan Lievens, Philosopher with an Hourglass (17th century)
'If no one asks me, I know. If I try to explain it, I do not.'
'What is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I try to explain it, I do not,' wrote Augustine. The past is gone, the future not yet here, the present has no length. So where does time live?
2272: Any experience you want, all feeling real, for life. Would you plug in?

A machine can give you any experience you want, love, triumph, discovery, all feeling real, for life. Would you plug in? Most people say no, which suggests we want more than pleasure. We want reality.
2273: Ivan Shishkin, Backwater in the Forest (1889 to 1890)
Not the same river twice, and not the same person stepping in.
'You cannot step into the same river twice,' Heraclitus is quoted as saying, for fresh waters keep flowing past. Everything is change, he taught; even the person stepping in is no longer the same.
2274: Christian Morgenstern, Reeds on Lake Starnberg (1866, Hamburger Kunsthalle)
A drop of water can kill him, yet he knows it, and the universe knows nothing.
'Man is only a reed, the weakest in nature, but a thinking reed,' wrote Pascal. A drop of water can kill him, yet he knows he dies and the universe knows nothing. Our dignity lies in thought.
2275: USDA / Scott Bauer, sow with piglet
A storm at sea, panic on deck, and one pig calmly eating: the wise man's model.
Caught in a storm at sea, Pyrrho pointed to a pig calmly eating on deck: this is how the wise should be. Skeptics suspended judgment on everything, and peace of mind followed, like a shadow.
2276: USDA / Scott Bauer, cow and newborn calf
Not 'Can they reason?' but 'Can they suffer?' One footnote that planted a movement.
'The question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?' Bentham wrote in 1789. That one footnote became a seed of the modern case for animal rights.
2277: Razor of Hatnefer, Egypt, about 1492 to 1473 BCE (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
When two explanations fit, prefer the one that assumes less.
Do not multiply entities beyond necessity: when two explanations fit the facts, prefer the one that assumes less. The rule is named after the friar William of Ockham, and it still trims theories.
2278: Fable of the Lion and the Fox, Dutch print (1608, Rijksmuseum)
A lion to frighten wolves, a fox to spot traps: a ruler needs to be both.
A prince must be a lion to frighten wolves and a fox to spot traps, Machiavelli wrote. Politics, in his view, should be judged by what actually works, not by how rulers ought to behave.
2279: William Stott of Oldham, Hide and Seek in the Garden of Epicurus
The philosopher of pleasure asked for little: friends, bread and a garden.
Epicurus taught that pleasure is the goal of life, but he meant no pain in the body and no fear in the mind: friends, bread, a garden. 'Death is nothing to us,' for where death is, we are not.
2280: Jacques Goullons, watch (about 1645, Metropolitan Museum of Art)
Find a watch on a heath and you know someone made it. And a living thing?
Find a watch on a heath, Paley wrote in 1802, and you know someone designed it. Living things are far more intricate, so surely they had a designer too. Darwin showed how complexity can build itself.
2281: Belief as a bet: gain everything, or lose little. But which God?
If God exists and you believe, you gain everything; if not, you lose little. Pascal argued that belief is the smart bet. Critics asked: which God, and can anyone simply choose to believe?
2282: Andries van Eertvelt, The Battle of Lepanto (1623, Museum of Fine Arts, Ghent)
Is tomorrow's battle already true or false today? If so, where is choice?
Is 'there will be a sea battle tomorrow' already true or false today? If it is, the future is fixed and choice is an illusion. Aristotle suggested some statements about the future are not yet either.
2283: Caravaggio, Narcissus (about 1597 to 1599, Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Antica, Rome)
He looked inside for his self and found heat, cold, love and pain, but no 'me'.
When Hume looked inward for his self, he found only a stream of perceptions: heat, cold, love, pain, never a 'me' holding them. Perhaps the self is a bundle, as elusive as the face Narcissus loved.
2284: Hakuin Ekaku, The Buddhist Layman Vimalakirti (Minneapolis Institute of Art)
Asked to define the truth, he said nothing at all, and gave the best answer.
One by one, sages tried to define non-duality in words. When Vimalakirti's turn came, he said nothing at all, and was praised for the best answer. Some truths can be pointed at but not spoken.
2285: Sengai Gibon, Circle, Triangle, Square (Edo period)
Three shapes in ink, and no key to read them.
'Two hands clap and there is a sound; what is the sound of one hand?' Zen teachers set riddles like Hakuin's to exhaust logical thinking. Sengai drew three shapes and left no key: a koan in ink.
2286: Thomas Eakins, The Chess Players (1876, Metropolitan Museum of Art)
A chess bishop is not its wood or shape, only the moves it may make. So are words.
What is a bishop in chess? Not its wood or shape, but the moves it is allowed. Wittgenstein said words work like that: their meaning is their use in a 'language game', not a thing they point to.
2287: Alive and dead until someone looks? Schrödinger meant it to sound absurd.

Seal a cat in a box with poison released if one atom decays. Quantum rules say the atom is both decayed and not until someone looks. So is the cat alive and dead? Schrödinger meant it to sound absurd.
2288: A young woman, or an old one? What you saw before decides what you see first.
A young woman looking away, or an old woman in profile? What you see first can depend on what you saw before: in 1935, people first shown a clear version of one face nearly always saw that one.
2289: William Hogarth, Satire on False Perspective (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
A man on a distant hill lights his pipe from a nearby window.
A man on a distant hill lights his pipe from a candle in a nearby window. Hogarth broke every cue the brain uses to judge distance, such as size, overlap and perspective, and the scene turns absurd.
2290: After Hermann Ebbinghaus (vector diagram, Wikimedia Commons)
The two orange circles are exactly the same size. Really.
The two orange circles are exactly the same size. Ringed by giants, one shrinks; among dwarfs, the other swells. The brain never judges size alone; it measures it against whatever is nearby.
2291: After Ludimar Hermann (vector diagram, Wikimedia Commons)
Gray dots flicker at the crossings, but never at the one you look at.
Gray dots flicker at the white crossings, yet vanish from any crossing you look at directly. Ludimar Hermann described them in 1870; the eye's wiring invents them, though exactly how is still argued.
2292: After James Fraser (vector diagram, Wikimedia Commons)
There is no spiral here. Trace one with a finger and see.
There is no spiral here. These are perfect circles, one inside another; trace one with a finger and see. The twisted stripes fool the brain's edge detectors, and it builds a spiral that is not there.
2293: Phenakistiscope disc, c. 1835 (Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum)
Every picture is still. The dancing happens in your brain.
Spin this disc behind its slits and the little man dances. Each picture is still; the brain fills the gaps with motion. Every film and screen relies on that guess, 24 or more times a second.
2294: Charles Wheatstone's mirror stereoscope (Popular Science Monthly, 1882)
Two mirrors, one drawing for each eye, and flat lines leap into depth.
Your eyes view the world from points about 6 cm apart. In 1838 Wheatstone used two mirrors to give each eye its own drawing, and flat lines leapt into depth: the brain builds 3D from the difference.
2295: Michel Eugène Chevreul, chromatic circle, 1861 (Linda Hall Library)
The black dye looked dull. Nothing was wrong with it; its neighbors were to blame.

The Gobelins tapestry works complained that their black dyes looked dull. Chemist Chevreul found nothing wrong with the dye: the colors woven beside it changed how it looked. Color lives in relations.
2296: Giuseppe Arcimboldo, Reversible Head with Basket of Fruit
A basket of fruit. Turn it over, and someone stares back.
A basket of fruit; turn it over and a face stares back. The brain is so primed for faces that it finds them in clouds, sockets and toast, and newborns already turn toward simple face-like patterns.
2297: Francis Galton, composite photographs of three sisters
He blended faces to expose 'types'. The blends kept looking better than the people.
Galton layered photos of several faces into one, hoping to expose 'types'. The blends kept looking better than the people. Later studies agreed: averaged faces tend to be rated more attractive.
2298: M. H. Reamy, Civil War veteran Henry A. Seaverns (Library of Congress)
The leg was gone, and it still itched.
After the Civil War, doctor Silas Weir Mitchell met many amputees who still felt their missing limbs itch, cramp and ache. He named them phantom limbs: the brain's map of the body outlives the body.
2299: After Hieronymus Bosch, The Conjurer (Musée Municipal, Saint-Germain-en-Laye)
While the crowd stares at the trick, someone behind them lifts a purse.
While the crowd stares at the trick, a man behind them lifts a purse. Attention is a narrow beam: in a famous test, about half of viewers counting basketball passes missed a person in a gorilla suit.
2300: Jan Steen, Merry Company on a Terrace (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
You tune out the whole room, until someone across it says your name.
In a noisy room you follow one voice and tune out the rest, until someone across the room says your name. Your brain was quietly listening to everyone all along, just in case.
2301: Dante Gabriel Rossetti, The Day Dream (Victoria and Albert Museum)
Almost half the time, our minds are somewhere else, and we are less happy for it.
An app pinged thousands of people at random moments: what are you doing, and are you thinking about it? Almost half the time, minds were elsewhere, and people were less happy when they were.
2302: Ouija board, Kennard Novelty Company, c. 1890
The pointer glides to YES, and no one is lying about not pushing it.
The pointer glides to YES and no one admits pushing it. Nobody is lying: muscles make tiny moves that follow our expectations without our noticing. The same effect drives dowsing rods.
2303: Le Baquet de Mr. Mesmer, French print, 1780s (Bibliothèque nationale de France)
Blindfolded, they reacted only when they believed the magic was on.
Parisians fainted and convulsed around Mesmer's magnetic tubs. In 1784 a commission including Benjamin Franklin blindfolded patients: they reacted only when they believed they were being magnetized.
2304: John Margolies, drive-in theater, Columbus, Ohio, 1980 (Library of Congress)
'Eat Popcorn', flashed too fast to see. It caused a panic, and was made up.
In 1957 a marketer claimed that flashing 'Eat Popcorn' on a movie screen, too fast to notice, boosted sales. Panic followed; in 1962 he admitted the study was made up. Hidden messages barely sway us.
2305: Freud likely never said 'iceberg'. The gist holds: most of the mind works out of sight.
Freud seems never to have likened the mind to an iceberg; that image came later. But research backs the gist: most of what the brain does, from reading faces to forming habits, happens out of sight.
2306: Elihu Vedder, Memory (Los Angeles County Museum of Art)
Retold again and again, the ghost story grew shorter, and canoes became boats.
In 1932 Bartlett had English students retell a Native American ghost story. Each retelling grew shorter and more familiar; canoes became boats. We don't replay memories; we rebuild them.
2307: National Photo Company, car accident, c. 1920 (Library of Congress)
Say 'smashed' instead of 'hit', and people remember broken glass that wasn't there.
People watched a film of a car crash. Asked how fast the cars went when they 'smashed', they guessed higher than for 'hit', and a week later twice as many recalled broken glass. There was none.
2308: Years later their stories had changed completely, and they still felt sure.
The day after Challenger exploded, students wrote down how they heard the news. Two and a half years later many accounts had changed completely, yet people felt sure. Vivid is not accurate.
2309: Johann Erdmann Hummel, The Chess Game (Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin)
Five seconds, and masters rebuild the board. Scatter the pieces and the magic fades.
Shown a real game for five seconds, chess masters rebuild the board almost perfectly. Scatter the pieces at random and their edge nearly vanishes. Experts see patterns, not pieces.
2310: W. H. Matthews, Mazes and Labyrinths (1922)
The rats seemed to learn nothing, until food appeared and they raced straight to it.
Rats that roamed a maze with no reward seemed to learn nothing, until food appeared; then they raced to it. They had built an inner map. A 2014 Nobel went for finding the brain cells that draw it.
2311: Eyes dart under closed lids, again and again through the night. Wake them now.
In 1953 a graduate student watching sleepers saw their eyes dart under closed lids, again and again through the night. Woken then, they usually reported vivid dreams. Sleep has its own seasons.
2312: Thomas Cole, The Voyage of Life: Childhood (National Gallery of Art)
You learned to walk, talk and love, and remember almost none of it.

You learned to walk, talk and love in your first years, and remember almost none of it. Most adults' earliest memories date from about age three, perhaps because the young brain cannot yet store them.
2313: After Charles Le Brun, Expressions of the Passions of the Soul, 1732 (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
The same grimace reads as disgust or triumph, depending on the body below it.
Le Brun drew a dictionary of the passions, one face for each. Modern experiments complicate it: the same grimace reads as disgust or triumph depending on the body around it. We read faces in context.
2314: Joseph Ducreux, Self-Portrait, Yawning (J. Paul Getty Museum)
Just looking at this may make you yawn.
Just looking at this may make you yawn; even reading about yawning can. Yawns spread between people, and some studies find they spread most between friends and family, a small trace of empathy.
2315: Most laughter follows ordinary remarks, not jokes.
We laugh about 30 times more often with others than alone. Robert Provine eavesdropped on everyday laughter: most of it follows ordinary remarks, not jokes. Laughter is more about bonding than humor.
2316: Vilhelm Hammershøi, Interior with a Woman Seen from Behind (Randers Kunstmuseum)
Loneliness ranks with smoking as a health risk.
A review of 148 studies found that people with stronger social ties were about 50% more likely to survive the follow-up period. Loneliness ranks with smoking and inactivity as a health risk.
2317: Vilhelm Hammershøi, Interior, Sunlight on the Floor
Fifteen minutes alone with their thoughts, and many chose electric shocks instead.
Left alone in a room for 15 minutes with nothing but their thoughts, many people chose to give themselves electric shocks rather than do nothing: two thirds of the men and a quarter of the women.
2318: Diederik Franciscus Jamin, The Grieving Widow (Rijksmuseum)
The famous five stages were never shown to fit mourning. Most people ache, and cope.
The five stages of grief came from interviews with dying patients and were never shown to fit mourning. Long-term studies find most people who lose someone close are resilient: they ache, yet cope.
2319: Louis Ducros, Night Storm at Cefalù (Musée cantonal des Beaux-Arts, Lausanne)
Feeling small before a storm, and oddly, it feels good.
Before a storm at sea or a starry sky we feel small, and oddly that feels good. Studies of awe suggest it quiets the self's chatter and nudges people to be more generous toward others.
2320: Capilano Canyon bridge, North Vancouver, c. 1908 (UBC Library)
High on a swaying bridge, a pounding heart was mistaken for attraction.

On this swaying bridge high over a canyon, a woman gave men her number. Far more called than men she met on a low, steady bridge. In this 1974 study, a heart pounding from fear was read as attraction.
2321: Herbert James Draper, Ulysses and the Sirens (Ferens Art Gallery, Hull)
He knew he could not resist, so he had himself tied to the mast.
Ulysses knew he could not resist the Sirens, so he had himself tied to the mast. Knowing our future self will be weak, we can bind it today, like savings plans that raise contributions automatically.
2322: Jean Siméon Chardin, Young Student Drawing
Children who loved to draw were promised a prize. Afterward, they drew half as much.
Preschoolers who loved to draw were promised a prize for drawing. Later, in free time, they drew about half as much as unrewarded kids. Pay for what people enjoy and it can start to feel like work.
2323: Hard enough, but not too hard, and time simply vanishes.
When a task stretches our skill just enough, time vanishes and the self goes quiet. Csikszentmihalyi called it flow; too easy bores us, too hard makes us anxious, and the sweet spot absorbs us.
2324: Robert M. Yerkes, The Dancing Mouse (1907)
A famous rule about stress grew from one study of mice, and fits loosely at best.
In 1908, mice learning a hard choice did best with medium-strength shocks. That one study grew into the famous rule that some stress helps and too much harms, a loose fit at best.
2325: The '10,000-hour rule' explains far less than its fame suggests.

The '10,000-hour rule' grew from a study of top violinists. Focused practice matters, but a large review found it explains only about a fifth of the differences between performers in music and sports.
2326: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Wheel of Fortune, c. 1470 (Utrecht University Library)
A rigged wheel stopped at 10 or 65, and that meaningless number steered every guess.
Volunteers spun a wheel of fortune rigged to stop at 10 or 65, then guessed the share of African countries in the UN. Those who saw 65 guessed far higher. A meaningless number had become an anchor.
2327: Sem, La Roulette in the Casino, from Monte-Carlo (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
Black came up 26 times running. Fortunes went on red. The wheel has no memory.
On 18 August 1913 at Monte Carlo, the ball fell on black 26 times running. Gamblers bet fortunes on red, sure it was due. But a wheel has no memory: each spin starts fresh, at nearly even odds.
2328: Angelos Akotantos, Saint John the Baptist (Byzantine and Christian Museum, Athens)
Rated handsome, and somehow also smarter, braver and kinder.
In 1920 Thorndike noticed that officers who rated a soldier handsome and fit also rated him smarter, a better leader and of finer character. One good trait casts a glow over the rest, like a halo.
2329: The Eiffel Tower at the Exposition Universelle, Paris, 1889
Leading artists called it useless and monstrous. Now Paris adores it.
In 1887 leading Parisian artists protested Eiffel's 'useless and monstrous' tower. Today it is the city's beloved emblem. Psychologists find we tend to like things simply because we see them often.
2330: Johann Franz Michiels, Cologne Cathedral, south side, 1853
Begun in 1248, finished in 1880. We all plan for the best case.
Students asked when they would finish their theses guessed about 34 days; they took 56. We plan for the best case and forget past delays. Cologne Cathedral, begun in 1248, was finished in 1880.
2331: Matthew Hopkins, The Discovery of Witches (1647)
To a witch-finder, almost anything counted as proof of guilt.
Witch-finders like Matthew Hopkins took almost anything as proof of guilt. We all lean that way: testing a hunch, many people seek only cases that fit it, never ones that could prove it wrong.
2332: Limbourg brothers, Anatomical Man, Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry (Musée Condé)
Every student got the same 'personal' profile, and rated it 4.3 out of 5.
In 1948 a professor gave each student a 'personal' profile; all got the same text, much of it from a horoscope book. They rated its accuracy 4.3 out of 5. Vague, flattering words feel tailor-made.
2333: The world was due to end in 1844. When it didn't, many kept believing.
Thousands of Millerites expected the world to end in 1844. When it didn't, many reinterpreted the prophecy instead of quitting. Festinger saw the same in a modern cult: deep belief often beats facts.
2334: 24 jams or 6? A famous finding about too much choice, and it mostly faded.
A famous 2000 study found shoppers offered 24 jams bought far less often than those offered 6. Later reviews put the average effect near zero: too much choice paralyzes only under certain conditions.
2335: US World War II poster (National Archives)
Hear it twice and it starts to feel true, even if you knew better.
Hear a claim twice and it starts to feel truer, even if you knew better the first time. Repetition breeds familiarity, and the brain mistakes familiar for true. Slogans and propaganda lean on that.
2336: Londoners saw a pattern in where the bombs fell. The map showed pure chance.
As V-1 bombs fell on London, people saw patterns: some districts seemed targeted, others spared. In 1946 an actuary split south London into 576 squares and found the hits matched pure chance.
2337: Georges Delaw, The Emperor's New Clothes
Everyone praises the invisible clothes, each sure the others can see them.
Everyone praises the emperor's invisible clothes, each sure the others see them. Likewise, Princeton students believed their peers were far more at ease with heavy drinking than they themselves were.
2338: Domenico Fetti, Parable of the Good Samaritan (Museum of Fine Arts, Boston)
On their way to talk about the Good Samaritan, the hurried ones walked past.
Seminary students on their way to give a talk, some on the Good Samaritan, passed a man slumped in a doorway. Of those told they were late, 10% stopped to help; of those with time to spare, 63%.
2339: Rembrandt, Landscape with the Good Samaritan (Czartoryski Museum, Kraków)
The story of 38 silent neighbors was exaggerated. On real streets, someone usually helps.
The 1964 tale of 38 neighbors ignoring a murder was badly exaggerated. Crowds do make each person less likely to act in the lab, yet street cameras show someone helps in about 9 of 10 real fights.
2340: Bain News Service, six-day bicycle race, Madison Square Garden, 1908 (Library of Congress)
Cyclists rode faster against each other than against the clock.
In 1898 Norman Triplett saw that cyclists rode faster racing others than racing the clock. In what is often called the first social psychology experiment, many children reeled faster side by side.
2341: Jessie Tarbox Beals (attributed), tug of war at the 1904 Olympics, St. Louis
Eight men on a rope pull far less than eight times one.
Ringelmann had men pull a rope alone and in teams. Eight together pulled far less than eight times one man's force. Partly that is poor coordination, but people also ease off when effort is pooled.
2342: Split by a taste for Klee or Kandinsky, and already loyal to their side.
Schoolboys were split into two groups, supposedly by whether they preferred Klee or Kandinsky. Strangers to each other, they still favored their own side. A trivial label is enough to make an 'us'.
2343: Jean-Léon Gérôme, Pygmalion and Galatea (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
Pupils picked at random were said to be about to bloom, and they did, a little.
Teachers were told some pupils, picked at random, would soon bloom, and those pupils gained more IQ points. The 1968 study drew criticism, but the core holds modestly: expectations nudge outcomes.
2344: Édouard Manet, Masked Ball at the Opera (National Gallery of Art)
Take one candy each, they were told. The unnamed, in groups, took more.
On Halloween, researchers watched over 1,300 trick-or-treaters told to take one candy each. Unnamed children in groups took extra far more often than those asked their names. Anonymity loosens rules.
2345: US Army Signal Corps, volunteers bound for infantry training, France, 1945
7% against 62%: white soldiers who served beside Black volunteers, and those who never did.
In 1945 Black volunteers joined white companies in Europe. Only 7% of white soldiers in those companies then disliked the idea, against 62% in units that never mixed. Shared work erodes prejudice.
2346: After André Brouillet, A Clinical Lesson at the Salpêtrière (1887)
She swooned on cue before the elite of Paris. Was she sick, or performing?
Charcot's star patient swooned on cue before Paris's elite. Critics later argued she had learned to perform what doctors expected. Subjects in experiments, too, guess what is wanted and supply it.
2348: Punch and Judy show, Melbourne, 1944 (Australian War Memorial)
The marble was moved while she was gone. Where will she look for it?
A puppet hides a marble and leaves; another moves it. Where will the first look? Most 3-year-olds point to where the marble is now; by about 4, children grasp that others can believe what isn't true.
2350: Sandra Uecker / US Fish and Wildlife Service
Goslings follow the first moving thing they see. He made sure it was him.
Goslings follow the first moving thing they see in a short window after hatching. Konrad Lorenz made sure it was him, and a line of geese trailed him like a mother. Some learning has a deadline.
2352: Vincent van Gogh, First Steps, after Millet (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
Open arms, just far enough away: that gap is where learning happens.
A father kneels with open arms, just far enough away. Vygotsky saw learning thrive in that gap, which he called the zone of proximal development: what a child can't yet do alone but can with help.
2353: John Heil / US Fish and Wildlife Service
Sick just once, hours after a sweet drink, and the rat shuns that taste for good.
Make a rat sick hours after it tastes sweet water, just once, and it shuns that taste. Garcia found the brain ties nausea to food above all; ranchers even tried sickening baits on coyotes.
2354: Wolfgang Köhler's chimpanzee research, Tenerife (reproduced in Creation by Evolution, 1928)
Bananas out of reach, a pause, and then: stack the crates and climb.
On Tenerife in the 1910s, chimpanzees faced bananas hung out of reach. After some failures, one might pause, then stack crates and climb. Köhler saw sudden insight, not trial and error.
2355: Mills Novelty Company advertisement for the Liberty Bell, 1909
Pigeons pecked hardest when food came unpredictably. So do we, at our feeds.
Skinner found pigeons pecked most stubbornly when food came at unpredictable times. Slot machines like the Liberty Bell run on that rule, and so do the feeds we keep refreshing for something new.
2356: From Four Temperaments to Five Traits
Pieter de Jode I after Maerten de Vos, The Sanguine Temperament (Rijksmuseum)
Four temperaments for 2,000 years, then thousands of words boiled down to five traits.
For 2,000 years personality meant four temperaments: sanguine, choleric, melancholic, phlegmatic. Sifting thousands of trait words, psychologists found five broad traits that recur across cultures.
2357: Phineas Gage holding the tamping iron, cabinet card (Gage family collection)
An iron bar shot through his head, and friends said he was 'no longer Gage'.
In 1848 an iron bar shot through Phineas Gage's head, and friends said he was 'no longer Gage'. The case showed the frontal lobes shape character, though he later drove stagecoaches in Chile.
2358: Johannes Sobotta, Atlas of Human Anatomy (1911)
He says he saw nothing, yet his left hand picks out the object. Two minds?
To stop severe epilepsy, surgeons cut the bridge between the brain's halves. Show such a patient an object on the left only and he says he saw nothing, yet his left hand picks it out. Two minds?
2359: What do you see in the ink? A century later, science is still divided on what it means.
Rorschach published ten inkblots in 1921, hoping what people saw would reveal their minds. A century of research is mixed: some scores help spot disordered thinking; many popular uses lack support.
2360: It measures nerves, not lies: a nervous innocent can fail, a calm liar pass.
A polygraph tracks pulse, breathing and sweat: signs of arousal, not lying. A nervous innocent can fail and a calm liar pass, and in 2003 the US National Academy of Sciences found its basis weak.
2361: Tony Robert-Fleury, Pinel at the Salpêtrière (1876)
The chains came off. The doctor got the credit; his aide had led the way.
Around 1795 Paris asylums began striking the chains off patients and treating them with routine, work and kindness. Philippe Pinel got the credit, though his aide Jean-Baptiste Pussin led the way.
2362: US War Department, soldiers taking an army intelligence test, Camp Lee, 1917 (National Archives)
The average person of 1920 would score well below today's average IQ.
Through the 20th century, raw IQ scores rose about three points a decade in many countries; an average person of 1920 would score well below today's average. Schooling and nutrition likely helped.
2363: Frances Benjamin Johnston, Hampton Institute classroom, 1899 (Library of Congress)
Visual learner? Auditory? Most teachers believe it. The evidence keeps saying no.
Most teachers believe students learn best in their preferred style, such as visual or auditory. Reviews keep finding no evidence that matching style to student helps. Matching method to content does.
2364: James M. Lawson, Lottery Wheel (National Gallery of Art, Index of American Design)
Lottery winners became famous for being no happier. A bigger study disagreed.
A 1978 study made lottery winners famous for being no happier than others. We do adapt to good and bad fortune, but less than claimed: a big Swedish study found winners more satisfied years later.
2365: Caspar David Friedrich, Woman at a Window (Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin)
Patients facing trees went home sooner than those facing a brick wall.
Surgery patients whose window faced trees went home sooner and needed fewer strong painkillers than those facing a brick wall. That 1984 study helped launch research on nature's restorative power.
2366: Henri Rousseau, The Dream (Museum of Modern Art)
Signaling to the lab with their eyes, from inside a dream.

Some dreamers know they are dreaming. Skeptics doubted it until the late 1970s, when lucid sleepers moved their eyes in a pre-agreed pattern during REM sleep, signaling from inside a dream to the lab.
2367: Possibly Mazhar Ali Khan, Elephant with a Mahout, c. 1840 (Victoria and Albert Museum)
A small rider on a huge elephant, mostly explaining where it already went.
Jonathan Haidt pictures the mind as a small rider on a huge elephant: reasoning sits on top, but fast intuition and emotion do most of the walking. The rider often just explains where it went.
2368: Jean Siméon Chardin, The House of Cards (National Gallery of Art)
100 studies redone, and only about a third held up.
In 2015, 270 researchers redid 100 published psychology studies; only about a third got the same result. Famous findings like ego depletion and power posing wobbled, and the field began to reform.
2369: The first words and the last stick. The middle disappears. Go first or last.
Hear a list of 20 words and you will recall the first few and the last few best, and lose the middle. The first get rehearsed into memory; the last are still echoing. Go first or last.
2370: Given the choice, most picked the longer dose of pain, because it ended gentler.
People held a hand in painfully cold water for 60 seconds, and in another trial for 60 seconds plus 30 slightly less cold. Most chose to repeat the longer one: memory keeps the peak and the end.
2371: Three dots you just know. Seven you must count.
Glance at 3 dots and you know it is 3 instantly; at 7 you must count. In 1871 Jevons tossed beans into a box and judged their number at a glance: he never erred up to 4, then mistakes crept in.
2372: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations (Cannan edition)
The baker isn't feeding you out of kindness, and yet the whole city eats.
We do not get dinner from the baker's kindness but from his self-interest, Adam Smith wrote, and yet the city eats. Millions chasing their own gain can end up serving one another.
2373: Bernard Mandeville, The Fable of the Bees (1924 edition)
A hive thrived on greed and vanity, then collapsed when its bees turned virtuous.

Mandeville's scandalous poem told of a hive that thrived on greed and vanity, then collapsed when its bees turned virtuous. His claim that selfish spending feeds jobs shocked 1714 and shaped economics.
2374: Water keeps us alive and costs nearly nothing. Diamonds are useless and cost a fortune.

Water keeps us alive yet costs almost nothing; diamonds are useless and costly. The answer, found in 1871: value comes from the next unit, and one more glass of water is worth little when water is plentiful.
2375: The Leader of the Luddites, engraving (1812)
The machines did take their jobs, and made others no one could yet picture.

From 1811, English textile workers smashed the machines that were taking their jobs. Machines did destroy those jobs, and created others no one could yet picture: the bargain every new technology still offers.
2376: No government could print money at will. In a crisis, that cut both ways.
Under the gold standard every banknote could be swapped for a fixed weight of gold, so no government could print money at will. That kept prices steady, and also tied its hands in every crisis.
2377: A wall around local factories, paid for at the checkout by shoppers.
A tariff is a tax on goods from abroad. It shields local factories, but shoppers pay it in higher prices, and when every country raises one, as in the 1930s, world trade shrinks for everyone.
2378: The octopus was cut into 34 pieces, by order of the court.

A company with no rivals can raise prices and stop improving. In 1911 the US Supreme Court split Standard Oil, the octopus in this cartoon, into 34 companies, proving competition can be enforced by law.
2379: Albert Hahn, poster for Philips Arga lamps (1917 to 1918)
Rival bulb makers secretly agreed to make bulbs die sooner, and fined any that lasted.

In 1924 the big light bulb makers, Philips among them, secretly agreed to cap bulb life at 1,000 hours and fined members whose bulbs lasted longer. A cartel turns rivals into partners against the buyer.
2380: John Messina, EPA Documerica, Chalmette, Louisiana (1973)
The factory sells the aluminum. The neighbors breathe the smoke for free.

The factory sells aluminum; the neighbors breathe its smoke for free. Economist Arthur Pigou named this hidden cost in 1920 and proposed the fix: tax the harm so its price finally appears on the bill.
2381: 20% of Italians owned 80% of the land, and the same split keeps turning up.
Vilfredo Pareto noticed that about 20% of Italians owned 80% of the land. The same lopsided split keeps turning up: a few customers bring most sales, a few bugs cause most crashes.
2382: Lady Jane Lindsay, Sealing of the Bank of England Charter, 1694 (1905)
It began as a loan to a king short of money for war.
The Bank of England began in 1694 as a loan to a king short of money for war. It grew into a central bank, the lender of last resort that keeps a panic from turning into a collapse.
2383: Rai stones, Yap, Micronesia (photo Scot Nelson)
One stone of money lay on the seabed, and it still counted.
On Yap, giant stone discs served as money, too heavy to move, so ownership passed when everyone agreed who owned what. One stone lay on the seabed and still counted. Money is a record of trust.
2384: In a slump, one person's cut spending is another's lost wage. Who breaks the spiral?

In a slump, Keynes argued, one person's cut spending is another's lost wage, and the spiral feeds itself. A government that hires and builds can break it; the WPA employed about 8.5 million Americans.
2385: Reception of a Debtor in the Fleet Prison, Cassell's (1865)
Jailed for debt, where they could earn nothing to pay it.

For centuries debtors who could not pay were jailed, where they could earn nothing to pay. Bankruptcy law flipped the logic: clear the slate and let people try again, a safety net that makes risk possible.
2386: Some things are bought precisely because they cost so much.
Some goods are bought precisely because they are expensive: the price is the point, a signal of status. Thorstein Veblen named it conspicuous consumption in 1899, aiming at Gilded Age millionaires.
2387: Ban It and a Black Market Is Born
Prohibition agents in New York (1921), Library of Congress
Drinking didn't stop. It just went underground, and the gangsters took over.

When the US banned alcohol in 1920, drinking did not end; it went underground. Smugglers and gangsters took over the trade, and in 1933 the country repealed the ban it had written into its constitution.
2388: Rowlandson and Pugin, Auction Room, Christie's (1808)
If the winner pays the second-highest bid, honesty becomes the smartest move.
If the winner pays the second-highest bid, the smartest move is simply to bid what the thing is truly worth to you. William Vickrey proved it in 1961, and online ad auctions were built on the idea.
2389: Wenceslaus Hollar, Abraham and Lot Separating (17th century)
One cuts, the other chooses: the oldest fair-division trick, now proved by math.

To split a cake fairly between rivals, one cuts and the other chooses. The cutter makes both halves equal, since either may be left to him. Abraham let Lot choose his land; mathematicians now prove such rules.
2390: Harold Robson, Christmas Truce on the Western Front (1914), IWM
Kindness for kindness, a shot for a shot: how enemies in the trenches learned to live.

Enemies who meet again and again learn to cooperate: answer kindness with kindness, a shot with a shot. Political scientist Robert Axelrod found trench soldiers of 1914 doing exactly that: live and let live.
2391: US Air Force, Minuteman II in its silo (1980)
A weapon built never to be fired, and it only works if they believe you would.

A weapon built never to be fired: deterrence works only if the enemy believes you would fire it. Strategists like Thomas Schelling mapped its strange logic, which many credit with keeping the Cold War cold.
2392: Nobody wants segregation, yet a mild wish for a few similar neighbors produces it.
Schelling showed that if each household wants just a third of its neighbors to be like it, a mixed city still sorts itself into sharp enclaves. Nobody intends the segregation; the system produces it.
2393: Albert Hahn jr., SDAP election poster (1929)
'Not alms but a right!' Old age, no longer a privilege of the rich.
'Not alms but a right!' cries this 1929 Dutch poster. Germany had led in 1889 with the first national old-age insurance, turning retirement from a privilege of the rich into a stage of ordinary life.
2394: One worker who quits is replaced by morning. Twenty thousand cannot be.

One worker who quits is replaced by morning; thousands who stop together cannot be. In 1912 some 20,000 textile workers in Lawrence, Massachusetts walked out, many of them women and children, and won a raise.
2395: A dozen pioneers, no private property, one shared table.
In 1910 a dozen young pioneers by the Sea of Galilee founded Degania on a radical rule: no private property, shared work, a shared table, children raised together. More than 250 kibbutzim followed.
2396: Rent since 1516: 0.88 euros a year, plus three daily prayers.

In 1516 banker Jakob Fugger founded a walled quarter in Augsburg for poor working families. It is the oldest social housing still in use, and the yearly rent is still 0.88 euros, plus three daily prayers.
2397: A voting district twisted so badly that a cartoonist gave it wings.

Draw district lines cleverly and you can win more seats with fewer votes. In 1812 one Massachusetts district was twisted into such a shape that a cartoonist gave it wings and a name: the Gerry-mander.
2398: Why rivals drift to the center: one voter in the middle decides it all.
Line voters up from left to right and the one in the middle decides any two-way race. That is why rival candidates so often drift toward the center: whoever wins the median voter wins.
2399: Each option loses to another, so the group prefers in a circle.

Three voters, three options: one ranks A over B over C, one B over C over A, one C over A over B. Each option loses to another by majority, so the group prefers in a circle. Condorcet found it in 1785.
2400: Elections favor the rich and famous. Chance favors no one.

Athenians filled most offices by lottery, not election, using slotted stone machines like this to pick citizens at random. Their logic still provokes: elections favor the rich and famous, chance favors no one.
2401: The first free Landsgemeinde in Glarus (engraving, about 1900)
No representatives, just a show of hands in the town square, once a year.
Once a year the voters of the Swiss canton of Glarus still gather in the town square and pass laws by a show of hands. No representatives: the people themselves are the parliament, as for centuries.
2402: Guilty or not: the gravest call a state makes, handed to twelve ordinary people.
Trial by jury hands the gravest decision a state can make, guilty or not, to twelve ordinary citizens picked almost at random. Power over liberty stays with the people, not with the crown.
2403: Let truth and falsehood grapple in the open. Truth wins, Milton bet.
In 1644 Milton argued that no one should need a licence to print, because truth wins in open combat with falsehood. Licensing in England lapsed in 1695, and a free press was born.
2404: Gerard ter Borch, The Ratification of the Treaty of Münster (1648)
Two sides swear to peace, and a rule nations still live by is born.
The 1648 Peace of Westphalia, which ended the Thirty Years' War, is credited with the rule nations still live by: each state governs its own territory. Here Spain and the Dutch swear to their peace.
2405: Edouard Armand-Dumaresq, Signing of the First Geneva Convention (Geneva City Hall)
Even war has rules: the wounded, and those who treat them, are spared.

In 1864 twelve states promised that wounded soldiers, and those who treat them, would be spared on every side. The idea that even war has rules grew into today's Geneva Conventions, ratified by every country.
2406: Qiu Ying, Viewing the Pass List (about 1540)
For 1,300 years, officials were chosen by exam, not by birth.
For 1,300 years China chose officials by written exam rather than birth, from 605 until 1905. Crowds gathered to read the pass lists, and Europe later borrowed the idea for its own civil services.
2407: He measured heads, arms and ears to unmask repeat offenders, and gave us the mug shot.

To catch repeat offenders hiding behind new names, Alphonse Bertillon measured each suspect's head, arm and ear and photographed front and side. He gave us the mug shot; fingerprints soon replaced the rest.
2408: An Image That Moved a Nation
Description of a Slave Ship, printed by James Phillips (1789)
Hundreds of people, packed like cargo, drawn to scale. One diagram made it visible.

Abolitionists drew the slave ship Brookes to scale, with hundreds of people packed like cargo, and printed thousands. One diagram made distant cruelty visible and helped end Britain's slave trade in 1807.
2409: Josiah Wedgwood / The Metropolitan Museum of Art
300,000 people protested slavery at the breakfast table: they stopped buying sugar.

In 1791 some 300,000 Britons stopped buying sugar grown by enslaved people, a protest made at the breakfast table. It was the first mass consumer boycott, long before the word 'boycott' was coined in 1880.
2410: Thomas Rowlandson, A Mad Dog in a Coffee House (about 1800)
For a penny, anyone could read the papers and argue politics with strangers.
For a penny, anyone could enter a London coffeehouse, read the papers and argue politics with strangers. Jürgen Habermas saw there the birth of public opinion, a power even kings had to reckon with.
2412: Rank was won not by hoarding blankets, food and copper, but by giving them away.
At a potlatch, chiefs of the Pacific Northwest gained rank not by hoarding but by giving away blankets, food and copper. Canada banned the feast from 1885 to 1951, yet it never really stopped.
2413: About 150 relationships: roughly a village, and perhaps the limit of our brains.

Robin Dunbar argued that a primate's brain size caps its social circle, and for humans the cap is about 150 stable relationships, roughly a village or an army company. Critics dispute the exact figure.
2414: A letter passed hand to hand toward a stranger arrived in about six steps.

In 1967 Stanley Milgram asked people in Nebraska to pass a letter, hand to hand, toward a stranger in Boston. Letters that arrived took about six steps: in a world of billions, we are all a few friends apart.
2415: Laurentius de Voltolina, a lecture in Bologna (14th century)
Students hired their own teachers, and the guild they formed became the university.

In Bologna, traditionally from 1088, students hired their own teachers and banded together to protect themselves. That guild grew into the university, a self-governing community whose business is knowledge.
2416: Levin C. Handy, Buffalo Public Library children's room (1900)
A radical bet: knowledge should not depend on wealth.
A library open to all, free, paid for by taxes: a radical bet that knowledge should not depend on wealth. Boston founded the first large one in 1848, and soon children had rooms of their own.
2417: 'Scholars captured by the dreaded attendance officer', National Library of Ireland (about 1910)
The day the state decided a child's days belong to learning, truant officers included.
