Compulsory schooling meant the state, not parents or employers, decided that a child's days belonged to learning. Prussia led in 1763; by 1918 every US state required it, truant officers included.
2418: United Cigar Stores, US daylight saving poster (1918)
An hour moved from sleepy mornings to busy evenings, first to save coal for a war.
Moving the clocks an hour forward in summer shifts daylight from sleepy mornings to busy evenings. Germany did it first in 1916 to save coal for the war; the United States followed in 1918.
2419: Giovanni Francesco Brunetti, the Lazzaretto of Milan (1631)
Forty days of waiting, long before anyone knew about germs.

Quarantine comes from the Venetian 'quaranta giorni', forty days. Long before anyone knew of germs, port cities isolated ships and travelers to wait out the plague, in walled compounds like this one in Milan.
2420: A haberdasher added up London's death lists and found order in the chaos.

London's weekly death lists were kept to warn of plague. In 1662 a haberdasher, John Graunt, added them up and found order in the chaos: more boys born than girls, and a city kept growing by newcomers.
2421: T. R. Malthus, An Essay on the Principle of Population (6th edition, 1826)
Every gain eaten by more mouths. It held for most of history, then broke.
Malthus warned in 1798 that people multiply faster than food, so every gain is eaten by more mouths. It held for most of history; then farming leapt ahead and families chose to shrink.
2422: A small random sample beat 2.4 million biased replies.
Ask 1,000 people chosen truly at random and you can estimate a whole nation's opinion within about three points. In 1936 Gallup's far smaller sample beat a magazine's 2.4 million biased replies.
2423: About 30% of real numbers start with 1. Fakers rarely know that.
In real-world numbers, from tax returns to river lengths, about 30% start with 1 and under 5% with 9. Invented figures rarely follow this pattern, which is why auditors use it to catch fraud.
2424: Charles Booth, Map of London Poverty (1898 to 1899)
Every street colored from gold to black, and a third of the city was poor.
Charles Booth colored every London street by its residents' means, from gold for the wealthy to black for the poorest. The maps showed that poverty was not a rare vice but about a third of the city.
2425: John Randel Jr., the Commissioners' Plan of 1811 (1821 printing)
Numbered streets drawn over a Manhattan that was still mostly farms and hills.
In 1811 New York laid a grid of numbered streets over a Manhattan that was still mostly farms and hills. Plain and rigid, it made every lot easy to sell and every address easy to find.
2426: Ildefons Cerdà, plan for Barcelona's Eixample (1859)
Cut-off corners so carts could turn, and light and air could reach every home.

Ildefons Cerdà planned Barcelona's extension in 1859 as a grid of identical blocks with cut-off corners, so carts could turn and light and air could reach every home. He also coined the word urbanization.
2427: Ebenezer Howard, To-morrow: A Peaceful Path to Real Reform (1898)
Town is one magnet, country the other. He drew a third.

Town pulls with jobs, the country with fresh air; Howard drew them as two magnets and added a third, the garden city, joining the best of both. His 1898 diagram seeded Letchworth and suburbs worldwide.
2428: Double a city and wages, patents and crime per person all rise. Roads per person shrink.

Double a city and each resident gets roughly 10 to 15% more wages, patents and crime, while the city needs about 10 to 15% less road per person. A city is not a big village but an engine that speeds up with size.
2429: Shang dynasty oracle bones (about 1200 BCE), photo Gary Lee Todd
Questions to the gods, carved beside cracks in bone: ancestors of today's characters.

Shang kings put questions to their gods by cracking ox bones with heat, then carved the question beside the cracks. Those 3,000-year-old signs are ancestors of the characters over a billion people read today.
2430: Writing Was Invented More Than Once
Writing was not invented once. It was invented at least three times.

Writing was not one lucky invention that spread. It arose separately at least three times: in Mesopotamia, in China, and in Mesoamerica, where Maya scribes filled bark books like this with gods and Venus tables.
2431: Letters shaped like the mouth making each sound, learnable in a morning.

In 1443 King Sejong, pitying subjects who could not master thousands of Chinese characters, designed letters that sketch the mouth making each sound. A wise person, it promised, learns them in a morning.
2432: He could not read any language, and built a script for his people alone.
Sequoyah could not read any language, yet he grasped that marks on paper could carry speech and alone built 85 signs for Cherokee syllables. Within a few years thousands of his people were reading.
2433: No spaces between words, until some Irish scribes began leaving gaps.

Ancient Greek and Latin were written with no spaces between words, as in this 4th-century Bible, read aloud to be understood. Irish scribes around 700 began inserting gaps, and silent reading grew easier.
2434: Long dismissed as mere gestures, it has a grammar as rich as any spoken tongue.

Sign languages were long dismissed as mere gestures. In 1960 linguist William Stokoe showed that American Sign Language has its own grammar, as rich as any spoken tongue; Israel has a sign language of its own.
2435: 16 grammar rules, no irregular verbs, and a dream that anyone could share it.
Zamenhof, an eye doctor who grew up among quarreling Poles, Russians, Germans and Jews in Białystok, built a language with 16 grammar rules and no irregular verbs, so anyone could share it.
2436: The top word in almost any language appears twice as often as the second. Cities obey the same curve.

In almost any language the top word appears about twice as often as the second and three times as often as the third. George Zipf found the same curve in city sizes, a hidden order in how we talk and settle.
2437: Otto Schrader, Prehistoric Antiquities of the Aryan Peoples (1890)
Sanskrit, Greek and Latin shared too much to be chance. Somewhere behind them stood a lost mother tongue.

In 1786 William Jones noticed that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin share too much to be chance: they must descend from a lost common ancestor. Linguists later drew the family as a tree, from Hindi to English.
2438: Turbinia at speed, Charles Parsons' test ship
No piston, just steam blowing through blades. It raced past the navy at 34 knots.
Instead of pushing a piston, steam can blow through rows of blades and spin them. In 1897 Parsons' Turbinia raced past the navy at 34 knots; turbines still make most of our electricity.
2439: Reproduction of Volta's pile, Science History Institute
Before this stack of coins and wet cloth, electricity came only in brief sparks.
Stack copper and zinc discs with brine-soaked cloth between them, and a steady current flows. Volta's pile of 1800 was the first battery; before it, electricity came only in brief sparks.
2440: Francis turbine runner, Imatrankoski power plant, Finland
Water spirals in and leaves more than 90 percent of its energy behind.
Water falling through a dam spirals into curved blades and leaves almost all its energy behind, over 90 percent in big turbines. This one made electricity in Finland from 1936 to 1989.
2441: Crossley Brothers gas engine on Otto's design, Technisches Museum Wien
Suck, squeeze, bang, blow: one piston, four jobs, and most cars still keep the rhythm.
Suck, squeeze, bang, blow. Otto's 1876 engine draws in fuel and air, compresses, ignites and exhausts them, one piston doing four jobs in turn. Most car engines keep this rhythm.
2442: First Austrian-built diesel engine, Vienna (1898), Technisches Museum Wien
No spark needed: squeeze air hard enough and it lights the fuel by itself.
Squeeze air hard enough and it grows hot enough to light fuel by itself, with no spark. That high compression makes Diesel's engine thrifty; it moves most of the world's ships and trucks.
2443: Whittle W.1X engine, Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
Gulp, squeeze, burn, hurl. This engine was shipped across the ocean to start America's jet age.
A jet gulps air, squeezes it, burns fuel in it and hurls it out the back, and the plane is pushed forward. A Whittle engine flew in 1941; this one was shipped to America to start its jet age.
2444: 1886 Rover safety bicycle, Carnegie Science Center, Pittsburgh
A chain and a small rear wheel, and riders stopped falling from high up.
The penny-farthing needed a giant front wheel for speed, and riders fell from high up. The Rover geared up a small rear wheel with a chain instead, and cycling opened to almost everyone.
2445: The Archimedes steamer with F. P. Smith's screw propeller, lithograph (1839)
The navy tied a screw ship to a paddle ship. The screw towed it away.
Paddle wheels splash much of their effort into the air; a screw under the stern pushes water all the time. In 1845 the navy tied a screw ship to a paddle ship, and the screw towed it away.
2446: Modern model of Leonardo da Vinci's aerial screw
Leonardo sketched a linen screw to bore into the sky, 450 years too early.
Around 1489 Leonardo sketched a linen screw to bore up into the air. A real rotor is a set of spinning wings, each lifting like a plane's; Sikorsky made one practical in 1939.
2447: The first jump swung so wildly he was sick. The cure was a hole in the top.
In 1797 Garnerin cut loose from a balloon over Paris and drifted down under silk. He swung so wildly he was sick; a hole at the top, letting trapped air out steadily, cured it.
2448: Bushnell's American Turtle, Library of Congress
A one-man barrel crept up on a British warship. The attack failed; the trick never did.
To sink, let water into a tank; to rise, pump it out. In 1776 Bushnell's one-man Turtle crept up on a British warship this way. The attack failed, but every submarine still dives the same way.
2449: Elisha Otis demonstrating his safety elevator, New York (1854)
Hoists existed; trust did not. So he rode up before a crowd and had the rope cut.
Hoists existed; trust did not. In 1854 Otis rode a platform up before a crowd and had the rope cut. Spring-loaded teeth bit the rails and he stopped. Safe elevators made skyscrapers possible.
2450: It began with a vacuum cleaner and two tins. Now it can carry a tank.
Blow air under a rubber skirt and a heavy craft floats on a cushion over water, sand or ice. Cockerell tested it with a vacuum cleaner and two tins; this Navy hovercraft can carry a tank.
2451: Stephenson's Rocket, National Railway Museum, York
Its secret was hidden inside: 25 tubes of fire running through the boiler.
Rocket's secret was inside: 25 tubes carried the fire's heat through the boiler, and spent steam blasted up the chimney to fan it. It won the 1829 Rainhill trials and set the pattern for a century.
2452: A faint signal steering a strong current: the tube that let voices cross a continent.

Put a wire grid between a hot filament and a plate, and a faint signal on the grid steers a strong current. That is amplification. It let voices cross a continent and made radio broadcasting possible.
2453: SCR-270 radar antenna, National Electronics Museum
On 7 December 1941 a radar like this saw the planes coming. The warning was waved off.
Send out a radio pulse and time its echo: the delay gives the distance. On 7 December 1941 a radar like this saw Japanese planes 200 km from Pearl Harbor. The warning was waved off.
2454: Harris & Ewing: Herbert Grove Dorsey and his fathometer (1937), Library of Congress
Sailors once dropped a weighted rope. This sends a sound down twenty times a second.
Sailors once measured depth with a weighted rope. Dorsey's fathometer sends a sound down and times the echo from the bottom, twenty times a second. Echoes like these mapped the ocean floor.
2455: News crossing France in hours, decades before electric wires, one tower copying the next.
A chain of towers in sight of each other, each copying the coded arm positions of the last. From 1794 France sent news this way across hundreds of kilometers in hours, decades before electric wires.
2456: US Army photo of EDVAC, Ballistic Research Laboratory
Before this, a new task meant new wires. After it, just new numbers.
Early computers were reprogrammed by rewiring them. EDVAC's 1945 plan kept the program in memory beside the data, so a new task meant new numbers, not new wires. Nearly every computer since works so.
2457: Kelvin-type tide-predicting machine, National Museum of Nature and Science, Tokyo
Pulleys and one wire, drawing a whole year of tides in a few hours.
A tide is many simple waves added together. Kelvin gave each wave a pulley and ran one wire over them all, and the wire drew a year of tides in hours. Ports used such machines into the 1960s.
2458: Slide one scale along another and you multiply. Engineers did it for 350 years.
Place numbers at distances equal to their logarithms, and sliding one scale along another adds lengths, which multiplies the numbers. Engineers worked this way for 350 years, until calculators.
2459: Blow cold air into molten iron and it gets hotter, not colder.

Blow cold air through molten iron and you might expect it to freeze. Instead it burns out the carbon, and the burning heats the metal. Tons of iron became steel in twenty minutes, and steel got cheap.
2460: Joseph Monier's patent drawing for a reinforced concrete beam (1878)
Each covers the other's weakness, and a French gardener first patented it for flower pots.
Concrete shrugs off crushing but cracks when stretched; steel is the opposite. Bury steel where a beam is pulled and each covers the other's weakness. A French gardener patented it for flower pots.
2461: Woodcut from Vegetius, De re militari (1529), Science History Institute
Turn the screw and water climbs uphill, one pocket at a time. Dutch polders still do it.
Tilt a big screw in a tube, foot in the water, and turn it: each pocket of water climbs a little with every turn and spills out the top. Dutch polders and sewage plants still lift water this way.
2462: Forging press at Bochum steelworks, from Ledebur's metallurgy manual (1895)
A narrow piston, a wide one, and one person squeezes with the weight of many tons.
Push water with a narrow piston and the pressure reaches a wide one undiminished, multiplying the force. Bramah's 1795 press let one person squeeze with the weight of many tons.
2463: HAER drawing of Hayden Bridge, Oregon, Library of Congress
Push a square and it folds. Push a triangle and it holds.
Push a square of sticks and it folds; push a triangle and it holds, since no corner can move unless a side changes length. In a bridge of triangles, every bar is pulled or pushed, never bent.
2464: Diagram of a sextant in use, Pearson Scott Foresman
Two mirrors, the Sun and the horizon in one view, and the ship knows where it is.
Two mirrors let a navigator see the Sun and the horizon in one view and slide them together. The angle between them at noon tells how far north or south the ship is.
2465: Tommaso da Modena, Hugh of Provence, fresco (1352), Treviso
This friar wears the oldest pair of glasses known in any picture.
Curved glass bends light so tired eyes can focus again. Glasses appeared in Italy around 1286; this friar, painted in 1352, wears the oldest pair known in a picture.
2466: Hargreaves' improved spinning jenny, Popular Science Monthly (1891)
One worker, eight spindles, then dozens. Cloth got cheap and hand spinners lost their living.
A spinning wheel makes one thread at a time. Hargreaves' jenny let one worker drive eight spindles, soon dozens. Cloth got cheap, hand spinners lost their living, and the factory age began.
2467: Blanchard copying lathe, Springfield Armory National Historic Site
A broken rifle, fixed from a box of spares: every part now fit every gun.
A wheel traces a model gunstock while a cutter carves the same shape in fresh wood. Such machines made parts so alike that any one fit any rifle, and a broken gun was fixed from a box of spares.
2469: Model of a cotton gin, Eli Whitney Museum
Meant to save labor, it helped US slavery grow from 700,000 people to nearly 4 million.
Wire teeth pull cotton through slots too narrow for the seeds. It was meant to save labor, but cotton boomed, and US slavery grew from about 700,000 people in 1790 to nearly 4 million by 1860.
2470: Singer sewing machine patent model, No. 8,294 (1851), Smithsonian
The trick is a needle with its eye at the point. Shirts took hours instead of days.
A hand sewer pulls the whole thread through each stitch. A machine needle has its eye at the point: it pokes a loop through and a second thread locks it below. Shirts took hours instead of days.
2471: Sholes and Glidden typewriter prototype (about 1870, replica 1938), Wisconsin Historical Museum
It opened offices to women, and its odd QWERTY layout is still under your fingers.
Press a key and a lever swings up to strike a letter through an inked ribbon. Sholes' machine was the first big seller and opened offices to women. Its odd QWERTY layout is still under your fingers.
2472: Gideon Sundback, patent for a separable fastener (1917)
Tiny hooks that cannot grip alone, and a name taken from its sound on rubber boots.
Rows of tiny hooks and hollows that cannot grip alone are pressed together by a slider at just the right angle. Sundback perfected it in 1913; it was named for its sound on rubber boots.
2473: Reinhold Burger, patent drawing for a double-walled vacuum vessel (1907)
Built to hold frozen gases. We fill it with coffee.

Heat travels by touch, moving air and glowing light. Empty space between two glass walls stops the first two; a silver coating sends the glow back. Dewar made it for cold gases; we fill it with coffee.
2474: Steam digester after Denis Papin, Écomusée d'Alsace
His pot softened bones, and to stop it exploding he invented the safety valve.
Water cannot get hotter than its boiling point, but trap the steam and the boiling point rises. Papin's 1679 pot softened bones; to stop it exploding, he invented the safety valve.
2475: McCormick reaper in the field (19th century), Wisconsin Historical Society
A few people now harvested what took a crowd with scythes, and farmhands headed for cities.

A horse pulls, a reel bends the wheat into a moving blade, and the cut stalks fall on a platform. A few people could now harvest what took a crowd with scythes, and farmhands began leaving for cities.
2476: Joseph Glidden's barbed wire patent drawing (1874), National Archives
Two twisted wires, pennies a mile, and the cowboy's open range was gone.
The treeless American plains had no wood for fences. Two twisted wires with barbs between them kept cattle in for pennies a mile, and within decades the cowboy's open range was fenced off.
2477: Yale pin tumbler lock, Ottův slovník naučný
Egyptians did it with wooden pins. Yours is guarding the front door right now.
Small pins of different lengths block the cylinder from turning, and only the right key lifts each one exactly to the gap. Egyptians used wooden pins; Yale's 1860s design guards most front doors.
2478: Model of Marc Brunel's tunneling shield, Brunel Museum, London
Under the river, 36 cells of miners, each digging a little before the iron crept on.

Under a river, soft mud would bury the diggers. Brunel's iron shield held up the face in 36 cells, each miner digging a little before the frame crept on. The first tunnel under a river opened in 1843.
2479: NBS cesium beam frequency standard, National Institute of Standards and Technology
Count 9,192,631,770 waves and one second has passed. Officially.
Every cesium atom absorbs microwaves at exactly the same frequency. Count 9,192,631,770 of those waves and one second has passed: since 1967 that is the official definition of the second.
2480: The first dialysis machine at Rambam Hospital, Haifa (1965)
The first one was built in wartime Holland from sausage casing.
Blood flows past a thin membrane with clean fluid beyond it; waste seeps across while blood cells stay. Kolff built the first in wartime Holland from sausage casing; this one reached Haifa in 1965.
2481: Warren K. Leffler: a doctor holding a Medtronic pacemaker (1961), Library of Congress
The first patient to get one lived another 43 years.
A heart beats to tiny electrical pulses; when its own rhythm fails, a device can send them instead. The first was implanted in Sweden in 1958, and its patient lived another 43 years.
2482: Westinghouse microwave oven (1956), National Electronics Museum
It was discovered when a radar tube melted the candy bar in an engineer's pocket.
Microwaves make water molecules flip back and forth billions of times a second, and that jostling is heat. Percy Spencer found out in 1945 when a radar tube melted the candy bar in his pocket.
2483: Replica of Chester Carlson's original copier, Battelle Memorial Institute (HAER)
The first copy ever made read: '10.-22.-38 ASTORIA'.

Charge a plate with static and shine a page on it: light wipes the charge wherever the paper was white, and powder sticks only to the letters. Carlson's first copy, in 1938, read '10.-22.-38 ASTORIA'.
2484: Tape could be cut and spliced, and recording became editing.
Sound becomes current, current a magnet, and the magnet lines up iron grains on moving tape; play it past a coil and the sound returns. Tape could be cut and spliced: recording became editing.
2485: Foucault's gyroscope, from Arago's Astronomie populaire
However its frame turns, the spinning wheel keeps pointing the same way in space.
A fast-spinning wheel keeps its axis pointing the same way in space, however its frame turns. Foucault named it in 1852; gyroscopes later steered ships, planes and rockets with no outside guide.
2486: Brewster F2A fighter in NACA's Full-Scale Tunnel, Langley (1938)
Fixing rivets and gaps made this fighter about ten percent faster.
Rather than fly a plane through air, blow air past a plane standing still; the physics is the same. Tested here in 1938, this fighter got about ten percent faster after fixing rivets and gaps.
2487: Edwin Drake (right) at his well, Titusville, Pennsylvania (retouched photo, about 1890), Library of Congress
Oil was once skimmed from seeps. Drake drilled 21 meters down, and an age began.
Oil had long been skimmed from seeps. In 1859 Drake drove a pipe through loose ground and drilled 21 meters down to it. First for lamps, soon for engines: the age of oil began.
2488: Experimental Breeder Reactor I crew, Idaho (1951), US Department of Energy
The first electricity from the atom lit exactly four light bulbs in the Idaho desert.
Splitting uranium atoms makes heat, heat makes steam, and steam turns a generator. On 20 December 1951 a reactor in the Idaho desert lit four bulbs this way, the first electricity from the atom.
2489: Researcher examining solar cells for Vanguard I, US Army CECOM
Light in, current out, and not a single moving part.
Light knocks electrons loose in silicon, and a built-in field pushes them out as current, with no moving parts. Bell Labs made the first practical cell in 1954; Vanguard I ran on sunlight in 1958.
2490: James Nasmyth, Steam Hammer in Full Work, from his autobiography (1883)
The same hammer that forged a ship's shaft could gently crack an egg in a wine glass.
Steam lifts a huge iron block and drops or drives it down with whatever force the operator chooses. Nasmyth liked to show it could gently crack an egg in a wine glass, then forge a ship's shaft.
2491: Strowger switches, Telephone Museum, Waltham, Massachusetts
An undertaker reportedly built it because an operator kept sending his calls to a rival.
Each digit dialed sent a burst of clicks, each stepping a switch one notch until it found the right line. Strowger, an undertaker, reportedly built it because an operator sent his calls to a rival.
2492: Pneumatic mail tube terminal, General Post Office, New York, postcard (1926)
For 56 years New York shot its mail through tubes under the streets, faster than any truck.
Put letters in a canister, seal it in a tube, and let air pressure do the rest. From 1897 to 1953 New York shot mail between post offices through tubes under its streets, faster than any truck.
2493: Western Electric telephone with a Bakelite case (1928), Museum für Angewandte Kunst Köln
A material that heat could never melt again: the shell of countless phones.

Baekeland cooked phenol and formaldehyde under pressure and got a hard material that heat could never melt again. Bakelite, of 1907, was the first fully synthetic plastic, the shell of countless phones.
2494: Nine horses drawing a seed drill, South Australia (about 1925), State Government photographer
Seed thrown by hand lands too thick, too thin, or on top for the birds.
Seed thrown by hand lands too thick, too thin, or on top for the birds. A drill cuts a furrow, drops seeds evenly spaced and covers them. Jethro Tull's 1701 design got more grain from the same seed.
2495: Prisms of the Bodie Island Lighthouse lens, National Park Service
528 pieces of glass, bending one light into a beam that reaches 30 km out to sea.

A lens big enough for a lighthouse would be too thick and heavy. Fresnel cut it into rings of prisms that bend light into one flat beam. This one has 528 pieces of glass and shines about 30 km to sea.
2496: SSG James I. Hatton: a crane lifts a Sea-Land container at Da Nang (1967), National Archives
Steel boxes cranes could lift whole, and loading fell from $5.86 a ton to 16 cents.
Ships once sat in port for days while sacks and crates were loaded by hand. In 1956 McLean shipped 58 steel boxes cranes could lift whole. Loading cost fell from $5.86 a ton to 16 cents.
2497: Trap jet water closet principle, Popular Science Monthly (1887)
A little water trapped in a bend is all that keeps the sewer out of your house.
The bend under every sink and toilet always holds a little water, and that plug keeps sewer gas out of the house. Alexander Cummings patented the S-bend in 1775, and indoor plumbing became bearable.
2498: Project Whirlwind core memory, MIT, Charles River Museum of Industry
Each tiny ring is one bit, and it remembers even with the power off.
Each tiny magnetic ring holds one bit: magnetized one way it is 1, the other way 0, and it remembers with the power off. From 1953, computers remembered with woven rings like these for 20 years.
2499: The Governor: Machines That Correct Themselves
Brotherhood centrifugal governor, from Rankin Kennedy, Modern Engines (1905)
Spin too fast and the balls fly out, closing the steam. Every thermostat thinks this way.
Two weighted balls spin with the engine. Too fast, they fly out and close the steam valve; too slow, they drop and open it. Watt's 1788 governor is pure feedback, the idea behind every thermostat.
2500: Cartoon of a doctor with a Laennec stethoscope (1906)
Too awkward to press his ear to her chest, he rolled up a sheet of paper instead.
In 1816 Laennec felt awkward pressing his ear to a young woman's chest, so he rolled paper into a tube. Her heart sounded louder and clearer than ever, and doctors began listening inside the body.
2501: Rockets used to be thrown away. By August 2026, one Falcon 9 booster had flown 37 times.
Rockets used to be thrown away after one flight. These two Falcon Heavy boosters landed side by side in 2018, and by August 2026 one Falcon 9 booster had flown 37 times, making launches far cheaper.
2502: Fusion Ignition: Inside the NIF Chamber
For the first time, a fuel pellet gave back more energy than the lasers put in.
In 2022 lasers in this chamber made a fuel pellet release more energy than they put in, a first; by 2025 the gain passed 4. Fusion could bring clean, abundant power, but plants are years off.
2503: We hit an asteroid on purpose, and its orbit shrank by 32 minutes.
In 2022 NASA's DART probe hit this 160-meter asteroid on purpose and cut its orbit by 32 minutes, the first proof we can nudge a space rock. Europe's Hera is due to arrive in November 2026.
2504: A short-lived instruction: cells read it, build one harmless protein, and learn.

An mRNA vaccine is a short-lived instruction: cells read it, build one harmless protein and train immunity. After billions of COVID doses, a personal mRNA melanoma vaccine met its phase 3 goals in 2026.
2505: NASA / Bill Stafford, James Blair, Regan Geeseman
Built to work where people cannot, and still few, slow and closely watched.
NASA built Valkyrie in 2013 to work where people cannot. Humanoid robots are now starting trial jobs in factories and warehouses, but in late 2026 they are still few, slow and closely supervised.
2506: Artemis II: Back Around the Moon
Four astronauts around the Moon, the first crew to go there since 1972.
On 1 April 2026 this rocket sent four astronauts around the Moon, the first crew to go there since 1972. They splashed down on 10 April, and NASA now aims to land people in early 2028.
2507: Landing on a Ship at Sea
A rocket fell back from space and stood upright on a barge. Now it is no longer news.
In April 2016 a rocket stage fell back from space and stood upright on a robotic barge, a first. By April 2026 Falcon boosters had landed 600 times, and a landing is no longer news.
2508: Crew Dragon: A Taxi to Orbit
NASA once flew its own spaceships. Now it buys seats.
NASA once flew its own spaceships; since 2020 it buys seats from a company. By early 2026 Crew Dragon had flown 21 crewed missions, and it is still the only American craft carrying astronauts.
2509: 23 internet satellites in one streak, and astronomers worried about the trails.
This streak carried 23 internet satellites. By October 2026 about 11,000 Starlinks were working in orbit, serving over 12 million users, while astronomers worry about the trails they leave.
2510: Too big for any rocket, so the mirror folded up and opened only in space.
A mirror 6.5 meters wide was too big for any rocket, so it was built from 18 gold-coated segments that folded up and opened in space. Webb has worked since 2022 and has fuel for about 20 years.
2511: A Sunshade the Size of a Tennis Court
Five layers thinner than a hair: one side near 110 C, the other near minus 233.
Five layers of film, each thinner than a hair, keep the Sun's heat off Webb. One side can reach about 110 C while the telescope stays near minus 233 C, cold enough to see faint infrared light.
2512: A gold box that made oxygen on Mars: about what a small dog breathes in 10 hours.
This gold box rode to Mars and turned its carbon dioxide air into oxygen, 122 grams over 16 runs, about what a small dog breathes in 10 hours. A big version could fuel rockets home.
2513: Mars Samples Waiting for a Ride
Ten sealed tubes of Mars rock, left on the ground. The ride home was cancelled.
In 2023 Perseverance left ten sealed rock tubes on the ground as a backup cache. The mission meant to bring them home was cancelled in its current form in 2026, so for now they wait on Mars.
2514: Asteroid dust holding 14 of the 20 amino acids life uses, made in space.
On 24 September 2023 this capsule fell into the Utah desert carrying 121.6 grams of asteroid Bennu. Inside, scientists found 14 of the 20 amino acids life uses, made in space, not on Earth.
2515: Parker Solar Probe: Touching the Sun
NASA / Johns Hopkins APL / Ed Whitman
1,400 C on the front of this shield. Behind it, the instruments stay cool.
Behind this heat shield, the fastest object humans have built dives to 6.2 million km from the Sun's surface at about 687,000 km/h. The shield faces some 1,400 C while the instruments stay cool.
2516: An 8.5 meter arm, reaching for a salty ocean hidden under ice.
This 8.5 meter boom will sense the salty ocean under Europa's ice. Launched in 2024, the probe passes Earth in December 2026 and reaches Jupiter in 2030 to ask if that ocean could host life.
2517: A gentle shove that never stops, all the way to a metal-rich asteroid.
Psyche pushes itself with thrusters that fire charged xenon, a gentle shove that never stops. It swung past Mars in May 2026 and should reach a metal-rich asteroid in 2029.
2518: Video from deep space at 267 megabits a second, sent by laser instead of radio.
This telescope aimed a laser at a probe hundreds of millions of km away. The test sent data from 494 million km and video at 267 megabits a second, at least ten times faster than radio of that size.
2519: Sunlight pushes on everything it touches. Could it carry a ship with no fuel?
Sunlight pushes on everything it touches, very gently. NASA unfurled this 80 square meter sail in orbit in 2024; a boom bent and it tumbled, but sails like it could one day travel without fuel.
2520: A heat shield wider than the rocket it rides in. The trick: inflate it.
A heat shield wider than any rocket can still fit inside one if it inflates. In November 2022 this 6 meter shield came back from orbit intact, a way to land heavy cargo, or people, on Mars.
2521: A Nuclear Reactor for the Moon
Lunar night lasts two weeks, and solar panels go dark the whole time.
Solar panels go dark for two weeks of lunar night. This small reactor passed a full-power test in 2018, and in 2026 NASA and the Energy Department agreed to aim for a reactor on the Moon by 2030.
2522: An Engine That Rides an Explosion
An engine that rides a detonation racing around a ring thousands of times a second.
Inside this engine a detonation wave races around a ring thousands of times a second, squeezing more push from less fuel. In 2023 a 3D-printed one fired for 251 seconds; it is still a test design.
2523: A long needle nose, shaped to turn a sonic boom into a soft thump.
Its long needle nose is shaped to turn a sonic boom into a soft thump. The X-59 first flew in October 2025 and passed Mach 1 in 2026; next it flies over towns to ask people what they hear.
2524: Blue Ghost: A Company Lands on the Moon
Landing on the Moon was once a superpower feat. This time a company did it.
Landing on the Moon was once a superpower feat. In March 2025 this private lander, Firefly's Blue Ghost, touched down upright and ran NASA experiments for a full lunar day, about 14 Earth days.
2525: Blown up like a balloon for a two-year test, and still in use ten years later.
This room was launched folded and blown up like a balloon at the space station in 2016. Meant for a two-year test, it was still in use in 2026, a hint of how big, light homes in space could be built.
2526: X-62 VISTA: An AI at the Controls
Software against a human pilot in a mock dogfight, with safety pilots aboard.
In 2023 software flew this modified F-16 in a mock dogfight against a human pilot, with safety pilots aboard. Testing went on through 2026; no AI flies a combat jet on its own yet.
2527: Staff Sgt. Jake Jacobsen / U.S. Air Force
No cockpit. It flies beside a pilot and takes the riskiest jobs.
This jet has no cockpit: it is meant to fly beside a piloted fighter and take the riskiest jobs. It first flew in August 2025, and in June 2026 the Air Force picked it for production.
2528: A weapon whose every shot costs about as much as its electricity.

In 2014 this became the first laser weapon deployed on a warship, and a shot costs about as much as its electricity. In 2025 a newer Navy laser downed four drones at sea, but only one ship carries it.
2529: Maps and night vision over a soldier's eyes. After $1.8 billion, back to the drawing board.
These goggles lay maps, targets and night vision over what a soldier sees. After about $1.8 billion, the Army decided in 2026 to shelve some 10,000 sets and start again with a new design.
2531: The first salad grown in orbit: red romaine under pink lights.
In August 2015 astronauts ate the first salad grown in orbit, red romaine raised under pink LEDs. A trip to Mars would last years, and fresh food grown on board could keep crews healthy.
2532: The First Flower Grown in Space
It nearly died of mold, until an astronaut nursed it back to bloom.
This zinnia nearly died of mold before astronaut Scott Kelly nursed it back to bloom in January 2016. Flowers are harder to grow than lettuce, a step toward growing tomatoes and peppers in orbit.
2533: Three flying cubes on tiny fans, practicing for outposts with no one aboard.
Since 2019 three cube-shaped robots have flown around the space station on small fans, filming and taking inventory. They let ground teams test machines that could tend outposts with no crew aboard.
2534: NISAR: Radar That Feels the Ground Move
From orbit it can feel the ground shift by a centimeter, before it slides or shakes.
Built by NASA and India, NISAR launched in 2025 and scans nearly all of Earth's land and ice every 12 days. Its radar can spot ground shifting by a centimeter, a warning before landslides and quakes.
2535: PACE: Reading the Colors of the Sea
Over 200 colors of the sea, read from orbit to tell tiny plants apart.
This instrument splits sunlight bouncing off the ocean into more than 200 colors. Since 2024 it has told apart kinds of plankton from orbit, the tiny plants that make about half of Earth's oxygen.
2536: CubeSats: Satellites the Size of a Shoebox
A satellite once cost as much as a building. Now students build them shoebox-sized.
A satellite once cost as much as a building. CubeSats are built from 10 cm cubes; thousands have flown since 2003, many built by students, small nations and start-ups on tiny budgets.
2537: Sea Hunter: A Ship With No Crew
San Diego to Hawaii and back, almost entirely with nobody aboard.
This 40 meter trimaran can sail for weeks with nobody aboard. In 2019 it went from San Diego to Hawaii and back almost entirely on its own, a glimpse of fleets where robots stand the long watches.
2538: Gliders That Dive Into Hurricane Season
No propeller: it sinks and rises for months, tasting the warm water that feeds hurricanes.
This robot has no propeller; it sinks and rises by changing buoyancy, gliding for months down to 1,000 meters to measure the warm water that feeds hurricanes and sharpen forecasts.
2539: The surgeon sits a few meters away, steering thin arms through small cuts.

The surgeon sits at a console a few meters away and steers these thin arms through small cuts. In 2025 such robots helped in more than 3.1 million operations, though they do not decide anything alone.
2540: Living cells, printed layer by layer, so drugs can be tested on tissue instead of animals.
This printer lays down living cells layer by layer to build small pieces of tissue. Labs already test drugs on such tissue instead of animals; printed organs for transplant are still many years off.
2541: Release millions of sterile males, and the next generation simply never hatches.
Release millions of sterile male flies and their mates lay no eggs. The trick once drove the flesh-eating screwworm out of North America; in 2026 the US opened a Texas base to do it again.
2542: A Sensor That Reads Blood Sugar All Day
A filament as thin as a hair, reporting your blood sugar to your phone all day.
A hair-thin filament under the skin sends glucose readings to a phone every few minutes. Since 2024 such sensors are sold in the US without prescription, even to people without diabetes.
2543: Less a doughnut, more a cored apple, and that shape may shrink future power plants.
This fusion machine is shaped more like a cored apple than a doughnut, which may let future power plants be smaller. It last ran in 2016; after long repairs it is expected to restart in 2027.
2544: Solar panels floating on a lake left by mining sand, the very stuff solar cells are made of.
On this Dutch lake the panels float on water left by sand mining, the very sand solar cells are made from. Water keeps panels cooler and more efficient, and saves farmland for crops.
2545: U.S. Department of Energy / Merrill Smith
The sheep trim the grass under the panels, then nap in their shade.
These sheep trim the grass under a Hawaiian solar farm and rest in its shade. Sharing land between power and farming, called agrivoltaics, is spreading; some crops grow better in partial shade.
2546: Five turbines off a small island, and America's first offshore wind farm.
Block Island's five turbines became America's first offshore wind farm in 2016. Sea winds blow steadier than land winds; in 2026 two large farms reached New England's grid after court fights.
2547: Batteries the Size of a Town
Each box holds the midday sun until the evening, when everyone switches on.
Each container here is packed with lithium batteries that store midday solar power for the evening peak. By mid-2026 the US had about 50 gigawatts of grid batteries, up from almost none in 2015.
2548: A Nuclear Fuel Grain That Holds Its Own
Smaller than a poppy seed, each grain wears its own ceramic armor against 1,600 C.
Each grain of this fuel, smaller than a poppy seed, wraps uranium in its own ceramic shells that survive about 1,600 C. A full core of it reached Idaho in 2025 for a portable military reactor.
2549: The Machine That Redefined the Kilogram
For 130 years a kilogram was a metal cylinder in a vault. Now it is a law of nature.
For 130 years a kilogram was a metal cylinder locked in a vault near Paris. Balances like this tied it to a constant of nature, and since 2019 a kilogram means the same thing everywhere, forever.
2550: Two atoms floating above a gold chip, each one a quantum bit.
Two atoms float above this gold chip, held by electric fields and used as quantum bits. In 2026 the best such machines hold about 100 qubits; breaking codes would need thousands of error-free ones.
2551: Starship: The Biggest Rocket Ever Flown
U.S. Department of Defense / Alexander Kubitza
A 52 meter spaceship meant to land and fly again within hours.
These black tiles shield a 52 meter spaceship meant to land and fly again within hours. On 28 September 2026 Starship reached orbit for the first time; catching it whole is the next test.
2552: Up and Back in One Picture
One long exposure, a whole round trip: up to space, and back down beside the pad.
A long exposure caught a round trip: the rocket's climb, then its first stage falling back to land near the pad minutes later. In 2016 this was startling; by 2026 it happens several times a week.
2553: New Glenn: A Second Reusable Giant
Only its second try, and the booster landed on a ship at sea.
On this November 2025 flight Blue Origin's booster landed on a ship at sea, only its second try. It flew again in April 2026, so a second company can now reuse orbital boosters.
2554: A Solar Panel That Rolls Out Like a Carpet
A solar panel that rolls out in orbit like a tape measure.
This solar array was tested in 2017, rolled up like a tape measure and unrolled in orbit. Since 2021 bigger versions have covered the station's aging wings, adding 20 to 30 percent more power.
2555: It came home with chunks missing from its heat shield. Then a crew had to ride it.
On its uncrewed 2022 flight this capsule came home with chunks missing from its heat shield. NASA traced it to trapped gas, changed the return path, and the Artemis II crew landed safely in 2026.
2556: Wind and sun only, and it sailed straight through the eye of a hurricane.
Powered only by wind and sun, these drones sail for months. In 2024 one rode through the eye of Hurricane Debby, measuring waves over 5 meters, and in 2026 ten joined NOAA's hurricane fleet.
2557: 908 days in orbit, doing what exactly? Then it landed on a runway.
This robot space plane spent 908 days in orbit before landing on a runway in 2022. Its eighth mission, launched in 2025, tests laser links and a quantum sensor that navigates without GPS.
2558: Dream Chaser: A Cargo Plane for Orbit
Built to glide home from orbit and land on a runway like a jet. It is still waiting to go.
This small space plane is built to glide home and land on a runway like a jet. Its first orbital flight, now planned without docking at the station, slipped from 2021 to late 2026 at the earliest.
2559: NEO Surveyor: Watching for Dangerous Asteroids
Dark asteroids are hard to see, but they glow in heat.
Dark asteroids are hard to see but glow in heat. This infrared telescope, due to launch by 2028, should find most space rocks big enough to wipe out a city, years before any could hit.
2560: A Weather Satellite That Also Watches the Sun
From 36,000 km up it maps lightning, and keeps one eye on the Sun.
Launched in 2024, this satellite now watches the Americas every few minutes from 36,000 km up, mapping lightning and storms. It also carries a camera that spots solar storms heading for Earth.
2561: A Rover That Thinks for Itself
Mars is up to 22 minutes away by radio, so the rover has to choose its own path.
Radio takes up to 22 minutes to reach Mars, too slow to steer by joystick. In March 2026 this NASA prototype crossed a California desert choosing its own path, practice for robots on other worlds.
2562: A Robot That Digs the Moon
Two drums spinning opposite ways, so it can dig in low gravity without pushing itself off.
Its two drums spin in opposite directions, so it can dig in low gravity without pushing itself away. Moon dirt holds oxygen and maybe water; mining it could save hauling every kilogram from Earth.
2563: DNA read in space for the first time, on a machine the size of a phone.
In 2016 Kate Rubins read DNA in space for the first time, on a sequencer the size of a phone. Such pocket devices now identify germs in field clinics and outbreaks in hours instead of weeks.
2565: It walks into chemical leaks so that people do not have to.
This four-legged robot sniffs for chemical and radiation leaks so people need not walk into danger. Legged robots now inspect plants, bases and tunnels, though a human still steers most missions.
2566: Spinning lasers on the roof redraw the street in 3D many times a second.
Spinning lasers and cameras on the roof let this test car build a 3D map of the street many times a second. By March 2026 robotaxis gave 500,000 paid rides a week in ten US cities.
2567: The Blue Glow of a Test Reactor
That blue glow is particles outrunning light, in water.
The blue light is Cherenkov radiation, from particles outrunning light in water. This Idaho reactor tests new fuels, and in 2026 four new reactor designs nearby went critical for the first time.
2568: Five times the speed of sound, and still steering, which makes it very hard to stop.
Missiles in these tubes glide at over five times the speed of sound while steering, which makes them very hard to stop. America's first battery was activated in December 2025, after Russia and China.
2569: On the space station, yesterday's coffee becomes tomorrow's coffee.
On the space station yesterday's coffee becomes tomorrow's coffee. In 2023 its machines began recovering 98 percent of all water, including sweat and urine, the level a trip to Mars would need.
2570: Lucy: Visiting Fossils of the Solar System
Off to asteroids that have barely changed in 4.5 billion years.
Lucy is the first probe sent to the Trojans, asteroids sharing Jupiter's orbit that have barely changed in 4.5 billion years. It passed a practice asteroid in 2025 and meets its first Trojan in 2027.
2572: A Year on Mars in Houston
Four volunteers, sealed in a printed Mars for a year, with delays in every call home.

Behind this red sand stands a 3D-printed habitat where four volunteers lived sealed in for a year, with delays in their calls home. The second crew went in on 19 October 2025 and was set to leave on 31 October 2026.
2573: Boards glued crosswise, strong enough for a 25-floor tower that stores carbon.
Glue layers of boards crosswise and you get panels strong enough for towers. This timber stores carbon instead of emitting it as concrete does; the tallest wooden tower, in Milwaukee, has 25 floors.
2574: Perovskite: A Solar Cell You Could Print
A solar cell you could print like ink. The catch: it still wears out too fast.
This thin film can be printed like ink, far cheaper than silicon. Stacked on silicon, lab cells passed 34 percent efficiency, but in 2026 few panels are sold because they still wear out too fast.
2575: Blue Moon: A Lander Waiting for the Moon
Eight meters tall, tested in a vacuum chamber, and waiting for the lunar south pole.
Blue Origin's first Moon lander, eight meters tall, finished space-like testing in a NASA vacuum chamber in 2026. It is meant to deliver cargo to the lunar south pole; a crewed version would follow.
2576: Gateway: A Moon Station on Pause
Parts of this Moon station were already built. Then it was paused.
Gateway was meant to be a small station circling the Moon, a stopover for astronauts on their way down. Parts of it were already built, but in 2026 NASA paused it to fund a base on the lunar surface.
2577: Every chatbot answer runs on a building like this.
Every chatbot answer runs on buildings like this, packed with chips and cooling towers. US data centers used 4.4 percent of the nation's power in 2023, and could need up to 12 percent by 2028.
2578: A Robot Farmhand That Never Sleeps
The cows push their feed out of reach. The robot pushes it back, all night long.
Cows push their feed out of reach; this orange robot circles the barn around the clock and pushes it back. On farms short of workers, robots now feed, milk and clean, and cows keep their own hours.
2579: A Farm in a Shipping Container
A farm in a box. The big ones burned billions; the small ones carry on.
Inside, greens grow in stacked racks under LEDs, using a fraction of the water of a field. Big vertical farms burned billions and several failed by 2025; small ones near cities carry on.
2580: A Bus That Exhales Only Water
Only water drips out. Clean, but only if the hydrogen is.
This Tokyo bus makes electricity from hydrogen and oxygen, and only water drips from it. The catch: almost all hydrogen today is made from natural gas, so it is clean only if the hydrogen is.
2581: A plane flying behind airliners, sniffing the exhaust of fuel made from fat and waste.
In 2023 NASA's DC-8 flew behind airliners burning fuel made from fats and waste, sampling their exhaust. Such fuel cuts soot and lifecycle carbon, yet in 2025 it was only 0.6 percent of all jet fuel.
2582: Drones That Start Fires to Stop Fires
A drone that starts fires, to starve the next wildfire.
This drone drops small spheres that ignite on the ground, setting controlled burns that clear the brush wildfires feed on. It lets crews burn steep or smoky land without risking a pilot.
2583: ALIA: An Electric Plane Takes Passengers
A battery plane that flew all the way to Washington.
This battery plane flew to Washington in 2023 with Air Force help. On 20 October 2026 its vertical-lift sister made the first FAA-approved flight with potential customers; full approval is pending.
2584: Picking up rocks underwater, practicing for the Moon.
Astronaut Loral O'Hara practices picking up rocks underwater in the suit built for the next Moon landing. It must resist sharp dust and deep cold, and auditors warned in 2026 that time is tight.
2585: NASA / Johns Hopkins APL / Ed Whitman
A car-sized drone with eight rotors, built for the thick air of a moon of Saturn.
This frame will become an eight-rotor drone the size of a car, to fly through the thick air of Saturn's moon Titan. Hanging from bungees for shake tests in 2026, it is due to launch in July 2028.
2586: The First Metal Printer in Space
A laser melted steel wire into the first metal part ever made in space.
In August 2024 this printer melted steel wire with a laser and built the first metal part ever made in space. Crews far from Earth could one day print spare parts instead of waiting months for them.
2587: A Clock That Would Not Lose a Second
A clock that would drift less than a second in 40 billion years.
This tangle of lenses guides lasers that count the ticks of strontium atoms. Such clocks would drift less than a second in 40 billion years, and could redefine the second around 2030.
2588: ITER: The Giant Fusion Machine, Delayed
35 nations building one fusion machine, and the start keeps slipping.
These superconducting strands carry current for the central magnet of ITER, a fusion reactor 35 nations are building in France. In 2024 its start slipped to 2034, with fusion fuel not before 2039.
2589: Satellites worth hundreds of millions die when the fuel runs out. This arm wants to save them.
Satellites worth hundreds of millions die when fuel runs out. This 3 meter robotic arm launched in July 2026 on a servicer that will bolt life-extension packs onto aging satellites 36,000 km up.
2590: Waves carry huge, steady energy. They also smash the machines sent to catch it.
Waves carry huge, steady energy, but they also smash machines. This Navy site in Hawaii tests wave converters, and Oregon opened a grid-linked test berth in August 2026; no big wave farm runs yet.
2591: Coral hung on underwater trees, grown like saplings, then planted back on the reef.
Divers hang coral fragments on underwater trees, grow them, then replant reefs. The 2023 marine heatwave killed many Florida nursery corals, so teams are now breeding strains that survive heat.
2592: Current with zero resistance. The price: keeping it as cold as liquid nitrogen.

Cooled with liquid nitrogen, the tapes around this cable carry current with zero resistance, several times more than copper of the same size. Short city links use them; costly cooling keeps them rare.
2593: Algae Fuel: A Promise That Faded
Oil giants once hailed it as the fuel of the future. The last one quietly quit.
Algae grow fast on sunlight and carbon dioxide, and oil giants once hailed them as the fuel of the future. By 2023 the last, ExxonMobil, had quietly quit; algae now serve mostly food and chemicals.
2594: Ten thousand mirrors heat salt above 500 C, and the salt makes power after dark.
Ten thousand mirrors aim sunlight at a tower to heat salt above 500 C, and the hot salt makes power after dark. The idea works, but this Nevada plant struggled and filed for bankruptcy again in 2026.
2595: Vogtle: America's First New Reactors in Decades
No carbon at all, but seven years late and over 30 billion dollars.
Inspectors tour a reactor that started in 2023, its twin in 2024, the first US reactors built from scratch in decades. They emit no carbon, but came seven years late and cost over 30 billion dollars.
2596: Moon rock is nearly half oxygen. You just have to melt it at 1,600 C to breathe.
Moon rock is nearly half oxygen by weight, locked in minerals. This rig melts fake lunar soil at over 1,600 C and pulls the oxygen out with electricity, a way to make air and rocket fuel on the Moon.
2597: 26 million amps for a split second, into a target smaller than a spool of thread.
For a split second this machine drives about 26 million amps into a target smaller than a thread spool, throwing off these arcs. It tests a path to fusion and how matter behaves inside giant planets.
2598: One in Four New Cars Is Electric
A quarter of all new cars, and they rarely need a petrol station.
Plugging in has become ordinary. More than 20 million electric cars were sold in 2025, a quarter of all new cars worldwide, most of them made in China, and they rarely need a petrol station.
2599: A Balloon That Circles the World
A balloon as big as a stadium, circling the globe in 46 days.
This sealed balloon, as big as a stadium when inflated, holds its shape day and night 33 km up. In 2016 it circled the globe in 46 days, a cheap way to lift telescopes above most of the atmosphere.
2600: Atlas: From Lab Robot to Factory Worker
It began as a heavy robot for a rescue contest. Next stop: the car assembly line.
Atlas began in 2013 as a heavy hydraulic robot for a DARPA rescue contest. An electric version went into production in January 2026, and Hyundai plans to put it on car assembly lines from 2028.
2601: Nine misses, then a plane reeled in a jet drone on a cable, like a fish on a line.
A cargo plane reels in a jet-powered drone on a cable, like a fish on a line. After nine misses, DARPA's crew caught one in October 2021, a step toward reusable drone swarms launched from planes.
2602: A Robot Tanker for Fighter Jets
No pilot aboard, and it refueled a fighter in flight.

In 2021 this pilotless tanker refueled a fighter in flight for the first time, then rolled around a carrier deck in tests. Production began in 2026; the Navy expects it in service no earlier than 2029.
2603: Flying a Drone Through Its Eyes
Cheap drones like this one, by many estimates, now cause most front-line casualties.
Goggles show this Marine what his small racing drone sees as he steers it. Cheap drones like this reshaped the war in Ukraine, where by many estimates they cause most front-line casualties.
2604: A missile can cost far more than the cheap drone it hits. So: cheap hunters.
This soldier readies a small interceptor that flies into enemy drones to knock them down. A missile can cost far more than the cheap drone it hits, so armies are racing to build cheap defenders.
2605: About 4,400 nautical miles to California, almost entirely without human hands.
This former supply boat now sails itself across oceans for the Navy's robot ship tests. In 2021 it went about 4,400 nautical miles to California almost entirely without human control.
2606: Starliner: When a New Spaceship Stumbles
An eight-day test that turned into nine months, and a ride home in a rival's ship.
Boeing's capsule brought two astronauts to the station in June 2024 for an eight-day test. Thruster trouble kept it from flying them home; they returned on a SpaceX Dragon nine months later.
2607: A Greenhouse That Runs Itself in Orbit
180 sensors gardening in orbit, because the crew has no time to.
This sealed chamber on the space station waters, lights and monitors its lettuce with little help from the crew, using some 180 sensors, practice for long missions where nobody has time to garden.
2608: X-57: The Electric Plane That Never Flew
An electric plane that never flew, and still taught everyone who came after.
NASA gave this small plane electric motors to show quiet, efficient flight. Safety problems and missing parts ended it in 2023 before it flew, but builders of electric planes use its lessons.
2609: Testing the Wings of Air Taxis
Many propellers on one wing, and the swirling air between them can get loud.
Air taxis spin many propellers along their wings, and the swirling air can make them loud or unstable. In 2025 NASA tested this 2 meter wing in a wind tunnel to help design quieter craft.
2610: A camera trick that makes the invisible visible: shock waves around a supersonic jet.
These ripples are shock waves around a jet flying faster than sound, revealed by a camera trick that reads tiny bends in light. Such images helped NASA shape the X-59 to turn the boom into a thump.
2611: A torpedo that tastes the lake for poison before anyone drinks it.
This torpedo carries a tiny lab that samples lake water and tests it for algal toxins underwater. In Lake Erie it gives cities earlier warning when a bloom threatens their drinking water.
2612: An Atomic Clock Smaller Than a Coffee Bean
The heart of an atomic clock once filled a room. Now it sits beside a coffee bean.
The heart of an atomic clock once filled a room; this glass cell of rubidium atoms beside a coffee bean does the same job. Tiny clocks could keep phones and drones on time when GPS is jammed.
2613: A Car Printed in One Piece
A sports car body printed in one piece, layer by layer.
In 2015 a printer the size of a room built this sports car's body from carbon-fiber plastic, layer by layer. Printers that big now make boat hulls, factory molds and even army barracks.
2614: A battery that changes color as it charges. Want more storage? Get a bigger tank.

Vanadium changes color as it stores and releases charge. Flow batteries keep this liquid in big tanks, so more storage just means bigger tanks; in 2026 one in China began holding 1,000 megawatt-hours.
2615: A Robot That Tests Chemicals Day and Night
Every tiny well is its own experiment, and the robot never stops feeding them.
This robot arm feeds plates of tiny wells, each a separate experiment, to machines that test chemicals against disease targets nonstop. Hundreds of thousands of compounds can be screened in weeks.
2616: This rotor once counted as big. The biggest blades now are about 150 meters long.
In 2011 this 2 megawatt rotor counted as big. In 2025 a Chinese test turbine reached 26 megawatts, with blades 153 meters long, longer than one and a half football fields.
2617: A Collider Reborn as a Proton Microscope
The collider made its last collisions. Its tunnel is being reborn to look inside matter.
This laser source spin-aligned protons for a New York collider that made its last collisions in February 2026. Its tunnel is being rebuilt as a collider to see how quarks and gluons build matter.
2618: X-rays bright enough to watch a battery from the inside as it charges.
At this X-ray source scientists look inside chips, batteries and proteins down to the atom. Rebuilt in 2024, its beams are up to 500 times brighter, sharp enough to follow a battery as it charges.
2619: Fake stars, 90 km up, made so a telescope can stop the real ones from twinkling.
These beams make sodium atoms glow 90 km up, creating fake stars. A telescope watches them twinkle and reshapes its mirror hundreds of times a second to cancel the blur, giving sharp views.
2620: On Earth, printed tissue sags. In orbit, it holds its shape.
On Earth soft printed tissue sags under its own weight; in orbit it holds its shape. In 2023 this printer on the space station made the first human knee meniscus printed in space, then heart tissue.
2621: Stop, start, stop, start: wasteful for fuel, perfect for batteries that recharge on braking.
A bus stops and starts all day, which wastes fuel but suits batteries that recharge as it brakes. In 2025 electric buses were over half of new city buses in more than 20 countries.
2622: Oil-field drills, pointed at hot dry rock instead of oil.

Oil-field drills bored kilometers into hot dry rock here and cracked it so water can carry the heat up. Since autumn 2026 this Utah plant, the first of its kind, has sold 33 megawatts of steady power.
2624: Roman: A Telescope With a Wider Eye
A mirror the size of Hubble's, with a view about 100 times wider.
This 2.4 meter mirror is the size of Hubble's, but its camera sees a patch of sky about 100 times wider. Roman launched on 30 August 2026 and is due to start mapping billions of galaxies next year.
2625: The Coldest Place in Space Is a Fridge
The coldest place in space is a box the size of a minifridge.
Jessica Meir upgrades a minifridge-sized box that chills atoms to a ten-billionth of a degree above absolute zero. In orbit it ran the first quantum sensor in space, a step toward precise navigation.
2626: Around the Moon, a laser beamed home 474 gigabytes and live HD video.
Technicians build the laser terminal that flew on Artemis II. Around the Moon in April 2026 it beamed home 474 gigabytes, over 20,000 images and live HD video, far more than radio could carry.
2627: GPS was never aimed at the Moon. This receiver caught the spillover anyway.
GPS satellites aim their signals at Earth, yet this small receiver caught the faint spillover near the Moon. In March 2025 it fixed its position on the lunar surface, a cheap way to navigate there.
2628: VIPER: The Moon Rover That Came Back
Cancelled after 450 million dollars, then brought back to life.
This rover was built to drill for ice at the Moon's south pole, then cancelled in 2024 after 450 million dollars. Revived in 2025, it could land in late 2027 if Blue Origin's first lander succeeds.
2629: In 2029 an asteroid will pass closer than many satellites, and this probe will be waiting.

After bringing asteroid dust home in 2023, this probe was renamed OSIRIS-APEX and sent on. On 13 April 2029 asteroid Apophis will pass closer to Earth than many satellites, and the probe will meet it.
2630: A Wing Held Up by Braces
The future of fuel-saving wings may look like an old biplane.
Long, thin wings waste less fuel but sag, so this design props them on struts, like an old biplane. Tunnel tests went on into 2025, though plans for a full-size test plane were put on hold.
2631: A Drone Dropped Into a Hurricane
Planes cannot fly low in a hurricane, so they dropped a small drone into Ian.
Hurricane hunter planes cannot fly low in a storm, so they drop this small drone. In September 2022 one flew into Hurricane Ian for nearly two hours, measuring winds near 350 km/h just above the sea.
2632: A turret that burns through drones in seconds. Dust, rain and heat still fight back.
The turret on this light Army vehicle is a laser that burns through small drones in seconds, for the price of electricity. Such systems are in trials; dust, rain and heat still limit their reach.
2633: A Factory in a Shipping Box
A broken bracket used to mean weeks of waiting. Now it means one night.
These rugged printers travel with Marines and print spare parts in plastic and carbon fiber on the spot. Instead of waiting weeks for a broken bracket, a unit can make one overnight.
2634: A doctor in Spain, colleagues in Italy, and one exam guided across the sea.
A urologist in Spain waves to colleagues in Italy during a remote-guided exam in 2021. Since the pandemic video visits have become routine, letting one specialist see patients in many places.
2635: The Spike That Taught Vaccines a Shape
Two small changes froze the spike before its attack, and vaccines learned that shape.
This is a printed model of the coronavirus spike. NIH scientists found two small changes that lock it in its pre-attack shape, and within weeks in 2020 that recipe went into the first mRNA vaccines.
2636: Same carbon, different size, different color.
These vials hold specks of carbon a few nanometers wide; their size alone sets the color they glow. Such quantum dots won the 2023 Nobel Prize and already sharpen the colors of many TV screens.
2637: 2.5 quadrillion calculations a second in 2013. Today's fastest do hundreds of times more.
2638: Fuel From Corn Stalks: Harder Than It Looked
Ethanol from the whole plant, not just the kernels. Cost had other plans.
The kernels make ethanol easily; the idea was to make it from the stalks and husks too. Several big plants for this opened in the 2010s, but most shut within a few years, beaten by cost.
2639: A pump that adjusts insulin on its own, every few minutes, even while you sleep.
Paired with a glucose sensor, this pump adjusts insulin by itself every few minutes, day and night. The first such system was approved in 2016; now they keep many with diabetes in range even asleep.
2640: A Printed Hand for a Few Dollars
Free designs online, and volunteers printing hands for children born without fingers.
FDA scientists printed and tested this hand from free online designs. Volunteers worldwide print similar ones for children born without fingers, for a tiny fraction of a commercial prosthesis.
2641: A Grocery Robot on the Sidewalk
Six wheels, a bag of groceries, and it waits at the crossing like a polite pedestrian.
This six-wheeled robot carries groceries down Helsinki sidewalks, waiting at crossings like a polite pedestrian. Fleets like it have made millions of deliveries on campuses and in suburbs worldwide.
2642: Lunar Trailblazer: A Small Mission Lost
Built to map water on the Moon. A day after launch, its panels missed the Sun.
This instrument was built to map water on the Moon from a satellite the size of a dishwasher. Launched in February 2025, it lost contact a day later when its solar panels missed the Sun.
2643: No metal frame, just straps and cables, and stroke patients walking again.
Instead of a metal frame, this suit uses straps and cables pulled by small motors to help the legs at each step. The research led to a version cleared in 2019 to help stroke patients walk again.
2644: CRISPR: Editing the Code of Life
Search and cut, inside the code of life.
CRISPR works like search and cut: a guide RNA finds a spot in DNA and a protein snips it. The first CRISPR cure, for sickle cell, was approved in 2023, and in 2026 it opened to children from age two.
2645: The Robot Mule That Was Too Loud
It could carry 180 kg over rough ground. It just could not keep quiet.
This four-legged robot could carry 180 kg of gear over rough ground behind soldiers. The Marines shelved it in 2015 because its engine was too loud for patrols; quieter electric robot dogs took over.
2646: Three times more accurate, and far harder to jam.
This rocket carried the ninth of a new generation of GPS satellites in January 2026. They are about three times more accurate and far harder to jam, matters for phones, farms and planes alike.
2647: Set routes, home every night: a delivery truck is a battery's dream job.
Delivery trucks drive set routes and return to a depot each night, ideal for batteries. In 2025 sales of electric trucks and buses topped half a million worldwide, nearly 90 percent of them in China.
2648: An Early Warning for Space Storms
1.5 million km toward the Sun, tasting the solar wind half an hour before it hits.
Launched in 2025, this probe sits 1.5 million km sunward, sampling the solar wind before it reaches us. Its live data can give about half an hour's warning of storms that threaten satellites.
2649: A record 10.7 megawatts of fusion in 1994, and three decades later, still the long road.
This glow is a hydrogen plasma inside a Princeton reactor that made a record 10.7 megawatts of fusion in 1994. Three decades on, compact private machines like SPARC aim for first plasma in 2027.
2650: Silicon: A Battery That Holds More
Ten times more lithium, if only it would stop swelling and cracking.

Silicon can hold about ten times more lithium than the graphite in today's batteries, but it swells and cracks. Coatings tamed it, and by 2026 silicon anodes shipped in gadgets and were reaching cars.
2651: The Moon Rocket and Its Price Tag
About 4 billion dollars a launch, and the rocket is thrown away.
The Space Launch System carried Artemis II around the Moon, but each launch costs about 4 billion dollars and the rocket is thrown away. NASA is weighing cheaper reusable rockets for later missions.
2652: Robot Floats Taking the Ocean's Temperature
Dropped overboard in a box that dissolves, it rises every ten days to report the heat.
Dropped overboard in a box that dissolves, this float sinks to 2,000 meters and rises every ten days to radio its data. About 4,000 such floats show how much heat the oceans are soaking up.
2653: An Airliner That Is All Wing
No body and wings, just one wing: the whole plane makes lift.

In this wind tunnel model the body itself is a wing, so the whole plane makes lift. A startup is building a flying demonstrator with Air Force money, due to fly in late 2027, aiming for much less fuel per seat.
2654: Lasers a Hundred Times the World's Power
For an instant, 100 times the world's electric output, in one laser pulse.

A petawatt laser squeezes modest energy into a pulse lasting quadrillionths of a second. In 2025 a US laser hit 2 petawatts, for an instant 100 times the world's electric output, to probe extreme matter.
2655: A welder in a small Iowa factory, one of about 4.7 million robots at work.
A robot welder at work in a small Iowa factory in October 2026. About 4.7 million industrial robots were working worldwide by the end of 2024, more than half of new ones installed in China.
2656: Once a costly curiosity, now the light in most new lamps on Earth.
In 2008 lamps like these were costly curiosities. LEDs use at least 75 percent less power than old bulbs and last many times longer, and they are now the most common new lighting worldwide.
2657: More than 99 percent air, and NASA used it to catch comet dust.

This ghostly block is more than 99 percent air, among the lightest solids ever made. NASA used it to catch comet dust; thin aerogel sheets now slow fire spreading between cells in electric-car batteries.
2658: He is downing drones that exist only in software.

With a headset and two controllers, this soldier practices jamming and downing drones that exist only in software. Virtual training lets units rehearse rare, dangerous situations again and again, cheaply.
2659: Bureau of Land Management / Blythe Mesa Solar
Panel prices fell about 90 percent in a decade, and the desert turned into a power plant.
Rows of panels stretch across the California desert. Solar panel prices fell about 90 percent in a decade, and solar now adds more new power capacity worldwide each year than any other source.
2660: An ultrasound that once filled a cart, now plugged into a phone in the Arctic.

Navy medics scan a simulated casualty in the Arctic with an ultrasound probe that plugs into a phone. A machine that once filled a cart now fits a pocket, bringing imaging to ambulances and battlefields.
2661: The Railgun That Wore Itself Out
Magnets, not gunpowder, at 2,500 meters a second. The rails could not take it.
Magnets, not gunpowder, hurled this 3.2 kg slug at over 2,500 meters a second in 2008. The rails eroded too fast, so the Navy shelved the program in 2021; Japan has since tested one on a warship.
2662: It burns methane, a fuel that could one day be made on Mars from air and ice.
This is the first test firing of SpaceX's Raptor engine, in 2016. It burns methane, which could one day be made on Mars from air and ice, and 33 of its successors lift the Starship booster.
2663: Printing Buildings Out of Moon Dust
Why ship concrete to the Moon when you can print with its dust?

At NASA's Swamp Works this printer tests how to build with simulated lunar soil in a vacuum-like chamber. The goal is landing pads and shelters made on the Moon, instead of shipping concrete at huge cost.
2664: No motors, no hinges: a metal that remembers its shape folded the wingtips in flight.
A heated metal that remembers its shape folded this test plane's wingtips 70 degrees upward in flight in 2017, with no motors or hinges. Folding wings could let future jets change shape to save fuel.
2665: A Chip That Gives Sight Back
A chip beneath the retina, and patients with failing sight read letters again.

This tiny chip sits beneath the retina, turning light into signals the surviving cells pass on. In a 2025 trial of a newer chip, 84 percent of patients with advanced macular degeneration read letters again.
2666: Reading a Genome for the Price of Dinner
The first genome took 13 years and billions. Now: about the price of dinner.
The first human genome took 13 years and billions of dollars. Machines like this one cut the cost to about 560 dollars by 2021, and makers now claim 100 to 200, cheap enough for routine care.
2667: Three Mile Island Comes Back for AI
The site of America's worst nuclear accident, waking up to power AI.
This plant suffered America's worst nuclear accident in 1979. Its undamaged unit closed in 2019, and it is being restarted, aiming for 2027, to power Microsoft's data centers for 20 years.
2668: U.S. Department of the Interior / Tami Heilemann
Pores too fine for salt, and most of Israel's drinking water comes through them.
These tubes hold membranes that push seawater through pores too fine for salt. Israel now gets most of its drinking water this way, though the plants use about a tenth of the country's electricity.
2669: GLP-1: The Weekly Shot That Changed Weight Loss
A pen that copies a gut hormone telling the brain: you are full.
This pen copies a gut hormone that tells the brain the stomach is full. Users lose about 15 percent of their weight on average, and since 2025 and 2026 the same drugs also come as daily pills.
2670: The minutes that decide survival, saved by a drone carrying blood.

Soldiers load a drone that flies blood to the wounded, saving the minutes that decide survival. In Rwanda drones have flown blood to clinics since 2016; one company passed 2 million deliveries in 2026.
2671: America's Bullet Train, Still Being Built
A viaduct for trains at 300 km/h, and a line still waiting to connect.
This viaduct belongs to a line meant to run trains at over 300 km/h across California. In 2025 Washington pulled 4 billion dollars; the state builds on alone, aiming to link north and south by 2038.
2672: A Nuclear Plant Brought Back From Retirement
Shut down in 2022, now loading fuel again: a retired reactor coming back.
The Palisades reactor on Lake Michigan shut down in 2022. In late August 2026 workers began loading its fuel again, aiming for the first restart of a retired American nuclear plant.
2673: A Jet Engine With No Moving Parts
An engine with no moving parts, breathing air at supersonic speed.

Under this bomber's wing hangs the X-51, powered by a scramjet that burns fuel in air rushing through at supersonic speed. In 2013 it flew at Mach 5.1 for over three minutes; such engines remain experimental.
2674: Superconducting Cavities for an X-Ray Laser
Chilled near absolute zero, it pushes electrons with almost no energy lost.
Pure niobium cavities like this, chilled near absolute zero, push electrons with almost no energy loss. Since 2023 a California X-ray laser built on them can fire up to a million pulses a second.
2675: The Strongest Ion Thruster Yet Built for Flight
Four times stronger than Psyche's thruster, and its station is on pause.

This 12 kilowatt thruster, about four times Psyche's, arrived in 2025 for NASA's Moon station. The station is on pause, but thrusters this strong could one day haul heavy cargo to Mars on little fuel.
2676: An astronaut's bone marrow flew around the Moon beside its donor, on a chip.

Each clear chip holds living bone marrow cells from an Artemis II astronaut. They flew around the Moon beside their donors in 2026, so doctors can see how deep space harms the body without risking people.
2677: A Power Grid That Fits a Base
Roll out the mats, plug in the batteries, and the camp keeps running when the grid fails.
Rolled-out solar mats, batteries and a smart controller form a microgrid that keeps a camp running when the main grid fails. Hospitals, islands and towns now use the same idea to ride out storms.
2678: A Sensor That Tells Crops When to Drink
Water only when the soil asks for it.
Buried probes like this measure moisture at the roots and radio it to the farmer's phone. Watering only when the soil asks can cut water use sharply, a big deal where farms drink most of the water.
2679: An air conditioner running backward, and it now outsells the gas furnace.
A heat pump is an air conditioner that can run backward, moving warmth into a home instead of burning fuel. In the US they have outsold gas furnaces every year since 2022.
2680: A Cabin for the Next Moon Crews
A second Moon lander, so one failure cannot stall the whole program.

This full-size mock-up of Blue Origin's crewed lander cabin opened for astronaut training in May 2026. It is NASA's second Moon lander, beside SpaceX's Starship, so one failure cannot stall the program.
2681: They once required a doctor and thousands of dollars. Now they sit on the shelf.
Tiny hearing aids once required a doctor's visit and cost thousands. Since October 2022 Americans can buy them over the counter, and prices for many have dropped to a few hundred dollars.
2682: Charcoal That Locks Carbon in the Soil
Bake forest waste without oxygen, and its carbon stays out of the air for centuries.
Bake forest waste without oxygen and you get biochar, which holds water in soil and keeps its carbon out of the air for centuries. It is now one of the most common ways companies buy carbon removal.
2683: Vulcan: A New Rocket's Rocky Start
The rocket flew perfectly. Its passenger sprang a leak and never landed.
