This rocket's first flight in January 2024 worked perfectly, yet its passenger, a private Moon lander, sprang a leak and never landed. Methane engines like Vulcan's are now the standard for new heavy rockets.
2684: Air Taxis Near Their First Riders
Rises like a helicopter, flies like a plane, and waits on the last signature.

Six tilting rotors let this quiet electric aircraft rise like a helicopter and fly like a plane. In October 2026 it was in the last stage of FAA certification, hoping to fly its first passengers in Dubai soon.
2685: Eleven Parachutes for a Moon Capsule
40,000 km/h on the way in, and eleven parachutes to make it a gentle splash.
Back from the Moon, a capsule hits the air at about 40,000 km/h; after the heat shield, eleven parachutes slow it to a gentle splash. Tested in 2017, they brought the Artemis II crew home in 2026.
2686: A Crewed Launch, Then a Landing
Minutes after sending four people to space, the booster came home and landed.
Minutes after sending four astronauts toward the space station on 1 October 2026, this booster flew back and landed on the Florida coast. Flying people on a rocket that comes home is now routine.
2687: From Laser Test to Iron Beam
It shot down rockets but was too bulky to field. Two decades later, Iron Beam.

This US-Israeli laser shot down rockets in tests in the 2000s but was too bulky to field. Two decades later Israel's Iron Beam laser was declared operational and handed to its air force in December 2025.
2688: A vaccine that had to travel frozen, hard to bring to the places that needed it most.

Early mRNA vaccines had to travel frozen, hard for poor and remote places. A newer version approved in 2025 still ships frozen but then lasts 90 days in an ordinary fridge, making it easier to deliver.
2689: The Promise of Thousands of Cheap Drones
Thousands of drones promised in two years. Hundreds arrived.
In 2023 the Pentagon promised thousands of cheap autonomous drones within two years. By the August 2025 deadline only hundreds had arrived, a reminder that building in bulk is harder than inventing.
2690: Scooping rocks in a pressurized suit, rehearsing the search for water on the Moon.
In a pressurized suit, a crew member practices scooping rocks with new lunar tools in January 2026. Samples from the Moon's south pole, planned for 2028, could show where future bases can find water.
2691: A Christmas launch, then 344 steps that each had to work the first time. All did.
On 25 December 2021 this rocket carried Webb folded up like origami. Unfolding in space involved 344 steps that each had to work the first time; all did, and the telescope has worked since 2022.
2692: An empty capsule sent farther than any spacecraft built for people.
In November 2022 this launch sent an empty Orion capsule beyond the Moon, about 432,000 km from Earth, farther than any spacecraft built for people. It cleared the way for the crewed flight of 2026.
2693: A Buoy That Listens for Tsunamis
The seafloor feels a tsunami pass, and this buoy tells the coast.

A sensor on the seafloor feels the slight pressure change of a passing tsunami and sends it to this buoy, which radios it by satellite. About 60 such stations now give coasts minutes to hours of warning.
2694: It lets go with one end and grabs with the other, inching like a caterpillar.
This 11 meter European arm, installed in 2021, can let go with one end and grab a new anchor with the other, inching across the station like a caterpillar. Arms like it could build future stations.
2695: An astronaut in orbit, photographing a rocket trying to join him.

From the space station, astronaut Don Pettit photographed the glowing plume of Starship's sixth test flight in November 2024. Two years later the rocket reached orbit itself, still learning to come back whole.
2696: The size of a microwave, and the first to fly the orbit planned for Moon stations.

This satellite, about the size of a microwave oven, was the first to fly the stretched orbit planned for lunar stations, arriving in November 2022. It showed a tiny, cheap craft can scout deep space routes.
2697: Living yeast past the Moon: the first biology beyond low orbit in 50 years.

This shoebox satellite carried living yeast past the Moon on Artemis I in 2022, the first biology study beyond low orbit in 50 years. Yeast repairs DNA much like we do, a guide to risks for Mars crews.
2698: A Laboratory the Size of a Stamp
A whole lab bench, shrunk to the size of a stamp.

Channels as thin as a hair carry drops of fluid through this chip, mixing and testing them like a whole lab bench. Chips like this now power quick tests in clinics that give answers in minutes instead of days.
2699: Soy and wheat, shaped like chicken. Taste and price still decide.
These tenders are made from soy and wheat protein shaped to mimic chicken. After a boom around 2020, US sales of plant-based meat fell for several years; taste and price still decide who switches.
2700: Wearables That Warn Before You Feel Sick
A ring that may notice you are getting sick a day or two before you feel it.

Soldiers in a 2023 exercise wore rings and watches that track pulse, temperature and sleep. Such data can flag fatigue or infection a day or two before symptoms, though the readings are hints, not diagnoses.
2701: In 2014 its beard came off during cleaning and was glued back crooked.

The beard was already detached when the mask was found in 1925, and it was fixed back on with a wooden dowel in 1944. In 2014 it came off again during cleaning, and quick-drying epoxy left it off-center. A German and Egyptian team later reattached it using beeswax.
2702: No head was ever found, but her palm turned up 87 years after her body.

A French consul found part of her bust and body on Samothrace in 1863. Her head and arms never turned up, but in July 1950 a Louvre curator working with New York University excavators found the palm of her right hand on the site. She still lands on a stone base shaped like the bow of a warship.
2703: For centuries his outstretched arm was a guess, until a marble arm surfaced in a builder's yard.

The group was dug up in a vineyard in February 1506 with Laocoön's right arm missing, and Michelangelo was called to the site at once. In 1532 Montorsoli gave him a straight outstretched arm. In 1905 Ludwig Pollak found a marble arm in a builder's yard in Rome; it was attributed to the group and installed in 1957.
2704: Emperor, in armor, and barefoot: a detail once reserved for gods.

Being barefoot had previously been allowed only on images of the gods, so the bare feet may mean this marble was made after his death. The small Cupid riding a dolphin at his feet points to the family's claimed descent from Venus. The statue was almost certainly painted once, though little color survives.
2705: Probably the book stolen in 1007 and found under sod, its golden cover gone.

An Irish chronicle records a gospel book stolen at night in 1007, generally assumed to be this one. It came back months later from under a sod, without its golden, jeweled cover. On this page Christ sits enthroned, flanked by peacocks.
2706: A bishop in mid-battle, rallying the troops with a raised baton or mace.

Bishop Odo brandishes his baton or mace and rallies the Norman troops, in a work he is generally thought to have commissioned himself. Despite its name it is technically an embroidery, stitched rather than woven, nearly 70 meters long.
2707: Even the angels wear the king's badge.

Richard II and the angels around the Virgin all wear badges with his livery, a very unusual idea for religious art. Closed, the panel shows his emblem, a white hart. The painter has never been identified.
2708: Anatomical Man, Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry
The zodiac laid over the human body, an image found in no other book of hours.

The twelve signs of the zodiac appear over the parts of the body they were linked to, and astrology was one of the duke's interests. The page may not have been part of the book's original plan. The duke and the Limbourg brothers all died in 1416, leaving the manuscript unfinished.
2709: Mary holds his head, Magdalene his feet, and John flings his arms wide in despair.

Giotto painted this fresco around 1305 in a private chapel built by the wealthy Scrovegni family. Mary, Mary Magdalene and John each grieve in a different way, while Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea wait on the right to prepare the body for burial.
2710: Her knees press through the robe: a holy figure with real weight.

Giotto used a scale of light and dark to build volume, so his figures feel weighty, like three-dimensional sculptures. The contours of the body show under the drapery, above all at the Virgin's knees. Yet she and the Child still tower over the saints around them.
2711: Siena shut its workshops to parade it; 460 years later it was sawn apart.

On 9 June 1311 it was carried in a loop around the city and installed in the cathedral, and a witness wrote that all workshops stayed closed. In 1771 it was sawn up to share between two altars, damaging the paintings. Pieces were sold or lost, and some now sit in museums across Europe and the United States.
2712: When he died, this painting lay at the head of his catafalque.

Raphael's last painting tells two stories: Christ transfigured above, and below, the apostles failing to cure a possessed boy. He died on 6 April 1520, and for a couple of days it lay at the head of his catafalque at his house. Critics have argued about whether the two halves belong together.
2713: The chariot is pulled by cheetahs, probably modeled on a duke's own menagerie.

Ovid's text had tigers, but the cheetahs here were probably modeled on the menagerie of Duke Alfonso I d'Este, who ordered the picture. Raphael had first held the commission and died in 1520 with only a drawing done, so it passed to Titian. He signed his name on the gold urn in the foreground.
2714: X-rays found a Cupid at her feet, painted out in the 19th century.

A seated Cupid once sat beside her feet until it was painted over in the 19th century, and X-rays in the 20th century confirmed that other elements lay beneath. The picture was unfinished when Giorgione died in 1510, and it has long been thought that Titian completed it. The landscape and sky are generally accepted as mainly his.
2715: Many of Toledo's landmarks are in the wrong place, and the sky grows dark above them.

It is one of two surviving landscapes by El Greco, and many of its landmarks are not where they stand in the real city. The scholar Walter Liedtke thinks he painted it more as a future or a hope for what the city might look like. Near the city, the sky turns exceptionally dark.
2716: Expulsion from the Garden of Eden
A duke had fig leaves painted on them; a 1980s cleaning took them off.

Three centuries after Masaccio painted it around 1425, Cosimo III de' Medici demanded fig leaves. They stayed until the fresco was fully restored and cleaned in the 1980s. What remains is the force of Eve's howling, deeply felt pain.
2717: Below the fresco, a skeleton speaks: I once was what you are.

Above the skeleton are the words 'I once was what you are and what I am you also will be.' Around 1570 Vasari built a new altar in front of the fresco, hiding it, and it was rediscovered only when that altar came down in 1860. Its two parts, the Crucifixion and the tomb, were reunited in 1952.
2718: A walnut tree with bark as white as the skin of the man beside it.

The white bark of the walnut echoes the white skin of Christ, and the tree separates him from the angels. Christ, John's hand and bowl and the dove form a central axis that divides the picture in two. Piero was an authority on perspective and geometry, and the town in the distance may be Sansepolcro.
2719: The robe's pattern runs upside down on the front: a sign he painted what he actually saw.

He wears white silk damask woven with gold and silver thread, and the design runs upside down on the front, which suggests Bellini painted exactly what he saw. The buttons were called 'golden bells'. The signature sits on a slip of paper that looks freshly unfolded and stuck onto the marble.
2720: Its details may come from a real public execution he saw in 1599.

Caravaggio may have drawn on the public execution of Beatrice Cenci in 1599. His Judith, probably modeled by the Roman courtesan Fillide Melandroni, shows a mix of determination and repulsion. The canvas was rediscovered only in 1950.
2721: The letter in her hand is not in the biblical story, and was not in his first idea.

The letter carries King David's demand, though the Book of Samuel never mentions one, and it was not part of the original conception. Rembrandt began the life-sized work around 1647 and kept altering it until 1654. Her expression has been read as resignation, a solemn moment of thought.
2722: Nazis seized it from the Rothschilds and stamped a small swastika on the back.

In 1940 the Nazis seized it from the home of Édouard de Rothschild and stamped a small swastika on the back, declaring it property of the Third Reich. It returned to the Rothschilds after the war. In 1983 the French state acquired it as payment of inheritance taxes, and it has hung in the Louvre since.
2723: He probably once looked down. Vermeer turned his head to the window.

Vermeer changed his mind as he painted: the head likely looked down at first, the dividers stood upright, and a sheet of paper lay on the stool. The same young man modeled for The Astronomer. Some scholars suggest he was Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, but no document connects the two men in Vermeer's lifetime.
2724: The general who won dismounts to greet the one who lost.

Spinola took Breda in June 1625, and here he greets and embraces his defeated opponent with a kindly expression. Velázquez painted the scene in 1634 and 1635, about a decade later. The philosopher José Ortega y Gasset called the upright lances the backbone of the whole picture.
2725: A bare patch on her lap: nobody knows what was meant to go there.

The picture is finished except for one area on her lap. A popular idea says a pheasant was planned, but the standing corn makes that unlikely; a work bag, a book, a fan, a lapdog or even a baby yet to be born have been proposed. By 1750 Robert Andrews owned almost 3,000 acres, including most of the land you can see.
2726: The Inquisition demanded to know why he painted it. His answers do not survive.

Probably commissioned by Manuel Godoy for a private cabinet of paintings, it was recorded in his inventory by 1800. Goya was later summoned on a charge of moral depravity and asked why he made the picture and at whose request, but he escaped prosecution. Who posed for it has never been established.
2727: The man leading the line was real: Kanin, a defrocked priest.

Repin based the men on real people he met while preparing the work, among them a former soldier and a former priest. In the distance a tiny steamboat hints that their labor was becoming unnecessary. Dostoevsky expected a lecture, but instead saw 'barge haulers, real barge haulers, and nothing more.'
2728: Lost in the Second World War, and how it was lost is still disputed.

In November 1849 Courbet stopped on the road to watch two men breaking stones and asked them to come to his studio the next morning. He did not show their faces, perhaps so they could stand for all workers. The canvas is often said to have burned on a transport during the bombing of Dresden in 1945, but one scholar argued it had gone missing in 1944.
2729: A village funeral, painted at a size reserved for heroes.

At 3.15 by 6.6 meters, it gives a provincial funeral the grand scale traditionally kept for heroic or religious history paintings, and the people of Ornans posed as the models. Critics attacked its size, its ugliness and its crowded composition. Whose funeral it shows is not known for certain.
2730: One critic looked at these women and saw the scaffolds of 1793.

Three women collect stray stalks of wheat while a rich harvest glows in the sunlit distance. To the upper classes it recalled the labor their society rested on, and one critic invoked the Reign of Terror. Millet sold it for 3,000 francs, below his asking price; in 1889 it fetched 300,000.
2731: Dalí insisted a coffin was hidden here. X-rays show a shape; few agree.

Dalí thought the piety verged on grief, and that the couple might be mourning a child, with the basket standing in for a small coffin. He asked the Louvre to X-ray the picture, and the images show an oblong geometric shape at their feet. His reading has not been widely accepted.
2732: If I haven't fought for my country, at least I'll paint for her.

Delacroix wrote those words to his brother while painting this barricade of the July Revolution of 1830. The French government bought it in 1831 for 3,000 francs, then took it down within months because of its political message. After the June Rebellion of 1832 it went back to the artist.
2733: Everyone calls it his last painting. It probably isn't.

The belief that this was his final work was helped along by the 1956 film Lust for Life, but scholars say that was likely Tree Roots. Around 10 July 1890 he wrote that he had painted large canvases of wheat fields to express sadness and extreme loneliness.
2734: Bal du moulin de la Galette
Its smaller twin sold for 78 million dollars. The buyer reportedly wanted it cremated with him.

Renoir painted two near-identical versions, this larger one and a smaller one, and it is not known which came first. The smaller sold at Sotheby's in May 1990 to the paper tycoon Ryoei Saito, who reportedly said he would be cremated with it and later claimed it was a joke aimed at the taxman. While he worked outdoors, the wind kept threatening to blow the canvas away.
2735: Before bronze, she was wax, in a real bodice and a wig of human hair.

Marie van Goethem, a student at the Paris Opera Ballet school, was the model. Degas showed the wax figure in 1881, dressed in real clothes and a human-hair wig, and J.-K. Huysmans called it 'the first truly modern attempt at sculpture I know.' The bronzes were cast only after his death, from 1920 to 1936.
2736: The Salon rejected it. Its dots were added about three years later.

Seurat was 24 when he finished it in 1884, and the Salon jury turned it down. X-rays lack the small pointillist touches, dated to around 1887. Behind the calm bathers rise the bridges and factories, and the bank they sit on is really Courbevoie, across from the island of La Grande Jatte.
2737: Two titles for one woman: Loving Woman, and Madonna.

Munch used both titles for this composition, which he worked on in several versions between 1892 and 1895. His friend Dagny Juel-Przybyszewska is identified as the model, and the picture reflects his idealized view of her. One version, from the Munch Museum, was stolen by armed men in 2004 and recovered in 2006.
2738: Critics called it madness; the Steins paid 500 francs.

Matisse painted his wife, Amélie, between September and October 1905 and showed the picture at the Salon d'Automne. Its bright palette and loose brushwork drew the largest crowd and the harshest words, from infantile to madness. Gertrude Stein and her family bought it anyway, a turning point for both her and the painter.
2739: The Dessert: Harmony in Red (The Red Room)
Green, then blue, then red: he repainted the whole background twice.

The background started out green, and Matisse changed it to blue before the 1908 Salon d'Automne, where Sergei Shchukin bought the work. In 1909 he repainted the background red and retitled the picture. It now hangs in the Hermitage in Saint Petersburg.
2740: An old face broken into squares, like a mask or a harlequin's patches.

Klee divides an elderly face into rectangles of orange, pink, yellow and white, flat squares that resemble a mask or a harlequin's patches. The picture has also been called Head of a Man Going Senile. Its title is said to refer to an artist-performer named Senecio.
2741: Unique Forms of Continuity in Space
Never cast in bronze in his lifetime, it now rides on Italy's 20-cent coin.
Boccioni's figure of 1913 existed only in plaster during his life. Bronze casts came later, starting in 1931. Today it appears on the Italian issue of the 20 cent euro coin.
2742: Dream Journey to the Peach Blossom Land
A prince described a dream; three days later it was a painting.

In 1447 Grand Prince Anpyeong of Korea asked An Gyeon to recreate his dream of visiting a paradise, the peach blossom land from a story by the Chinese poet Tao Yuanming. An finished in three days. The painting was reportedly taken to Japan during the Imjin War and is kept today at Tenri University.
2743: Only three prints survive, and no two are alike.

Steichen made this photograph in 1904 in Mamaroneck, New York, then applied light-sensitive gums by hand, which gave the print more than one color. Because of that hand-layering, each of the three known versions is unique. In February 2006 one sold for 2.9 million dollars, at the time the highest price ever paid for a photograph at auction.
